Executive summary

Overall risk: high. Five confirmed high findings sit on the default code paths that untrusted documents and caller-supplied assets reach: a document can make the engine fetch file:, ftp: and ldap: as well as http(s) URLs, internal hosts included, through its AIA caIssuers URLs (and through CRL/OCSP URLs for chains that reach a trust anchor) (F-001); an OutOfMemoryError raised inside DSS aborts the whole process with SIGABRT instead of the documented error result (F-186), and a 194 KB PNG (F-032) or a 200 KB TTF (F-222) needs hundreds of MB to gigabytes of heap, which under a heap cap is expected to trigger it (shown on the JVM; the native abort was reproduced with other inputs); and a snapshot-started engine that loses one LOTL download publishes an inconsistent trust pool that turns every trusted-chain validation into INTERNAL_ERROR while reporting completed=true (F-213). The 28 mediums cluster around the same themes (no admission control or CPU bounds in the sidecar, trusted-list cache poisoning and silent staleness, unverified TSA tokens, missing supply-chain automation and an LGPL source-distribution gap). None of this is "critical": the project is pre-release with zero tags, the cryptographic core (TL signature checking, external-CMS digest binding, snapshot deserialisation) is sound and well tested, and every high has a contained fix. The risk is high because, as it stands, exposing dss-server or the library to documents from outside the trust boundary is unsafe.

What it is. dss-native wraps the EU Digital Signature Service (DSS 6.5.1) in a thin Java engine (6,232 main LOC, 32 classes) compiled with GraalVM CE 25 Native Image into libdssnative, a shared library with an 11-function C API. Rust crates (dss-sys, dss, dss-cli, dss-server; 3,529 main LOC) and a copy-in Laravel PHP client sit on top. It validates CAdES and PAdES, extends PAdES to T/LT/LTA, signs with an external key (HSM or remote service) in cms and signature_value modes, owns the EU trusted lists (on-disk cache, online refresh, exportable snapshots) and runs as an HTTP sidecar. The repository is young and pre-release: 14 commits by one author over 10 days, 0 tags, no release ever cut, CI never run on GitHub. Against that, it carries an unusually complete design record (docs/DECISIONS.md, 11,145 words) and a real test estate: 152 JVM tests, 150 of them also passing in the native image, 44 Rust tests, a C smoke test with 80 concurrent validations, a JVM-vs-plain-DSS parity test and a JVM-vs-native differential.

What the audit did. 21 finder dimensions (Java engine security and correctness, external signing, visible signatures, FFI and native image, Rust core, Rust CLI, server security and correctness, PHP client, build/CI/supply chain, dependencies, licensing, two documentation lenses, tests, repository hygiene, configuration and operations, performance, API design, threat model) ran in round 1 (287 raw findings, 164 confirmed). Round 2 re-ran the 10 deep dimensions (Java security, Java correctness, signing, visible signatures, FFI, Rust core, server security, server correctness, build/CI, threat model) plus ten targeted gap probes (20 finders, 85 raw, 62 confirmed). A partial round 3 ran 1 of its 10 finders (2 confirmed). Every candidate went through adversarial verification: reproduce, impact and severity lenses for medium and above, reproduce alone for low and info. Result: 228 confirmed findings (5 high, 28 medium, 184 low, 11 info), 6 plausible (not confirmed by verification), 49 refuted. Finders read the DSS, PDFBox, BouncyCastle, HttpClient and GraalVM sources, ran offline probes against the compiled classes and the prebuilt macOS library, fuzzed the PNG and JPEG parsers (30,000 cases each), ran a 45-font hostile TTF corpus and drove fake TSA, TL and OCSP-less scenarios on loopback. Two things the process could not complete: the account usage limit cut round 2 verification, so 17 late findings, 14 of which are now confirmed (F-265, F-267, F-269 to F-278, F-280, F-282) and 3 refuted, had their missing lenses re-run in a follow-up workflow with the same prompts and models, and round 3 lost 9 of its 10 deep re-probe finders and the round-2 completeness critic, so nine of the ten deep dimensions had two rounds instead of three and no round-3 gap probes exist.

Headline results by area. The Java engine's trusted-list machinery and its network egress carry most of the weight: a document-controlled SSRF/file-read path (F-001), no size cap or deadline on certificate-driven and TL downloads (F-002, F-208, F-260), a trust pool that can be emptied, poisoned or made inconsistent by one bad or failed download while status reports success (F-213, F-180, F-272, F-010), TLS off by default for TL downloads with no rollback protection (F-003), and quadratic validation cost on crafted PDFs (F-248, F-264, F-265). Signing is cryptographically careful at its core (digest binding, signature-value verification, deterministic prepare) but trusts the TSA's token blindly (F-219), refuses augmentation on mixed-level PDFs (F-214) and spends external signatures before some refusals (F-274). Visible signatures are robust against malformed bytes but not against resource cost: F-032, F-222, F-259, F-224. The FFI boundary is sound except that an OOM inside DSS kills the process (F-186). The Rust crates are clean (clippy and fmt pass; unsafe is confined to the dss and dss-sys crates, with none in the binaries) with API-hygiene gaps and one trust footgun in the binaries, the cwd fallback for the OJ keystore (F-064). The sidecar has correct auth and error handling but no admission control, request deadline or readiness gate (F-052, F-080, F-090). Build, dependencies and licensing are well pinned but lack automation (F-115), run a superseded GraalVM with known CVE fixes outstanding (F-129) and distribute LGPL object code with only a pointer to the DSS source (F-132). Documentation is extensive and mostly accurate, but several safety claims are contradicted by the code (F-186, F-052, F-151, F-025). Tests are strong offline and never exercise OCSP or the real HTTP loaders (F-164).

The six top risks below the scorecard are: untrusted documents reaching the network and filesystem; trust-list fragility that fails open on staleness and fails closed with a false success signal; small inputs that abort the process or pin workers for minutes with nothing to shed load; verdict semantics in which TOTAL_PASSED hides post-signing modification and DocMDP violations and no aggregate verdict exists; signing that trusts the TSA and the external CMS more than the contract promises; and a release pipeline that is pinned but unverified and never exercised.

Verdict. Do not release or expose dss-server to documents from outside the trust boundary at commit 7e697c9. Before a first public release: ship the P0 set (egress policy with size and time bounds; a fail-safe refresh that stages, validates and promotes; bounded visible-signature inputs; admission control plus an honest OOM story; cost caps on PAdES/CMS validation; TSA token verification and the mixed-level fix; removal of the cwd keystore fallback; a readiness gate), then the P1 set (aggregate verdict and structured modification fields, stricter CMS checks, supply-chain automation, LGPL source distribution, proxy support, OCSP test coverage, CI on pull requests). After release: the remaining documentation sweep (the two false safety claims, that the isolate stays usable on OOM and that --max-request-mb bounds memory, are corrected before release under the P0 OOM item), the configuration-validation sweep, the API polish and the reproducibility, notarization and Docker items can follow in normal cadence, and a third deep round over the engine, signing and server dimensions should be run, since this audit could not complete it.

Closing assessment

dss-native is a well-designed, well-documented and unusually well-tested pre-release project whose hard parts (strict trusted-list signature synchronisation, immutable trust publication, defensive snapshot deserialisation, digest-bound external signing, an FFI boundary that never lets an exception reach C and a sound Rust thread model) are right. What is not right is the perimeter: the engine inherits DSS's permissive network loaders and default validation policy without the bounds a sidecar for untrusted documents needs, the refresh pipeline writes before it validates, a small image or font or a crafted PDF can abort the process or pin workers while the server has no way to shed load, and the TSA's word is taken on trust. These are well-understood gaps with contained fixes, concentrated in the engine (DssEngine, TrustedListManager, ExternalSigning), the visible/ package and rust/dss-server. Land the eight P0 items and the seven P1 items before the first public release, cut that release with CI running on every push, schedule a third deep round over the engine, signing and server dimensions that this audit could not complete, and re-assess the overall risk after the P0 items land.

Findings overview

Only findings that survived adversarial verification are counted. Plausible and refuted findings are in the appendix.

Top risks

A submitted document can steer the engine's network and filesystem access

With the defaults (revocation online, aia true) every caIssuers (AIA) URL in a document's certificates is fetched, and CRL/OCSP URLs are fetched for chains that reach a trust anchor, all through DSS's CommonsDataLoader, which opens file:, ftp: and ldap: URLs, follows redirects and has no host or private-range filter (F-001). Nothing caps the response size or bounds the whole transfer, so a server named in a certificate can stream an arbitrarily large or slow body into memory (F-002); the same gap applies to TSA responses (F-260) and TL downloads (F-208). Online revocation sources are rebuilt per call with no cache, so every document re-downloads its CRLs (F-187), and OCSP requests carry no nonce while stale responses are accepted silently (F-207). Signature-policy fetching is off only because DSS 6.5.1 happens to read a null field (F-253). The engine therefore gives anyone who can submit a document a blind SSRF into the sidecar's network position plus a memory and thread exhaustion vector; the safe configuration (revocation offline, aia false) is not the default and is not documented as the setting for untrusted input.

F-001 F-002 F-208 F-260 F-187 F-207 F-253 F-261

The trusted-list pipeline fails open on staleness and fails closed with a false success signal

Downloads go straight into the cache the offline loader reads, before validation. A badly signed LOTL empties the published pool and is cached, so restarts load nothing (F-180); any non-XML HTTP 200 body overwrites a good cache file and the list vanishes at the next restart (F-272); after a snapshot import, a failed LOTL download publishes a pool whose summary has zero TLs while trust properties still reference the snapshot, and every trusted-chain validation then dies with INTERNAL_ERROR until a refresh succeeds, with completed=true all along (F-213). run() reports success whenever DSS did not throw and discards snapshot provenance (F-010); cache files are rewritten in place with no temp-and-rename, and two processes defaulting to ./dss-cache can tear each other's files (F-014, F-212). TLS verification is off by default for TL hosts, sequence numbers are not checked and accept_expired is true, so a replayed older list can bring a withdrawn trust service back (F-003). On the operations side, a restart from any cache waits a full --refresh-hours regardless of age (F-090), /health returns 200 with no lists loaded (F-080), and unmatched countries codes or unenforced tl_versions are silent (F-268, F-267). The unpackaged binaries fall back to a cwd-relative keystore and cache and never log which keystore is in use (F-064).

F-213 F-180 F-272 F-010 F-003 F-014 F-212 F-090 F-080 F-064 F-011 F-267 F-268 F-273

Small inputs abort the process or pin workers for minutes, and nothing sheds load

An OutOfMemoryError raised inside DSS (not at the document copy) lands on GraalVM's Reference Handler thread and aborts the whole process with SIGABRT, contradicting docs/native-library.md (F-186); the ffi-boundary finder reproduced it with a 16-32 MB zero-filled input on a 64 MB isolate. Cheap triggers exist: a 194 KB 25-megapixel RGBA16 PNG needs about 400 MB of heap per prepare or complete (F-032), a TTF with one oversized loca entry makes TTFSubsetter allocate the claimed glyph length (F-222), and a 200-byte cmap edit makes FontBox allocate gigabytes or spin for minutes (F-259). CPU is equally unbounded: visible text re-wraps the whole template at each of up to 82 shrink steps (F-224), PAdES validation is quadratic in signature revisions, /Annots size and page count (F-248, F-264, F-265), and CMS cost grows with embedded certificate count (F-211). dss-server adds no admission control: bodies are buffered whole onto an unbounded channel with a 512-thread blocking pool, there is no request deadline, read timeout or cancellation, and /health queues behind engine calls (F-052, F-078, F-079, F-233). A handful of requests from one client can take the sidecar down, and --max-heap makes the abort more likely rather than less.

F-186 F-032 F-222 F-259 F-224 F-248 F-264 F-265 F-211 F-052 F-078 F-079 F-233 F-043 F-227

TOTAL_PASSED does not mean what integrators will assume

The engine runs DSS's default constraint.xml unchanged and sets visual comparison to zero pages. DocMDP, FieldMDP, SigFieldLock, UndefinedChanges and PdfVisualDifference are all WARN there, so a certified PDF whose content was replaced after signing (F-256, F-004), or one that gained /OpenAction JavaScript or embedded files (F-257), still validates TOTAL_PASSED with errors: [], and dss-cli exits 0; the visual-comparison setting cannot change that (F-258). There is no aggregate verdict, the documented 'check signatures[].indication' guidance ignores nested[] and passes vacuously on an unsigned PDF with signatures: [] (F-098), standalone document timestamps are invisible (F-009), a PDF inside a .p7m is never validated (F-216), errors mixes AdES and qualification messages so a passing signature can carry an 'error' (F-250), and private-anchor verdicts are indistinguishable from EU-TL verdicts (F-269). A related plausible but unconfirmed finding (F-255) says post-signing annotations and form fills can pass with no warning in the summary at all. Hosts that gate on TOTAL_PASSED, which is what the docs/server.md integration example does, will accept documents they should not.

F-256 F-004 F-257 F-258 F-098 F-009 F-216 F-250 F-254 F-269

Signing trusts the TSA and the external CMS more than the contract promises

The configured TSA's token is embedded after only BouncyCastle's status, policy and imprint check: signature, chain, EKU, validity, algorithm and genTime are never verified, so a rogue or misconfigured TSA yields T/LT/LTA documents that validate TOTAL_PASSED with the timestamp INDETERMINATE and the loss is noticed only when the signer's certificate expires (F-219); requests carry no nonce (F-261). In cms mode the external CMS is checked for digest binding and signature validity but not for ESSCertIDv2 hash match (F-024), certificate validity at signing time despite the README saying so (F-025), signature algorithm (SHA-1 and MD5 pass, F-218), unsigned attributes (F-221) or a valid signature-time-stamp (F-023). In both modes no key-usage or basicConstraints check is made, so CA and TSA certificates sign (F-220). Several refusals happen only at complete, after a paid or OTP-confirmed signature is spent: broken earlier signatures at LT/LTA (F-274), too-small content_size (F-027), missing revocation data on B→LT (F-262). The throwing augmentation alert means that once any signature in a PDF is LT/LTA, no other signature in it can ever be augmented (F-214).

F-219 F-261 F-214 F-274 F-023 F-024 F-025 F-027 F-218 F-220 F-221 F-262 F-026

The release pipeline is pinned but unverified and never exercised

CI runs only on release:published and workflow_dispatch, so nothing runs on push or pull request (F-111) and a release is public before any gate (F-110); the workflow has never run on GitHub. There is no Dependabot or Renovate, no scheduled cargo-deny, cargo-audit or OSV scan and no SBOM for a library that parses untrusted PDF, CMS and XML (F-115); cargo deny check fails locally only because no deny.toml exists. The pinned GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1, whose JDK and cacerts are compiled into the library, is superseded by 25.5.5.0.3 with CVE-2026-91403 and CVE-2026-114820 fixes (F-129). Cargo.lock is never enforced because set-version.sh leaves it stale (F-113), Maven artifacts are never hash- or PGP-verified and the cache is restored by prefix (F-114), the Dockerfile pins nothing and checks no checksum (F-086), release assets carry only same-pipeline .sha256 files (F-112), and the seed-cache step can ship a release missing national lists without failing (F-243). On the licensing side, LGPL object code ships with only a pointer to the DSS source although §4 governs the project's own releases (F-132), and GraalVM, MPL, W3C and UPL source or notice duties are unmet (F-133, F-135, F-139, F-140).

Confirmed findings

Grouped by calibrated severity. Each card opens to the mechanism, the evidence quoted from the code, the impact, the recommendation and the verifiers’ verdicts.

High (5)

F-001HighsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:479

Document-controlled AIA caIssuers URLs are fetched with no scheme/host policy (file: reads, blind SSRF with redirects, unbounded and blocking reads); CRL/OCSP URLs are only fetched for chains that reach a trust anchor

With the defaults (revocation online, aia true), every CRL DP, OCSP and caIssuers URL in a submitted document's certificates is fetched by CommonsDataLoader. That loader opens file:, ftp: and ldap: URLs, follows redirects, and has no host or private-range filter.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

certificateVerifier() wires OnlineCRLSource and DefaultAIASource to httpLoader and OnlineOCSPSource to ocspLoader, with no URL filtering. CommonsDataLoader.get dispatches by scheme: fileGet/ftpGet use url.openStream() with no size or time bound, and ldapGet uses JNDI with no host restriction. DefaultAIASource accepts every Protocol value, and redirectsEnabled defaults to true. AIA is requested whenever the issuer is unknown, so a self-made CA is enough to trigger it and no trust anchor is needed. The responses are parsed and then discarded, which makes this a blind SSRF plus an existence and timing oracle. file:///dev/zero exhausts the heap, and a FIFO or /dev/stdin blocks the thread indefinitely. In the native image ldap: is likely unavailable, but file: and http(s) work. README and docs do not mention that validation makes outbound requests to URLs chosen by the document.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:469-479 'OnlineCRLSource crl = new OnlineCRLSource(); crl.setDataLoader(httpLoader); ... verifier.setAIASource(config.aiaFetching ? new DefaultAIASource(httpLoader) : null);'; DSS CommonsDataLoader.get: 'if (Protocol.isFileUrl(urlString)) return fileGet(urlString); ... ftpGet ... ldapGet'; DefaultAIASource:62 'acceptedProtocols = Arrays.asList(Protocol.values())'; CommonsDataLoader:170 'redirectsEnabled = true'

Impact

Anyone who can submit a document can make the host open local paths, reach internal hosts such as cloud metadata and admin interfaces from the sidecar's network position, and hang or exhaust worker threads and the heap.

Recommendation

Wrap the CRL/OCSP/AIA loaders in a DataLoader decorator that allows only http/https and rejects loopback, link-local and private ranges by default (config: http.allowed_hosts / allow_private_networks). Call DefaultAIASource.setAcceptedProtocols(HTTP, HTTPS) and setLdapTrustedHostnames(empty). Disable redirects or re-validate them. Add a regression test with file: AIA/CRL URLs. Document that revocation 'offline' plus aia false is the safe setting for untrusted input.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

DssEngine.create now builds every outbound loader through DssEngine.Loaders.of(config): the CRL/AIA CommonsDataLoader, the OCSPDataLoader, the TL loader and the TSA TimestampDataLoader are each wrapped in OutboundFetchPolicy.wrap (scheme allow-list, private/loopback/link-local refusal, size cap, deadline); test-injected loaders (5/6-arg constructors) stay unwrapped. DefaultAIASource is built by DssEngine.aiaSource() with setAcceptedProtocols(HTTP, HTTPS) only, so file:/ldap:/ftp: caIssuers URLs are never opened even when the policy allows other schemes. setRedirectsEnabled(config.httpFollowRedirects) is applied on every client.

After review: Must-fix: EngineHardeningTest.realLoadersSitBehindThePolicyAndTheCache now asserts the current redirect design. With follow_redirects (default true) the CommonsDataLoader behind the policy has isRedirectsEnabled()==false and its response handler is an OutboundFetchPolicy.RedirectInterceptingHandler (the policy checks each hop); with follow_redirects:false the flag is false AND the handler is not a RedirectInterceptingHandler, so the two configurations are distinguished. The production wiring was unchanged. Tests F-002/F-006/F-181/F-208/F-260/F-263 that run through this method are green again (17/17 in EngineHardeningTest).

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java, java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/EngineHardeningTest.java

Test: EngineHardeningTest.realLoadersSitBehindThePolicyAndTheCache, EngineHardeningTest.aiaFetchesOnlyHttpUrls (a certificate with file:/ldap:/ftp: caIssuers yields zero loader hits, http: yields one)

The code reads as the finding says. DssEngine.java:468-479 wires OnlineCRLSource/DefaultAIASource to httpLoader and OnlineOCSPSource to ocspLoader; both are plain CommonsDataLoader/OCSPDataLoader from withTimeouts(...) No allowed_hosts, setAcceptedProtocols, setLdapTrustedHostnames or redirect setting exists anywhere in java/ or rust/ (grep: none).

Impact in this system is real, with one correction to scope. DSS's SignatureValidationContext requests AIA "only when no issuer has been found yet" (line 618-623), i.e. during chain building, before any trust decision, so a self-made two-cert chain with caIssuers = file:///dev/zero or http://10.0.0.1/... triggers the fetch; aia defaults to on (README.md:281 "default: revocation == online", revocation default "online"). By contrast, revocation is fetched only if (checkRevocationForUntrustedChains || containsTrustAnchor(certChain)) (line 1070) and CommonCertificateVerifier.checkRevocationForUntrustedChains = false (line 199), so CRL/OCSP URLs are attacker-controlled only when the chain already contains a TL/extra-trusted anchor, which the attacker does not control. The AIA path alone carries the full impact; the title is corrected accordingly. LDAP: reachability-metadata.json has zero ldap/jndi entries, so ldap: is probably dead in the native image, as the finding already allows.

Not a documented or intended trade-off. The only network statement for the sidecar is inbound ("There is no TLS: the server is meant for the same host or a private network", DECISIONS.md:856-857; server.md:216), which does not neutralise outbound requests that a document chooses; the sidecar must have outbound access to refresh TLs and fetch real CRLs, so it sits on the Compose network with the app, DB and any cloud metadata endpoint. The authors clearly treat "client makes the server read any file it can read" as a concern worth refusing (DECISIONS.md:840-841, detached_contents[].path refused) and treat hostile documents as in scope (README.md:512 "a hostile file attacking the process"), and they restrict operator-supplied TSA URLs to http/https (EngineConfig.java:173-185 httpUrl), yet document-supplied AIA/CRL URLs get no equivalent check. Nothing in README.md or docs says validation makes outbound requests to URLs chosen by the document.

Mitigations are partial: the Docker image runs as the unprivileged dss user (Dockerfile USER dss), the http timeouts bound http(s) stalls (60 s), and responses are parsed as certificates and discarded, so this is a blind SSRF plus a timing/existence oracle, not data exfiltration. But file: reads have no bound at all: /dev/zero (world-readable in every container) is read into the heap until OutOfMemoryError or the container is OOM-killed, and dss-server has no per-request timeout layer (grep in rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs: none); each stalled or crashed worker is one of available_parallelism() validation threads (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:244-247, DECISIONS.md:355). The FIFO//dev/stdin hang is less practical (stdin is usually /dev/null in a container; an attacker cannot create a FIFO), so heap exhaustion is the realistic DoS. Any party whose signed document the application validates can trigger this with the default config, which makes the impact high rather than medium: one crafted document takes down the shared sidecar and lets its network position be probed. Actionable fix is as recommended, with revocation: "offline" + aia: false as the documented safe setting; the only correction needed is that CRL/OCSP URLs are attacker-reachable only on trust-anchored chains.

The mechanism is accurately described. DssEngine.java:461-480 (certificateVerifier) contains OnlineCRLSource crl = new OnlineCRLSource(); crl.setDataLoader(httpLoader);, ocsp.setDataLoader(ocspLoader); and verifier.setAIASource(config.aiaFetching ? new DefaultAIASource(httpLoader) : null);. None of these sets a protocol or host filter.

In production, DssEngine.create (line 130) builds the loaders as plain new CommonsDataLoader() and new OCSPDataLoader(). withTimeouts (line 146) only sets timeouts and a truststore.

EngineConfig makes this the default: revocation defaults to "online" (line 123) and aiaFetching = f.bool("aia", revocation == Revocation.ONLINE) (line 129).

I checked the DSS 6.5.1 sources in ~/.m2:

  • CommonsDataLoader.get (line 798) dispatches isFileUrl -> fileGet, isFtpUrl -> ftpGet, isLdapUrl -> ldapGet.
  • ftpGet/fileGet (lines 906-922) do url.openStream() followed by an unbounded DSSUtils.toByteArray, so a file:///dev/zero URL can exhaust the heap. The HTTP timeouts do not apply to this path.
  • redirectsEnabled = true at line 170.
  • DefaultAIASource line 62 has acceptedProtocols = Arrays.asList(Protocol.values()).
  • OnlineCRLSource only has a preferredProtocol ordering, not a filter.

The docs do not state that document-chosen URLs are fetched. README:281 only says "fetch missing intermediate certificates".

Calibration: the cited line, 469, falls inside the right block, which starts at 461. The impact needs tempering, because this is upstream DSS's stock default behavior and is inherent to online validation, which has to fetch URLs embedded in certificates. The SSRF is blind and GET-only, and the fetched bytes are parsed as CRL, OCSP or certificate data rather than echoed back. dss-server listens on 127.0.0.1 by default and supports an optional bearer token (docs/server.md), although signature validation of third-party documents is the core use case, so untrusted input is expected. The realistic impacts are:

  • probing internal hosts or cloud metadata, with timing and existence leaks;
  • worker or heap DoS through file:/dev/zero or a FIFO, which bypasses the HTTP timeouts.

There is no direct data exfiltration and no integrity impact. That puts it at medium rather than high, roughly CVSS AV:N/AC:L/PR:N-L/UI:N/C:L/I:N/A:L-H.

F-032HighperformanceFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/PngDecoder.java:110

PNG decode of a 194 KB 5000x5000 RGBA16 image needs ~400 MB of heap per prepare/complete and, under a heap cap, aborts the engine process

MAX_PIXELS is 25,000,000. The decoder allocates the inflated rows, an unfiltered copy, the samples and the alpha plane, then re-deflates at BEST_COMPRESSION, and does this again on every call.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Measured: a 5000x5000 RGBA16 PNG added 404-649 MB of heap. Over HTTP, /sign/prepare took RSS from 42 MB to 578 MB, four concurrent requests reached 1.42 GB, and with --max-heap 256m the result was OOM.

Evidence

SignatureImage.java:29 'MAX_PIXELS = 25_000_000'; PngDecoder.java:110, :135, :157, :197-198

Impact

A client can exhaust the engine heap with a few hundred KB, which can abort the process.

Recommendation

Bound decoded bytes to a few MB, decode row by row, and cache the parsed image between prepare and complete.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-visible)

PngDecoder now decodes row by row: the chunk structure is checked first (lengths, CRCs, header), then IDAT chunks are fed to one Inflater a row at a time, unfiltered against the previous row and converted to 8-bit samples/alpha that SignatureImage feeds straight into two Deflaters (RowDeflater, BEST_COMPRESSION, same bytes as the former one-shot deflate: verified by test). Peak heap is a few row buffers plus the compressed output; the 194 KB 5000x5000 RGBA16 PNG that needed 400-650 MB now allocates ~3 MB and takes ~0.4 s (measured with ThreadMXBean; regression test asserts < 32 MB). A new side cap (SignatureImage.MAX_SIDE = 16384) bounds the row buffers; the documented 25-megapixel cap is kept. Decoded PNGs are cached (static LRU, 16 entries / 64 MB, keyed by SHA-256 of the bytes), so complete does not decode again what prepare did (second parse returns the same instance in 1 ms).

After review: Cache bound: SignatureImage.cacheBytes() = min(64 MB, Runtime.maxMemory()/16), read when caching rather than in a static initialiser (native-image may initialise classes at build time, which would bake in the builder's heap): 16 MB under --max-heap 256m, 64 MB from 1 GB up; MAX_CACHE_BYTES = 64 MB stays as the ceiling. Alpha: decodePng starts the alpha RowDeflater only at the first row that is not fully opaque, feeding it the preceding rows as 0xFF then, so an opaque PNG never compresses width x height bytes of 255 for nothing and a transparent one gets a byte-identical stream. SignatureImageTest.theAlphaStreamIsTheSameWhereverTransparencyStarts (RGBA PNGs transparent from row 0, 5 and 10 compared with the one-shot deflate of the whole alpha; an opaque RGBA image has no soft mask), SignatureImageTest.theCacheIsSizedToTheHeap, rowByRowCompressionEqualsOneShot and the recorded fixtures (bytes unchanged).

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/PngDecoder.java, java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java, java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImageTest.java

Test: SignatureImageTest.aLargePngIsDecodedInBoundedMemoryAndCached (JVM only), SignatureImageTest.rowByRowCompressionEqualsOneShot, SignatureImageTest.pngParserGuardsRefuseWithAReason, VisibleSignatureTest.theRecordedVisibleFixturesStillComplete (bytes unchanged)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: High · confidence 0.92

Code confirms the allocation pattern. SignatureImage.java:29 MAX_PIXELS = 25_000_000 bounds pixels only; PngDecoder.checkHeader (line 116) accepts colour type 6 at depth 16, so stride = width*8. PngDecoder.java:110 allocates the inflate buffer of (stride + 1) * height bytes (line 135 new byte[(int) expected]), unfilter (line 157) a second stride * height buffer, toSamples (lines 197-198) width*height*3 samples plus width*height alpha, and SignatureImage.parse (lines 61-62, 101-115) then deflates both at BEST_COMPRESSION. Nothing caches the result: DssJsonApi.completeSignature (line 147) calls SigningOptions.fromJson(optionsJson) again, which re-runs VisibleSignature.fromJson -> SignatureImage.parse (VisibleSignature.java:136), and dss-server's lib.rs:169 comment says complete must receive the same options as prepare.

Experiment (scratchpad, read-only for the repo): a generated 5000x5000 RGBA16 PNG of all zeros is 194,471 bytes. Through SignatureImage.parse on the JVM: OOM at -Xmx256m and -Xmx384m (stack at PngDecoder.decode:110), success at -Xmx512m with peak heap used ~390 MB. Through the shipped native library via dss-cli ... --max-heap 256m sign prepare document.pdf --visible-page 1 --visible-rect 10,10,200,100 --visible-image bomb.png: exit 134 on 3/3 runs with "Fatal error: Reference processing and cleaners must handle all potential exceptions: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Garbage-collected heap size exceeded", i.e. the whole process aborts rather than returning INTERNAL_ERROR; the same prepare without the image at 256m succeeds, and at --max-heap 1g it succeeds with 577 MB maximum RSS (matching the finding's 578 MB). This contradicts the guarantee in docs/DECISIONS.md:277-285 ("a 128 MB document on a 64 MB heap returns INTERNAL_ERROR and the isolate keeps working") and the test heap_limit_is_an_error_not_a_crash, which only cover the document copy path. The 25 MP cap is documented in README.md:460-461 but bounds pixels, not decoded bytes (8 bytes/pixel at RGBA16, held twice), so it is not a mitigation for this case. Severity raised from medium: a few hundred KB from an API client deterministically kills dss-server when a heap cap is configured, and costs ~0.4-0.6 GB per request otherwise.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: High · confidence 0.9

Impact lens: the claimed impact is real and, in one respect, worse than stated, because the documented mitigation for heap exhaustion does not hold on this path.

Code and contract. java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java:28-29 "Larger images are refused: they would only be scaled down into a signature box. static final int MAX_PIXELS = 25_000_000;" and README.md:461 documents "up to 25 megapixels" as the public contract, so a host that follows the docs forwards such images. PngDecoder.java:109-112 allocates inflate(idat.toByteArray(), (long) (stride + 1) * height) (200 MB for 5000x5000 RGBA16), then unfilter makes a second new byte[stride * height], toSamples adds samples (75 MB) and alpha (25 MB), and SignatureImage.parse re-deflates both. The image is parsed from the options in engine/VisibleSignature.java:136 on every call; README.md:430 says the options "must be the same in both calls", so prepare and complete each pay this. No document (README.md, docs/DECISIONS.md "After Phase 6: visible signatures", docs/server.md "Security") states the memory trade-off of the 25 MP limit; DECISIONS.md only says "Not done" items, none about size.

The documented mitigation fails here. docs/native-library.md:111-113 claims "A document or report that does not fit the heap fails as {"ok":false,...INTERNAL_ERROR...OutOfMemoryError} and the isolate stays usable" and docs/server.md:220-222 says "--max-request-mb and --max-heap bound both". I generated a 5000x5000 RGBA16 PNG (299,619 bytes; 200,005,000 raw bytes) and ran the shipped native library through rust/target/release/dss-cli offline (--allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation, no refresh) with a visible signature on testdata/fixtures/content/form.pdf:

  • no heap limit: success, peak RSS 577 MB (text-only baseline: 58 MB), i.e. ~520 MB for a 300 KB input, matching the finding's measurement;
  • --max-heap 1g: success, 577 MB; --max-heap 512m: success;
  • --max-heap 256m, three runs: two returned error: InternalError: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError (exit 2, the documented behaviour), one died with exit 134 (SIGABRT): "Fatal error: Reference processing and cleaners must handle all potential exceptions: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Garbage-collected heap size exceeded", stack in com.oracle.svm.core.heap.ReferenceHandlerThread.run (the Inflater/Deflater cleaners run there);
  • --max-heap 384m: exit 134, same fatal error.

So with a heap limit (the setting docs/server.md:192 recommends in containers, "DSS_MAX_HEAP: 1g"), the OOM is nondeterministically fatal to the process. In the sidecar the engine runs in-process (docs/server.md: "runs one engine"), so one such request kills dss-server for every client; the Compose example in docs/server.md has no restart policy. Four concurrent 25 MP requests at the default --workers = CPUs exceed a 1 GB heap, so the crash is reachable with the documented configuration.

Threat model: docs/server.md "Security" places the sidecar on a private network behind a bearer token, which limits who can send the request to the host application. But README.md:429 names "a scanned handwritten signature" as the use case, which is typically end-user supplied, and the library contract invites 25 MP images; the host has no documented reason to reject them. The impact is therefore not negligible: a few hundred KB from an authenticated client (or an end user via the app) costs ~0.5 GB of heap per call and can abort the engine process, breaking a guarantee the docs make (native-library.md:111-113, server.md:220-222). The recommendation to cache the image between prepare and complete conflicts with the stateless design (README.md:430), but bounding decoded bytes (a signature box never needs 25 MP) or decoding row by row is actionable. Severity raised to high because the process abort is reachable with the documented deployment and contradicts the documented OOM handling; the only reason it is not critical is the token and private-network placement.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.8

The finding is accurate. Two details need correcting.

What the code does:

  • SignatureImage.java:29 sets the only bound, static final int MAX_PIXELS = 25_000_000;. checkSize (around :190) enforces it from the IHDR, and nothing limits the decoded byte count. So 5000x5000 RGBA16 passes.
  • PngDecoder.java:110 runs byte[] raw = unfilter(inflate(idat.toByteArray(), (long) (stride + 1) * height), ...).
  • inflate allocates the whole expected size up front at :135: byte[] out = new byte[(int) expected];. For RGBA16 that is (5000*8+1)*5000, about 200 MB.
  • unfilter allocates a second copy at :157: byte[] out = new byte[stride * height];. That is another ~200 MB, and the inflated buffer is still reachable while unfilter runs.
  • toSamples allocates samples (75 MB) at :197 and alpha (25 MB) at :198. The alpha plane is allocated even when the image turns out to be opaque.
  • SignatureImage.parse (:54-63) then runs deflate(...) at BEST_COMPRESSION, with a ByteArrayOutputStream pre-sized to raw.length / 2 + 64.
  • Deflate tops out at roughly 1030:1, so ~200 MB of IDAT fits in about 194 KB. The "~194 KB" figure is plausible.

Reachability: VisibleSignature.java:136 calls SignatureImage.parse(base64(v, "image")) on every request, and nothing is cached. That is consistent with the cost repeating on prepare and on complete.

Corrections to precision:

  1. The four buffers are never all live at once. Peak is about 400 MB: the inflated and unfiltered arrays together, plus the idat copy. After that, raw + samples + alpha is about 300 MB. Total allocated per call is about 500 MB, so "~0.5 GB" holds as total allocation, not as a simultaneous peak. The finding's own 404-649 MB measurement agrees.
  2. The worst case needs 16-bit RGBA. An 8-bit RGBA image at the cap costs roughly half.

Severity calibration:

  • Impact is availability only. Each request is bounded at ~0.5 GB because MAX_PIXELS caps it, but concurrent requests multiply that.
  • dss-server listens on 127.0.0.1 by default (main.rs:37) and can require a bearer token (lib.rs:66). The direct attacker is therefore the calling application.
  • However, signature images are typically supplied by end users and passed through. A hostile 200 KB upload therefore reaches the engine in normal use.
  • The "can abort the process" claim is weakened by DECISIONS.md:277-285. Large allocations were deliberately moved out of the entry frames, so an OOM returns INTERNAL_ERROR and the isolate keeps working. The realistic effect is failed or slow requests and heap pressure on other in-flight work, not a guaranteed crash. I did not reproduce the OOM.

Overall this is a real, actionable amplification issue (about 2000x), and medium severity is appropriate. The recommendation stands: cap decoded bytes, stream row by row, and skip the alpha plane when the image is opaque.

OutOfMemoryError raised during DSS processing (not at the document copy) can land on GraalVM's Reference Handler thread and abort the whole process with SIGABRT, contradicting docs/native-library.md "the isolate stays usable"

An OOM during DSS processing often hits reference processing and cleaners, and the process aborts with SIGABRT.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Heap sweep: 128m, 144m and 176m gave rc=134 'Reference processing and cleaners must handle all potential exceptions'.

Evidence

native-library.md:111-113 'the isolate stays usable'; dss-cli --max-heap 128m rc=134

Impact

One large request kills the sidecar or the host process.

Recommendation

Document OOM as fatal, bound admission, investigate the GraalVM option, and add a regression test.

Remediation: Fixed (package docs)

java-ffi handoff applied. The DECISIONS Phase 3 OutOfMemoryError bullet has a 'Revisited (2026-11-09)' paragraph, and there are new Phase 3 bullets 'Isolate-thread handle checked at entry' and 'C strings decoded strictly'. README's C API paragraph covers strict UTF-8, INTERNAL_ERROR vs NULL, the possible abort and fatal handle misuse. native-library.md cross-references dss-server's --max-in-flight/--request-timeout. The server.md sizing text was already present (rust-server).

Files: docs/DECISIONS.md, README.md, docs/native-library.md

Test: Documentation only; DssLib.failure, ffi/StrictUtf8 and -H:+CheckIsolateThreadAtEntry verified in the tree.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: High · confidence 0.95

CONFIRMED by reproduction. The repo only handles the OOM that occurs at the document copy: DssJsonApi.call (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssJsonApi.java:197-214) catches Throwable in the calling worker thread, and the only tests are the copy case: rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:520-533 heap_limit_is_an_error_not_a_crash (128 MB of zeros on a 64m heap) and java/src/test/c/smoke.c:350-379 small_heap_check (same). docs/native-library.md:111-113 then generalises this to "A document or report that does not fit the heap fails as {...INTERNAL_ERROR...OutOfMemoryError} and the isolate stays usable", and docs/DECISIONS.md:277-285 records the same conclusion. Nothing guards an OOM raised on GraalVM's own "Reference Handler" thread, which is fatal by design: the shipped library contains the string (strings build/native/macos-aarch64/libdssnative.dylib | grep -> "Reference processing and cleaners must handle all potential exceptions").

Experiment (offline, scratchpad cache, no TL refresh): built a 40 MB CAdES attached .p7m with openssl from testdata/fixtures/pki/test-pki.p12 (random content), then ran rust/target/release/dss-cli --allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation --trust testdata/fixtures/pki/root-ca.pem --max-heap <H> validate big40.p7m --json. Results, repeated 3 times each: 64m rc=2 INTERNAL_ERROR; 96m rc=2 INTERNAL_ERROR; 128m rc=134 (3/3); 144m rc=134 (3/3); 176m rc=2 INTERNAL_ERROR; 256m/512m rc=0 TOTAL_PASSED. The rc=134 stderr begins "Fatal error: Reference processing and cleaners must handle all potential exceptions: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Garbage-collected heap size exceeded" and the failing thread is "Reference Handler" (STATUS_IN_JAVA, PREVENT_VM_FROM_REACHING_SAFEPOINT) with frames VMError.shouldNotReachHere <- com.oracle.svm.core.heap.ReferenceHandlerThread.run(ReferenceHandlerThread.java:127). So when the heap is exhausted at the moment the reference-handler thread runs cleaners, the OOM bypasses every catch in DssJsonApi/DssLib and the whole host process aborts (SIGABRT). Exact outcome depends on which thread allocates last, which is why neighbouring heap sizes succeed as INTERNAL_ERROR; it is deterministic at a given size/document here.

Note: trailing-junk PDFs up to 120 MB on a 128m heap did not trigger it (PDFBox does not copy), so the trigger needs processing-time allocation (CMS/BouncyCastle parsing here), not raw document size; this matches the finding's "during DSS processing". Impact as stated holds: dss-server is documented to run with --max-heap in containers (docs/server.md:43) and --max-request-mb (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120) only bounds bytes received, not processing memory, so one admitted request can take down the sidecar; for an embedding host the host process dies. Severity high: process-killing from a single under-limit request, reachable with a plain CMS document, and the documentation/tests assert the opposite behaviour. Corrected locations: the false claim is docs/native-library.md:112-113 ("the isolate stays usable"); the missing coverage is rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:520.

The finding's central claim ("an OOM during DSS processing often hits reference processing and cleaners, and the process aborts with SIGABRT") could not be reproduced in this system under read-only experiments, and the surrounding mitigations make the claimed impact (one large request kills the sidecar/host) unsupported.

What I ran (release dss-cli, offline, no real-TL refresh), all in the scratchpad:

  • Heap sweep 48m..512m on testdata/fixtures/pades/b-lta.pdf: rc=0 every time.
  • 60 MB, 100 MB and 120 MB PDFs (fixture + zero padding) at 96m..512m: rc=0 or a clean error: InternalError: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: ... (rc=2). Notably --max-heap 104m on the 100 MB doc returned "Garbage-collected heap size exceeded" as INTERNAL_ERROR, i.e. an OOM raised *inside DSS processing*, not at the entry-point copy, still came back as a structured error.
  • validate-batch --parallel 4 (24 docs, 8-64 MB each) with the synthetic trusted-list cache at 96m/128m/144m/176m: 19/18/15/8 validations failed with OutOfMemoryError and the rest succeeded in the same isolate; rc=0 every run.
  • validate-batch --parallel 8 (48 docs) at 64m/80m/96m: 47/48/47 OOM errors, rc=0, no abort.

  • 90 MB returned a clean InternalError OutOfMemoryError (rc=2).

So an OOM thrown mid-processing, when it lands in a cleaner or in reference handling, kills the process rather than producing INTERNAL_ERROR. The doc's claim is inaccurate, and nothing tests this path. The mechanism, file and line are as described.

Severity calibration:

  • dss-server accepts requests of up to 100 MB by default (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:47 default_value_t = 100, applied through DefaultBodyLimit at lib.rs:120).
  • The heap is unbounded by default ("grows with physical memory", main.rs:81-83), so in the default configuration a single request is unlikely to trigger this.
  • The exposure appears when an operator sets --max-heap / DSS_MAX_HEAP small relative to the request limit, or when many concurrent large requests push the heap. Then one unauthenticated network request can crash the server.
  • It is also nondeterministic: in my run 90 MB gave a clean error while 50 and 70 MB aborted.

That makes it medium rather than high. It is real and needs a doc correction plus a regression test, but it depends on configuration.

The cache-loaded path is unaffected. checkUsable only iterates the summary's TLInfos (now empty), so a poisoned export is accepted. No test covers a failed refresh after import. A snapshot-started engine that hits one transient LOTL outage answers INTERNAL_ERROR (HTTP 500) for every trusted-chain validation, while status reports success. Snapshots exported in that state break every engine that loads them.

Before publishing, check that every TLInfo/LOTLInfo referenced by staging's trust properties resolves in staging.getSummary(). If not, keep the previous snapshot and return completed=false.   • The outcome is reported as success: completed=true, and dss-server logs "online trusted-list refresh completed ... N trusted certificates" (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:127-128). Monitoring has no signal.

I did not rerun the probe. Its output matches this reading of the code exactly.

Intent: README.md:517-518 says a failed list "stays missing until a later refresh succeeds". The comment at line 318 says staging is filled "so that a later refresh that cannot run keeps these lists". Neither describes this outcome: the certificates are kept, the summary is emptied, every trusted-chain validation throws, and status reports success. So this is not a documented decision.

The finding is accurately described (file, line and mechanism are right). Severity calibration, which brings it down from high to medium:

  • It fails closed. Validations error out (INTERNAL_ERROR); nothing invalid gets accepted.
  • It needs three things: an engine started from a snapshot, an operator- or schedule-initiated online refresh, and a LOTL outage at that moment.
  • It recovers on the next successful refresh.
  • The persistent part, a poisoned export, also needs someone to export during that window and ship the file.

Air-gapped snapshot deployments that try an online refresh would hit it every time, which raises the likelihood. Even so, the impact is availability and correctness of error reporting, not a trust bypass. Medium.

The oversized-loca font (last entry 0x7ffffff0) is refused at options parse with INVALID_ARGUMENT instead of allocating 1.9 GB at template.save().

F-002MediumreliabilityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:146

No response-size cap or whole-transfer deadline on CRL/OCSP/AIA downloads driven by certificate URLs

withTimeouts() sets only connect and inactivity timeouts. A server named in a certificate can stream an arbitrarily large or slow body, and CommonsDataLoader reads it fully into memory.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

setTimeoutSocket and setTimeoutResponse bound the gap between packets, not the whole transfer, and CommonsDataLoader has no maximum response size (DSSUtils.toByteArray). Revocation sources are created per validation with no cache, so each submission repeats the cost.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:146-150 'loader.setTimeoutResponse(config.httpResponseTimeoutMs); loader.setTimeoutSocket(config.httpResponseTimeoutMs);'; CommonsDataLoader.java:909 'return DSSUtils.toByteArray(inputStream);'

Impact

A single crafted document can exhaust host memory and worker threads.

Recommendation

Wrap the loaders to enforce a byte cap per fetch and an overall deadline per validation, and expose both in the http config.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

CRL, OCSP and AIA requests now go through OutboundFetchPolicy (http.max_response_bytes cap, http.request_deadline_ms whole-request deadline) from DssEngine.create; the per-fetch body bound and the wall-clock bound are the policy's. GET responses are additionally cached across calls (F-187), so a repeated CRL is not re-downloaded per document.

Test: EngineHardeningTest.realLoadersSitBehindThePolicyAndTheCache asserts the wiring and that the policy settings equal OutboundFetchPolicy.Settings.of(config); the bounds themselves are covered by OutboundFetchPolicyTest (java-trust)

The finding's cited CommonsDataLoader.java:909 is actually the ftpGet/fileGet path (also unbounded, reachable through get()'s protocol dispatch at lines 798-806), so the HTTP citation is corrected above. DSS ships a MaxSizeInputStream (dss-spi eu/europa/esig/dss/spi/client/http/MaxSizeInputStream.java) but only NativeHTTPDataLoaderCall uses it (line 176); grep for MaxSize/maxSize in CommonsDataLoader.java returns nothing, and DssEngine never calls setHttpClientResponseHandler.
  1. Per-validation sources, no cache: DssEngine.java:468-479 certificateVerifier() builds new OnlineCRLSource(), new OnlineOCSPSource(), new DefaultAIASource(httpLoader) on every call, and revocation: "online" plus aia: true are the defaults (README.md:280-281, EngineConfig). No caching revocation source is wired.
  1. No overall deadline elsewhere: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:302-310 run is a bare spawn_blocking with no timeout; grep for timeout/deadline in rust/dss/src finds only the config passthrough (config.rs:91-93). EngineConfig exposes only connect_timeout_ms/response_timeout_ms (EngineConfig.java:112-115).

Mitigation that lowers but does not remove the impact: an optional --max-heap (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:81-83, 248-250; default "grows with physical memory") and the OOM handling in docs/DECISIONS.md:277-284 turn an allocation failure into INTERNAL_ERROR with the isolate surviving, so with -Xmx set the memory part degrades to a failed validation rather than a crash. The worker-starvation part stands regardless: a slow-drip or huge CRL/AIA/OCSP body occupies a validation worker (default workers = available_parallelism in dss-server, 1 in the library) for an unbounded time, and nothing in the Java or Rust layers can cancel it. Severity stays medium: it needs a document whose certificate names an attacker-controlled URL and the default online revocation, and the effect is denial of service of the validator, not integrity loss.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.8

Impact is real but narrower than stated, and part of the claimed impact is already mitigated.

What is reachable from an untrusted document. CRL/OCSP are NOT a practical vector: DSS only fetches online revocation when the chain reaches a trust anchor — dss-spi SignatureValidationContext.java:1070 if (checkRevocationForUntrustedChains || containsTrustAnchor(certChain)), with checkRevocationForUntrustedChains = false by default (CommonCertificateVerifier.java:199) and never changed in DssEngine.java (grep for UntrustedChains in java/src/main finds nothing). So CDP/OCSP URLs come from CA-issued certificates, not from the attacker. AIA is the real vector: SignatureValidationContext.java:617-622 requests the issuer from AIA for any CertificateToken whose issuer is not found, before any trust decision; DssEngine.java:479 wires new DefaultAIASource(httpLoader) whenever aia is on, and README.md:280 says aia defaults to revocation == online, i.e. on by default. DefaultAIASource.java:62 accepts every Protocol (FILE, HTTP, HTTPS, LDAP, FTP) and tries each caIssuers URL in turn (lines 110-128). For HTTP the whole body is read with no cap (CommonsHttpClientResponseHandler.java:110-111 DSSUtils.toByteArray(content)); the line the finding quotes, CommonsDataLoader.java:906-909, is actually ftpGet, which uses url.openStream() and therefore ignores every timeout set in withTimeouts() (DssEngine.java:145-150) — an ftp:// caIssuers URL has no connect, socket or response timeout at all. Nothing in the engine or sidecar adds an overall deadline: rust/dss/src has only connect_timeout_ms/response_timeout_ms (config.rs:91-93) and dss-server has no request timeout layer (lib.rs:105-120 only sets DefaultBodyLimit).

Memory impact is largely mitigated, so "exhaust host memory" is overstated: docs/DECISIONS.md:277-285 and docs/native-library.md:111-113 document and test that an OutOfMemoryError returns INTERNAL_ERROR and the isolate stays usable, and docs/server.md:221 documents --max-heap to bound the heap. Without --max-heap the heap "grows to a large share of physical memory" (native-library.md:100-101), but that is the same exposure as any large document and is a documented operator choice.

Worker starvation is real. docs/server.md:42: --workers defaults to CPUs and "more wait in a queue". A certificate whose caIssuers points at an attacker-run server that trickles one byte every <60 s (HTTP) or any slow FTP server (no timeout) holds a worker indefinitely; a document with several such certificates serialises several fetches. A handful of such uploads (documents from untrusted parties reach the sidecar through the trusted-network client, which is the intended deployment per server.md:216) stall all validations. This is not a documented decision (DECISIONS.md:134 only says "All share the http timeouts", no trade-off on size or total time) and not covered by tests (HttpsLoopbackTest.java:142 runs with "aia":false). Severity stays medium: availability only, needs an attacker-controlled slow server, no integrity or confidentiality effect. The fix is actionable (cap bytes and total time per fetch, restrict DefaultAIASource.setAcceptedProtocols to http/https, or add a per-validation deadline). The file:// protocol being accepted for AIA is a separate concern not assessed here.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.75

The mechanism is real, but one piece of the evidence is cited wrongly.

Confirmed:

  • DssEngine.java:146-150 withTimeouts sets only setTimeoutConnection, setTimeoutConnectionRequest, setTimeoutResponse and setTimeoutSocket, all taken from config. The response timeout defaults to 60s (EngineConfig.java:115 http.integer("response_timeout_ms", 60_000)). Nothing caps the body size or the total transfer time. A server that sends a little data every <60s can keep one fetch going indefinitely.
  • certificateVerifier (DssEngine.java:461-481) builds a new OnlineCRLSource, OnlineOCSPSource and DefaultAIASource on every validation, with no cache. AIA fetching defaults to on (EngineConfig.java:129 aiaFetching = f.bool("aia", revocation == Revocation.ONLINE), and revocation defaults to "online"). So an AIA URL inside a submitted document's certificate is fetched again on every submission.

Correction to the evidence:

  • The cited CommonsDataLoader.java:909 DSSUtils.toByteArray(inputStream) is inside ftpGet, not the HTTP path.
  • The HTTP path is httpGet -> requestGet -> executeHttpRequest (CommonsDataLoader.java:1031-1045), which uses the default CommonsHttpClientResponseHandler. Its getContent does return DSSUtils.toByteArray(content); with no limit. So the conclusion stands.
  • The fix point is also clear: setHttpClientResponseHandler (CommonsDataLoader.java:779) accepts a size-capped handler.

Severity calibration (medium, possibly lower):

  • Attack vector: network, through the document. dss-server accepts uploads, which travel lib.rs:120 (DefaultBodyLimit) and then spawn_blocking. No privileges are needed when the server is exposed.
  • Memory impact is partly contained. docs/DECISIONS.md:277-286 and 386 state that OutOfMemoryError is caught inside the isolate ("a 128 MB document on a 64 MB heap returns INTERNAL_ERROR and the isolate keeps working"). Even so, the default heap is large, a big download inflates memory for all concurrent validations, and a slow-drip body ties up a blocking worker for an unbounded time.
  • The claim "exhaust host memory" is therefore overstated. Thread and worker exhaustion through slow transfers, plus heap pressure, is the realistic impact.
  • This is DSS's default behaviour, not something the project introduced, which also argues against high. Medium is fair for a deployable validation server. Low would apply for library-only, trusted-input use.

F-003MediumsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:128

Trusted-list downloads skip TLS by default (TrustAllStrategy) and nothing rejects a replayed older, validly signed LOTL/TL: sequence numbers are not checked and accept_expired defaults to true

tl_verify_tls defaults to false, so the LOTL/TL loader trusts any TLS certificate. DSS does not reject a list with a lower sequence number, and accept_expired defaults to true. A network attacker, or anyone who can write the cache, can replay old signed lists and bring back withdrawn trust services.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

TrustAllStrategy is installed globally because two national hosts (ES, HU) fail PKIX. The hostname check that remains only inspects a certificate that TrustAll has already accepted. ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy checks the signature and, only when accept_expired=false, NextUpdate. TSLSequenceNumberErrorDetection is not registered, and even when registered it only raises an alert. The default policy rates TLNotExpired and TLFreshness as WARN, so a signature that chains to an anchor present only in the replayed list validates TOTAL_PASSED. Old LOTLs remain verifiable against the OJ keystore until 2027-2029. DECISIONS.md says a MITM 'can block a list but cannot inject one', which overlooks replay.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:123-129 'tlLoader.setTrustStrategy(TrustAllStrategy.INSTANCE);'; EngineConfig.java:116 'tlVerifyTls = http.bool("tl_verify_tls", false);' and :104 'tlAcceptExpired = sync.bool("accept_expired", true)'; TrustedListManager.java:188-189 setAcceptExpired...; TrustedListManager.java:198-209 registers only OJUrlChange, LOTLLocationChange, TLSignatureError, TLExpiration; constraint.xml 'TLFreshness Level=WARN, TLNotExpired Level=WARN'

Impact

A trust service that was withdrawn (for example after a compromise) can be made trusted again, and its signatures validate as qualified. The TLS gap also enables block, eviction and freeze attacks from any network position.

Recommendation

Default tl_verify_tls to true and handle the known bad hosts with a per-host exception list or an additive trust store. Track per-list sequence numbers and issue dates and refuse to go backwards relative to the published snapshot (tl_rollback alert, completed=false). Bound accept_expired with a grace period. Update DECISIONS.md.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

docs/DECISIONS.md records tl_verify_tls=false as an explicit owner decision (ES and HU TL hosts fail PKIX), and the loopback test pins it. The verifiers' point (a replayed, validly signed older list is accepted because nothing compares sequence numbers) is real but its fix is rollback detection in TrustedListManager (java-trust's file), not the TLS default: a per-host TLS exception would need a custom HostnameVerifier re-running PKIX and still not stop replay over a compromised host. Kept the decision; recorded a handoff to java-trust for the sequence-number rollback check and a docs update that states the replay caveat and recommends tl_verify_tls:true plus tl_sync.accept_expired:false where ES/HU are not needed.

After review: Rollback protection in TrustedListManager + TlCacheLoader + TlDocumentCheck. TlDocumentCheck.check now returns Identity(sequenceNumber, issueDate) read in the same StAX pass (TSLSequenceNumber / ListIssueDateTime under SchemeInformation). TlCacheLoader takes a Guard and runs every document through it (online downloads, cache-expiry hits and offline cache reads) before DSS sees it. TrustedListManager.admit() refuses a list whose sequence number is lower than the one last published for the same URL, or equal with an earlier issue date (seconds precision): the refusal is a DSSExternalResourceException ('rollback refused: ...'), so DSS records a download error for that list and keeps its previous result; the download is never staged or promoted; a tl_rollback alert is raised with url, message and structured fields previous_sequence_number, previous_issue_date, sequence_number, issue_date. After every publication (run() and importSnapshot) recordPublished() raises the floor from the summary for lists that are used for trust only (usable LOTL/pivots, usable TLs under a usable LOTL, usable other TLs), so a forged list cannot raise the bar, and persists it atomically to <cache_dir>/tl-sequence-numbers.json (read at construction; unreadable file = warning and fresh start; unwritable = cache_write_error alert). Status: every lotls[]/tls[]/pivots[] entry gains last_published_sequence_number (null when none). The hostname verifier that remains is DSS's CommonsDataLoader default (hostnameVerifier = new DefaultHostnameVerifier(), dss-service 6.5.1 sources line 239), which only checks the name inside a certificate TrustAll has already accepted, so a self-signed cert with the right CN passes. The repo's own test confirms the default: HttpsLoopbackTest.java:195 trustedListDownloadsSkipTlsVerificationByDefault loads lists over HTTPS from a server whose CA is not in the JDK store and asserts TOTAL_PASSED.
  1. No rollback protection. TrustedListManager.java:186-189 installs ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy with setAcceptExpired...(config.tlAcceptExpired), and EngineConfig.java:104 tlAcceptExpired = sync.bool("accept_expired", true). DSS's strategy source (isSyncSupported) checks only NextUpdate (skipped when accept-expired is true) and the signature validation result; it never compares sequence numbers or issue dates. TrustedListManager.java:198-209 registers only OJUrlChangeDetection, LOTLLocationChangeDetection, TLSignatureErrorDetection and TLExpirationDetection; TSLSequenceNumberErrorDetection exists in dss-tsl-validation 6.5.1 but is not used (grep of java/src for "SequenceNumber" hits only the status report at TrustedListManager.java:513 and the test helper), and even in DSS it is an AlertDetector whose state is an in-memory map, i.e. it can only raise an alert and forgets everything across restarts. DSS's AbstractAnalysis.download (dss-validation-job 6.5.1) replaces the cache whenever the digest differs: if (!cacheAccess.isUpToDate(downloadResult)) { cacheAccess.update(downloadResult); expireCache(); }, so an older signed list served by a MITM becomes the cached, parsed and validated list. Default policy/constraint.xml:642-643 in dss-policy-jaxb 6.5.1: <TLFreshness Level="WARN" .../>, <TLNotExpired Level="WARN" />, so a replayed list only warns at validation time.
  1. Documentation. docs/DECISIONS.md:193-197 records the choice and its rationale: "a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one". That rationale covers forgery but not replay of a genuine older list, which is exactly the finding's point; the decision is documented but rests on an incomplete threat model, so it does not refute the finding.

Severity calibration: I lower it from high to medium. The attack is real but needs a chain: a network position during an explicit online refresh of the TL hosts, an archived older list that is still signed by a TL-signing certificate the (current or replayed) LOTL lists, and, to do real damage, control of the withdrawn trust service's key (re-trusting an honest-but-withdrawn CA only revives its legitimately issued certificates). A cache-write attacker is a local compromise and out of scope for TLS. The TLS gap also enables cheaper block/freeze attacks, but those degrade availability, not trust. Still, for a qualified-signature validator the default configuration lets a network attacker roll back the trust-anchor set with no time bound (accept_expired=true), so it is a genuine defect, not a misread.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.65

The code reads as the finding says: DssEngine.java:123-129 installs TrustAllStrategy when tlVerifyTls is false; EngineConfig.java:116 defaults tl_verify_tls to false and :104 defaults accept_expired to true; TrustedListManager.java:198-209 registers only OJUrlChange, LOTLLocationChange, TLSignatureError and TLExpiration alerts. DSS 6.5.1 does ship eu.europa.esig.dss.tsl.alerts.detections.TSLSequenceNumberErrorDetection, but its source shows it keeps an in-memory map per job and only returns true to raise an alert, so even registering it would not refuse a lower sequence number across restarts.

Is it a documented, reasonable decision? It is documented three times (docs/DECISIONS.md:192-198 "TLS for trusted-list downloads: not verified ... a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one"; README.md:277; docs/native-library.md:140), was an explicit owner decision ("The user answered the four open questions"), mirrors the DSS demo's tl.loader.trust.all, and is pinned by HttpsLoopbackTest.trustedListDownloadsSkipTlsVerificationByDefault (line 195). That would normally refute under this lens. But the stated trade-off is factually incomplete: an on-path attacker cannot forge a list, yet can serve a stale genuine one, and nothing rejects it. The replay is not a no-op in this system: TrustedListManager.java:153-155 installs GrantedOrRecognizedAtNationalLevelTrustAnchorPeriodPredicate when use_sunset_date is true (EngineConfig.java:101 defaults it to true), so under the current list a withdrawn service's certificate stops being a trust anchor, and serving the previous list restores it. The OJ keystore (trust/oj-keystore.p12, keytool listing) holds LOTL signing certificates valid until 2027-2029, so previous LOTL versions remain verifiable. The decision was therefore made without the replay case in view, which makes the finding actionable at least as a correction of DECISIONS.md and a reconsideration of the default (a per-host exception for the two PKIX-failing hosts would keep the operational benefit).

Why medium rather than high: (1) The attacker needs an on-path position on the server's egress to EU/national hosts plus a signature from a certificate of a withdrawn service, a targeted adversary. (2) Silent replay is bounded by the list's NextUpdate (typically up to 6 months); beyond that TLExpirationDetection raises tl_expired and the status marks expired: true (TrustedListManager.java:517), and the status also exposes sequence_number and issue_date per list (:513-516), so rollback is observable by an operator. (3) The "block, eviction and freeze" part of the impact is not new: DECISIONS.md:196 already states a MITM can block a list, and with accept_expired=true a blocked refresh keeps the cached list in use regardless of TLS, so TLS verification would not remove it. (4) "anyone who can write the cache" is explicitly outside the threat model: README.md:507-509 says whoever can write the snapshot can make any certificate trusted and the application must protect its files; the cache directory sits at the same trust level. (5) Rollback protection by sequence number is a DSS-wide limitation that also applies with TLS on (a compromised national host or CDN could serve an old list), so that recommendation is a hardening feature rather than a defect introduced by this code. The actionable core is the tl_verify_tls default and the incomplete rationale in DECISIONS.md.

The cited facts check out.

  • EngineConfig.java:116 contains tlVerifyTls = http.bool("tl_verify_tls", false); and EngineConfig.java:104 contains tlAcceptExpired = sync.bool("accept_expired", true);.
  • TrustedListManager.java:184-189 installs ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy. It checks only the signature and, when accept_expired is false, expiry. There is no sequence-number or issue-date monotonicity check.
  • TrustedListManager.java:197-209 registers only these alerts: OJUrlChangeDetection, LOTLLocationChangeDetection, TLSignatureErrorDetection and TLExpirationDetection.
  • docs/DECISIONS.md:196 says "a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one". That covers forged lists, not replay of genuine older ones. The rollback gap is therefore real and is not addressed by the documented decision.

Corrections on precision and severity:

  1. Turning off TLS for TL downloads is itself a documented, user-approved decision (DECISIONS.md:192-197, README.md:277), and it matches DSS's own tl.loader.trust.all demo option. It is not the defect by itself. The real defect is the missing rollback check (TrustedListManager), which TLS-off makes easy to exploit from a network position. So the actionable location is TrustedListManager.java:184-209 rather than DssEngine.java:123.
  2. I could not find constraint.xml with TLFreshness/TLNotExpired in the repository (the grep over java/src and rust returned nothing). That claim rests on DSS's bundled default policy and is unverified here.
  3. Exploitation is narrow:
  • The attacker needs an on-path position against the TL refresh.
  • The attacker needs an archived older list whose signature still validates. For the LOTL, the signing cert must still be in the OJ keystore. For a TL, the signing cert must be in the LOTL pointer that is accepted.
  • The gain is limited to services withdrawn or changed inside that window.
  • Rollback acceptance is also stock DSS behaviour.

Impact is integrity of qualification verdicts, which is serious for a signature validator. However, attack complexity is high, a network position is required, and the scope is bounded. Medium is more appropriate than high.

F-010MediumcorrectnessFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:294

Online refresh that downloads nothing drops the snapshot provenance and republishes the kept snapshot certificates as loaded online, with a status whose tls[] is empty

run() calls publishSnapshot with completed=true whenever DSS's job did not throw. Per-list download, parse and validation errors are not aggregated, and snapshot provenance (tl_snapshot, lists_loaded) is replaced with mode 'online' even when nothing was downloaded.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Probe D1: an engine started from a snapshot, with the LOTL unreachable, produced RefreshRecord mode=online completed=true, tl_snapshot=false, and download.status=ERROR. A later export records lists_loaded mode online. dss-server logs 'online trusted-list refresh completed ... N trusted certificates', so a blocked or stale engine looks healthy.

Evidence

TrustedListManager.java:292-294 'RefreshRecord record = new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), true, null, staging.getNumberOfCertificates()); publishSnapshot(record, null);'; dss-server lib.rs:127-130 describe_refresh 'completed in {} ms'

Impact

Operators and applications that rely on completed, tl_snapshot or lists_loaded get false provenance and no signal that trust is frozen on stale lists.

Recommendation

Derive completed (or a degraded field with counts) from the per-list states. Keep the snapshot provenance and loadedBy when the pool was not rebuilt. Surface failure counts in logs and /health.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-trust)

Provenance half fixed: when a refresh produces nothing publishable (LOTL not downloadable after a snapshot start, LOTL unusable, or every national list undownloadable while the previous pool was loaded) the snapshot provenance and loadedBy are kept and the record says completed=false with an error; the failure is also a refresh_not_published alert and cache write failures a cache_write_error alert. The 'derive completed from per-list states' half was not done: the verifier confirmed completed's documented contract (false only when the run produced nothing usable; per-list problems in the status), which this keeps, refined as above. The DECISIONS text 'DSS has no earlier results to keep for a list that fails to download, so that list stays missing' still holds for partial failures.

After review: server.md: 'Give each server its own --cache-dir, or at least do not expect a dss-cli tl refresh on the same directory to update a running server (it writes safely, but the server's lists change only on its own refresh)' under Refreshes, and 'give each container its own' cache volume in the Docker section.
