Mechanism: TrustedListManager.run() (lines 283-296) only catches a RuntimeException; otherwise it unconditionally builds new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), true, null, staging.getNumberOfCertificates()) (line 292) and calls publishSnapshot(record, null) (line 294), which sets current = new Snapshot(copy, staging.getSummary(), Instant.now(), loadedBy, tlSnapshot=null) (line 452). DSS 6.5.1's TrustedListCertificateSourceSynchronizer.sync() (extracted from the sources jar) only calls synchronizeCertificates() when isCertificateSyncNeeded(summary) is true, i.e. when some parsing record is null/DESYNCHRONIZED/ERROR; a failed LOTL download on an empty cache leaves parsing REFRESH_NEEDED, so the staging source keeps the snapshot's certificates untouched, while certificateSource.setSummary(summary) replaces the summary with one that shows a download ERROR and no TLs. The library then publishes the snapshot's certificates as if loaded by this online run: tl_snapshot is dropped, loadedBy becomes the online record, exportSnapshot() (line 429) writes lists_loaded = that online record, and the status is self-contradictory (trusted_certificates=3, loaded=true, but tls=[] and the LOTL used_for_trust=false). This also contradicts README.md:517-518 and docs/DECISIONS.md:973-975 ("An online refresh replaces the snapshot's lists with what it downloads... A list that fails to download stays missing"): the lists are not replaced, they are silently kept and relabelled.

Correction to the finding: the completed=true part is a documented, deliberate semantics, not a defect. TrustedListManager.java:95 "Outcome of one refresh run. Per-list problems are in the TL status, not here."; rust/dss/src/types.rs:178 "False only if the refresh could not run at all; per-list problems are in the status."; and rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:613-617 (validation_keeps_working_during_a_refresh) asserts record.completed together with status.lotls[0].download.error.is_some(). dss-server's describe_refresh (lib.rs:125-131) follows that contract; /health exposes trusted_lists_loaded, which is also true here. The real defect is narrower than the title: the provenance (tl_snapshot, loadedBy/lists_loaded) is replaced and the summary is replaced even when DSS did not rebuild the certificate pool, so a snapshot-started engine whose LOTL is unreachable looks like it was loaded online. Severity medium: operators lose the only signal that trust is still frozen on the snapshot, and the exported file lies about which load validated its lists; no trust anchors are added or removed.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Verdict through the IMPACT lens: half of F-010 is a documented decision and is refuted; the other half (provenance) is real but narrower and lower-impact than stated.

REFUTED PART: "completed=true even when per-list downloads failed". This is the documented contract, not a defect. docs/openapi.yaml:871-873 completed: ... description: False only if the refresh could not run at all; per-list problems are in the lists' state.; rust/dss/src/types.rs:178 /// False only if the refresh could not run at all; per-list problems are in the status.; TrustedListManager.java:95 /** Outcome of one refresh run. Per-list problems are in the TL status, not here. */. The per-list signal exists: status() (TrustedListManager.java:456-500) emits download/parsing/validation status, error, last_success_synchronization, expired and used_for_trust per list, and dss-server passes it through at /tl/status (DECISIONS.md:849-851). OnlineTrustedListTest.java:54-60 already relies on download.status == "ERROR" as the failure signal. A TL that fails to download after a snapshot start going missing is also documented (DECISIONS.md:973-975, README.md:517-519). The dss-server log line (lib.rs:127-129) and /health (lib.rs:251-266, only trusted_lists_loaded/refresh_in_progress) are consistent with that contract. Changing completed as the finding recommends would break a documented API.

CONFIRMED PART, with experiment: I compiled a probe in the scratchpad against java/target/classes + test-classes using the project's synthetic LOTL harness (FakeHttp.offline(true), no network, no real EU lists). Results:

  • A (snapshot start, LOTL unreachable): record completed=true, trusted_certificates=3; status after: loaded=true trusted_certificates=3 tl_snapshot=false, lotl download=ERROR parsing=REFRESH_NEEDED used_for_trust=false, and tls EMPTY; export header lists_loaded={mode=online, completed=true, trusted_certificates=3}. Mechanism: DSS's TrustedListCertificateSourceSynchronizer.sync() only calls synchronizeCertificates() when isCertificateSyncNeeded() (parsing entry null/desync/error); with a fresh cache the LOTL parsing entry is REFRESH_NEEDED, so the staging source is left holding the snapshot's certificates, while run() at TrustedListManager.java:292-294 unconditionally does publishSnapshot(record, null), i.e. loadedBy = the online record and tlSnapshot = null. exportSnapshot (lines 429-430) then writes lists_loaded = snap.loadedBy().toMap().
  • B (cache start, LOTL unreachable): certificates kept, every list download=ERROR parsing=SYNCHRONIZED used_for_trust=true -> DSS last-known-good, visible in status; fine.
  • C (snapshot start, one TL unreachable): that TL dropped (3 -> 1 certificates) exactly as documented.
  • D (cache start, one TL unreachable): kept, download=ERROR visible.

So the real defect is scenario A only: README.md:493 promises lists_loaded is "the load that validated the lists" and README.md:517 says an online refresh "replaces the snapshot's lists with what it downloads"; here nothing was downloaded, nothing replaced, yet the label flips to online and tl_snapshot disappears, and the status becomes internally inconsistent (loaded=true, 3 certificates, but tls=[] and the LOTL used_for_trust=false). DECISIONS.md:976-978 states the intent that when a refresh cannot run "the published lists, and where they came from, stay as they were", but only the exception path implements it; the LOTL-download-error path (DSS reports it in cache state rather than by throwing) escapes it. No test covers it (TlSnapshotTest.onlineRefreshAfterASnapshotReplacesItsLists only tests the success path).

IMPACT CALIBRATION (low): no trust is widened and no validation verdict changes; the trust pool is exactly the snapshot the application itself chose to load (README.md:508-511 puts snapshot trust on the application). The library sits in a host app or a sidecar on a trusted network; no untrusted party influences this. Status still carries a signal (LOTL download=ERROR, used_for_trust=false, empty tls). What is wrong is provenance metadata: a re-exported snapshot is labelled online-validated and fresh (finished_at now), and operators of a snapshot-started sidecar behind an egress block lose tl_snapshot after the first 6-hourly refresh. Actionable and small: in run(), keep the previous Snapshot's loadedBy/tlSnapshot when DSS did not resynchronize (e.g. no LOTL/TL reached a parsed result), or record it in the RefreshRecord.

refutedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.65

The finding describes the code correctly, but the behaviour is the documented contract rather than a defect, and parts of the impact are wrong.

The code does what the finding says. TrustedListManager.java:292-294 builds new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), true, null, staging.getNumberOfCertificates()); publishSnapshot(record, null); whenever refresh.run() does not throw. publishSnapshot (line 441) sets tlSnapshot to null for an online refresh, so status reports tl_snapshot: null.

completed is documented as "the job ran", not "every list loaded". The record's javadoc (line 95) says "Outcome of one refresh run. Per-list problems are in the TL status, not here." The catch block (lines 283-285) says "DSS records per-list failures itself; reaching here means the job could not run at all." Those per-list failures are visible: status() lists every LOTL and TL with its download, parsing and validation state and used_for_trust. The probe itself saw download.status=ERROR there, so failures do get a signal.

Replacing the snapshot provenance is also documented, and it is accurate. docs/DECISIONS.md, "Behaviour around a snapshot", says "An online refresh replaces the snapshot's lists with what it downloads ... a list that fails to download ... stays missing until a refresh succeeds". After an online refresh, the published pool really is the online job's output, rebuilt from staging. So tl_snapshot=null and an exported lists_loaded of mode online (lines 429-430) describe the lists correctly. Keeping the snapshot provenance on lists the snapshot no longer supplies would be the false provenance.

The impact claim is imprecise. It says trust is "frozen on stale lists" behind a healthy-looking status. Per DECISIONS, in the snapshot case cited, lists that fail to download disappear rather than stay frozen. The certificate count in the record and in the dss-server log line (lib.rs:127-128, "completed in {} ms, {} trusted certificates") falls accordingly. Stale lists are only kept when a cache_dir holds them, which is the documented fallback, and the TL status still shows the per-list errors and expiry alerts.

What remains real is minor. dss-server's log line and the RefreshRecord carry no count of failed lists, so an operator who reads only the log line or completed misses partial failures. That is a low-severity observability improvement, worth adding failure counts to the log and /health, not a medium correctness bug. Exploiting it needs network control over the LOTL/TL fetches, and the full status shows the degradation.

F-052MediumreliabilityFixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120

No admission control: per-request DefaultBodyLimit is the only cap; bodies are buffered and copied onto an unbounded engine mpsc channel with no concurrency limit, and server.md wrongly says --max-request-mb/--max-heap bound memory

Each request is buffered whole, copied into a Job (to_vec) on an unbounded mpsc channel, and holds a blocking thread (512 max). The only limit is per-request DefaultBodyLimit.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Measured with 2 workers: 12 concurrent uploads of 37 MB took RSS from 42 MB to 1.74 GB, and 1.56 GB stayed resident afterwards. Rust-side copies are outside --max-heap. The library API has no try or timeout variants and no queue-depth metric. docs/server.md:221-222 says --max-request-mb and --max-heap 'bound both'.

Evidence

rust/dss/src/engine.rs:395 'mpsc::channel::<Job>()'; :159 'document: document.to_vec()'; lib.rs:120 '.layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_request_bytes))'; lib.rs:336 'field.bytes().await'

Impact

A burst of large uploads (or abusive clients) gets the sidecar OOM-killed and latency grows without bound.

Recommendation

Add a semaphore weighted by bytes or a ConcurrencyLimit with 503/429 and Retry-After, a bounded sync_channel, and queue metrics. Correct server.md with the real bound.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

Admission control in the server: Settings::max_in_flight (flag --max-in-flight / DSS_MAX_IN_FLIGHT, default 2 x --workers, clap range 1..=256) is a tokio Semaphore; every document handler takes a permit before reading its body and the permit moves into the spawn_blocking closure, so it is released only when the engine call returns (also when the client went away). The request over the limit is answered 503 SERVER_BUSY with Retry-After: 1 and its body is never read. /health reports in_flight and max_in_flight. docs/server.md no longer claims --max-request-mb/--max-heap 'bound both': a new 'Sizing' section gives the real bound (max_in_flight x max_request_mb x 2 on the Rust side, heap >= largest document x workers x 3) and states that --max-heap is not a safety boundary (F-186). A bounded channel inside the engine is unnecessary now: the server never submits more than max_in_flight jobs.

Files: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs, docs/server.md, docs/openapi.yaml

Test: rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs admission_control_refuses_the_request_over_the_limit (two concurrent /validate with max_in_flight 1: one 200, one 503 SERVER_BUSY + Retry-After; slot released afterwards; /health counters)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.9

Confirmed by reading the code paths. rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120 applies only .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_request_bytes)), a per-request cap; grep of rust/dss-server/src finds no ConcurrencyLimit, Semaphore, timeout or 429/503-on-busy (the only 503s are NOT_INITIALIZED / TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED). lib.rs:336 let bytes = field.bytes().await?; buffers each part whole; lib.rs:303-312 run() uses tokio::task::spawn_blocking, bounded only by Tokio's default 512 blocking threads. rust/dss/src/engine.rs:395 let (job_tx, job_rx) = mpsc::channel::<Job>(); is the unbounded std channel, and engine.rs:157-162 does document: document.to_vec() before submit, so every queued request holds two copies (Bytes in the handler + Vec in the job) while only b.workers threads (engine.rs:399-407, worker_main 601-626) drain it. docs/server.md:221-222 states "--max-request-mb and --max-heap bound both", which is false for aggregate memory: neither bounds requests in flight, and --max-heap covers only the isolate heap, not the Rust-side copies. main.rs:50 documents --workers as "requests the engine runs at the same time", which caps engine concurrency, not queue depth. docs/DECISIONS.md:357-358 only says the per-call copy is "negligible next to validation" and records no decision to forgo admission control. Mitigation: server.md:213-216 positions this as a private, token-protected sidecar not exposed publicly, so the abusive-client case needs a token holder; a burst from the owning app is the realistic trigger. The specific RSS figures (1.74 GB / 1.56 GB) were not re-measured here, but the structural defect and the incorrect doc statement are real as described. Medium severity: real OOM/latency risk under bursts, limited by private deployment.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.8

Impact lens, code reading taken as given and confirmed: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120 applies only a per-request DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_request_bytes); lib.rs:336 let bytes = field.bytes().await? buffers each part whole; lib.rs:307 tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || call(&engine)) with no semaphore or ConcurrencyLimit anywhere (grep for Semaphore/ConcurrencyLimit/timeout in rust/dss-server/src returns nothing but the health-check socket timeout); rust/dss/src/engine.rs:395 mpsc::channel::<Job>() is unbounded and :159 document: document.to_vec() makes a second Rust-side copy per queued job, so a queued request holds roughly 2x its size on the Rust side before the engine copies it again into its heap.

Part of the claimed impact IS neutralised by the deployment model and should be dropped: docs/server.md:215-217 and docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857 place the sidecar on the same host or a private network with a bearer token and say "never expose it publicly", so "abusive clients" is not the realistic threat. The sole client is the application (php/DssClient.php).

What remains is real and not documented as a trade-off: (1) The application forwards documents from untrusted end users, so a burst of legitimate large uploads (default --max-request-mb = 100, server.md:41) is the normal load shape of a validation service, and nothing caps how many are in flight or queued; (2) server.md:221-222 states "A request is held in memory whole, and the engine copies it into its own heap. --max-request-mb and --max-heap bound both." That is true per request and false in aggregate: --max-heap bounds the engine side (DECISIONS.md:277-282 even handles the engine OOM gracefully as a 500), but nothing bounds the Rust-side total. An operator who follows server.md:43 ("Set it in containers") and sizes the container as heap + one request will be OOM-killed by the container runtime under a burst, and DECISIONS.md:842-843 says the orchestrator then restarts the process, losing every request in progress. (3) php/DssClient.php:26 sets a 120 s client timeout, but the server has no cancellation, so abandoned jobs keep their place in the unbounded queue and client retries only deepen it. (4) rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs has no concurrency test (grep for concurren/parallel/join_all finds nothing), and docs/DECISIONS.md:357-358 only says the job copy "is negligible next to validation", which is a time statement, not a memory bound; the sidecar section (DECISIONS.md:817-870) does not discuss admission control at all. The finding's "measured 1.74 GB RSS" figure was not reproduced here (it would require starting the server, which refreshes trusted lists when nothing is cached), but the per-request arithmetic from the code suffices for the conclusion.

Severity: medium. The mitigation is cheap (a tower ConcurrencyLimit / bounded queue returning 503 plus one corrected sentence in server.md), the failure mode is a container OOM under ordinary peak load, and the documentation currently steers operators toward exactly that undersizing. Not critical because the network is trusted and the application's own upload limits and worker count usually bound concurrency in practice.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.85

I confirmed every part of the mechanism in the code.

  • rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120 sets .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_request_bytes)). That is a per-request cap only. The server has no Semaphore, ConcurrencyLimit or load-shed layer (grep for Semaphore/ConcurrencyLimit/concurren in rust/dss-server/src finds nothing).
  • lib.rs:336 let bytes = field.bytes().await? buffers each part whole.
  • lib.rs:307 tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || call(&engine)) holds a blocking-pool thread for each request in flight.
  • rust/dss/src/engine.rs:159 document: document.to_vec() makes a second copy.
  • engine.rs:395 let (job_tx, job_rx) = mpsc::channel::<Job>(); is unbounded. Only the per-job reply channel is sync_channel(1).

So aggregate memory grows with the number of concurrent requests, up to blocking-pool size times max-request-mb times about 2, plus the Java-side copy. Neither flag bounds that.

docs/server.md:221-222 says "A request is held in memory whole, and the engine copies it into its own heap. --max-request-mb and --max-heap bound both." That is misleading. --max-request-mb bounds a single request, and --max-heap bounds only the isolate heap, not the Rust-side Bytes and Vec copies. The queue itself is intended: server.md:42 says "more wait in a queue", and DECISIONS.md:355 says workers "share a job queue". But nothing documents an unbounded queue or the absence of admission control as an accepted trade-off.

I did not reproduce the RSS measurement myself, but the code path makes it plausible.

Severity: medium is right, at the low end of it. The documented deployment is a sidecar on a private Compose network behind a bearer token. A remote attack therefore needs network adjacency plus the token (AV:A/PR:L), and the impact is availability only (an OOM kill). Legitimate burst traffic, such as a batch of large PDFs, can trigger it without any attacker, which raises the likelihood in normal use. A maintainer can act on the finding as written: add a byte-weighted semaphore or concurrency limit returning 429/503, a bounded sync_channel, and a docs fix.

Small precision note: the blocking-thread hold is at lib.rs:307 (the spawn_blocking in the request path), which the finding implies but does not cite.

F-064MediumsecurityFixedrust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:610

OJ keystore (LOTL root of trust) and default cache dir fall back to cwd-relative paths in unpackaged dss-cli/dss-server, and neither the path nor the keystore digest is ever logged or exposed by status/version

dss-cli and dss-server fall back to ./trust/oj-keystore.p12 and ./dss-cache. A directory that supplies both decides which certificates are trusted, and nothing logs the path or digest of the keystore in use.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

A cargo-built CLI has no keystore next to the executable. dss-server main.rs:258-269 has the same fallback. The keystore password is public.

Evidence

dss-cli main.rs:603-614 'candidates.push(PathBuf::from("trust/oj-keystore.p12"));'; dss-cli main.rs:66 default 'dss-cache'; dss-server main.rs:258-269

Impact

Running inside an untrusted directory can make arbitrary signatures validate as trusted.

Recommendation

Drop the cwd fallback (or require an explicit flag), log the resolved path and oj_keystore_sha256, and expose them in status and version.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-cli)

The current directory is no longer used for either fallback. The OJ keystore is looked up from --oj-keystore/DSS_OJ_KEYSTORE, then next to the executable, then bin/../share/dss-native/. Development builds (built without DSS_RELEASE_RPATH_ONLY=1) also fall back to the repository's trust/oj-keystore.p12, by an absolute path that build.rs bakes in. Release packages get no such fallback, the same treatment as the dev rpath, so README examples that run target/release/dss-cli from the repo still work. The default cache directory is no longer ./dss-cache: it is dss-native in the user cache directory ($XDG_CACHE_HOME (absolute only) or ~/.cache; ~/Library/Caches on macOS). With HOME unset it errors and asks for --cache-dir/DSS_CACHE_DIR. The resolved keystore path (absolute) is printed by version and by the text output of tl status/tl refresh ('OJ keystore: <path>'), and on stderr at --log-level info|debug|trace together with the cache directory. Remaining: oj_keystore_sha256 cannot be shown, because the library computes it only into snapshot settings and does not report it in dss_tl_status or dss_init (handoff java-trust + rust-dss). dss-server has the same fallback (handoff rust-server).

After review: TrustedListManager now keeps ojKeystoreInfo = {path (as configured), sha256 (the certificatesSha256 digest snapshots record as oj_keystore_sha256)}, puts it into status() as oj_keystore (present from init, before any refresh), exposes it through the package-private accessor TrustedListManager.ojKeystore(), and logs at INFO on init: 'OJ keystore <path>: <n> LOTL signing certificate(s), sha256 <hex>'. dss_tl_status therefore carries oj_keystore through DssEngine.trustedListStatus() with no change elsewhere. Not done here: putting it into the dss_init result, which lives in DssJsonApi.init (java-engine's file): handoff below.

After review: New OjKeystoreInfo { path: String, sha256: String } and TrustedListStatus.oj_keystore: Option<OjKeystoreInfo> (None for libraries that do not report it), unit-tested on fixture JSON; the integration test empty_cache_refuses_to_validate checks the shape (path ends with oj-keystore.p12, 64 hex sha256) when the library reports it and prints a note otherwise, because build/native predates the Java change (dylib 16:02, TrustedListManager.java modified later). InitInfo is NOT mirrored: the Java dss_init result (DssJsonApi.java:51-53) emits only trusted_lists_loaded, log_level, initial_load, so there is nothing to mirror there yet.

After review: Late handoff from rust-cli. package.sh runs the packaged dss-cli version with neither --oj-keystore nor --cache-dir, with DSS_OJ_KEYSTORE unset. It requires the line OJ keystore: $out/bin/../share/dss-native/oj-keystore.p12, accepting the package path as given or with symlinks resolved, since Linux current_exe resolves them. Release builds use DSS_RELEASE_RPATH_ONLY=1 and have no dev fallback, so this proves the packaged lookup. The scratch cache dir and its trap are gone. The assertion was unit-tested with a symlinked package path (both forms accepted, a foreign path rejected). Not run end to end: the release dss-cli build fails on rust-dss's in-progress engine.rs, and the old dist/ CLI predates the OJ keystore line.

After review: TrustedListStatus now carries oj_keystore {path, sha256} (rust-dss). The 'OJ keystore:' line of tl status/tl refresh prints '<absolute path> (sha256 <hex>)' when the library reports it, and the CLI's own description otherwise. This takes effect once the native library with the java-trust change is rebuilt. version still cannot show the digest, because it builds no engine.

After review: Late handoff (rust-cli) mirrored: the OJ keystore is --oj-keystore/DSS_OJ_KEYSTORE, then <exe dir>/oj-keystore.p12, then <exe dir>/../share/dss-native/oj-keystore.p12, then (development builds only, not with DSS_RELEASE_RPATH_ONLY=1) the absolute path build.rs records as rustc-env DSS_SERVER_DEV_OJ_KEYSTORE; the cwd-relative trust/oj-keystore.p12 fallback is gone. --cache-dir is Option: without it (or DSS_CACHE_DIR) the cache is $XDG_CACHE_HOME/dss-native or ~/.cache/dss-native (~/Library/Caches/dss-native on macOS), and without HOME the server exits 2 with 'no cache directory: HOME is not set, pass --cache-dir or set DSS_CACHE_DIR'. The resolved keystore (or --config file) and cache directory are the first log line ('dss-server: OJ keystore <abs>, cache directory <abs>'). Tests: process.rs keystore_comes_from_the_installation_not_the_current_directory (a planted trust/oj-keystore.p12 in the cwd is ignored, the logged path is the repository's, the server becomes ready; skipped in release builds) and start_failures_name_their_cause (no HOME -> exit 2, nothing created in the cwd). A test now checks both. version (no engine) still prints the resolved path only, as intended, because the library computes the digest only when the engine loads the keystore.

Next it checks exe_dir/oj-keystore.p12 and exe_dir/../share/dss-native/oj-keystore.p12. If neither exists it falls back to the relative path candidates.push(PathBuf::from("trust/oj-keystore.p12")); at line 610, which resolves against the cwd. The cache default default_value = "dss-cache" at line 66 is also relative to the cwd. dss-server/src/main.rs:254-269 contains the same function. Neither binary logs or reports the resolved keystore path or digest: a grep of dss-cli/src and dss-server/src finds no logging of oj_keystore and no oj_keystore_sha256.

The severity should come down from medium to low:

  1. The fallback is a documented decision. docs/DECISIONS.md:380-381 says "The OJ keystore is taken from --oj-keystore, DSS_OJ_KEYSTORE, next to the executable, or trust/oj-keystore.p12." The --help text (main.rs:75-76) says so too.

That means a local attack vector, user interaction and a non-default install, which is low likelihood. The impact if it happens (attacker-chosen trust anchors) is high.

The observability gap (no path or digest reported) is real but is a hardening item. Its line and file citations are correct.

F-080MediumoperationsFixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:256

--health-check gates only on HTTP 200, which /health returns with trusted_lists_loaded:false, and a failed/empty first refresh is not retried before --refresh-hours

/health returns 200 'ready' whenever the engine exists, so Docker and Compose service_healthy pass while every validation returns 503 TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED. A failed refresh waits a full period (6 h) with no backoff.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Live run with an empty cache and an unreachable LOTL: /health returned ready with trusted_lists_loaded:false, /validate returned 503, and the log said 'refresh completed ... 0 trusted certificates'. Expired lists, alerts and refresh age are not reflected.

Evidence

lib.rs:256-264 'json_response(StatusCode::OK, ...)'; main.rs:198 checks only 200; schedule.rs:52-69 fixed interval; main.rs:155

Impact

Orchestrators route traffic to an instance that cannot validate, for hours after a cold start.

Recommendation

Return 503 (or offer a /ready endpoint) until lists are loaded when require_trusted_lists is set, retry failed refreshes with exponential backoff, and include degraded fields.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

/health answers 503 {"ok":false,"status":"waiting_for_trusted_lists",...} while the lists are required (the library's require_trusted_lists: derived from --allow-without-trusted-lists, or from the --config JSON) and not loaded; dss-server --health-check therefore fails too, so Compose service_healthy and the Docker HEALTHCHECK gate on an instance that can validate. /health also carries last_online_refresh (completed/error/finished_at) and in_flight/max_in_flight. A refresh that fails, publishes nothing or yields 0 trusted certificates (refresh_failed()) is retried after 1, 2, 4, ... minutes, capped at the period, instead of after a whole --refresh-hours; the backoff resets on success and RefreshInProgress is not counted as a failure. This changes the DECISIONS.md statement 'Healthy once the engine is up' (new decision recorded). scripts/ci/docker-smoke.sh already runs with DSS_ALLOW_WITHOUT_TRUSTED_LISTS=true, so CI is unaffected.

After review: Late handoff from rust-server. The Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK comment now says: healthy once the engine is up and the trusted lists are loaded (unless DSS_ALLOW_WITHOUT_TRUSTED_LISTS is set), in seconds from the cache volume, and with an empty cache only after the first online refresh, which can take minutes. --start-period went from 60s to 300s so a slow first refresh does not mark the container unhealthy first. A passing probe still marks it healthy at once, so nothing is delayed. docker-smoke.sh is unaffected (it sets DSS_ALLOW_WITHOUT_TRUSTED_LISTS=true and waits up to 120 s for healthy).

After review: server.md Docker section: the health check passes only once the trusted lists are loaded, from the cache volume in seconds, with an empty cache only after the first online refresh (minutes), covered by the --start-period of 300 s (failed probes during it do not count, a passing one marks the container healthy at once), unless DSS_ALLOW_WITHOUT_TRUSTED_LISTS is set.

DssEngine.java:419-420 throws TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED when require_trusted_lists and !loaded; lib.rs:486 maps it to 503. docs/server.md:184-200 recommends Compose condition: service_healthy on dss-server --health-check, so the app starts against an instance whose every validation is 503. Partial mitigation / documented decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:845-850 and docs/server.md:16-21 state that /health reflects engine start-up and that on first start 'validations fail with TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED' until the refresh finishes, and tests/http.rs:157-160 pins 200 + trusted_lists_loaded:false (ran cargo test -p dss-server --test http health_and_requests_wait_for_the_engine: passes). So the 200-while-not-loaded body is deliberate and the ~15 s window is accepted. What is not documented or handled anywhere is the failure case: with an unreachable LOTL the server stays 'ready' for --refresh-hours with no retry, the decision's own purpose ('so a container's health check ... see starting') is defeated, and --health-check never looks at trusted_lists_loaded even though it is exposed. Severity medium: operational, cold-start plus transient LOTL outage leaves a health-passing instance that cannot validate for up to 6 h; recoverable manually via POST /tl/refresh, and --allow-without-trusted-lists / seed cache / snapshot reduce exposure.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.65

But the claimed impact ("orchestrators route traffic to an instance that cannot validate, for hours") does not hold for this system. (1) The health semantics are a documented, intentional decision: docs/openapi.yaml:331 "200 once the engine is up, 503 while it starts. For container health checks"; docs/DECISIONS.md:845-848 "/health answers 503 and the other endpoints NOT_INITIALIZED until the engine is up, so a container's health check and the client both see 'starting'". The first-start trade-off is stated with mitigations in docs/server.md:20-24: "Until it finishes, validations fail with TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED. To skip that wait, extract a seed cache ... or start from a trusted-list snapshot"; the cache is a Docker volume (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile VOLUME /var/lib/dss/cache) so the window occurs once per volume, not per restart, and is ~10 s with a reachable LOTL (DECISIONS.md:888-889 measured 9.7 s), during which clients get an explicit retryable 503 TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED (server.md:112). (2) The documented topology (docs/server.md:184-212) is a single sidecar beside one app on a Compose network; there is no second instance to route to. With an unreachable LOTL, a 503 health would only make condition: service_healthy block the app indefinitely and restart loops would not help; the remedy is the same either way (POST /tl/refresh, 202, or fix the network), and /health already exposes trusted_lists_loaded while /tl/status and the start-up log (main.rs:146-153 "trusted lists not cached yet") show the state. (3) The backoff recommendation is not actionable as framed: a refresh against an unreachable LOTL is reported as completed=true with 0 certificates (finding's own log line; rust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs:38-40 asserts record.completed against a closed port), so the scheduler has no failure signal to back off on without changing library semantics. confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.8

The finding is accurate. Half of it is a documented choice, and the other half is a real gap that nobody documented.

  1. /health. In rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-268, health returns 503 only when state.engine() fails. Otherwise it returns json_response(StatusCode::OK, ...) with "status": "ready", "trusted_lists_loaded": s.loaded, so it answers 200 even when loaded is false. The health check in main.rs:181-198 only tests response.starts_with("HTTP/1.1 200"). The Dockerfile (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:39) uses --health-check. The Compose example in docs/server.md:198-200 uses condition: service_healthy, so the app starts while validations still return 503 TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED (docs/server.md:112). This behavior is documented on purpose. openapi.yaml:331 says "200 once the engine is up, 503 while it starts". DECISIONS.md:845-847 says the same, and docs/server.md:20-21 says validations fail with TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED until the first refresh finishes. Taken alone, this part is a liveness-versus-readiness design choice, which lowers its weight.
  1. No retry. In rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:52-69 (the finding's "schedule.rs" is in the dss crate, not dss-server), a fixed interval_at(first, every) runs, and after every outcome the code calls ticker.reset(). A failed first refresh therefore waits a full every (6 h by default, main.rs:128). There is no backoff and no early retry. main.rs:154-162 only logs the outcome. Nothing in docs/server.md or DECISIONS.md says that failures wait a full period. So after a cold start with an empty cache and a short network or DNS outage, the instance reports healthy but cannot validate for hours, unless an operator calls POST /tl/refresh.

Precision: the line numbers are about right (health starts at lib.rs:251, the 200 is at about line 264). I did not reproduce the "refresh completed ... 0 trusted certificates" log from the live run, but it does not change the mechanism. describe_refresh (lib.rs:125-137) separates completed refreshes from failed ones.

Severity: availability only. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, and no attacker gains anything. It needs a network failure during a cold start with an empty cache, and POST /tl/refresh is a manual fix. The /health semantics are documented. Medium is defensible because of the undocumented 6-hour outage window and because the Compose recipe promises readiness. Low-medium overall; I keep medium.

F-090MediumoperationsFixedrust/dss-server/src/main.rs:155

First online refresh after a restart from any cached copy waits a full --refresh-hours regardless of cache age; restarts more frequent than the period keep the lists from ever being refreshed online

refresh_on_start is set to !loaded, and cache age is never considered, while the offline loader's cache never expires.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Seed caches and snapshots make 'loaded' true.

Evidence

main.rs:155; schedule.rs:47-51; TrustedListManager.java:166 'setCacheExpirationTime(-1)'

Impact

Stale or withdrawn trust is served indefinitely.

Recommendation

Schedule the first refresh at max(0, period - age) and refresh at start when lists are expired.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

The age of the loaded lists is computed at start (newest regular file under <cache_dir>/tl, or the snapshot file's mtime via /tl/status tl_snapshot.path when initial_load.mode == "snapshot"). Lists older than --refresh-hours, or of unknown age, are refreshed at once (RefreshScheduler::try_spawn with refresh_on_start); younger ones get a one-off request_refresh() after (period - age), after which the scheduler's own period restarts, so restarts more frequent than the period no longer prevent refreshes. The age is logged ('loaded, downloaded N h ago' / 'first online trusted-list refresh in N min'). Partial because the aged-cache branch is only verified by reading: an offline test would need a real cache with old mtimes; the empty-cache branch is covered by process.rs refresh_schedule_runs_logs_and_retries.

After review: trusted_list_age's snapshot branch now dates the lists by trusted_list_status().snapshot_published_at (parsed with the new pub fn dss_server::parse_rfc3339, which takes java.time.Instant's output and RFC 3339 offsets) and falls back to the snapshot file's mtime only when that is null; the 'age unknown -> refresh at once' rule stands. The parser is tested (http.rs rfc3339_instants_are_parsed); the snapshot branch itself is still only read-verified, since an offline test would need a real snapshot with an old published_at.

After review: No README/DECISIONS text in my files needed changing for this rust-server item. The handoff notes that the TL status fields and the content_size INVALID_ARGUMENT live in server.md and openapi.yaml, which rust-server owns. The TL status fields are in README's 'Trusted-list status', and the content_size refusal is already in the README signing rules and the CHANGELOG.

Cache age is never considered. If the process restarts more often than --refresh-hours (crash loops, frequent deploys, short-lived containers built from an image with a seeded cache), no scheduled refresh ever runs. TrustedListManager.java:166 offline.setCacheExpirationTime(-1) means a cache load never re-fetches. EngineConfig.java:104 tlAcceptExpired = sync.bool("accept_expired", true) means that, by default, lists past their nextUpdate are still trusted, so stale trust is not cut off by expiry either.

Two corrections: (1) The cited file is wrong. schedule.rs is at rust/dss/src/schedule.rs, not in dss-server. (2) "At start only when nothing was cached" is documented as intended in docs/DECISIONS.md:849-850 and docs/server.md:20. What is not documented is that restarts starve the schedule. The fix is a small, clear improvement: schedule the first refresh at max(0, period - age).

Severity: I calibrate it as low rather than medium. Nobody can trigger it from outside (no attack vector). It needs an operational pattern of restarts more frequent than the refresh period. POST /tl/refresh and /tl/status (with the last refresh time) give operators a workaround and visibility. Revocation of trust in a TL usually goes along with OCSP/CRL revocation, which validation checks separately. The impact is real but limited: trust anchors that are stale, but signature-valid and published by the EU, are served past the intended 6-hour freshness. Saying "indefinitely" overstates the normal case.

Rust's all_passed() handles both cases correctly. PHP and HTTP clients have to reimplement it.

ValidationResult.toMap() emits a top-level all_passed: true only when at least one signature exists at any nesting level and every signature at every level is TOTAL_PASSED (same rule as Rust's Reports::all_passed); false for an unsigned or timestamp-only document. Mirrors for Rust/PHP and the server.md example are handoffs.

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ValidationResult.java

Test: EngineHardeningTest.unsignedDocumentsNeverPass, EngineHardeningTest.aPdfInsideACadesEnvelopeIsValidatedToo, DssJsonApiTest.validationResultCarriesTheAggregateVerdictAndLimitsApply

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.82

  1. No aggregate verdict in the JSON. ValidationResult.toMap() (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ValidationResult.java:103-122) emits only container, transformations, signatures, the report XML keys and, when non-empty, nested; nothing else. The HTTP server passes that JSON through unchanged (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:151 run(engine, move |e| e.validate_json(&document, &options)); rust/dss/src/engine.rs:155-166 returns the raw string after check_ok). docs/openapi.yaml:672-704 (Reports schema) confirms: required [container, signatures, simple_report_xml], no verdict/all_passed. grep -rn all_passed rust/dss-server/src java/src/main finds nothing. The aggregate only exists in Rust: rust/dss/src/types.rs:52-55 pub fn all_passed(&self) -> bool { let all = self.all_signatures(); !all.is_empty() && all.iter().all(|s| s.indication == Indication::TotalPassed) }, used by the CLI exit code (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:650). PHP (php/DssClient.php:18 "check signatures[*].indication") and server.md:85-86 ("check each signatures[].indication") give the same incomplete guidance; php/DssClient.php has no helper (its only public methods are validate/extend/prepareSignature/completeSignature/trustedListStatus/refreshTrustedLists).

DssEngine.validate (DssEngine.java:213-225) rejects only UNKNOWN input types; a plain PDF is a valid PDF container and goes to validateLevel, which summarizes whatever DSS found. Running the built CLI on the unsigned fixture testdata/fixtures/content/document.pdf (dss-cli --allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation --trust testdata/fixtures/pki/root-ca.pem validate --json) returned {'container': 'PDF', 'nested': [], 'signatures': [], 'transformations': []} (an ok result, over HTTP this is a 200). The CLI itself exited 1 because it uses all_passed(), but the documented PHP loop foreach ($result['signatures'] as $signature) (docs/server.md:159) executes zero times, so any "throw if indication != TOTAL_PASSED" body accepts the document.
  1. Nested signatures are ignored by the documented loop. cades/nested.p7m.p7m produced an outer signatures list with one entry plus nested[0].signatures with a second (all_signatures().len() == 2 is asserted at rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:85). The inner level is validated independently (DssEngine.java:274-281, validateLevel(inner, ..., depth + 1)), and the outer indication does not depend on the inner, so an outer TOTAL_PASSED over an already-tampered inner envelope is structurally possible; the top-level loop never sees nested[]. (The repo's tampered nested fixture fails at both levels, FixtureValidationTest.java:106-111, so the mixed case is not covered by a test, but the code path is plain.)

Not a documented decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:123-125 documents nested and notes "DSS itself validates only the outer envelope", but nothing documents leaving the aggregate out of the JSON, and the Rust API's own all_passed shows the intended semantics (non-empty and every level TOTAL_PASSED). Severity: medium. It is an API/documentation ergonomics gap, but the documented client guidance leads directly to accepting an unsigned PDF, which is the realistic failure the finding describes. Recommendation stands: add a verdict/all_passed field (or a DssClient helper) and fix the server.md example to check non-emptiness and recurse into nested.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.72

Impact is real in this system. (1) Positive evidence for the vacuous case: running dss-cli validate --json offline (--allow-without-trusted-lists, --offline-revocation, no refresh) on the unsigned fixture testdata/fixtures/content/document.pdf returns a successful result {"container":"PDF","nested":[],"signatures":[],"transformations":[]}; the CLI exits 1 only through result.all_passed() (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:650). (2) Nested: unwrap_nested defaults to true (ValidationOptions.java:101 f.bool("unwrap_nested", true)), each level is summarised independently in DssEngine.validateLevel, and docs/DECISIONS.md:122-124 says 'DSS itself validates only the outer envelope' - i.e. the inner verdicts are the whole point of the feature, yet the example discards them. (3) The authors recognised both hazards for Rust callers - rust/dss/src/types.rs:51-55 'True when there is at least one signature and every signature at every level is TOTAL_PASSED' - but ValidationResult.toMap() (ValidationResult.java:103-122) emits no equivalent, and server.md:85-86, openapi.yaml:13-14 and php/DssClient.php:17-18 all say only 'check signatures[].indication', nothing about emptiness or nested. (4) Not a documented trade-off: DECISIONS.md:838-840 ('results pass through verbatim') explains the shape but records no decision to omit an aggregate, and openapi.yaml:13 says results 'may gain fields', so adding all_passed is compatible. No PHP test or other layer mitigates it. The sidecar exists precisely for a Laravel app validating documents from untrusted parties, so an integrator following the only example silently accepts unsigned or inner-failed documents. Severity medium rather than high because the library's own data is correct and complete; the defect is an API/doc footgun in the integration path, and the fix is cheap (recursive boolean in toMap, a DssClient::allPassed helper, and fixing the example at docs/server.md:159).

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The facts hold. ValidationResult.toMap() (ValidationResult.java:103-122) writes only "container", "transformations", "signatures", the report XMLs and, when present, "nested". It writes no verdict or all_passed field. Rust has the aggregate in types.rs, quoted here:

  • all_signatures() recurses into self.nested.
  • all_passed() returns !all.is_empty() && all.iter().all(|s| s.indication == Indication::TotalPassed).

So Rust covers both the nested case and the case with no signatures. The CLI exit code also reports the verdict, per DECISIONS.md: "the exit status still reports the verdict (0 passed, 1 not)". PHP has nothing like this. php/DssClient.php has only validate, extend, prepareSignature, completeSignature, trustedListStatus and refreshTrustedLists, with no verdict helper. The docs/server.md example (around lines 158-161) is foreach ($result['signatures'] as $signature) { // $signature['indication']: TOTAL_PASSED, ... } and never mentions nested. The README documents nested as a separate key with the "same shape, for the envelope inside" (README.md:326).

The finding overstates two things:

  1. The PHP snippet is a sketch with a comment as its body. It never makes an accept decision, so "passes vacuously" is an inference about how an integrator would complete it, not something the code does.
  2. The missing nested loop matters only for .p7m.p7m inputs. In that case the outer signature is still validated at the top level.

Severity: the impact depends on an integrator writing a naive check on their own side. There is no attacker-controlled bypass in the service itself. An attacker would have to submit an unsigned document, or a doubly wrapped one with a failing inner signature, to an integration that copied the example literally. The likelihood is moderate, because the docs offer no helper and no warning. The impact can be accepting an unsigned document, but only in the client's code. That makes this a hardening and API-ergonomics issue: low, not medium. A maintainer can act on it as stated: add all_passed or a verdict field in toMap, add a DssClient::allPassed helper, and fix the server.md example.

The GraalVM CE releases page lists graal-25.5.5.0.3 (03 Nov, marked Latest) above graal-25.4.4.1.1; the 25.5 release notes say it is "based on OpenJDK 25.0.5.0.3" and its only security content is the eMudhra update (compromised intermediates distrusted, eMudhra and Comodo roots removed, links to CVE-2026-91403 and CVE-2026-114820). The OpenJDK 2026-10-21 advisory lists exactly one CVE, CVE-2026-91403 (security-libs, CVSS 9.1), affecting "25.0.5 ... and earlier". keytool -list -cacerts on the pinned JDK shows emsignrootcag1, emsignrootcag2, emsigneccrootcag3, comodoaaaca, comodoeccca, comodorsaca still present, and docs/native-library.md:144-149 confirms this exact file is captured into the library at build time ("the host's system CA store is *not* consulted ... Updating the embedded bundle means rebuilding"). Reachability: DssEngine.java:469-479 wires OnlineCRLSource, OnlineOCSPSource and DefaultAIASource over the HTTPS loader that verifies against the embedded bundle, and the URLs they contact come from certificates inside documents supplied by untrusted parties. No doc states an update cadence (the only related text is native-library.md:149 and reflection-audit.md:235 "On every DSS or dependency upgrade"); DECISIONS.md:4/11 records the pin as "Latest Community Edition release" as of 2026-10-28, which was true then, so this is a pin that went stale six days later (the audited commit is dated 2026-11-06), not a wrong decision. The fix is cheap and concrete (bump pom.xml:47, install-graalvm.sh:12-19 and the three hashes, rebuild), so the finding is actionable and not refuted.

Impact, however, is overstated. (1) The missed security content is only the eMudhra distrust, not a broad CPU batch: both the OpenJDK advisory and the 25.5 notes name nothing else. (2) In this system a TLS MITM holding a certificate from a compromised eMudhra intermediate cannot forge a validation outcome: CRLs and OCSP responses are signature-checked against the issuer, AIA-fetched intermediates must chain to TL-anchored roots, and timestamp tokens are validated against the TLs; TLS is only transport. The project already treats TLS as non-load-bearing for trusted-list downloads (DECISIONS.md:192-197, native-library.md:140: "Server certificate not verified ... Each list's XML signature is verified"). The practical exposure is confidentiality of revocation queries and denial of service, not integrity of signatures. (3) A documented runtime mitigation exists: http.trust_store (DssEngine.java:155-159, native-library.md:142 "Replaces the embedded bundle") lets a host drop the emSign roots without rebuilding, and -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore does so at build time. (4) Nothing has shipped: no git tags, dist/ holds only local 0.0.0-dev and 0.1.0-SNAPSHOT tarballs, and .github/workflows/ci.yml:6-12 builds only when a GitHub release is published. Severity therefore low, with the recommendation standing: bump the pin before the first release and write down a rebuild rule for JDK security releases.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.75

The finding is accurate and a maintainer can act on it. Its location and mechanism are correct; two details need correction.

Location: java/pom.xml:46-47 reads <!-- Must match the GraalVM CE release used to build (graal 25.4.4.1.1). --> and <graalvm.sdk.version>25.4.4.1.1</graalvm.sdk.version>. The evidence path is imprecise: the install script is scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh, not install-graalvm.sh. Line 12 of that script reads release="graal-25.4.4.1.1" and is pinned by SHA-256 (docs/DECISIONS.md:503). The same pin also appears in:

  • .github/actions/setup/action.yml:17 (cache key graalvm-ce-25.4.4.1.1)
  • docs/DECISIONS.md:11 ("Latest Community Edition release ... 2026-09-22")
  • LICENSING.md:72

All of these must change together.

Newer release: gh release view -R graalvm/graalvm-ce-builds returns graal-25.5.5.0.3 2026-11-03T14:43:07Z (JDK 25.0.5.0.3), now marked Latest. It came out three days before this audit. The graalvm.org/release-notes/25.5 page cites CVE-2026-91403 and CVE-2026-114820. It also says eMudhra-related root CA certificates were removed and compromised intermediates distrusted. Correction: the page gives no CVSS scores, so "CVSS 9.1" is unverified.

Embedding: docs/native-library.md:145 and DECISIONS.md:299 say the library embeds the build JDK's cacerts at build time ("Build-time capture of GraalVM CE's cacerts"). Running keytool -list -v -cacerts on the installed 25.4.4.1.1 JDK shows emsignrootcag1, emsignrootcag2 and emsigneccrootcag3, all with "O=eMudhra Technologies Limited". The claim about eMudhra roots is therefore true. Picking up the fixes needs a rebuild, as the finding states.

Severity: medium, perhaps low-medium.

  • The embedded cacerts only governs TLS for online fetches (AIA, OCSP, CRL, TL). Signature trust comes from the EU trusted lists, not cacerts.
  • TL downloads already skip TLS verification by default (DECISIONS.md:304).
  • Hosts can replace the CA set at runtime with http.trust_store (EngineConfig.java:58).
  • The impact of the JDK CVEs on this library's reachable code is not established.
  • The release is three days old, so this is normal patch lag, not long neglect.

A routine version bump plus a rebuild policy for each Critical Patch Update is the right fix.

F-132MediumlicensingFixedLICENSING.md:38

libdssnative is LGPL object code whose DSS source is only pointed to (github.com/esig/dss); LICENSING.md rests on §6 although §4 governs dss-native's own releases

SOURCE links to esig/dss on GitHub, and embedders are told a pointer is enough.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

LICENSING.md:38; package.sh:46

Impact

LGPL object code is distributed without source.

Recommendation

Attach the source to each release and rewrite the rationale around §4.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

Release job attaches the corresponding source next to the packages: dss-native-<v>-source.tar.gz (git archive of the tag), dss-<dss.version>-source.tar.gz (esig/dss tag), plus GraalVM sources (F-133), via scripts/ci/fetch-sources.sh. LICENSING.md rewritten around LGPL-2.1 section 4 for the project's own distributions (object code of the Library must be accompanied by source or equivalent access from the same place), states the duties embedders inherit, and adds a 'Source of the release packages' section. package.sh SOURCE file now names those archives and the canonical repository URL.

Files: scripts/ci/fetch-sources.sh, .github/workflows/ci.yml, LICENSING.md, scripts/package.sh

Test: fetch-sources.sh --print-urls against build/native/macos-aarch64/licenses/graalvm/release: all three URLs answer HTTP 200; test-scripts.sh checks the DSS tag, substratevm commit and jvmci tag URLs; packaged SOURCE inspected in scratchpad. Release upload itself not runnable here.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.72

Reproduced from the cited files; the documentary facts the finding rests on are all present.

  1. The §6 framing. LICENSING.md:38-39: "dss-native meets LGPL-2.1 §6 by giving users everything needed to rebuild the native library against a modified DSS". But the project licenses the wrapper itself under the LGPL (LICENSING.md:9-10 "The licence covers everything in this repository", and the package's LICENSE is described at LICENSING.md:109 as "LGPL-2.1: dss-native and DSS"). LICENSE:271-273 defines §6 as "an exception ... [to] combine or link a 'work that uses the Library' with the Library", i.e. for non-LGPL applications. libdssnative is instead "the Library (or a portion or derivative of it, under Section 2) in object code" (LICENSE:227-228), so §4 applies to dss-native's own releases: "provided that you accompany it with the complete corresponding machine-readable source code" (LICENSE:229-230), with the only relaxation being "offering equivalent access to copy the source code from the same place" when distributing from "a designated place" (LICENSE:234-237).
  1. What is actually shipped. The DSS source is never in the repository or the build: java/pom.xml:43 <dss.version>6.5.1</dss.version> and the eu.europa.ec.joinup.sd-dss dependencies (pom.xml:84-137) pull binary jars from Maven Central; scripts/build-native.sh fetches no DSS sources (the only -sources.jar use is in scripts/audit-reflection.sh:17, an audit tool). The release job uploads only the packages, the seed cache and the keystore (ci.yml:196-212: pattern: dss-native-*, tl-cache-snapshot, cp trust/oj-keystore.p12 release/, gh release upload "$TAG" release/*). GitHub's automatic "Source code" asset covers the wrapper and build scripts at the tag (so that part of the corresponding source is at the same place), but the DSS source is represented only by a URL in the SOURCE file, package.sh:46: DSS $dss_version source: https://github.com/esig/dss/tree/$dss_version, and the GraalVM runtime likewise, package.sh:47-48. The Docker image carries the same SOURCE file (LICENSING.md:104-111). LGPL-2.1 §4 has no GPLv3-style "different server operated by ... a third party" allowance; a pointer to esig/dss is not "the same place".
  1. Embedders. LICENSING.md:53-55 tells them to "ship the native library as a separate file ... and point to this repository's source and build instructions, or ship them." A pointer is none of §6(a)-(e): 6(a) "Accompany the work with the complete corresponding machine-readable source code for the Library" (LICENSE:286-288), 6(c) a written offer (LICENSE:306-309), 6(d) "equivalent access ... from the same place" (LICENSE:311-313); 6(b) concerns a library "already present on the user's computer system" (LICENSE:299-300), not one the embedder ships. So the summary "embedders are told a pointer is enough" matches the text.

Mitigating points, which keep this at medium rather than high: (a) the licence is "2.1 or later" (LICENSING.md:5-7, third-party/dss.txt), and under LGPL-3.0 + GPLv3 §6(d) a third-party server with clear directions next to the object code is permitted, so a distributor could elect v3 and the current SOURCE file would be close to compliant; but the project's own rationale cites 2.1 §6 and does not make that election. (b) The wrapper source is effectively at the same place via GitHub's auto-attached release source archive. (c) Remediation is cheap: attach the DSS 6.5.1 source archive (and optionally the GraalVM CE source) to each release / package and rewrite LICENSING.md around §4 (and §6 only for embedders). docs/DECISIONS.md:513 and :915 describe SOURCE as "for the LGPL rebuild path" and name only the commit, tag and release, confirming this was a deliberate pointer-based design rather than an oversight, but it is a legal misreading, not a reasonable documented decision that handles the §4 requirement.

Small correction to the finding: §6 does genuinely govern embedders' applications (they are "works that use the Library"); the finding's "§4 applies, not §6" is exact for dss-native's own distribution and only approximately so for embedders, where the shipped copy of the Library still needs 6(a)/(c)/(d), not a pointer. Severity stays medium: a compliance gap in a project explicitly preparing to go public (DECISIONS.md:895 "licensing review before going public"), with no code or runtime impact.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

Impact lens. The claimed impact ("LGPL object code is distributed without source") does not hold in this system, and the §4-vs-§6 distinction changes nothing operationally.

  1. The §4/§6 distinction is immaterial to the obligation. LICENSE:234-238 (§4 ¶2) and LICENSE:311-313 (§6(d)) use the identical mechanism: "If distribution ... is made by offering access to copy from a designated place, [offer] equivalent access to copy the source code from the same place". Whichever section governs, the question is only whether source is accessible from the same place. The finding's premise is also doubtful: DSS is consumed unmodified (java/pom.xml:43 <dss.version>6.5.1</dss.version> from Maven Central; grep finds zero @TargetClass/@Substitute substitutions and no eu/europa packages under java/src/main/java), so the wrapper is a "work that uses the Library" and libdssnative is "a work containing portions of the Library" (LICENSE:271-274), which is exactly what §6 governs. LICENSING.md:38 citing §6 is defensible, not wrong.
  1. The project's own LGPL source is already at the same place as the binaries. .github/workflows/ci.yml:206-212 uploads the packages with gh release upload "$TAG" release/* to the GitHub release of the repository itself, and a GitHub release always carries the tagged source archive next to its assets. scripts/package.sh:42-48 writes SOURCE with the exact commit and remote URL. So for everything dss-native authored (wrapper, build scripts, Rust crates), "same place" is satisfied without any change.
  1. What is only pointed to is third-party, unmodified, public source: DSS at its exact tag (package.sh:46 https://github.com/esig/dss/tree/$dss_version, also sources jars on Maven Central) and GraalVM CE at its exact release (package.sh:47-48, plus licenses/graalvm/release with component commits). The FSF's GPL FAQ treats a clear cross-reference to source kept on another site as "equivalent access" under GPLv2's "same place" wording, which LGPL-2.1 copies verbatim. DSS's copyright holder is the European Commission, which publishes that source itself; realistic enforcement exposure from pointing at it by tag is negligible. The finding also ignores that the same reasoning (and a GPLv2 §3 obligation) applies to the GraalVM runtime, whose complete corresponding source (JDK class library + Substrate VM) is multi-gigabyte; "attach the source to each release" is disproportionate and the finding does not scope it.
  1. Documented, intentional decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:896-915 records a dedicated "licensing review before going public" that settled on "SOURCE names the full commit, the DSS source tag and the GraalVM CE release" (line 915), and DECISIONS.md:512-513 "a SOURCE file with repository and commit, for the LGPL rebuild path." The Docker image inherits the same files (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:14,25).
  1. Embedder guidance (LICENSING.md:53-55) tells applications to ship the library "as a separate file, not statically linked, and point to this repository's source and build instructions, or ship them." A separately shipped shared library is §6(b) (LICENSE:296-302), which requires no source shipment at all for the host work; pointing to or shipping this repository covers §6(a)/(d). The advice is reasonable, not harmful.

Residual: at most a documentation-polish item (LICENSING.md could add that GitHub releases carry the tagged source and that DSS sources jars are on Maven Central, or attach DSS -sources.jar to releases as belt-and-braces). No actual loss of source access for any recipient; severity low/info, not medium.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

The finding is accurate. LICENSING.md:38 says "dss-native meets LGPL-2.1 §6 by giving users everything needed to rebuild the native library against a modified DSS". Its justification (lines 41-51) is the §6 relinking argument. But per lines 34-36, libdssnative is a single image that contains DSS itself ("compiles DSS ... into one shared library"). Distributing that image means distributing the Library's object code, which is the §4 case. §4 requires the complete corresponding source to accompany the object code, or equivalent access to it "from the same place".

scripts/package.sh:42-49 writes only a SOURCE file into the tarball:

  • "DSS $dss_version source: https://github.com/esig/dss/tree/$dss_version"
  • a GraalVM CE releases link (GPLv2 + Classpath Exception, so GPLv2 §3 needs the same source availability)
  • the git origin URL for the wrapper

No source archive is included. .github/workflows/ci.yml:12 confirms that only "the packages, the seed cache and the OJ keystore are uploaded to that release". LICENSING.md:53-55 also tells embedders to "point to this repository's source and build instructions, or ship them".

The wrapper's own source sits in the same GitHub repository as the releases, so that part plausibly meets the "same place" clause. The DSS and GraalVM sources are on third-party repositories (esig/dss, graalvm/graalvm-ce-builds) that the distributor does not control, and under GPLv2 and LGPL-2.1 such a pointer is generally not considered sufficient.

Precision corrections:

  • The mechanism is in scripts/package.sh:42-49, not line 46 alone. The finding's file and line (LICENSING.md:38) is the wrong rationale, not the code that ships.
  • The problem also covers the GraalVM runtime (LICENSING.md:72), not only DSS.
  • The title's "only by pointers to third-party hosts" overstates it for the wrapper's own code.

Severity: low. This is a licence-compliance gap, not a security issue, and there is no attacker or user-data impact. The source is publicly available at pinned tags and commits, so practical enforcement risk is small. The fix is cheap: attach source tarballs for the DSS and GraalVM tags to each release, and reword the rationale around §4 plus the §6 relinking point. It still matters, because LGPL §8 terminates the licence on non-compliant distribution, and the project publicly claims compliance.

F-164MediumtestingFixedjava/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/testsupport/TestPki.java:333

OCSP is never exercised by any suite, and CRL/OCSP/AIA never go through the real HTTP loaders; only in-memory CRL via FakeHttp is tested

FakeHttp is used everywhere, the test PKI has no OCSP, and real-stack tests force offline revocation.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

TestEngines.java:51; HttpsLoopbackTest.java:142; smoke-test-c.sh:32

Impact

Native-image regressions in the default path ship unnoticed.

Recommendation

Add a local OCSP and CRL responder test on the JVM, native and C paths.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-tests)

New RevocationLoopbackTest drives the production outbound stack (DssEngine.create: CommonsDataLoader/OCSPDataLoader behind OutboundFetchPolicy and the CRL/AIA cache, revocation "online", aia on) against a plain-HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 that serves the synthetic LOTL/TLs, an OCSP responder (POST, BouncyCastle-built responses signed by the issuing CA, nonce echoed/wrong/omitted, good/revoked, or internalError), CRLs (root and intermediate, with revoked entries), caIssuers certificates and an RFC 3161 TSA. The PKI is issued at test time: root (on the IT TL) -> intermediate CA that is in no list and in no document, so it can only be fetched over AIA -> signer whose certificate names the OCSP responder, the intermediate CRL and the intermediate caIssuers URL; a TSA issued by the root that names the root CRL. Tests: (1) a B signature made through prepareSignature/completeSignature (signature_value, signing certificate only) validates TOTAL_PASSED online, with the intermediate fetched over AIA, OCSP queried with a nonce and Content-Type application/ocsp-request, the root CRL fetched for the intermediate and no signer-CRL fetch; offline validation of the same B document does not pass; engine.extend B->LT then embeds the OCSP response, CRL and intermediate, and an engine with revocation offline and aia false validates the result as PAdES-BASELINE-LT TOTAL_PASSED. (2) OCSP revoked -> sub-indication REVOKED*. (3) An OCSP 'good' answer carrying another nonce (replay) is refused, the CRL fallback is used and its revocation is reported. (4) OCSP internalError -> CRL fallback, TOTAL_PASSED. (5) revocation offline + aia false makes no request at all. JVM: all pass. Native: built and ran the native JUnit image locally (./mvnw -o -Pnative test filtered to the new and changed classes), then scripts/run-native-tests.sh -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit: all 5 revocation tests pass natively, and no registration is reported missing. Because the native profile runs this class in CI, the native OCSP/CRL/AIA path is covered from now on. Not done: the C path (smoke.c). A C-level test would need a dynamic OCSP responder process next to scripts/smoke-test-c.sh (owned by scripts-ci). The test image's extra metadata holds only JUnit/surefire registrations, so the OCSP path in the native test image relies on the same main metadata as libdssnative; I therefore judged a C responder low value and did not hand it off. TestPki gained public helpers for this: Profile (now public), Pointers(crlUrl, ocspUrl, caIssuersUrl), Issued, issueNow(...), crl(issuer, key, revoked), ocspResponse(request, issuer, key, revoked, Nonce), ocspInternalError(), timestampResponse(request, key, chain). freshCrl/timestampResponse(byte[]) behave as before.

After review: Unchanged: partial. Nonce.OMIT is now exercised. In the new RevocationLoopbackTest.anOcspAnswerWithoutANonceIsAccepted, the responder leaves out the nonce while the CRL lists the signer as revoked. The test asserts the current engine behaviour: the request carried a nonce, the nonce-less answer is accepted with only a warning (DSS alertOnNonexistentNonce), the CRL is not fetched (zero hits on /intermediate.crl), and the result is TOTAL_PASSED. The C path (smoke.c / scripts/smoke-test-c.sh) is still open and now has a recorded owner: handoff to scripts-ci (see notes). Alternatively, docs can record in docs/DECISIONS.md that the native JUnit image is the accepted coverage of the native OCSP/CRL/AIA path.

A responder would need a signer certificate whose AIA/CRL-DP points at a run-time port, so a document signed at run time, plus a new smoke.c case outside my ownership. The accepted coverage is RevocationLoopbackTest in the native JUnit image, which CI runs in ci.yml via scripts/run-native-tests.sh -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit. test-scripts.sh now guards this with 3 checks: RevocationLoopbackTest exists, it has no @DisabledInNativeImage/@EnabledInNativeImage, and ci.yml still runs the native image with missing registrations fatal. The decision text for docs/DECISIONS.md is in notes under DOCS, for the docs package.

After review: New DECISIONS subsection 'Native OCSP/CRL/AIA coverage', using the handoff's text. Checked: RevocationLoopbackTest exists, and test-scripts.sh:204-207 guards that it runs in the native image with Exit mode.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.8

The native test image runs the whole JUnit suite (java/pom.xml:269-286, scripts/run-native-tests.sh), so OnlineCRLSource + CRL parsing is exercised natively too. So "never exercised by any suite" is false for CRL in-memory.

TestPki.issue adds only cRLDistributionPoints (TestPki.java:331-333); a grep for authorityInfoAccess|OCSP_URL|ocsp in TestPki returns nothing, so no certificate advertises an OCSP responder and OnlineOCSPSource never sends or parses a response. No OCSP responder exists in any test support class (grep for OCSP in java/src/test hits only PlainDssReference.java, which just instantiates OnlineOCSPSource). I scanned all 41 fixture files for the id-pkix-ocsp-basic OID (06 09 2B 06 01 05 05 07 30 01 01) and /OCSPs: zero matches. OCSP request building/response parsing (BC OCSP, DSS OCSPToken, OCSPDataLoader) therefore never runs in any suite, including the native test image built with --exact-reachability-metadata and run with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit (java/pom.xml:313-316, .github/workflows/ci.yml:89-90).
  2. CRL/OCSP/AIA over the real loaders. The only real-stack JVM test, HttpsLoopbackTest, hardcodes "revocation":"offline","aia":false (engine/HttpsLoopbackTest.java:142) and its loopback server serves only LOTL/TLs/TSA (:76-80; SyntheticTrustedLists.serveOn routes only lotl/IT/DE at :98-100, no CRL). scripts/smoke-test-c.sh:32 and :40 use "revocation":"offline","aia":false in both offline and --online modes; SyntheticCacheSeeder.java:40 writes "revocation":"offline","aia":false; Rust tests set Revocation::Offline (rust/dss/tests/common/mod.rs:47, rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:40, --offline-revocation in rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs:28), and the Rust online test starts from offline_config() (rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:759). OnlineTrustedListTest (the -Pintegration suite) validates no document at all (:63-109). AIA fetching is never exercised because TestPki certs carry no AIA extension.
  3. The only online-revocation run is scripts/diff-vs-jvm.sh:87 for testdata/private/, which is gitignored (.gitignore:7) and absent in CI.

Mitigations that lower severity: HttpsLoopbackTest does exercise CommonsDataLoader (and TimestampDataLoader, a subclass) over real TLS, redirects and Basic auth in the native image (class doc, :43-47), so the generic HTTP-stack reachability metadata is covered; OCSPDataLoader only adds a content type. DECISIONS.md:471 acknowledges "the fixtures set uses offline revocation. Real-world coverage comes from testdata/private/" but only in the differential-test context; it does not document a decision to leave OCSP untested. Since OCSP is the dominant revocation mechanism for real EU certificates and a native-only failure in OCSP parsing would go unnoticed by every automated suite, I keep medium, with the corrected, narrower title.

F-180MediumsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:292

A badly signed LOTL download empties the published trust pool and is cached, so restarts load nothing until the next successful online refresh

The online loader writes to the same cache before validation. When the signature is invalid, DSS empties the pool, which is published with completed=true and survives restarts.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Probe: after a good refresh certs=3; after a badly signed LOTL certs=0 and TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED; a restart from cache gives certs=0. With TLS unverified, one forged response is enough. DECISIONS.md's claim about MITMs is wrong.

Evidence

TrustedListManager.java:292-294; FileCacheDataLoader.getDocument 'createFile(fileName, bytes)'; TrustedListsCertificateSource 'super.reset()'

Impact

An outage of all validation that persists across restarts.

Recommendation

Download into staging, promote only validated lists, and keep the last-good pool when the LOTL is unusable. Add a test.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-trust)

New TlCacheLoader replaces DSS's FileCacheDataLoader for the TL job: downloads are pre-checked and staged under <cache_dir>/tl-staging/<pid>-<n>/, DSS parses/validates the staged file, and after the job TlCacheLoader.promote copies into <cache_dir>/tl/ only the lists the refresh found usable (LOTL/pivots when their signature validated or tl_sync lets them through; a national list only when it AND its LOTL are usable, so a forged LOTL cannot push its own TLs into the cache). A badly signed LOTL that would empty a loaded pool is not published (completed=false, previous lists kept). The in-place truncate-then-write is gone: temp file + fsync + atomic rename.

After review: Removed the unused TrustedListManager.cacheLoader() and alertKeys(), TlCacheLoader.pendingUrls(), stagingRoot() and directory(); MAX_ALERTS is private again. The stage/validate/promote fix itself is unchanged.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.72

The mechanism is real. TrustedListManager.java:165-173 gives the offline and online FileCacheDataLoader instances the same directory (offline.setFileCacheDirectory(tlCache.toFile()) and online.setFileCacheDirectory(tlCache.toFile())). The offline loader never expires its entries (setCacheExpirationTime(-1)), so a restart reloads whatever bytes the online loader last wrote, and the online loader writes them before DSS validates them. When job::onlineRefresh completes without throwing, run (lines 281-295) treats the refresh as a success, unconditionally. It builds new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), true, null, staging.getNumberOfCertificates()) and calls publishSnapshot(record, null). Nothing checks whether staging just dropped from N certificates to 0. The "keep the last pool" protection only covers the case where a RuntimeException is thrown (the comment at lines 286-287). The strict ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy (DECISIONS.md lines 88-95) rejects the invalid LOTL, staging ends up with no certificates, and validate then returns TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED (DECISIONS.md line 98). TLS on TL downloads is deliberately not verified (DECISIONS.md lines 192-198), so an on-path attacker can trigger this.

Calibration, and why this is medium rather than high: (1) The impact is availability only. DECISIONS.md says "a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one". That stays true, because nothing can be injected. What that sentence misses is that one block wipes the pool everyone already relies on and survives restarts. (2) "Persistent" is overstated. online_cache_expiration_ms defaults to 0 (EngineConfig.java:105), so every online refresh downloads again, and dss-server runs refreshes on a schedule (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:154-155 RefreshScheduler). The outage therefore lasts until the next good online refresh, not indefinitely. Only a restart that loads from the cache before any good refresh brings the empty pool back. (3) The attack needs a network-adjacent or on-path position against the TL hosts, and an attacker in that position can block refreshes forever in any case. (4) The more likely trigger in normal use is not an attack. An OJ keystore rotation or a LOTL signer change that the configured keystore does not cover would also publish an empty pool and stop all validation. That makes it a robustness problem worth fixing.

The recommendation is sound and a maintainer can act on it: keep the last good snapshot when an online refresh leaves the LOTL unusable or produces 0 certificates, and stage downloads separately from the offline cache. The cited line 292 falls inside the success branch at lines 291-294. I did not rerun the probe myself. The claim that DSS writes the cache before validating rests on how FileCacheDataLoader.getDocument behaves and on the reporters' probe, so my confidence is moderate.
