The finding is accurate, and it is a missing feature rather than a security vulnerability.

What the code does:

  • DssEngine.create (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:121-132) builds four loaders with nothing but withTimeouts(...) and optional TLS trust settings:
  • the TL loader: new CommonsDataLoader()
  • the HTTP loader for CRL/AIA: new CommonsDataLoader()
  • new OCSPDataLoader()
  • tsaLoader(config), which is new TimestampDataLoader() (lines 135-144)
  • withTimeouts (lines 146+) sets only timeouts and the trust store.
  • No call anywhere sets setProxyConfig or setUseSystemProperties. A grep for proxy, useSystemProperties and setProxy in java/src/main finds nothing. No proxy key or decision appears in README.md or docs/DECISIONS.md.

What DSS 6.5.1 does (from the dss-service sources jar):

  • CommonsDataLoader.java:173 declares private boolean useSystemProperties = false;.
  • getHttpClientBuilder (line 1286) starts with HttpClients.custom() and calls httpClientBuilder.useSystemProperties() only if (useSystemProperties) (lines 1289-1290).
  • configureProxy (line 1378) installs a route planner only when a ProxyConfig is set.
  • So Apache HttpClient 5 uses its default route planner, which ignores both -Dhttps.proxyHost and the OS proxy.
  • In a native-image shared library, the host application could not easily set JVM system properties anyway.

So the cited file, lines and mechanism are correct. One small note: the evidence "CommonsDataLoader:173" refers to the DSS library source, not to this repository. The custom-DataLoader constructors (lines 111-118) could take proxied loaders, but only Java callers can use them. The FFI/Rust path always goes through create().

Severity, CVSS-like view:

  • This is an operational and availability gap, not an exploitable flaw: no attacker, no confidentiality or integrity impact.
  • Impact in proxied enterprise networks is real. Online TL refresh, CRL/OCSP/AIA revocation fetching and TSA timestamping (B-T and higher signing) would all fail, so validation results come back INDETERMINATE.
  • The claim that the library is "unusable" is overstated. The TL part can be worked around with offline TL snapshots (config.tlSnapshot / importSnapshot, lines 101-102), and a pinned trust store is supported. Revocation fetching and the TSA have no workaround.

Medium is a fair rating for a deployment blocker in a common enterprise setup. The fix is simple: map an http.proxy config key to a DSS ProxyConfig, or call setUseSystemProperties(true) on all four loaders.

F-187MediumperformanceFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:468

DssEngine.java:468-474; EngineConfig.java:114-115

Impact

Latency, collapse under slow CAs, and load on CA servers.

Add a revocation cache and lower the timeouts.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

Parsing uses BouncyCastle ASN.1 (no reflection, native-image safe). Tests: CachingDataLoaderTest.theTtlDependsOnWhatTheBodyIs and aCrlIsFetchedAgainOnceItsNextUpdateHasPassed. The README note on http.cache_ms is a docs_updates item (see notes).

The code reads as the finding says: DssEngine.certificateVerifier() (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:461-481) creates new OnlineCRLSource() and new OnlineOCSPSource() on every validate/extend/sign call, over the shared CommonsDataLoader/OCSPDataLoader built in create() (DssEngine.java:130-131), and no FileCacheDataLoader or Jdbc cache source is involved. However the claimed impact is overstated for this system. (1) DSS 6.5.1 CommonCertificateVerifier defaults, which the engine does not change, are revocationDataLoadingStrategyFactory = new OCSPFirstRevocationDataLoadingStrategyFactory() (sources line 80), revocationFallback = false (line 91) and checkRevocationForUntrustedChains = false (line 199). EU qualified certificates carry OCSP, so a validation makes a few small live OCSP queries per chain; OCSP answers are current-status queries that validators (DSS demo, Adobe) fetch live by design, and a CRL is downloaded only when OCSP is missing or fails. "CRLs are downloaded again for every document" is therefore the exception path, not the normal one. (2) With checkRevocationForUntrustedChains = false, a document from an untrusted party whose chain does not reach an EU trust anchor triggers no revocation fetch, so the "collapse under slow CAs" scenario requires a real QTSP responder to be slow, which affects every DSS-based validator equally and is not something an attacker-supplied document can provoke through this path. (3) Mitigations exist and are documented: revocation: "offline" / --offline-revocation (README.md:280, docs/server.md:48); the 30 s/60 s timeouts are configuration (http.connect_timeout_ms/response_timeout_ms, README.md:276, EngineConfig.java:114-115); the sidecar's worker count is --workers/DSS_WORKERS with a request queue (docs/server.md:42, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:244-247) and the sidecar is documented for a private network (docs/server.md:216); a JVM host can inject its own caching DataLoader through the public constructor (DssEngine.java:85-92). (4) docs/DECISIONS.md:68-69 already records "Other caches (AIA, revocation) can sit next to it later", so a revocation cache is acknowledged deferred work rather than an oversight. Residual, informational point: the default timeouts (30 s connect, 60 s response) are generous compared with the DSS demo's few-second defaults, and a CRL file cache would help for CAs without OCSP; both are tuning, not a medium-severity defect.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

The core mechanism is real. DssEngine.java:461-482 certificateVerifier(snapshot) runs on every operation (called at lines 224, 309 and 365). With config.revocation == ONLINE it builds new OnlineCRLSource() with crl.setDataLoader(httpLoader) and new OnlineOCSPSource() with ocsp.setDataLoader(ocspLoader) (lines 468-474). httpLoader and ocspLoader are plain CommonsDataLoader/OCSPDataLoader wrapped by withTimeouts (lines 130-131, 146-150), not a FileCacheDataLoader. DSS's JdbcCacheCRLSource/JdbcCacheOCSPSource is not used either. So nothing caches revocation data across calls, and a batch of documents signed under the same CA downloads the same CRL again for each document. "online" is the default (EngineConfig f.string("revocation", "online")). docs/DECISIONS.md:68 says only that revocation caches "can sit next to it later", so the gap is acknowledged but not addressed.

Imprecisions: (1) The timeouts are http.integer("connect_timeout_ms", 30_000) and ("response_timeout_ms", 60_000) (EngineConfig.java:114-115). They are configurable defaults that match DSS's usual loader defaults, so they are not a defect in themselves. (2) "CPU-count workers" is wrong for the library: rust/dss/src/engine.rs:45 sets the default to workers: 1. Only dss-cli uses available_parallelism() (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:497), and only for its worker count, for example in validate-batch. (3) The DSS validation context may still reuse revocation data within a single document. The waste happens across calls.

Severity: this is not a security issue. It costs latency and repeated load on CA CRL/OCSP endpoints in batch or server use, and a slow responder can tie up a worker for up to 60 s per fetch. It happens in normal use but needs no attacker. I rate it low, or low-medium for dss-server deployments, rather than medium.

F-208MediumsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:122

TL/LOTL/pivot bodies are buffered and cached with no size cap; an on-path, DNS-level or compromised TL host can drive a refresh to multi-GB memory use (process abort unconfirmed; TLS default is a documented decision)

The TL loader is a CommonsDataLoader, which has no maxInputSize, behind FileCacheDataLoader. With tl_verify_tls=false by default, any TL host or on-path party can make a refresh allocate and cache arbitrarily large bodies.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

DssEngine.create builds tlLoader = withTimeouts(new CommonsDataLoader(), config) and sets TrustAllStrategy when tl_verify_tls is false. CommonsHttpClientResponseHandler reads bodies with DSSUtils.toByteArray(content), with no limit; only NativeHTTPDataLoader has maxInputSize. FileCacheDataLoader then writes the full byte[] to <cache_dir>/tl, and DSS builds several DOMs from it. The timeouts bound inactivity, not total size or duration. The cached oversized file is re-parsed on every offline load. Up to tl_threads downloads run in parallel. F-002 covers only certificate-driven CRL/OCSP/AIA URLs; this is the trust-refresh path, triggered by schedule or by POST /tl/refresh.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:122-128 `CommonsDataLoader tlLoader = withTimeouts(new CommonsDataLoader(), config); ... tlLoader.setTrustStrategy(TrustAllStrategy.INSTANCE);`. TrustedListManager.java:170-173 (online FileCacheDataLoader). CommonsHttpClientResponseHandler.java:111 `return DSSUtils.toByteArray(content);`. Native dss-cli with a 314,572,944-byte well-formed IT.xml: 12.24 s, 2,070,364,160 max RSS, cache file overwritten at 314 MB. With --max-heap 512m: 'OutOfMemoryError: Garbage-collected heap size exceeded'.

Impact

A refresh can be driven into OOM or multi-GB memory use with no document access. Per F-186 an OOM on a background thread can abort the process. The country's anchors are dropped and the oversized file recurs at every start.

Recommendation

Wrap the TL data loader in a size-capped reader (e.g. 64 MB max, checking Content-Length and counting while streaming) and add a whole-transfer deadline. The same decorator can serve the CRL/AIA loaders (F-002). Expose it as config (e.g. http.max_response_bytes). Consider defaulting tl_verify_tls to true.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

The TL loader is now OutboundFetchPolicy.wrap(tlLoader, config) in DssEngine.Loaders.of, so LOTL/TL/pivot bodies are bounded by http.max_response_bytes (64 MiB default) and http.request_deadline_ms before they are cached or parsed (java-trust's TlCacheLoader pre-checks the content as well).

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java

Test: EngineHardeningTest.realLoadersSitBehindThePolicyAndTheCache (tl loader is an OutboundFetchPolicy over a CommonsDataLoader with TrustAllStrategy by default); HttpsLoopbackTest and ProxyLoopbackTest exercise the wrapped TL loader end to end

The executor at :177 is newFixedThreadPool(config.tlThreads, ...) so downloads run in parallel. In DSS 6.5.1 (java/pom.xml:43), CommonsHttpClientResponseHandler.java:109-111 reads return DSSUtils.toByteArray(content); with no limit, CommonsDataLoader has no maxInputSize at all (grep of the extracted sources-jar: zero hits), and FileCacheDataLoader.java:290-296 does bytes = dataLoader.get(url); ... else if (toBeCached(bytes)) { createFile(fileName, bytes) } with toBeCached returning true when no cachePredicate is set (:315-318), i.e. the whole body is written to the cache before signature validation. This matches the finding's reported behaviour (whole buffering, multi-hundred-MB heap per list, OOM under a heap cap, oversized file persisted to <cache>/tl).

The TLS decision is documented in docs/DECISIONS.md:191-198 ("a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one"), but that reasoning covers integrity only, not resource exhaustion, and the missing size cap exists independently of TLS (a legitimate but compromised TL host triggers it with tl_verify_tls=true too). The refresh is reachable via POST /tl/refresh (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:112,213) and the scheduled refresh (main.rs:42). Severity stays medium: it is a DoS of the trust-refresh path requiring a hostile/compromised TL host or an on-path attacker, with no document or credential access needed, and the persisted oversized cache file recurs at each start.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.65

Every start re-parses the cache (trustedLists.offlineRefresh() in the DssEngine constructor, line 101). The heap is unbounded by default (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:56 "Default: Native Image's, which grows with physical memory"); docs/server.md:221 bounds only request bodies via --max-request-mb/--max-heap. (2) The "OOM aborts the process" part is unconfirmed: TrustedListManager.run (line 285) catches only RuntimeException, but per-list downloads run in DSS executor tasks whose FutureTask captures Throwable, and DECISIONS.md:277-283 says Native Image skips only the allocating frame's own catch, so with --max-heap an oversized list most likely just fails that list. confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.75

The finding is described accurately. java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:122-128 reads CommonsDataLoader tlLoader = withTimeouts(new CommonsDataLoader(), config); if (!config.tlVerifyTls) { ... tlLoader.setTrustStrategy(TrustAllStrategy.INSTANCE); }. EngineConfig.java:116 has tlVerifyTls = http.bool("tl_verify_tls", false);, so TLS is unverified by default. TrustedListManager.java:170-173 puts that loader behind an online FileCacheDataLoader that writes into the tl cache directory. No size cap appears anywhere in the project: a grep for maxInputSize, max_response or MaxInput in java/src and rust finds nothing. That is consistent with DSS's CommonsDataLoader, which reads the whole body. The cited line is correct.

docs/DECISIONS.md:192-198 documents the TrustAll choice. Its argument is that "a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one". That covers integrity and the loss of a single country's list. It does not cover memory exhaustion of the whole process from an oversized body, so the decision does not neutralize this finding. It does make the MITM precondition explicit and accepted. Hostname verification remains, but it means little under TrustAll because a self-signed certificate with the right name passes.

Severity calibration:

  • Attack vector: network, but it needs either an on-path position between the server and an EU TL or LOTL host, or a malicious or compromised national TL host. Both are uncommon.
  • Trigger: the scheduled refresh, or POST /tl/refresh. That endpoint sits behind the optional bearer token (DECISIONS.md:856), so an outside attacker usually cannot start a refresh and must wait for the schedule.
  • Impact: availability only, with no impact on integrity or confidentiality, because the XML signature check still rejects tampered lists. That availability impact can be severe: GB-scale RSS or OOM, a possible process abort, and a cached oversized file that keeps being re-parsed offline at every start.

High attack complexity combined with high availability impact fits medium, at its lower end. One part of the reported reproduction is unverified here: the 2 GB RSS figure. I did not rerun it, because it would need a local fake TL host.

F-212MediumoperationsFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:165

Two processes sharing one cache_dir (dss-cli and dss-server both default to ./dss-cache) race on TL files that DSS truncates and rewrites in place; a torn read silently drops the list (no alert) until the next refresh

Both FileCacheDataLoaders read and write <cache_dir>/tl/<name> directly, by truncate-then-write with no lock and no temp-and-rename. Nothing requires a single writer per directory, and README/server.md never say a cache belongs to one process.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

TrustedListManager builds an offline and an online FileCacheDataLoader on the same tlCache. DSS's createFile → DSSUtils.saveToFile is Files.newOutputStream (truncate) plus copy. A dss-cli tl refresh (cron or seeding) running beside dss-server's start-up offline load or its own refresh can hand one side a partial list. The XAdES signature then fails and the list drops from the pool until the next refresh (tl_signature_error alert). No trust injection results. A cron CLI refresh also never updates the running server's pool. This extends F-014 (single process) and F-073 (shared default directory) to concurrent processes. Torn-read outcome not reproduced end to end.

Evidence

TrustedListManager.java:165-173 (two FileCacheDataLoaders on tlCache.toFile()). DSS FileCacheDataLoader.java:397-401 `DSSUtils.saveToFile(bytes, file)`; DSSUtils.java:792 `Files.newOutputStream(file.toPath())`. dss-cli main.rs:66 and dss-server main.rs:54 `default_value = "dss-cache"`. No lock, synchronized, temp-file or move call in FileCacheDataLoader.

Impact

National lists can be silently lost from the server's trust pool for up to a refresh period, so valid signatures turn INDETERMINATE.

Recommendation

Document that a cache directory has exactly one owning process. Write downloads to a temp file and rename (also fixes F-014). Optionally take an advisory flock on <cache_dir>/tl during refresh and offline load.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-trust)

Every cache file is now written whole (temp sibling, fsync, ATOMIC_MOVE), so a reader in this or another process never sees a torn list; the offline loader also pre-checks each cached file and reports garbage as a download error of that list only. No advisory lock was added (not needed for torn reads; a refresh in another process still cannot update this process's pool, which must be documented: handoff to docs).

After review: Covered by the same Docker-section rewrite (checksum, BuildKit, VERSION, DSS_LISTEN, pinned base, volume per container, health-check timing).

Files: /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TlCacheLoader.java, docs/server.md

Test: TrustedListTest.cacheFilesAreWrittenWholeAndStagingIsCleanedUp (no temp files in tl/, garbage replaced only by a usable download, torn IT file -> IT download ERROR, DE still loads, tl-staging emptied on close)

  • java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:165-173 builds offline and online FileCacheDataLoaders and both call setFileCacheDirectory(tlCache.toFile()) on the same <cache_dir>/tl. No FileLock, temp file or Files.move anywhere under java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine (grep); the only synchronized/refreshLock is in-process.

Reproduction (read-only, in the scratchpad, using the seeded synthetic cache at rust/target/synthetic-tl): copied the cache twice and truncated tl/https___tl_dss_native_test_IT_xml to half its size in one copy (simulating the state a reader sees mid-write). dss-cli tl status on the intact copy: 3 trusted certificates, DE and IT "trusted". On the torn copy: [Fatal Error] :1:7054: The element type "tsl:ServiceStatus" must be terminated, Certificate synchronization is skipped for TL 'https://tl.dss-native.test/IT.xml', 1 trusted certificate, IT shown as NOT USED, and alerts: []. validate testdata/fixtures/pades/b-lta.pdf: TOTAL_PASSED (exit 0) on the intact cache, INDETERMINATE / NO_CERTIFICATE_CHAIN_FOUND (exit 1) on the torn cache. DSS's TrustedListCertificateSourceSynchronizer.java:149-150,173-176 confirms a parsing error excludes the TL from the pool.

Corrections: the failure is a parsing error ("not a valid XML"), not a signature failure, so no tl_signature_error alert fires; the loss is visible only in tl status. The long-running-server case (whether DSS keeps the previous parsed result when a later refresh hits a torn file) was not verified; the fresh-process case (server start-up, CLI one-shot) is. The race window is short (the duration of one list write) and needs two processes refreshing/loading at the same time, which keeps this at medium: real, no trust injection, availability/correctness only, and fixable by documentation plus temp-and-rename.

The server owns its refresh schedule (docs/server.md:25; DECISIONS.md:72-73 "the host application owns the refresh schedule"); the shipped image keeps the cache in a volume private to the container (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:33-35; docs/server.md:195-206); seed-cache extraction is documented as a first-start step (docs/server.md:20-23). Net impact: a fail-closed, logged, status-visible, self-healing availability hiccup for one country's lists, reachable only through a pointless deployment the docs do not describe. DSSUtils.java:790-797 is Files.newOutputStream(file.toPath()) followed by Utils.copy, which truncates the file and writes it in place with no temp file, no rename and no lock. FileCacheDataLoader has no lock, synchronized or move calls at all; its only "tmp" hit is the java.io.tmpdir default. README.md and docs/server.md never say a cache belongs to one process. DECISIONS.md:425 even describes a second TLValidationJob reading the same cache directory, though within one process.

Severity, calibrated from medium down to low: (1) There is no attacker vector. The issue only arises when an operator misconfigures things by running a CLI tl refresh against the live server's cache directory. The documented Docker setup (server.md:183-206) gives the server its own named volume. (2) The race window is narrow. A TL file is a few hundred KB, written in milliseconds, and a torn read needs a read to overlap that write. This was not reproduced. (3) The impact is limited to availability and does not affect integrity. ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy rejects a torn list because its signature fails, so no trust can be injected. The list then stays missing until the server's next refresh, which can turn validations INDETERMINATE for that country.

So the finding is real as an undocumented hazard: a single-owner rule or a temp-file-and-rename write is missing. It is still a low-likelihood operational issue, not a medium one. File and line are accurate (TrustedListManager.java:165).

F-214Mediumapi-designFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:461

certificateVerifier() keeps DSS's throwing augmentationAlertOnHigherSignatureLevel, so extend and LT/LTA/T signing refuse any PDF whose other signatures are already LT/LTA (mixed levels, and a second plain-CMS LT signature on an LT document)

SignatureRequirementsChecker.assertTLevelIsHighest runs over every signature in the PDF. The engine's verifier keeps ExceptionOnStatusAlert, so one higher-level signature blocks augmenting the others. The same check blocks completing an LT signature on an LTA document.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

DssEngine.certificateVerifier() never sets augmentationAlertOnHigherSignatureLevel. Extending [LTA, B] to LTA (which passes through T) throws, as do LT→T, LTA→T/LT, and completeSignature at LT on an LTA document. LTA→LTA and LT→LT/LTA succeed. README.md:353 documents only 'a signature is already at a higher level than the target'. This breaks sequential multi-party signing in which a later signer adds a B signature.

Evidence

`C2 extend that to LTA: EXTENSION_FAILED ... Error on signature augmentation to T-level. [S-B10DA1FC...: The signature is already extended with a higher level.]`; `extend pades/b-lta.pdf to LT: EXTENSION_FAILED`; `second signature at LT on pades/b-lta.pdf: SIGNING_FAILED`. DssEngine.java:309-313, 461-481.

Impact

Once any signature in a PDF is LT/LTA, a later B or T signature can never be augmented through dss_extend, dss-cli extend or POST /extend.

Recommendation

Set setAugmentationAlertOnHigherSignatureLevel(new LogOnStatusAlert(Level.WARN)) (or null) for extend and for the LT/LTA signing path, optionally behind an option. Add tests for [LTA,B]→LTA and [LT,B]→LT. Document the refused combinations.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.8

The mechanism checks out against the code.

Engine side

  • DssEngine.java:309 builds the service with new PAdESService(certificateVerifier(snapshot)).
  • certificateVerifier() at DssEngine.java:461-481 sets the trusted sources, CRL/OCSP and AIA. It never calls setAugmentationAlertOnHigherSignatureLevel. No StatusAlert or HigherSignatureLevel setting appears anywhere in java/src, apart from an unrelated one in AwtFreePdfObjFactory.

DSS 6.5.1 side (sources jar)

  • CommonCertificateVerifier.java:176 sets augmentationAlertOnHigherSignatureLevel = new ExceptionOnStatusAlert(), so the default throws.
  • PAdESLevelBaselineT.extendSignatures takes every signature in the PDF with pdfDocumentAnalyzer.getSignatures(). If isTLevelExtensionRequired holds, it calls assertExtendToTLevelPossible(signatures).
  • isTLevelExtensionRequired holds when the target is T, or when any one signature lacks hasTProfile() (line 172).
  • SignatureRequirementsChecker.java:321-333 runs checkTLevelIsHighest over every signature. That check reports "The signature is already extended with a higher level." for any signature with LT or higher (lines 343-346). The alert then throws.
  • PAdESLevelBaselineLT does the same for an LT target through assertExtendToLTLevelPossible.

Combinations confirmed

  • Extending [LTA, B] to LT or LTA fails, because the B signature needs T and the LTA signature trips the check.
  • Extending an LT/LTA document to T fails, and extending an LTA document to LT fails.
  • LTA→LTA passes, because no T is needed and LTA does not run the LT check when no T was added.

Precision

  • Line 309 is where the verifier is used. The missing setting belongs at line 461 (certificateVerifier), hence corrected_line.
  • README.md:353 ("a signature is already at a higher level than the target") reads as being about the target signature. It does not warn that some other signature in the PDF can block the extend.
  • The extend Javadoc at DssEngine.java:291-293 shows this was a deliberate choice to keep DSS's defaults. The consequence for mixed-level documents is not documented, and DECISIONS.md does not cover it.
  • I did not run the signing-path repro ("second signature at LT on b-lta.pdf"). It is consistent with DSS running the same extension profile after signing, but I have not verified it myself.

Severity

  • There is no security impact. Failing closed is conservative, and nobody can exploit it.
  • It is a functional block on a realistic workflow: countersigning a PDF that already has an LT/LTA signature, then raising the new signature to LT/LTA. That breaks dss_extend, the CLI and POST /extend, and callers have no way around it through the API.
  • Medium fits, at the lower end. It is DSS's own default behaviour, and the fix is a one-line verifier setting, optionally behind an option.

F-219MediumsecurityPartially fixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:97

Timestamp tokens from the configured TSA are embedded without trust/EKU/algorithm/genTime checks: a self-signed rogue TSA yields T/LT/LTA documents that validate TOTAL_PASSED with the timestamp INDETERMINATE

The engine hands DSS a plain OnlineTSPSource. Its only check is BouncyCastle's TimeStampResponse.validate (status, policy, imprint). The token's signature, chain, EKU, validity, algorithm and genTime are never checked before it is written at T/LT/LTA, in both signing and extend.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

OnlineTSPSource.getTimeStampResponse returns the DER token after BC's validate. PAdESTimestampService and CAdESSignatureExtension add it with no further check. Only the LT path re-checks intactness and revocation presence, not trust. Results through the JVM engine and native dss-cli with a loopback RFC 3161 responder:

  • Rogue self-signed TSA: B→T, B→LT and LT→LTA all OK; outputs validate TOTAL_PASSED while the timestamp is INDETERMINATE/NO_CERTIFICATE_CHAIN_FOUND.
  • No timeStamping EKU, SHA-1-signed, expired TSA certificate, genTime +1h, or a token with no certificates: accepted.
  • genTime -10y: LT→LTA on a TOTAL_PASSED file yields a TOTAL_FAILED/NOT_YET_VALID document.

In every case the result reports the requested level and dss-cli exits 0. The JSON summary has no per-timestamp verdict. F-006 (plain-http TSA) makes substitution by a man-in-the-middle possible.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:96-97 `new OnlineTSPSource(config.tsaUrl.toString(), tsaLoader != null ? tsaLoader : httpLoader)`. OnlineTSPSource.java:181-204 `timeStampResponse.validate(timeStampRequest); ... return new TimestampBinary(...)`. Harness: `[selfsigned] extend pades/b-b.pdf -> LT: OK ... validates: TOTAL_PASSED/null format=PAdES-BASELINE-LT ... timestamp: INDETERMINATE/NO_CERTIFICATE_CHAIN_FOUND`; `[past] extend pades/b-lt.pdf -> LTA: OK ... validates: TOTAL_FAILED/NOT_YET_VALID`; `[noeku] ... CHAIN_CONSTRAINTS_FAILURE`.

Impact

A faulty, misconfigured, compromised or spoofed TSA silently yields 'successful' long-term documents whose timestamps prove nothing. The loss is noticed only when the signer's certificate expires. A wrong-clock TSA can turn valid documents TOTAL_FAILED.

Recommendation

Wrap the TSPSource and check each returned token before accepting it:

  • signature and imprint are intact;
  • the chain reaches the trusted sources (with an explicit opt-out);
  • the id-kp-timeStamping EKU is present;
  • genTime is within a tolerance of the engine's clock and not before signing_time;
  • the algorithm meets the cryptographic constraints.

Fail with SIGNING_FAILED/EXTENSION_FAILED naming the TSA. Add fake-TSA tests, and expose per-timestamp verdicts in the summary.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package java-engine)

New CheckedTspSource wraps the OnlineTSPSource for every extend/sign call (built per call with the verifier's trusted sources). Before DSS writes a token it refuses: unparsable token or imprint not over the digest sent; no certificate in the token that verifies the signature; TSA certificate not valid at genTime or without id-kp-timeStamping EKU; MD2/MD5/SHA-1 signature or RSA < 2048 bits; genTime further than tsa.max_clock_skew_ms (default 300,000) from the host clock; and, with tsa.require_trusted (default true), a certificate that does not chain (through the token's certificates and the anchors) to the trusted lists or extra_trusted_certificates. The trust check is skipped with a warning when the engine has no trust anchors at all, keeping the recorded decision that T-level signing needs no trusted lists. All refusals and TSA transport/HTTP errors are the new code TSA_FAILED. Per-timestamp verdicts are now in the result (F-009).

After review: Option (b) taken: behaviour unchanged (the no-anchor bypass keeps the recorded 'T-level signing needs no trusted lists' decision), but it is now stated precisely in the CheckedTspSource Javadoc and pinned by a test: an engine with require_trusted_lists:true and tsa.require_trusted:true whose cache is empty refuses to extend (TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED, since extend goes through trustSnapshot()) but signs at cms-T through prepare/complete with the rogue TSA's token embedded unchecked; after refreshTrustedListsOnline() the same engine refuses the same TSA with TSA_FAILED 'does not chain to a trusted certificate' (EngineHardeningTest.tokensFromAnUntrustedTsaAreRefused). Note the reviewer's premise is narrower than stated: only signing at B/T (trustedLists.current()) is affected, not extend. Option (a) (an 'explicit require_trusted' flag that refuses with TSA_FAILED when there are no anchors) was not done: it is a contract change touching EngineConfig (java-trust's file) and needs a docs decision; the README/TSA_FAILED wording is left to docs (docs_updates in notes).

Impact lens; I assume the code reads as the finding says and checked whether the impact is real, documented, mitigated or non-actionable in this system.

Not documented as an intentional trade-off. docs/DECISIONS.md:634-637 says only "DSS's default CertificateVerifier alerts are kept. DSS throws on an invalid signature or timestamp; ..." and :640-643 that the TSA "uses DSS's TimestampDataLoader with the same timeouts and trust store as CRL/OCSP". README.md:356-357 says "The TSA's HTTPS server is trusted like the CRL/OCSP servers" (TLS only, docs/native-library.md:133-142). Nothing states that the token itself is accepted untrusted, nor the consequence. So the "documented decision" refutation does not apply.

Upstream behaviour confirms the mechanism and that it is not handled elsewhere: in DSS 6.5.1 (java/pom.xml:43) SignatureValidationContext.allTimestampsValid() only checks if (!timestampToken.isValid()) ... "Signature is not intact!" (scratch copy of dss-spi sources, lines 1356-1366), and TimestampTokenVerifier.isAcceptable (trust anchor + chain + crypto) is used only in isTimestampValid()/registerTimestampPOE (lines 906-925), i.e. to decide whether a POE is extracted, never as a gate for extension. The engine's certificateVerifier() (DssEngine.java:461-481) sets no TimestampTokenVerifier/TrustAnchorVerifier, so the default 'no configuration available' instance (TimestampTokenVerifier.java:73-77) applies.

The impact is real, not stylistic: the summary exposed to hosts and the sidecar is per-signature only (ValidationResult.java:30-39 and :111 m.put("signatures", sigs); grep for "timestamp" in ValidationResult/DssJsonApi returns nothing; README.md:315-318 shows only indication/sub_indication/signing_time/best_signature_time). A document whose LTA timestamp is INDETERMINATE therefore reads TOTAL_PASSED until the signer's certificate expires, exactly as the finding describes. The engine's own ExtensionTest re-validates results (DECISIONS.md:652-654) but with a TSA that is in the synthetic trusted list (TrustedListTest.java:73 "IT: root CA + TSA", :168), so no test covers a hostile TSA.

It is actionable and cheap: the engine already loads the EU trusted lists and the test TSA is already a TL entry, and DSS 6.5.1 ships TrustAnchorVerifier/TimestampTokenVerifier (dss-spi-6.5.1.jar listing) that could gate acceptance; qualified EU TSAs are TL entries, which is the stated use case.

Why medium rather than high: the TSA is operator configuration (EngineConfig.java:134-144), the same trust level as the trust store, so the realistic triggers are a misconfiguration (test/wrong TSA), a plaintext http:// tsa.url chosen by the operator (EngineConfig.java:178 allows it) under MITM, or a wildly broken TSA clock; a TSA compromised with its real key cannot be caught by any client-side check. There is no forgery or trust escalation, only silent loss of long-term proof (and a damaged output in the broken-clock case, with the input untouched). TLS to an https TSA is verified against the CA bundle (native-library.md:140), which neutralises the MITM branch for correctly configured deployments. The behaviour also matches upstream DSS defaults used across EU deployments. Hence: real as described, severity medium.

The finding describes the mechanism correctly. DssEngine.java:96-97 builds a plain DSS source with no wrapper or post-check: this.tspSource = config.tsaUrl == null ? null : new OnlineTSPSource(config.tsaUrl.toString(), tsaLoader != null ? tsaLoader : httpLoader);. A grep of java/src/main/java finds no other TSPSource implementation apart from the NoTsa stand-in (DssEngine.java:391), and no token validation anywhere.

The docs do not cover this case:

  • docs/DECISIONS.md:634-637 keeps DSS's default CertificateVerifier alerts. Those alerts concern the signatures and timestamps already in the document being extended ("DSS throws on an invalid signature or timestamp; a revoked, expired or not-yet-valid certificate; missing revocation data").
  • README.md:350-354 likewise refuses only when "a signature or timestamp does not verify" or "the TSA fails".
  • DECISIONS.md:640-643 and README.md:356-357 say only that the TSA's HTTPS server is trusted like the CRL/OCSP servers, which is about transport trust. Nothing documents a choice to skip checking the freshly issued token.

So the gap is real and a maintainer can act on it.

Severity is lower than "high", for these reasons:

  • The TSA URL is operator-trusted engine configuration (EngineConfig.java:135), not attacker input. Exploiting this needs a misconfigured or compromised TSA, or a man-in-the-middle on a plain-http TSA URL, which depends on F-006 and on the operator choosing http.
  • Nothing corrupts the signature itself. The harm is a timestamp that is worthless or untrusted, which validation does flag on the timestamp (INDETERMINATE/NO_CERTIFICATE_CHAIN_FOUND). The cost is false assurance at the long-term level, and it shows up late.
  • Upstream DSS behaves the same way by default (OnlineTSPSource only runs BC's validate), so this is defense in depth rather than a regression.

The wrong-clock case (genTime -10y making the output TOTAL_FAILED) is an availability and integrity nuisance caused by a faulty, trusted TSA.

I did not re-run the harness, so the specific outcomes it reports (TOTAL_PASSED and so on) are not independently confirmed here. The code path that makes them plausible is confirmed. On a CVSS-like view (AV:N with adjacent/MITM preconditions, AC:H, PR:N or high for the config, I:L-M, C:N, A:L), medium is the right calibration. File and line are correct.

F-224MediumperformanceFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.java:233

Visible text has no length cap and fit() re-wraps the whole text (measuring each word with the full growing line) at every one of up to 82 shrink steps, in both prepare and complete: never-fitting text costs tens of seconds of CPU (750 KB → 27.6 s; 32000 words in 600x10 → 9.3 s; 4000 words in a 14000-pt-wide box → 25.8 s) before INVALID_ARGUMENT

fit() steps from font_size down to 3 pt by 0.95, up to 82 steps. Each step calls wrap(), which measures every word with growing candidate strings and does not stop early once the lines exceed the box. The text template is bounded only by the request size.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The cost is O(text length × line length) per step, repeated in complete. Every case ends in INVALID_ARGUMENT, but only after the work is done.

Evidence

`ab x 250,000 (750 KB) -> prepare INVALID_ARGUMENT after 18539.6 ms`; `never-fits box 600x10, 32000 words: 3.59 s`; `14400x14400 page, never-fits ... 4000 words: 7.03 s`. Loop at AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.java:233.

Impact

A few large-text requests tie up engine workers for seconds to minutes. Combined with F-052, this starves other callers.

Recommendation

Cap visible text length after placeholder expansion. Stop wrapping as soon as the height is exceeded, and binary-search the font size.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-visible)

Text is capped at VisibleSignature.MAX_TEXT_LENGTH = 10,000 characters, checked on the template at parse and on the rendered text after placeholder expansion (INVALID_ARGUMENT). fit() now measures each word's glyph advances once (AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.Paragraph) and re-sums them per size step in exactly the order PDFont.getStringWidth adds them, so the wrapping decisions and the bytes drawn are bit-identical to before (the recorded visible fixtures still complete); wrap() stops as soon as the lines so far exceed the box height or a word is too wide. The 10,000-char text in a 14000-pt-wide box that never fits is refused in ~11 ms (tens of seconds before). The 0.95 shrink steps were kept on purpose: a binary search would pick different sizes and break the committed signing fixtures.

After review: Paragraph.measure now measures the space only when the paragraph has more than one word (float[] space = words.length > 1 ? advances(font, " ") : new float[0]); checkGlyphs has already encoded the whole paragraph (space included) before, so a text the font cannot show is still INVALID_ARGUMENT 'the font cannot show the text' and a one-word text with a font that has no U+0020 glyph signs. CraftedFonts.noSpaceGlyph() builds Liberation Sans with a cmap of one format-12 subtable mapping U+0021..U+007E only; VisibleSignatureTest.aFontWithoutASpaceGlyphShowsASingleWord signs 'Approvato' with it (prepare, complete, validate TOTAL_PASSED) and shows 'Approvato oggi' refused with INVALID_ARGUMENT, which also proves the font lacks the space (so the old unconditional encode(" ") would have thrown). FontCheckTest.realFontsPass checks FontCheck accepts that font. Bytes of the recorded fixtures unchanged (theRecordedVisibleFixturesStillComplete).

  • The work is repeated: ExternalSigning.visible() (engine/ExternalSigning.java:384-390) is resolved in both prepare (line 109) and complete (line 131), and the drawer javadoc says "prepare and complete draw the same bytes".

Experiments (scratchpad, sign prepare --mode cms --level b, engine startup is 0.06 s):

  • "ab " x 32000 in a 600x10 box: 9.33 s, then INVALID_ARGUMENT "does not fit ... even at 3 points".
  • "ab " x 250000 (750 KB) in a 200x60 box: 27.59 s, then INVALID_ARGUMENT.
  • 4000 words "parola " on a generated 14400x14400-pt page, box 14000x10: 25.77 s, INVALID_ARGUMENT; the same 4000 words in a 14000x14000 box (fits at the first step): 0.61 s — showing the 82-step repetition and quadratic candidate measurement are the multipliers.

My timings are larger than the finding's (9.3 vs 3.6 s, 27.6 vs 18.5 s, 25.8 vs 7.0 s), so the finding if anything understates the cost. Severity stays medium: it is CPU exhaustion from a single legitimately shaped request (bounded only by a 100 MB body), not a correctness or integrity defect, and every case ends in a clean INVALID_ARGUMENT.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

The mechanics are as described: fit() at java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.java:233 loops for (float size = appearance.fontSize(); ; size = Math.max(MIN_FONT_SIZE, size * SHRINK)) and calls wrap() for every paragraph at every step; wrap() (line ~258) builds String candidate = line + " " + words[i] and measures it with font.getStringWidth, with no early exit on height; and VisibleSignature.java:126-131 accepts text with only an isBlank() check and no length cap. So a pathological text is costly. But the claimed impact ("ties up engine workers ... starves other callers") does not hold against who can supply that text:

  1. The text is authored by the host application, not by an untrusted party. Every input to the rendered string comes from the signing options or the certificate the caller chose: VisibleSignature.appearance() (lines 190-221) fills {signer_name} from pades.signer_name or the signing_certificate CN, {reason}/{location} from pades.reason/pades.location, {signing_time} from a formatted date. Nothing from the PDF being signed (the only untrusted-party input in this system) feeds the text. README.md:388-394 and 453-456 document these as the caller's options. A 750 KB template or a 4000-word stamp on a 14400 pt page is the application attacking itself.
  1. In the sidecar the caller is authenticated and on a trusted network by design: docs/server.md "Security": "No TLS. Run the sidecar on the same host or on a private network ... never expose it publicly. The token stops other containers on the same network from using it." A client that holds the token can already occupy the single default worker (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:45, workers: 1) for as long with legitimate-looking work: the request cap is 100 MB (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:47, DSS_MAX_REQUEST_MB default 100), there is no per-request deadline anywhere, and validating or signing a large hostile PDF costs comparable CPU. The visible-text path adds no new trust boundary or amplification class.
  1. The stated measurements need inputs no real caller produces (a signature stamp is one to three lines; font_size is documented as "the largest size, 4-200" for a box that README.md:457 gives a 3-point margin). Every such case ends in INVALID_ARGUMENT ("the text does not fit in the box even at 3 points"), i.e. the caller's own misuse, and the README (line 469-470) documents that outcome.
  1. docs/DECISIONS.md "Visible signatures" documents the algorithm ("text wrapped at spaces and shrunk from font_size by 5% steps until it fits. One code path for all cases") as a deliberate simplification over DSS's layout. It does not state a performance trade-off, so this is not a fully documented decision, but it is a reasonable one for application-authored text.

Net: a cheap hardening (cap the expanded text length, stop wrapping once the block exceeds the box height) would be sensible defence in depth and I would keep it as a low-severity note, but the finding's medium-severity impact claim of worker starvation by "a few large-text requests" presupposes an attacker who is the trusted application itself, which already has equal or greater means. Not confirmed as a real impact in this system.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

The finding describes the code correctly, so I am not refuting it. I am lowering the severity to low.

What the code does

  • AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.java:233 is the shrink loop: for (float size = appearance.fontSize(); ; size = Math.max(MIN_FONT_SIZE, size * SHRINK)).
  • The constants are MIN_FONT_SIZE = 3 and SHRINK = 0.95f (lines 72-73).
  • The largest allowed start size is MAX_FONT_SIZE = 200 (VisibleSignature.java:41).
  • From 200 down to 3 that is ln(3/200)/ln(0.95) ≈ 82 steps, which matches the finding's "up to 82".
  • Every step calls wrap() on every paragraph. Inside wrap():
  • it builds String candidate = line + " " + words[i]; and measures it with font.getStringWidth;
  • it never checks the running line count against area.h;
  • it does not stop when a single word is too wide (fits &= ... just keeps going).
  • The height check only runs after the full wrap: if (fits && lines.size() * lineHeight <= area.h).
  • When nothing fits, the code throws INVALID_ARGUMENT only at size == MIN_FONT_SIZE, after all the work is done.

No cap on text length

  • VisibleSignature.java checks the font size (lines 153-155) but has no limit on text length.
  • The only limit I found is the HTTP body cap, DSS_MAX_REQUEST_MB with a default of 100 (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:47).

So the mechanism, file and line are all accurate, and the recommended fixes are actionable: cap the text after placeholder expansion, stop wrapping early once the height is exceeded, and binary-search the font size.

Why low rather than medium

  • The attacker has to be a client allowed to call prepare/complete. The server can require a bearer token (main.rs:39), and the API is meant for signing integrations, not anonymous users.
  • The damage is CPU time on an engine worker for each request. There is no effect on integrity or confidentiality, and nothing persists.
  • Normal signer text is a few lines and costs nothing.

In CVSS terms: network vector, low privileges, availability-only impact (low, or high only together with F-052). That fits low, or low-to-medium if the server is exposed to semi-trusted clients.

I did not reproduce the timings myself; the mechanism was confirmed by reading the code.

F-248MediumreliabilityPartially fixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:254

PAdES validation time grows super-linearly (~quadratically) with the number of signature revisions because DSS re-copies and re-parses each revision prefix twice; the engine and server add no signature-count cap, per-call deadline or queue admission control

For each signature, DSS's AbstractPDFSignatureService copies and re-parses the revision prefix twice (getRevisions and analyzePdfModifications), and each prefix grows. The engine has no signature-count or deadline check.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Measured with native dss-cli, offline: 1 signature 0.11 s, 50 → 1.07 s, 100 → 4.2 s, 200 → 18.1 s, 300 → 56 s, 400 → 91.5 s with 365 MB RSS. A second run measured 10 → 0.19 s, 50 → 1.2 s, 200 → 18.6 s. Extend and sign pay the same cost before any TSA call. There is no admission control (F-052).

Evidence

`n=400 size=22754306 real=91.53s rss=365 MB`; `N=200 (7.3 MB) 18.62 s`. DssEngine.java:239; AbstractPDFSignatureService.java:576-577, :928, :991-1007.

Impact

Modest valid uploads consume CPU-minutes. A few concurrent ones block every worker, and memory caps do not help.

Recommendation

Count signature revisions before validating and refuse above a configurable limit. Add a cooperative per-call deadline. Document the measured curve.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package java-engine)

New DocumentLimits pre-check (one PDFBox parse before DSS) refuses a PDF with more signature revisions (PDDocument.getSignatureDictionaries) than limits.max_pdf_signatures (default 100) for validate, extend, prepare and complete, with the operation's failure code and a message naming the limit. No cooperative per-call deadline: DSS's validation has no cancellation point, so a deadline would need the Rust/server layer (handoff noted for rust-dss as a note only).

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DocumentLimits.java, java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java, java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/EngineConfig.java

Test: EngineHardeningTest.structuralLimitsRefuseBeforeDssRuns (b-lta.pdf, two revisions, refused with max_pdf_signatures:1; b-b.pdf passes), DssJsonApiTest.validationResultCarriesTheAggregateVerdictAndLimitsApply

Experiment (read-only, offline, scratchpad /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f248/): chained N PAdES-B signatures with the fixture PKI via dss-cli sign prepare/complete + openssl, then timed dss-cli validate --offline-revocation --allow-without-trusted-lists: n=1 0.15 s (43 ms engine), n=10 0.21 s (110 ms), n=25 0.43 s (348 ms), n=50 1.22 s (1143 ms), n=100 4.66 s (4574 ms), 2.9 MB file, all 100 signatures reported. Doubling n quadruples time, matching the finding's 100 → 4.2 s and consistent with its 400 → 91 s. Engine start is ~0.1 s, so this is the validation cost itself.

Impact in this system: (1) the input is exactly what the product exists to accept, signed documents from end users of the host application; the sidecar's private network and bearer token (docs/server.md "Security") stop other containers, not the application's own uploads. (2) The only documented bounds are byte-based: server.md:221-222 "A request is held in memory whole… --max-request-mb and --max-heap bound both." Default is 100 MB (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:47), so a 23 MB/400-signature file passes, and the cost is driven by signature count, not bytes (a 2.9 MB file already costs 4.6 s). (3) No timeout: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs has no tower timeout layer (only DefaultBodyLimit at :120), run() at :302 just awaits spawn_blocking; the engine queue is unbounded mpsc::channel::<Job>() at rust/dss/src/engine.rs:395, workers default to CPU count (server.md:42 "more wait in a queue"). So a handful of such uploads occupy every worker for ~90 s each and later requests queue indefinitely. (4) Not documented or decided: docs/DECISIONS.md and README.md say nothing about signature count or per-call cost; the only "hostile file" statement (README.md:512) concerns snapshot deserialization. The measured validation figure in DECISIONS.md is "One validation (PAdES B-LTA) ~30 ms", so the quadratic case is not an acknowledged trade-off. (5) Actionable: counting /ByteRange/signature dictionaries before validation, or a cap in the server, is cheap.

F-256MediumsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:255

DocMDP /P 1 violations (annotation added or content replaced after certification) still validate TOTAL_PASSED: engine uses DSS default policy where DocMDP/FieldMDP/SigFieldLock/UndefinedChanges are Level=WARN, and all_passed()/CLI exit status ignore warnings

DSS detects the violation, but the default policy has DocMDP Level=WARN and the engine never overrides it. The only signal is a warning string.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

A document certified at P=1 and then given an added annotation or replaced content returns TOTAL_PASSED. DSS's own signer refuses to add a second signature, but validation of an externally crafted one is unaffected.

Evidence

`CERTIFIED P=1 then ANNOTATION added: TOTAL_PASSED/- warnings=[Document contains changes restricted by /DocMDP dictionary!, ...]`; `then CONTENT replaced: TOTAL_PASSED/-`; constraint.xml:64 `<DocMDP Level="WARN"/>`.

Impact

The author's explicit cryptographic lock is ignored by the verdict.

Recommendation

Treat DocMDP, FieldMDP and SigFieldLock violations as FAIL through a custom policy, or expose them as structured fields. Document the current behaviour.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

Took the finding's second option: per PAdES signature the result now carries modified_after_signing (true when DSS found annotation changes, undefined changes or page differences after the signature's revision) and changes_after_signing {extension, signature_or_form_fill, annotation, undefined, pages_differ, annotations_overlap, active_content}, from the diagnostic data's PDFRevisionWrapper. DocMDP/FieldMDP/SigFieldLock violations show as the counted changes plus DSS's warning text; the verdict is unchanged (DSS default policy, a recorded decision) and there is no DocMDP-specific flag. docs must say that all_passed and indication ignore these and that modified_after_signing must be checked.

The openapi_document_matches_the_router test still passes against the edited document.

The existing lines are unchanged, so the expect_line/grep -x checks in scripts/package.sh and package-smoke.sh still match. Against the rebuilt library it prints 'API version 1 (dss-cli expects 1)'.

The modifiedAfterSigning() docblock now says that changes_after_signing.pages_differ and annotations_overlap are lists of page numbers, empty when nothing changed, and not booleans. DssEngine.validateLevel (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:237-255) builds the validator and calls validator.validateDocument() without ever setting a validation policy. That file has <DocMDP Level="WARN" />, <FieldMDP Level="WARN" />, <SigFieldLock Level="WARN" /> and <UndefinedChanges Level="WARN" /> at lines 64-67, and again at 370-373 for counter-signatures. Under this policy, a DocMDP violation cannot change the indication: it only adds a warning. I did not re-run the crafted-PDF experiment, but the outcome follows directly from the policy levels.

I am lowering the severity from medium to low: (1) This is a documented decision. docs/DECISIONS.md:201 says "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now." (2) The behaviour matches upstream DSS and its reference demo, so this wrapper adds no new weakness. (3) The signal is structured per signature, not a loose string. ValidationResult.java:33/47/78 puts the AdES and qualification warnings into a per-signature warnings list in the result JSON. (4) Exploiting it needs a document certified with P=1 and then changed, plus a relying party that reads only the indication and ignores the warnings. Integrity of the signed revision is not affected: the signature still covers its own byte range.

The recommendation still makes sense as a hardening step and a documentation item: a custom policy, or failing on DocMDP/FieldMDP/SigFieldLock violations. One correction: line 255 is the validateDocument call. The root cause is that no policy is set at all, as decided in DECISIONS.md:201, not a specific override that is missing at that line.

F-259MediumsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/VisibleSignature.java:294

A ~200-byte cmap edit to a caller TTF makes FontBox allocate gigabytes or spin for seconds to minutes inside checkFont, ending in INTERNAL_ERROR/OOM

FontBox parses every cmap encoding record (duplicate offsets included) and expands each format-13 group into a HashMap of up to 1.1M entries per subtable. There is no limit on records, groups or font size. checkFont catches only IOException and RuntimeException.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Results:

  • 20 shared records (203 KB font): OOM at -Xmx512m.
  • 200 records, default heap: 48 s and 8.9 GB RSS.
  • Each format-13 group costs about 12 ms per parse.

The font is parsed in checkFont and again in prepare and in complete.

Evidence

`options UNCAUGHT(INTERNAL_ERROR) java.lang.OutOfMemoryError ... at CmapSubtable.processSubtype13(CmapSubtable.java:344)`; native `--max-heap 512m` → `InternalError: OutOfMemoryError`; default heap: `48.11 real ... 8897642496 maximum resident set size`; `1000 groups -> prepare OK 11988.1 ms`.

Impact

A small font can exhaust heap or host memory (container OOM, or a process abort per F-186), or pin a worker for minutes.

Recommendation

Pre-check font tables: cap the size; refuse many records, duplicate offsets, format 13, and oversized format-12 coverage. Catch OOM and StackOverflowError around checkFont. Add the crafted fonts to the tests.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-visible)

FontCheck bounds the cmap before FontBox parses it: at most 16 encoding records (MAX_CMAP_RECORDS), each subtable offset inside the table, format 13 refused, and the character coverage of all subtables together (duplicates counted, formats 0/2/4/6/8/10/12) capped at 1,000,000 (MAX_CMAP_ENTRIES), which bounds FontBox's hash maps to roughly 100 MB worst case instead of unbounded; checkFont also catches OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError. Crafted fonts (20+ duplicate records, format-13 group over all of Unicode, format-12 group over all of Unicode) are in the tests. The default PT Serif and Liberation Sans, and 16 duplicate records, still pass.

Test: FontCheckTest.characterMapsThatWouldMakeFontBoxAllocateAreRefused, FontCheckTest.realFontsPass, VisibleSignatureTest.craftedFontsAreRefusedWhenTheOptionsAreParsed

The location and mechanism are described correctly. In java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/VisibleSignature.java, lines 292-298, checkFont calls PDType0Font.load(scratch, new ByteArrayInputStream(font), false); at line 294 and catches only IOException | RuntimeException. No table, record or size limits are applied before FontBox parses it.

The finding's cost figures (OOM at -Xmx512m in CmapSubtable.processSubtype13, 48 s and 8.9 GB RSS) come from the reporter's experiments, which I did not re-run. They fit how FontBox expands cmap groups into per-codepoint maps.

The impact is worse than a clean error. DssLib.java (lines ~41-43) says Native Image does not deliver an OutOfMemoryError to a handler in the same compiled frame: it unwinds to the C entry stub, which aborts the process. An OOM here therefore results either in INTERNAL_ERROR (DssJsonApi catches Throwable) or in a process abort, and with the default heap ("a large share of physical memory", docs/native-library.md:100) it can pressure the host.

Exposure: dss-server exposes POST /sign/prepare and /sign/complete with multipart options (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:11-12, 109-110). A body limit applies (line 120), but it does not help because the font is small. The bearer token is optional (lib.rs:62-67, 279).

Calibration: the vector is network, complexity low, and privileges low (or none when no token is configured). The impact is availability only, with no confidentiality or integrity effect, and the caller is normally the integrating application rather than an anonymous party. CVSS AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/A:H comes to about 6.5. Medium is appropriate and not higher. The DoS is real and fixable as described: pre-check the cmap tables or cap the font size and records.

F-260MediumreliabilityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:149

TSA responses have no whole-transfer deadline or size cap: a trickling TSA holds an engine worker far beyond http.response_timeout_ms (validate queues behind it; /health does not)

withTimeouts() sets only per-read timeouts on the TSA loader. A TSA sending 1 byte/s kept B→T blocked for 40 s against a 3 s timeout. Bodies are buffered with no cap.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

F-002 covers the CRL/OCSP/AIA URLs driven by documents; this is the operator-configured TSA, which every T/LT/LTA operation depends on.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:146-151; `[trickle] extend pades/b-b.pdf -> T: EXTENSION_FAILED in 40047 ms`, vs `[stall] ... 3010 ms`; dss-cli `exit 1 in 40.15 s`.

Impact

A degraded TSA can occupy every worker, and validate and health requests queue behind them.

Recommendation

Bound the total TSA exchange time and cap the response size (~1 MB). Until then, document that response_timeout_ms is a per-read timeout.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

The TSA loader is wrapped in OutboundFetchPolicy in DssEngine.Loaders.of, so one RFC 3161 exchange is bounded by http.request_deadline_ms (default 120 s, on the policy's daemon pool, cancelled on timeout) and its body by http.max_response_bytes. TSA transport failures are now TSA_FAILED, distinct from the document's refusals.

Test: EngineHardeningTest.realLoadersSitBehindThePolicyAndTheCache (tsa loader is a policy over TimestampDataLoader); HttpsLoopbackTest.extensionToLtaUsesAnAuthenticatedHttpsTsa exercises it end to end (assertion updated to TSA_FAILED for the 401 case)

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

The mechanism is accurate. tsaLoader (DssEngine.java:135) wraps new TimestampDataLoader() in withTimeouts. withTimeouts (lines 146-151) sets only setTimeoutConnection, setTimeoutConnectionRequest, setTimeoutResponse(config.httpResponseTimeoutMs) and setTimeoutSocket(config.httpResponseTimeoutMs). Apache HttpClient applies these per connect or per read, not as a deadline on the whole exchange, and the code sets no limit on body size. A TSA that sends a byte at a time therefore keeps the call alive past response_timeout_ms. README.md:276 documents "response_timeout_ms": 60000 without saying it is a per-read timeout, and DECISIONS.md:640-641 says only that the TSA uses "the same timeouts and trust store as CRL/OCSP". No documented decision accepts this behaviour.

Two corrections:

  1. The impact overstates the reach to health. /health (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-256) calls e.trusted_list_status(), which goes through control_call (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:305-306, 339-342). That runs on the separate dss-control thread (DECISIONS.md:354: "A *control* thread ... serves status/version"), not on the validation workers, so health does not queue behind a stalled TSA. Validate requests do queue, because the workers "share a job queue" (DECISIONS.md:355) and there is 1 worker by default.
  2. Severity should be lower. The TSA URL is operator-configured engine config, not attacker-supplied (contrast F-002, where documents drive the URLs). It is fetched over the operator's chosen TLS trust. To exploit this, someone must control or badly degrade the operator's own trusted TSA, or sit on its network path. Neither is likely in normal use, and the effect is availability only: no integrity or confidentiality impact. The uncapped body is also bounded in practice by what a trusted TSA sends.

This is a real robustness gap that a maintainer can act on: add a total deadline and a size cap, or document per-read semantics. It rates low rather than medium.

F-264MediumreliabilityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:453

PAdES validation has no CPU-time bound: a small PDF with a huge /Annots array holds a dss-server worker for tens of seconds or more, and the documented size/heap limits do not cover it

DefaultPdfObjectModificationsFinder.compareArraysRecursively runs an unguarded nested loop over two arrays. The depth guard does not bound breadth, and the engine caps nothing.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Validation time by annotation count M:

  • M=2,000: 0.25 s
  • M=10,000: 2.70 s
  • M=40,000 (1.03 MB): 36.6 s

Cryptographic validity is irrelevant. With --workers 2 and 8 concurrent uploads, two requests were still running at 120 s.

Evidence

DefaultPdfObjectModificationsFinder.java:354/362/364 (nested loop, no break); `M=40000 (1.03 MB) 36.61 s real, peak RSS 221 MB`; jstack in compareArraysRecursively.

Impact

A small-input CPU amplification attack on dss-server.

Recommendation

Bound the object count and the largest array before validation (VALIDATION_FAILED), or skip modification detection above a threshold. Report the issue upstream (map-based matching). Make the cap configurable.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

DocumentLimits.checkPdf counts the /Annots array of every page while iterating the page tree and refuses a page with more than limits.max_pdf_annotations_per_page (default 5,000) annotations before DSS's O(M²) array comparison runs, for every operation on a PDF.

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DocumentLimits.java, java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java

Test: EngineHardeningTest.structuralLimitsRefuseBeforeDssRuns (11 link annotations against a limit of 10 → VALIDATION_FAILED naming limits.max_pdf_annotations_per_page)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: High · confidence 0.92

CONFIRMED as described. My lens was REPRODUCE; both the code paths and an offline end-to-end experiment confirm it.

  1. The unguarded nested loop exists. In the DSS 6.5.1 sources (dss-pades-6.5.1-sources.jar), DefaultPdfObjectModificationsFinder.compareArraysRecursively runs for (int i = 0; i < firstArray.size(); i++) (line 354) and, inside it, for (int j = 0; j < secondArray.size(); j++) (line 362) matching object keys, with no break when a match is found — it keeps scanning the whole second array for every i. Since every PDF /Annots entry is an indirect object (PdfBoxArray.getObjectKey returns a non-null key for each COSObject), both arrays have M keyed entries, giving O(M²). The reference guard (isProcessedReference / objectTree / processedObjects) only prevents re-descending the same reference; it does not bound the breadth of the j-loop. So "the depth guard does not bound breadth" is accurate.
  1. The engine caps nothing. DssEngine.pdfObjFactory() (java/.../engine/DssEngine.java:453-459) builds AwtFreePdfObjFactory and only calls differencesFinder.setMaximalPagesAmountForVisualComparison(0) (line 456), disabling *visual* comparison. The Javadoc at lines 450-451 states "Object-level modification detection between revisions stays on." No maximum object/array count is ever set on the pdfObjectModificationsFinder (DSS's AbstractPDFSignatureService uses the DefaultPdfObjectModificationsFinder, invoked from getModificationDetection -> pdfObjectModificationsFinder.find at AbstractPDFSignatureService.java:1005-1006). The finding cites DssEngine.java:455 as the integration point where the cap is missing — correct.
  1. Reproduced offline. I built single-page PDFs whose page /Annots array holds M indirect Link annotations, signed each PAdES-BASELINE-B via dss-cli external signing (test PKI), and timed dss-cli validate --json --allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation (warm JVM): M=100 -> 0.08s; M=2000 -> 0.21s; M=10000 -> 1.85s; M=40000 -> 26.25s real, 25.88s user, peak RSS 238 MB. From 10000->40000 (M×4) time grows ×14 — clearly superlinear, consistent with O(M²). This matches the finding's figures (M=40000: 36.6s / 221 MB; mine 26s / 228 MB — same order; my host is likely faster and my annotation encoding larger). Validation runs the full PAdES path (output shows format PAdES-BASELINE-B, INDETERMINATE only because the chain is untrusted — cryptographic validity is irrelevant to the cost, as claimed).
  1. dss-server exposure. rust/dss-server default DSS_MAX_REQUEST_MB=100 (main.rs:47), applied as DefaultBodyLimit (lib.rs:120); the router has no tower timeout layer, and each request runs on a spawn_blocking engine worker (lib.rs:302) bounded only by --workers (default = CPU count). A small PDF (well under 100 MB; my 40000-annot file was 5.6 MB and a compact encoding fits ~1 MB) therefore wedges a worker for tens of seconds; a few concurrent uploads exhaust the worker pool — a valid-input CPU amplification / DoS. Note requests pass an authorize token layer, so the attacker must be an authorized caller, but that is exactly the "adversarial valid input" gap. Severity high stands.

Minor: the title's "~1 MB" is the finding author's compact-encoding size; the cost is driven by object count M, not bytes, and is reproducible either way, so no correction to the claim is needed.

The impact is real in this system, though narrower than "attack on dss-server" suggests, so I lower it from high to medium.

  1. Not neutralised by the trusted-network placement. docs/server.md "Security" (lines 216-222) says: "No TLS. Run the sidecar on the same host or on a private network ... never expose it publicly. The token stops other containers on the same network from using it." That excludes direct unauthenticated access, but the sidecar's purpose is to validate documents the host application receives from third parties (README.md: curl -F document=@contract.pdf.p7m .../validate; server.md: "a tampered or untrusted signature is a 200 result"). Anyone who can get a signed PDF into the host app's validation path reaches the finder. The attacker needs an upload path, not network access; that gate is why this is medium rather than high.
  1. The documented mitigations bound bytes, not time. server.md line 221-222: "Size. A request is held in memory whole ... --max-request-mb and --max-heap bound both." The finding's input is ~1 MB against a 100 MiB default (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:46-47, default_value_t = 100) and peaks at 221 MB RSS, so neither limit is hit. With quadratic scaling, a 10 MB document inside the default cap would cost on the order of an hour per request.
  1. No timeout or cancellation anywhere in the chain. grep -i "timeout|cancel|deadline|abort" over rust/dss/src/engine.rs and rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs returns nothing. Requests go to a fixed pool (engine.rs:398 for i in 0..b.workers, default = CPUs per main.rs:244-247; server.md line 42: "Requests the engine runs at the same time; more wait in a queue"). lib.rs:302 says "The engine's own workers do the work; this thread waits." php/DssClient.php:26 has timeoutSeconds = 120, which abandons the HTTP call but does not free the worker. So N such documents wedge all N workers while /health keeps answering 200 (it is served by axum, not the engine), so an orchestrator will not restart it. That matches the finding's "two requests were still running at 120 s" with --workers 2.

The stated trade-off covers only the visual comparison; nothing in docs/DECISIONS.md or README.md mentions adversarial CPU cost of modification detection. The README's "hostile file attacking the process" guard (README.md:512) concerns snapshot deserialization only.

Actionable locally. pdfObjFactory() (DssEngine.java:453-458) already customises the factory (setPdfDifferencesFinder), so a bounded or threshold-skipping PdfObjectModificationsFinder can be set there, and dss-server could add a per-request wall-clock bound. Impact lens: the claimed impact (a small PDF occupying a validation worker for a long time) is real in this system and nothing documented or implemented neutralises it.

Code shape confirmed (upstream DSS 6.5.1 sources from ~/.m2, extracted to the scratchpad): DefaultPdfDifferencesFinder.getAnnotationOverlaps (dss-pades, line 83) loops for (int pageNumber = 1; pageNumber <= reader.getNumberOfPages(); pageNumber++) and calls reader.getPdfAnnotations(pageNumber). For a flat /Kids array chosen by the document author, page i costs O(i), so the scan is O(N²) with N the page count; the file author controls the tree shape, so worst case applies. It runs from AbstractPDFSignatureService.getModificationDetection (line 1000) once per signature revision and once per document-timestamp revision (lines 930-936), each time on the same finalRevisionReader, so the repeated work is pure recomputation of an identical result.

Project side: DssEngine.java:455-457 constructs DefaultPdfDifferencesFinder and only calls setMaximalPagesAmountForVisualComparison(0); docs/DECISIONS.md:112-114 says "Object-level modification detection between revisions stays on (it does not render)". The decision addresses rendering/AWT cost and says nothing about page-count cost, so this is not a documented trade-off for this behaviour. No page cap exists anywhere (the only getNumberOfPages call in the project is Placement.java:66, for visible-signature placement). dss-server has no per-request timeout (the only timeout in rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:189-193 is the 3 s --health-check probe); --workers defaults to CPUs and "more wait in a queue" (docs/server.md:46). docs/server.md:224-229 bounds memory (--max-request-mb, --max-heap) but nothing bounds CPU time per request.

Threat model: docs/server.md:224 and DECISIONS.md:857 place the sidecar on the same host or a private network, which makes the *clients* trusted, but the documents a client forwards are signed files from third parties, which is the service's purpose; README.md:519 shows the project does treat "a hostile file attacking the process" as in scope. docs/native-library.md:181 sets the expectation "A validation: tens of milliseconds"; the reporter's figures (20,000 pages / 231 KB → 17 s, growing quadratically, times the number of signature and timestamp revisions) are three orders of magnitude off that, and with CPUs-many such uploads every worker is busy and every other client's validations queue behind them. I did not re-run the timings myself, hence the moderate confidence; the quadratic structure is established from the code.

Calibration: medium, as reported. It is availability only (no crash, no memory blow-up, the request eventually completes), requires the host application to accept arbitrary PDFs (typical for a validation service), and legitimate documents of a few thousand pages are still handled in about a second. It is actionable in this repository without touching upstream: the project already subclasses PdfBoxNativeObjectFactory (AwtFreePdfObjFactory), so a DefaultPdfDifferencesFinder subclass that walks PDPageTree once (iterator) instead of get(i) per page, or a page cap, can be installed at DssEngine.java:455. Correction to the title: the per-page resolution happens twice per page, and the scan repeats per signature *and* per document timestamp on the same final reader, so its result could also be computed once per document.

F-272MediumreliabilityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:170

The online TL FileCacheDataLoader has no cache predicate, so a non-empty, non-XML HTTP 200 body replaces the good cache file. The running engine keeps the old lists and reports completed=true, but the next offline load (restart) drops that list, or all lists when it is the LOTL.

The online FileCacheDataLoader has no cache predicate, so any non-empty HTTP 200 body is written to disk before XmlDownloadTask checks it is XML. Memory keeps the old results, so the refresh reports completed=true. The next offline load drops the list.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

No signature or attack is needed: a captive portal, a CDN error page or a truncated transfer is enough, and so is any on-path party, since TLS is off by default. It hits every national TL as well as the LOTL, and is silent until restart. Distinct from F-180 (badly signed LOTL) and F-014 (interrupted write).

Evidence

Harness: `hostile refresh: completed=true certs=3` / `cache file size now=31 content=not xml at all: 502 Bad Gateway` / `after restart (offline cache load): certs=0`. Native: IT.xml rewritten to 1187 bytes; next process `1 trusted certificates`, IT 'NOT USED'. FileCacheDataLoader.getDocument writes before assertDocumentIsValidXML.

Impact

After one bad response the service looks healthy, then at the next restart loses a country's or all trust anchors for up to a refresh period.

Recommendation

Set a cache predicate (XML preamble plus isDOM, or a TrustServiceStatusList root check). Better, stage downloads and promote them only after successful parsing and signature validation (also fixes F-180 and F-014). Add a regression test.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-trust)

TlDocumentCheck (StAX, secure, no DTD) runs on every download before anything is staged and on every cached file before DSS reads it: must be well-formed XML with root {http://uri.etsi.org/02231/v2#}TrustServiceStatusList. A 200 with an error page is a download error of that list; memory keeps DSS's last good parse (completed=true, download.status=ERROR with the reason) and the cache file is untouched.

After review: TlCacheLoader.Online.getDocument: in the online_cache_expiration_ms > 0 branch a DSSException from the cached copy (torn/foreign file, or a rollback refusal) is logged at debug and the method falls through to the download. Test: TrustedListTest.garbageInAFreshCacheFileIsReplacedDespiteTheCacheExpiration (expiry one hour: a fresh copy is not re-downloaded; garbage written into it is re-downloaded and promoted, list SYNCHRONIZED, 3 anchors).

Test: TrustedListTest.nonXmlResponseIsReportedAndDoesNotReachTheCache (IT and LOTL cases, restart from cache still loads 3), TlDocumentCheckTest.nonXmlAndForeignRootsAreRejected

TrustedListManager.java:170-173 builds the online loader as FileCacheDataLoader online = new FileCacheDataLoader(); online.setCacheExpirationTime(...); online.setDataLoader(httpLoader); online.setFileCacheDirectory(tlCache.toFile()); and never calls setCachePredicate. It shares the tl/ directory with the offline loader at lines 165-168, which never expires (-1).

In DSS 6.5.1, FileCacheDataLoader.getDocument (dss-service sources, around lines 286-297) reads bytes = dataLoader.get(url), then else if (toBeCached(bytes)) { final File out = createFile(fileName, bytes); ...}. toBeCached returns true when cachePredicate == null ("No cache predicate is defined. Cache the retrieved data."). Only afterwards does XmlDownloadTask.java:69/85 run assertDocumentIsValidXML / DomUtils.isDOM. So the bad body is already on disk when it is rejected.

run() (TrustedListManager.java ~281-296) only reports failure when the whole job throws. Per-list download errors are recorded by DSS, and the record is completed=true with staging.getNumberOfCertificates(). That matches the claim that it "reports success" while memory keeps the previous results. On restart, offlineRefresh reads the non-XML file and the list is lost. The finding's own harness and native run show this (certs 3 -> 0).

Two corrections to the severity framing:

  1. The trigger is narrower than stated. DSS's CommonsDataLoader rejects non-200 statuses by default, so a real 502 response is not cached. Only a 200 response with a non-XML body is: a captive portal, a misbehaving proxy, or an on-path party. TLS verification for TL downloads is off by default (DECISIONS.md ~line 192), which makes the on-path case reachable. A truncated transfer usually fails on content-length rather than being cached.
  2. The impact is availability only, not trust injection. Signature checks (ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy) still block forged lists. The loss lasts until the next successful online refresh after restart, or the operator notices TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED / zero certs.

So: network attack vector, no privileges, but it needs an on-path or misconfigured network plus a restart, has a delayed and recoverable availability impact, and is silent. That is medium rather than high. The recommendation (set a cache predicate, or stage and promote only after validation) is concrete and actionable.
