F-274MediumcorrectnessFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:177

PAdES external signing at LT/LTA (and T in cms mode) on a PDF whose earlier signature is broken, or has an expired certificate with no POE, passes prepare and fails only at complete, after the external signature is spent

prepare never examines the PDF's existing signatures, but DSS's augmentation at complete re-checks every signature with throwing alerts. In signature_value mode T succeeds; in cms mode T fails.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Contradicts README.md:421 and DECISIONS.md:722 ('no external signature is spent on a document complete would refuse'). Co-signing a PDF whose first signer's certificate has expired is an ordinary case.

Evidence

`two-sigs-second-expired cms-LT: COMPLETE SIGNING_FAILED: ... Expired signature found`; `sv-T: OK`; `two-sigs-second-tampered cms-LT/sv-LT/cms-LTA/cms-T: COMPLETE SIGNING_FAILED ... Cryptographic signature verification has failed`; all passed prepare.

Impact

Remote or QES signatures, often paid or OTP-confirmed, are wasted, and callers cannot tell this case from a bad CMS.

Recommendation

At prepare for LT/LTA (and for T in cms mode), validate the existing signatures and refuse with the offending id. Alternatively, align cms-mode T with signature_value mode. Document and test this.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-signing)

ExternalSigning.prepare now runs assertExistingSignaturesExtendable for PAdES whenever complete will extend the PDF (mode cms at T; both modes at LT/LTA): it parses the PDF's existing signatures with PDFDocumentAnalyzer and runs the same PAdESSignatureRequirementsChecker assertions DSS's PAdESLevelBaselineT runs at complete (assertExtendToTLevelPossible, assertSignaturesValid, assertSigningCertificateIsValid) with the same verifier and alerts and without fetching revocation data (DSS's checker uses an offline verifier copy because checkCertificateRevocation defaults to false, so this mirrors complete exactly). A refusal is SIGNING_FAILED 'the PDF's existing signatures cannot be extended to <level> together with the new one, so complete would refuse it: <DSS reason with signature id>'. The LT chain/revocation assertion is deliberately not pre-run (needs the network; prepare is documented as offline). In signature_value mode at T nothing is extended, so nothing is pre-checked (documented asymmetry, see F-275). Test: aPdfWhoseExistingSignaturesCompleteWouldRefuseIsRefusedAtPrepare (tampered/pades/b-b.pdf refused at cms-T/LT/LTA and sv-LT/LTA, accepted at cms-B and sv-T; pades/b-b.pdf co-signed at LT with both signatures validating LT).

After review: Same Javadoc handoff as F-025: already applied.

After review: assertExistingSignaturesExtendable now mirrors DSS's choice of assertions. One correction to the reviewer's case (2): in mode cms the newly embedded signature is itself at B when extendDocument runs, so PAdESLevelBaselineT.isTLevelExtensionRequired is true and DSS takes the T path at LT/LTA regardless of the existing signatures; only mode signature_value (where PAdESService puts the signature timestamp inside the new CMS) can take the pure LT path. confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.85

The finding is accurate. Only the severity is overstated.

Mechanism, from the code. prepare (ExternalSigning.java:109-130) never looks at the PDF's existing signatures:

  • In cms mode it only calls externalCmsService().getMessageDigest(...).
  • In signature_value mode it only calls padesService().getDataToSign(...).

complete then hands the document to DSS, which embeds the signature and extends every signature in the PDF:

  • cms mode: service.signDocument(doc, padesParameters(o, visible), new InMemoryDocument(der)) at line 177. The comment there says DSS "embeds the CMS, then extends unless the level is B, or T and the CMS already has its timestamp".
  • signature_value mode: service.signDocument(doc, parameters, value) at line 149.

README.md:349-352 already states that when DSS extends, it refuses if "a signature or timestamp does not verify" or if "a certificate is revoked, expired or not yet valid". That refusal now happens inside complete.

The behaviour was confirmed empirically in the reporter's harness log (scratchpad/edgepdf/harness2.log, lines 41-56):

  • two-sigs-second-expired:
  • cms-T, sv-LT, cms-LTA: "COMPLETE SIGNING_FAILED ... Expired signature found ... The signing certificate has expired and there is no POE"
  • sv-T: OK
  • two-sigs-second-tampered:
  • cms-T, sv-LT, cms-LTA: "Cryptographic signature verification has failed"
  • sv-T: OK
  • B level works in every case.

All of these failures happen at the COMPLETE step, not at PREPARE. The cms-mode T vs signature_value T asymmetry is real: cms-mode T extends the whole PDF with a document timestamp, while signature_value T only timestamps the new signature.

Documentation contradiction: DECISIONS.md:721-722 says "no external signature is spent on a document complete would refuse". In context that sentence is about the signing certificate's validity (README.md:421-422 is limited to that), but as worded it is broader than what the code guarantees. The finding's citations are therefore fair.

Corrections:

  • Line 177 is right for cms mode. The signature_value path fails at line 149.
  • "Expired certificate" applies only when the earlier signature has no POE (proof of existence: a timestamp or archive data proving it existed before the certificate expired), i.e. a B-level signature. A timestamped earlier signature would not trip this check.

Severity calibration, high lowered to medium:

  • There is no security or integrity impact. Nothing invalid is produced, and the failure is loud (SIGNING_FAILED with DSS's reason and the offending signature id), not silent.
  • The cost is a wasted, possibly paid or OTP-confirmed, external signature.
  • In cms mode the same CMS can probably be completed again at B, since the digest does not depend on the level. That partially mitigates it, though I did not verify it.
  • Callers can work around it by validating the PDF first.
  • Likelihood: co-signing a document whose earlier B-level signature has an expired certificate is plausible in normal use. A tampered earlier signature is rare.
  • Net: a correctness and usability defect plus a documentation over-claim, which fits medium rather than high.

In DSS 6.5.1 PAdESWithExternalCMSService.getMessageDigest is just pdfSignatureService.messageDigest(toSignDocument, parameters) (dss-pades sources, lines 150-157); nothing validates the signatures already in the PDF. The external signature is NOT wasted. padesParameters (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:393-412) feeds the level only through p.setSignatureLevel(o.level.pades), which does not enter the signature dictionary or the signed attributes. My experiment (scratchpad/f274/src/F274.java, run against the project's compiled classes and TestEngines) shows prepare's digest is byte-identical for B, T, LT and LTA with the same signing_time and options, in both modes ("cms prepare digests: {B=1TPUp7..., T=1TPUp7..., LT=1TPUp7..., LTA=1TPUp7...} allEqual=true"; same for signature_value). Re-running completeSignature with the SAME external CMS / signature value and the same signing_time but level: "B" succeeds on both corpus PDFs ("cms reuse same external output at B: OK PAdES-BASELINE-B -> 3 sigs: TOTAL_PASSED/null TOTAL_FAILED/HASH_FAILURE TOTAL_PASSED/null"), and in signature_value mode level: "T" succeeds too. So the paid/OTP-confirmed signature is fully recoverable by the caller: complete again at B (or sv-T) with what the signer already returned. Nothing is lost.
  1. The caller CAN tell this case from a bad CMS. The checked-CMS refusals carry their own messages ("the CMS signs the digest ... not this document's", "the CMS has no message-digest attribute", ExternalSigning.java:214-262), while this case carries DSS's augmentation message naming the offending existing signature id ("Error on signature augmentation [S-7345B50C...: The signing certificate has expired and there is no POE..."). docs/DECISIONS.md:728-730 documents exactly this: SIGNING_FAILED "covers an unusable external result, an invalid certificate at prepare, and DSS failing to add a level ... These all mean 'this signature cannot be completed as asked', and the message says which."
  1. The behaviour is consistent with documented intent. README.md:355-359: "DSS checks the signatures first. It refuses (EXTENSION_FAILED...) when: a signature or timestamp does not verify; a certificate is revoked, expired or not yet valid; ..."; README.md:415-416 says LT/LTA in signing "adds the certificates and revocation data like dss_extend"; DECISIONS.md:635-638 "DSS's default CertificateVerifier alerts are kept." DECISIONS.md:714-716 documents the cms-mode mechanism that makes T differ ("PAdESWithExternalCMSService.signDocument embeds and then extends"). A PDF whose earlier signature is tampered or has an expired certificate without POE cannot be brought to LT by any path (ext-T/ext-LT/ext-LTA fail identically in the corpus log), so refusing is correct; the only question is when, and the caller has dss_validate (the corpus shows the input validates as TOTAL_FAILED/HASH_FAILURE or INDETERMINATE before signing) plus the B-level retry.
  1. Doing the check at prepare would break a documented property: DECISIONS.md:719-721 "prepare and B/T complete need none [trusted lists]: nothing is validated against trust anchors" and DssEngine.java:329 "Needs no network and no trusted lists"; detecting "expired with no POE" requires the full validation/revocation pass that complete already does. Not a reasonable trade for a recoverable failure.

Residual, low-severity: DECISIONS.md:722-723 ("so no external signature is spent on a document complete would refuse") is phrased more broadly than README.md:428-429 (correctly scoped to the signing certificate), and the useful fact that prepare's digest is level-independent (so a refused LT/LTA complete can be re-completed at B with the same signer output) is undocumented. That is a documentation precision item, not a high-severity correctness defect, and does not match the finding as described (wasted signature, indistinguishable error).

F-004LowsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:255

A PDF whose page content is replaced by a post-signing incremental update still validates TOTAL_PASSED (dss-cli exit 0); the change surfaces only as a warning string

A PDF changed by an incremental update after signing still gets TOTAL_PASSED. DSS's default constraint.xml rates UndefinedChanges, DocMDP, FieldMDP and PdfVisualDifference as WARN, and the engine sets visual comparison to 0 pages.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The engine uses DSS's default policy only. Its warnings appear as plain strings next to TOTAL_PASSED, and the README does not tell integrators to treat them as failures.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:455-457 'differencesFinder.setMaximalPagesAmountForVisualComparison(0);'; constraint.xml:61-67 '<PdfVisualDifference Level="WARN"/> <DocMDP Level="WARN"/> <FieldMDP Level="WARN"/> <UndefinedChanges Level="WARN"/>'

Impact

Hosts that gate on TOTAL_PASSED accept PDFs (the shadow-attack class) whose content was changed after signing.

Recommendation

Ship a stricter PAdES policy, or add a 'modified_after_signing' flag to the summary, and document that warnings must be inspected and that visual comparison is off.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

Same change as F-256: modified_after_signing and changes_after_signing expose a post-signing content replacement (an undefined change) as structured data next to TOTAL_PASSED. The verdict is unchanged (decision kept: DSS default policy). Docs must tell integrators to gate on modified_after_signing too; Rust/PHP mirrors are handoffs.

After review: dss-server tests that use loopback servers set block_private_addresses false: tests/http.rs Server::refreshing (closed-port LOTL on 127.0.0.1) sets config.http = Some(Http { block_private_addresses: Some(false), .. }); tests/process.rs refresh_schedule_runs_logs_and_retries passes the new --allow-private-addresses flag and asserts no 'refused by policy' line reaches stderr (the closed port is attempted and refuses the connection). A new process test private_addresses_are_refused_by_default shows the default against the rebuilt library: the library logs outbound request to http://127.0.0.1:<port>/eu-lotl.xml refused by policy: 127.0.0.1 is a loopback address, the refresh ends with 0 trusted certificates, /health reports trusted_lists_loaded false.

After review: Late handoff (http.block_private_addresses now defaults to true): no change needed in php/ or in the docs/server.md PHP section. The PHP client only talks HTTP to dss-server and never builds library config. The PHP section shows no TSA, LOTL, CRL or OCSP config on a loopback or private address. Its 127.0.0.1 stand-in server (tests/fixtures/router.php) is reached by Guzzle, not by the library, so the new policy does not affect it. The PHP suite still passes.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.85

REPRODUCED. Code facts: DssEngine.java:442-446 builds a plain new PDFDocumentValidator(doc) and :255 calls validator.validateDocument() with no setValidationPolicy, so DSS 6.5.1's bundled policy/constraint.xml applies (docs/DECISIONS.md:201 "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now."). That file (dss-policy-jaxb-6.5.1.jar, lines 58-67) has <PdfPageDifference Level="FAIL"/> but <PdfVisualDifference Level="WARN"/> <DocMDP Level="WARN"/> <FieldMDP Level="WARN"/> <UndefinedChanges Level="WARN"/>. DssEngine.java:456 sets differencesFinder.setMaximalPagesAmountForVisualComparison(0) (documented at DECISIONS.md:112-114). ValidationResult.java:73-78 copies report.getIndication(id) and the warning texts verbatim; there is no derived flag.

Experiment (scratchpad /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f004/append_update.py): appended an incremental update to testdata/fixtures/pades/b-lta.pdf and b-lt.pdf that redefines object 6 (the page's content stream) so the visible text becomes "ALTERED AFTER SIGNING: you now owe 1,000,000 EUR.", then ran rust/target/release/dss-cli validate --offline-revocation --trust testdata/fixtures/pki/root-ca.pem --allow-without-trusted-lists --json. Results: original b-lta.pdf -> TOTAL_PASSED, exit 0. Modified b-lta.pdf -> indication: TOTAL_PASSED, sub_indication: None, exit 0, warnings: ['The document contains undefined object modifications after the signature revision!', ...]. Same for b-lt. The detailed report shows the check BBB_FC_DSCNUOM with Status WARNING. dss-cli's exit rule (main.rs:17 "0 success (for validate: every signature TOTAL_PASSED)") therefore returns success for a document whose visible content was changed after signing.

Corrections to the finding: (1) the visual-comparison setting is immaterial to the verdict: with comparison on, PdfVisualDifference is also WARN in the default policy, so TOTAL_PASSED would still result; the operative cause is the unchanged default policy plus the absence of any derived flag or documentation. (2) Whole-page additions/removals do FAIL (PdfPageDifference Level="FAIL"), so only object-level/content edits are affected. (3) This is upstream DSS default behaviour, and the policy choice is recorded in DECISIONS.md:201, but neither README.md (line 320 only shows "warnings": [] with no guidance) nor DECISIONS.md states the consequence that a modified document still passes; hosts gating on TOTAL_PASSED or on the CLI exit code accept it. Medium severity: real and demonstrable, but the signature itself is cryptographically intact and the modification is reported, just not in a field integrators are told to check.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Experiment (read-only, offline, same flags as rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs:18-30): I appended an incremental update to testdata/fixtures/pades/b-lta.pdf that replaces the page content stream (object 6) with "CONTENT REPLACED AFTER SIGNING", then ran dss-cli validate. Result: "indication": "TOTAL_PASSED", "warnings": ["The document contains undefined object modifications after the signature revision!", ...], process exit 0. The human output prints only "2 warning(s)" without the text. So the core claim (content swapped after signing still yields TOTAL_PASSED, with the only signal a free-text warning) is confirmed in this system.

Impact assessment:

  • Docs actively steer hosts to the verdict alone. docs/openapi.yaml:14 "A signature that fails validation is a 200 result: check signatures[].indication"; docs/server.md:86 "check each signatures[].indication"; docs/server.md:160 "$signature['indication']: TOTAL_PASSED, TOTAL_FAILED or INDETERMINATE"; README.md:316-320 shows "warnings": [] with no explanation. rust/dss/src/types.rs:52-55 all_passed() and rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:650-653 (exit 0 iff all_passed) ignore warnings; main.rs:17 documents "0 success (for validate: every signature TOTAL_PASSED)". Nothing in README.md, docs/DECISIONS.md, docs/server.md or docs/native-library.md says that a TOTAL_PASSED PDF may have been modified after signing or that warnings must be inspected. For a sidecar validating documents from untrusted parties, a host following these docs accepts the modified document, so the impact is real, not stylistic.
  • The decision is only partly documented. docs/DECISIONS.md:201 records "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now." but states no trade-off about post-signing modifications. This is DSS's upstream default (constraint.xml:64-67 in dss-policy-jaxb-6.5.1: DocMDP/FieldMDP/UndefinedChanges WARN) and matches ETSI semantics (the signature is valid for its revision), so the engine itself is not defective; the gap is in the API/CLI ergonomics and documentation.

Corrections to the finding:

  • Visual comparison off (DssEngine.java:456) is not a contributing factor. constraint.xml:63 <PdfVisualDifference Level="WARN"/> — enabling it would add another WARN, never change TOTAL_PASSED; and object-level detection (documented at DECISIONS.md:112-114 as intentionally kept on, with the AWT/native-image trade-off stated) already produced the "undefined object modifications" warning in my experiment. That part is a documented, reasonable decision.
  • "Ship a stricter PAdES policy" is not clearly reasonable: UndefinedChanges=FAIL would reject many legitimately post-processed PDFs. The actionable part is: document that TOTAL_PASSED can coexist with post-signing modifications and that warnings (or the simple report) must be inspected, expose it as a structured field, and have dss-cli print warning text / consider the exit code.

Severity calibrated to low: behaviour equals upstream DSS and the standard, the signal is present in the warnings field and XML reports, and the fix is documentation plus a structured flag rather than an engine change; but the docs' explicit "check indication" guidance and the CLI's exit 0 make it a real, actionable gap rather than a non-issue.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

The facts in the finding are accurate. Its severity is overstated.

Confirmed:

  • In java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java, pdfObjFactory() at lines 453-459 does differencesFinder.setMaximalPagesAmountForVisualComparison(0); on line 456. Its javadoc says visual comparison is off and that "Object-level modification detection between revisions stays on".
  • The bundled policy is dss-policy-jaxb-6.5.1.jar, policy/constraint.xml. Lines 61-67 read <PdfPageDifference Level="FAIL" />, <PdfAnnotationOverlap Level="WARN" />, <PdfVisualDifference Level="WARN" />, <DocMDP Level="WARN" />, <FieldMDP Level="WARN" />, <SigFieldLock Level="WARN" /> and <UndefinedChanges Level="WARN" />. Lines 367-373 repeat these for the counter-signature section.
  • docs/DECISIONS.md:201 says "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now."
  • The README result example (around README.md:316-320) shows indication: TOTAL_PASSED with warnings: []. It does not say warnings must be inspected.
  • So an incremental update after signing that keeps the page count still yields TOTAL_PASSED, with the modification reported only in warnings.

Corrections and calibration:

  1. This is upstream DSS behaviour, not something the project introduced. Any DSS deployment on the default policy gives the same verdict. The only local change is that visual comparison is off. That is a documented decision (DECISIONS.md:112, "PDF visual comparison is off ... Object-level modification detection between revisions stays on"). Even with visual comparison on, the result would only add another WARN under this policy, so the verdict would not change.
  2. Not every change is a warning: PdfPageDifference is FAIL, so adding or removing pages after signing does fail.
  3. Exploiting this needs a host that gates only on indication and ignores warnings. The data needed to reject such a PDF is already in the result.

Real impact is therefore an integrator-guidance and hardening gap on top of standard DSS semantics, not a vulnerability. Fair severity is low, at most low-medium.

The recommendation to document that warnings must be inspected, or to add a modified-after-signing flag, is actionable. The location (DssEngine.java:456) and the mechanism are precise enough for a maintainer to act on.

F-005LowsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssJsonApi.java:245

log_level 'debug' writes the TSA HTTP Basic credentials to stderr via both the http.headers and http.wire loggers

applyLogLevel sets the default level for every logger. At DEBUG, HttpClient 5 logs request headers, including the preemptive Authorization: Basic header sent to the TSA.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

tsaLoader enables preemptive authentication, and DefaultManagedHttpClientConnection logs every request header when org.apache.hc.client5.http.headers is at debug. The README does not warn about this.

Evidence

DssJsonApi.java:244-246 sets org.slf4j.simpleLogger.defaultLogLevel; DssEngine.java:139-141 'loader.addAuthentication(...); loader.setPreemptiveAuthentication(true);'; httpclient5 'HEADER_LOG.debug("{} >> {}", this.id, header)'

Impact

Debug logging leaks the TSA password into log pipelines.

Recommendation

Pin the http.headers and http.wire loggers to info whatever level is requested, and document the risk.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

DssJsonApi.applyLogLevel pins org.slf4j.simpleLogger.log.org.apache.hc.client5.http.headers and ...http.wire to info before the default level is set, whatever log_level says, so the preemptive Authorization: Basic header to the TSA is never logged.

After review: DssJsonApiTest.reInitReplacesTheEngine now also asserts behaviour, not only the system properties: after an init with log_level debug, a logger created under each SECRET_BEARING_LOGGERS name (<name>.after-init, created after init so slf4j-simple reads the property) has isDebugEnabled()==false; as a positive control a logger under it.codingduck.dssnative has isDebug/isWarn/isErrorEnabled matching the level in force (the one init reports). No production change.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The finding is accurate. Severity should be low, not medium.

The mechanism holds up in the code:

  • DssJsonApi.java:39 calls applyLogLevel(config.logLevel). EngineConfig.java:145 reads log_level as a free string, defaulting to "warn".
  • applyLogLevel (DssJsonApi.java:243-248) runs System.setProperty("org.slf4j.simpleLogger.defaultLogLevel", level) when the property is unset, and sends the log to System.err.
  • Nothing pins the org.apache.hc.client5.http.headers or org.apache.hc.client5.http.wire loggers to a higher level.
  • DssEngine.java tsaLoader calls loader.addAuthentication(..., config.tsaUsername, config.tsaPassword); loader.setPreemptiveAuthentication(true);, so the Basic Authorization header is on the first request.
  • httpclient5 5.6.5 sources, DefaultManagedHttpClientConnection.java:65 and :208-212, define HEADER_LOG = LoggerFactory.getLogger("org.apache.hc.client5.http.headers") and, when debug is enabled, run for (final Header header : headers) { HEADER_LOG.debug("{} >> {}", this.id, header); }. Nothing is redacted.
  • The wire logger at :183 would also dump the raw bytes.
  • README.md:289 says only "log_level": "warn", // slf4j-simple level, logs go to stderr, with no warning about credentials.

Minor precision fix: the method starts at line 243 (the finding says 245, inside its body). "trace" triggers the leak as well as "debug".

Why low and not medium:

  • The leak only happens when whoever writes the engine config explicitly sets a non-default diagnostic level. The default is "warn", and the pom pins "warn" for tests.
  • The credential belongs to that same operator, and it is written to their own process's stderr. No remote or unprivileged attacker can trigger it.
  • The exposure is secondary: debug logs end up in shared log pipelines or bug reports, and a TSA account gets abused. That is a real hardening and documentation gap, but it needs an operator action plus a separate log-access exposure.

In CVSS-like terms: local or adjacent access, needs high privileges or a config change, confidentiality impact limited to a TSA credential, low likelihood in normal use.

The code reads as the finding says (ValidationResult.java:72 for (String id : report.getSignatureIdList()); only signatures is summarized, toMap() at lines 103-123 emits no timestamp array). Through the impact lens, though, the claimed consequences do not hold in this system.

  1. Scope and accuracy. README.md:7 states the library "Validates CAdES ... and PAdES signatures". A document timestamp is not a signature, so signatures: [] for a PDF with zero signatures is a correct statement, not a misclassification. The field is named signatures, not verdicts.
  1. The verdict fails safe. rust/dss/src/types.rs:52-55: pub fn all_passed(&self) -> bool { let all = self.all_signatures(); !all.is_empty() && all.iter().all(|s| s.indication == Indication::TotalPassed) }. A timestamp-only document therefore yields false, and dss-cli exits 1 (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:650-654). The sidecar contract tells hosts to check each signatures[].indication (docs/server.md:85-86; php/DssClient.php:18), so a host sees no passed signature and does not accept the document. For documents from untrusted parties this is the conservative direction: nothing is accepted on the strength of a timestamp. There is no security or correctness exposure, only a missing convenience.
  1. The information is not hidden. README.md:300 "simple report is always included" and README.md:322 "simple_report_xml"; rust/dss/src/types.rs:32 pub simple_report_xml: String (non-optional). The finding's own probe confirms the Timestamp element with Indication PASSED and TimestampLevel QTSA is in that report. So "Consumers cannot see document timestamps, their verdict or their qualification" is false: they are in every result, just not in the summary array.
  1. For signed documents, which are the stated scope, timestamp effects already surface in the summary: format carries the level (e.g. PAdES-BASELINE-LTA, README.md:317), best_signature_time depends on timestamps (DECISIONS.md:993 "best_signature_time of two untimestamped signatures, which is the validation time"), and DSS folds timestamp validity into the signature's indication/sub-indication and warnings. The gap is confined to timestamp-only documents, which are outside what the library claims to validate.

Not a documented decision (DECISIONS.md and README.md say nothing about timestamp-only documents), so a timestamps array would be a reasonable enhancement, but the medium severity and the stated impact are not supported: the behaviour is accurate, fails safe, and the data is available in the always-returned simple report. Calibrated severity: low (API convenience / feature request).

I am lowering the severity to low:

  2. The failure is fail-safe. For a document that is only timestamped, reporting no signatures is factually true, and all_passed=false is conservative: nothing gets accepted wrongly.
  3. On signed documents, a failing signature or archive timestamp already affects the signature's own indication in DSS. A failing standalone document timestamp is not surfaced, but neither direction lets an attacker get a false PASS.

The file, line and recommendation are precise enough to act on.

TL alerts are appended on every refresh (tl_expired re-fires unconditionally) and never deduplicated or cleared; one-shot alerts like oj_url_changed can be evicted from the 100-entry ring

DSS re-runs detections on every refresh. A chronically late list adds one identical tl_expired entry per refresh until the 100-entry ring evicts unique alerts such as oj_url_changed.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Alerts are cleared only by importSnapshot, and the duplicates are also written into exported snapshots.

TrustedListManager.java:241-246 'alerts.add(a); if (alerts.size() > MAX_ALERTS) alerts.remove(0);'

Key alerts by (type, url) with first_seen, last_seen and count, or clear them at the start of each refresh.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-trust)

Alerts are keyed by (type, url): a repeat updates message, at, last_seen and count; entries carry first_seen/last_seen/count; the ring of 100 distinct keys evicts the oldest key. Snapshot import normalises older alert entries. Also added LOTL alerts lotl_signature_error, lotl_expired, lotl_structure_error (a badly signed LOTL raised no alert before) and tl_structure_error.

By contrast OJUrlChangeDetection and TLSignatureErrorDetection are gated on isDesynchronized(), which CachedEntry.update() sets only when new content is stored and synchronizeCertificateSources() resets, so oj_url_changed is effectively one-shot per LOTL content change and can indeed be evicted by the ring: with dss-server's default --refresh-hours 6 one late list fills 100 slots in ~25 days, several late lists faster. F-014LowreliabilityPartially fixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:170

DSS saveToFile truncates and rewrites cache files. A SIGKILL, a full disk, or a concurrent reader (re-init builds the new engine before closing the old one, or several processes share one cache_dir) sees a partial LOTL or TL, which is then dropped from trust.

Recommendation

Write to a temp file, fsync it and rename it atomically. Close or stop the old engine before re-init. Document that cache_dir must not be shared, or lock it.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package java-trust)

Cache writes are atomic (temp + fsync + rename), so SIGKILL or a full disk cannot leave a torn list in the cache; a garbage cache file is now a per-list download error, not a crash of the load. Not in this package: dss-server's shutdown deadline (rust-server) and DssJsonApi.init closing the previous engine only after creating the new one (java-engine). Shared cache_dir: see F-212.

(2) In dss-server with the default schedule a damaged LOTL yields loaded=false, so RefreshScheduler::spawn(engine, every, !loaded) (main.rs:155, schedule.rs:43-51) starts an online refresh at once and overwrites the bad file; "comes up with no trust" is a transient ~15 s window identical to the documented empty-cache first start, not a stuck state. (3) The re-init concurrent-reader path (DssJsonApi.java:40-48 creates before previous.close()) is reachable only via the Java API: the Rust crate calls dss_init once per isolate (engine.rs:575). Sharing one cache_dir between processes is neither documented nor forbidden. The in-place write is upstream DSS behaviour the project inherits; a fix would be overriding FileCacheDataLoader.createFile with temp+fsync+rename, plus a shutdown deadline or a documented stop_grace_period. Given the self-heal in dss-server, the visibility in status, and the narrow window for a kill to land inside a single small write, severity is low rather than medium.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

MECHANISM (confirmed, not just assumed). DSS 6.5.1 dss-spi DSSUtils.java:790-793: saveToFile does Files.newOutputStream(file.toPath()) on the final cache path and copies into it: no temp file, no fsync, no rename. FileCacheDataLoader.java:397-401 createFile calls it for every downloaded LOTL/TL, and getDocument (lines 262-309) returns new FileDocument(out) from that same path. This repo wires both loaders to the same directory (TrustedListManager.java:165-173 offline.setFileCacheDirectory(tlCache.toFile()) / online.setFileCacheDirectory(tlCache.toFile())), with the online expiry defaulting to 0 (DECISIONS.md:70-72, "default 0 (always refetch)"), so every online refresh truncates and rewrites every cached list in place.

TRIGGER PLAUSIBILITY. The SIGKILL scenario is credible in this system: rust/dss/src/engine.rs:428-436 (impl Drop for Engine: "the refresh thread finishes a running refresh first" and t.join()), dss-server/src/lib.rs:84-89 and main.rs:172-177 block shutdown on a running refresh; a full-LOTL refresh takes ~10-15 s (DECISIONS.md:884-885 "9.7 s", server.md:20 "about 15 s"); neither docker/dss-server/Dockerfile nor the compose example in server.md:183-206 sets a stop grace period, so Docker's 10 s default can SIGKILL mid-refresh. However the truncated state only exists between open-with-truncate and close of one file (a few MB from memory to local disk, milliseconds), so the per-kill probability is on the order of 0.1-1 %, not "often". The re-init race (DssJsonApi.java:40-48 creates before previous.close()) is real but only reachable through the C API in one isolate; the Rust layer makes one isolate per Engine. Shared cache_dir between processes is nowhere suggested: server.md:3 and lib.rs:5 describe one engine per server, and the compose example gives the single container its own volume.

IMPACT, CORRECTED. (1) Security: none. A truncated XML fails parsing/signature validation and ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy (TrustedListManager.java:185-190) drops it; nothing is injected. (2) "Service comes up with no trust" (truncated LOTL): in dss-server this is transient and health-gated. main.rs:144-155 RefreshScheduler::spawn(..., !loaded) starts an online refresh immediately when loaded is false (schedule.rs:41-52), which re-downloads and overwrites the damaged file; /health reports trusted_lists_loaded, and validations meanwhile fail closed with TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED (DECISIONS.md:98). With --refresh-hours 0 the server logs "POST /tl/refresh loads them" (main.rs:166-167). So the LOTL case behaves exactly like a first start from an empty cache. (3) "A list may silently go missing" (one truncated national TL): this part survives. loaded stays true (other lists' certificates), so no immediate refresh; the list stays missing until the next scheduled refresh (default 6 h, server.md:40) or, for an embedded host that owns its own schedule (DECISIONS.md:72-73), until the host refreshes. It is visible in tl_status (used_for_trust, parsing error per list, TrustedListManager.java:490-520) but not in /health; affected signatures come back INDETERMINATE rather than wrongly accepted. A full disk produces the same partial file deterministically rather than probabilistically.

VERDICT. Not documented as a decision (DECISIONS.md "Trusted lists" section covers in-memory concurrency only, lines 74-83), no test covers a damaged cache file (only corrupt documents, DssJsonApiTest.java:138-155), and the fix is cheap and actionable in this repo (override the public FileCacheDataLoader.createFile to write temp+fsync+rename, and/or document a stop grace period). But the stated impact is overstated: the sidecar self-heals the LOTL case, everything is fail-closed, the trigger window is milliseconds, and the residual is a bounded trust gap for one country after a rare crash. Calibrated severity: low, not medium.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

Mechanism confirmed. In DSS 6.5.1 (dss-spi sources from ~/.m2), DSSUtils.java:790-797 saveToFile does Files.newOutputStream(file.toPath()). That uses the default CREATE+TRUNCATE_EXISTING+WRITE, with no temp file, fsync or rename. FileCacheDataLoader.createFile calls it for every downloaded LOTL/TL. TrustedListManager.java:164-172 points both the offline loader (setCacheExpirationTime(-1)) and the online loader at the same tlCache directory, so a torn file written by an online refresh is exactly what the next offline load reads. DssJsonApi.java:40-48 builds DssEngine.create(...) (an offline load from that directory) before previous.close(). The refreshLock (TrustedListManager.java:119) belongs to each manager instance, so it does not serialize the new engine's load against the old engine's refresh. Nothing locks cache_dir between processes. I found no atomic-write handling or shared-cache_dir guidance in README or DECISIONS.

Severity is lower than medium:

  • The write window is small. The bytes are already in memory and the copy takes milliseconds, so a torn file needs a SIGKILL or crash at that moment, a full disk, or a concurrent re-init or second process.
  • The failure is fail-closed. A truncated LOTL or TL fails parsing or ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy, so trust is lost (availability: validations go indeterminate). No untrusted anchor gets injected.
  • It recovers on the next successful online refresh: online_cache_expiration_ms defaults to 0 (EngineConfig.java:105), so the online loader always downloads again and overwrites the torn file.
  • Not attacker-triggerable. It needs local operational events.

So: real reliability or availability issue, local or operational vector, no integrity impact, low likelihood in normal single-process use. The cited line 170 is fine for where the shared cache dir is configured. The actual non-atomic write is in third-party DSS code (DSSUtils.saveToFile, called from FileCacheDataLoader.createFile), so the fix means overriding or wrapping the loader, or staging into a temp directory. The recommendation is still actionable.

F-016LowcorrectnessFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/EngineConfig.java:105

Numeric config not range-checked: negative online_cache_expiration_ms makes online refresh cache-only yet report success; HTTP timeouts cast to int unbounded (0 = no timeout, negative/overflowed = HttpClient system default)

DSS treats a negative cache expiration as 'never expires', so refreshes read only the cache and still report success. Timeouts are cast to int without bounds, so 0 means no timeout and large values overflow.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

FileCacheDataLoader.isCacheExpired returns false when the value is below 0. tl_threads is the only numeric key that is range-checked.

Evidence

EngineConfig.java:105 'onlineCacheExpirationMs = f.integer("online_cache_expiration_ms", 0);'; :114-115 '(int) http.integer("connect_timeout_ms", 30_000)'; FileCacheDataLoader.java:462-464

Impact

A configuration mistake silently freezes trusted lists or hangs network calls.

Recommendation

Reject negative expirations and out-of-range timeouts with INVALID_CONFIG, and document the semantics.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-trust)

online_cache_expiration_ms < 0 -> INVALID_CONFIG (a negative value would make online refreshes cache-only); connect_timeout_ms/response_timeout_ms must be 1..2147483647 (0 would mean no timeout, larger values overflowed the int cast).

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Reproduced by reading the code paths; the finding is real as described, with one nuance on negative timeouts.

EngineConfig.java:105 onlineCacheExpirationMs = f.integer("online_cache_expiration_ms", 0); and JsonFields.java:71-79 long integer(String key, long def) only checks v instanceof Long; no sign or range check. The only range-checked numeric is tl_threads (EngineConfig.java:106-109 if (threads < 1 || threads > 64) throw f.error(...)). The value is passed straight through at TrustedListManager.java:171 online.setCacheExpirationTime(config.onlineCacheExpirationMs);. In DSS 6.5.1 (dss-service-6.5.1-sources.jar, FileCacheDataLoader.java:462-464) private boolean isCacheExpired(File file) { if (cacheExpirationTime < 0) { return false; } ..., and getDocument (:273-283) returns new FileDocument(file) without calling dataLoader.get(url) whenever the file exists and is not expired. The project itself relies on exactly this semantics for the offline loader (TrustedListManager.java:166 offline.setCacheExpirationTime(-1); // never expires). So a negative online value turns the online loader into a cache-only loader once a cache exists. TrustedListManager.run (:280-295) records new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), true, null, ...) after job.onlineRefresh() returns normally, so the refresh reports success with no indication nothing was downloaded. README.md:274 documents only "0 = re-download on every online refresh"; negatives are not documented.
  1. Timeouts. EngineConfig.java:114-115 httpConnectTimeoutMs = (int) http.integer("connect_timeout_ms", 30_000); (same for response_timeout_ms) narrows a long to int with no bounds check; DssEngine.java:147-150 passes them to CommonsDataLoader.setTimeoutConnection/ConnectionRequest/Response/Socket. In CommonsDataLoader.java:1454-1460 toTimeoutMilliseconds(int millis) returns null for negatives ("Use system default") and otherwise Timeout.ofMilliseconds(millis); httpcore5 Timeout.java:58 DISABLED = ZERO_MILLISECONDS, so 0 disables the timeout (network call can hang indefinitely). A value >= 2^31 silently overflows: e.g. 2147483648 becomes Integer.MIN_VALUE, which DSS treats as "system default" rather than an error, and 4294967296 becomes 0 (no timeout). Nuance vs. the finding: negative/overflowed-negative timeouts do not hang, they silently fall back to HttpClient defaults; only 0 (directly or via overflow) removes the timeout.
  1. Reachability. The typed Rust API uses u64 (rust/dss/src/config.rs:30, :91-93) so it cannot emit negatives, but raw config_json is accepted as-is via EngineBuilder::with_config_json (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:41) and the CLI/server --config file (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:562, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:218), so negative or oversized values reach EngineConfig unchanged. No test in java/src/test or rust/ covers these keys with out-of-range values (grep found none).

Severity stays low: it requires an operator misconfiguration, is not attacker-reachable, and the cache-only behaviour is identical to what DSS documents for negative expiry; but the silent "success" on a frozen trusted-list refresh and the unbounded int cast are real and cheap to reject with INVALID_CONFIG as tl_threads already does.

F-018LowcorrectnessFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/Json.java:213

Json parser accepts non-conforming input: signed \u escapes, leading zeros, '1.', 1e999 (Infinity), lone surrogates, and duplicate keys (last wins); untested

Integer.parseInt(hex) accepts '+' and '-', and readNumber accepts any run of digit-like characters. Duplicate keys silently override earlier ones (for example accept_invalid_signature), and none of this is covered by tests.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Probes: '"\u+123"' parses to U+0123, '01' to 1, '1e999' to Infinity, and '{"a":1,"a":2}' to {a=2}.

Evidence

Json.java:208-217 'Integer.parseInt(s.substring(pos, pos + 4), 16)'; Json.java:140 'map.put(key, readValue(depth + 1));'

Impact

Malformed config and options are accepted, and parsers can disagree about duplicate security-relevant keys.

Recommendation

Validate hex digits, reject leading zeros, non-finite numbers and duplicate keys, and add tests.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

Json.parse is strict: duplicate object keys are a ParseException ('Duplicate key'); numbers must match RFC 8259 (no leading zeros, digits around '.', digits after the exponent) and non-finite doubles are rejected; \u escapes need exactly four hex digits (no sign) and a lone surrogate (escaped high without low, or a low alone) is rejected while a pair is kept. One existing test (SigningTest.preparingIsRepeatable) built options with a duplicate signing_time and was adjusted.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.95

Reproduced exactly as stated. I compiled java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/Json.java alone (it has no project dependencies) under GraalVM JDK 25 in the scratchpad and probed it; every listed input is accepted:

  • "\u+123" -> String U+0123 and "\u-001" -> U+FFFF. Cause: Json.java:213 sb.append((char) Integer.parseInt(s.substring(pos, pos + 4), 16)); — parseInt accepts a leading sign and no hex-digit check is done.
  • 01 -> Long 1, -01 -> Long -1, 1. -> Double 1.0, 1e999 -> Double Infinity. Cause: readNumber (Json.java:236-246) consumes any run of 0-9 . e E + - and hands it to Long.parseLong/Double.parseDouble (lines 250-252), which tolerate leading zeros, a trailing '.', and overflow to Infinity. The only number-shape check is the parse itself (1-2 is rejected).
  • {"a":1,"a":2} -> {a=2} and {"tl_sync":{"accept_invalid_signature":false,"accept_invalid_signature":true}} -> accept_invalid_signature=true. Cause: Json.java:140 map.put(key, readValue(depth + 1)); with no containsKey check.
  • "\ud800" -> a lone U+D800 is appended unchecked (line 213 again).

Tests: java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/JsonTest.java rejectsMalformedInput covers "01a" (rejected only because of trailing chars), none of the above cases, and no duplicate-key test exists; so the claim "none of this is covered by tests" holds. Intent: docs/DECISIONS.md:153 says "Unknown keys in config_json / options_json are errors, so typos fail loudly", i.e. the design intent is strictness, and nothing documents the leniency as a decision. Calibration (why low, not higher): the lenient path is reachable only from the Java/C API callers that hand raw JSON. The Rust API serializes typed structs with serde_json (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:36,151,178,209) and dss-server re-parses the options part with serde_json and re-serializes it (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:365-370, 178, 190), so duplicate keys collapse before reaching Java and both sides resolve them last-wins — the "parsers can disagree" impact is speculative in this codebase. JsonFields.integer (JsonFields.java:71-80) rejects Double, so 1e999 cannot reach integer config such as timeouts; Infinity can only reach VisibleSignature decimals (VisibleSignature.java:118-119,153,274). Net: real non-conformance in an operator-facing config/options parser with no test coverage, but no demonstrated security or correctness consequence beyond accepting malformed input.

Impact

Parse the TimeStampToken, check that its imprint matches the signature value and verify the TSA signature. Otherwise refuse, or strip it and add the engine's own timestamp. Add tests.

At LT the engine neutralises it: garbage -> accepted with tsaHitsAdded=1 (DSS adds a real signature timestamp before LT) and validates LT; wrong-imprint -> REFUSED SIGNING_FAILED … Broken timestamp(s) detected … Signature is not intact!. So the impact is confined to B and T.

Why not refuted on impact: docs/DECISIONS.md:715-717 and README.md:407-410 document the skip rule ("skips T when the CMS already has a signature timestamp"; "A timestamped CMS asked for at B is reported as T, the level it has") but do not state the presence-only trade-off, so a reader assumes a valid timestamp. DECISIONS.md:692 states the design intent "The external result is checked before anything is built, with reasons a caller can act on", and this is the one attribute that escapes that policy, so the finding is consistent with the project's own goals and actionable (parse the TimeStampToken, compare its imprint with the digest of the signature value, refuse with SIGNING_FAILED like the other checks).

Why low: the precondition is a bug in the host-chosen key holder (HSM/remote signing service, README.md:361), a trusted component that could sign anything anyway; untrusted parties supply documents, not the CMS. The output is still a valid signature (TOTAL_PASSED at B) with a wrong level label, never a broken document; dss_validate exposes the garbage case as B; LT/LTA repair or refuse; and upstream DSS behaves identically, so the project is not worse than the reference it mirrors (DECISIONS.md:413, :683). Severity: low, correctness/robustness gap with a clear, cheap fix.

The finding is accurate. I am keeping it (refuted=false) but lowering the severity to low.

Mechanism (confirmed in the code)

  • ExternalSigning.java:303-306 checks only that the attribute is present: return unsigned != null && unsigned.get(PKCSObjectIdentifiers.id_aa_signatureTimeStampToken) != null;
  • checkedCms (about :213-292) checks content-type, message-digest, the signing-certificate attribute, signing-time and the CMS signature. It never parses or verifies the timestamp token in the unsigned attributes.
  • CAdES: :192 extends only when o.level == Level.LT || o.level == Level.LTA || (o.level == Level.T && !timestamped). A junk token at T therefore skips the TSA.
  • PAdES: :175-177 hands the decision to DSS, as the comment says: "DSS embeds the CMS, then extends unless the level is B, or T and the CMS already has its timestamp."
  • Reported level: reached() at :207-210 turns B into T when timestamped is true. At T, the reported level is T whatever the token is.

The harness result in the finding (reported T, 0 TSA hits, validates as B) is consistent with this code.

Small precision note: the line-208 citation is right. The finding does not say that the PAdES skip happens inside DSS (PAdESWithExternalCMSService), not in this file. A maintainer fixing the PAdES path has to validate or strip the token before calling service.signDocument.

Severity: low, not medium

  • Not a third-party attack. The CMS comes from the caller's own chosen external signer, through complete. Unsigned attributes are not covered by the signature. Only whoever supplies the complete input can add or alter them, and that is the caller or the signer the caller trusts. No external attacker vector is shown.
  • Signature stays valid. Impact is integrity of the level label only. The signature still verifies, and any validator reports the true level (B). The harm is a mislabelled level and a missing long-term proof, not a forgery.
  • Unlikely in normal use. It needs a buggy or misbehaving external signer that emits a malformed token.
  • Matches DSS and is partly documented. It mirrors DSS's own presence-only check in isExtensionRequired. docs/DECISIONS.md:715-717 records the skip ("skips T when the CMS already has a signature timestamp ... A timestamped CMS asked for at B is reported as T"). However, that note does not say the token goes unverified.

Why it still stands: the project validates every other part of the external CMS, with "reasons a caller can act on", and leaves this one gap. A caller who asks for T can get a document labelled T that has no valid timestamp.

The recommendation is actionable: before deciding timestamped, parse the TimeStampToken, check that its imprint matches the signature value, and verify the token's signature. Otherwise refuse.

The docs set the expectation that this is covered. docs/DECISIONS.md:695 lists "signing-certificate(-v2)" among the checks, README.md:413 says "signing-certificate-v2", and checkedCms is meant to give "reasons a caller can act on".   • The code also accepts the v1 signing-certificate attribute, although the error message names only v2.
  • The fix needs to handle both ESSCertID (SHA-1) and ESSCertIDv2.

Severity calibration: I rate this low rather than medium.

  • Who can trigger it: only the caller's own configured external signer (HSM or remote signing service), during that caller's own prepare/complete flow. No attacker can inject the faulty CMS.
  • What goes wrong: the result fails closed. Every validator, including this project's own DSS validation, reports the document as INDETERMINATE. Nothing is accepted that should not be, and no integrity or authenticity property is broken.
  • Real impact: a misbehaving signer produces an unusable signature without an error at signing time, and the caller is told ok:true. It is found later instead of by the up-front check.
  • Likelihood in normal use: low, because conforming CMS signers compute this attribute correctly.

It is a real, actionable gap between the check and its documentation, but it is a correctness and usability issue, not a medium-severity security defect.

The mechanism is real, but the finding overstates the severity and the identity point.

What the code does

  • In ExternalSigning.java:118-123, cms-mode prepare returns early with externalCmsService().getMessageDigest(doc, padesParameters(o, visible)) or DSSUtils.digest(...). It does not call getDataToSign.
  • padesParameters (:409-412) attaches the certificate only when if (o.mode == Mode.SIGNATURE_VALUE) { p.setSigningCertificate(...). So a certificate passed in cms mode is never checked at prepare.
  • At complete, padesFromCms (:163-181) and cadesFromCms (:183-205) run checkedCms. Its only certificate-related checks are:
  • the signer's certificate is present (signerCertificate, :286-297);
  • it equals signing_certificate when one is given (:275-279);
  • the signature verifies cryptographically (:280-285).
  • No notBefore/notAfter check runs at B. For CAdES at B, no DSS service is called at all.

Why the documentation claim stands

The doc conflict is real. README.md:421 says "prepare refuses a signing certificate that is expired or not yet valid at the signing time". rust/dss/src/engine.rs:200-201 and rust/dss/src/error.rs:32 say the same, with no exception for cms mode.

DECISIONS.md:721-723 partly documents the gap: "In "cms" mode the certificate is only known from the result." That sentence is inaccurate when signing_certificate is supplied, because the certificate is then known at prepare and still not checked. It also does not say that complete skips the check.

Why medium overstates it

  • This is not an attack surface. The external signer is the caller's own trusted key holder, so there is no attacker-controlled path.
  • The worst outcome is wasted work: one external signature is spent on a document that validates as INDETERMINATE or fails. That shows up at once on validation.
  • "Signer identity never pinned" is weaker than stated. Callers can pin the signer by passing signing_certificate, and complete enforces it at :276. Making the field optional in cms mode is a design choice, and DECISIONS.md:723 explains it.

Calibrated severity: low. This is a documentation and correctness gap. The fix is either:

  • check validity at prepare (when signing_certificate is given) and at complete in cms mode, or
  • qualify README.md:421, engine.rs:200 and error.rs:32 for cms mode.

The file and line given in the finding (ExternalSigning.java:118) are accurate.

prepare accepts any content_size, and the overflow is detected only inside signDocument.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Harness: content_size 500 passed prepare, then complete failed with 'signature size [500] is too small ... [2255]'.

Evidence

ExternalSigning.java:124-128 has no size estimate

Impact

A paid or user-confirmed signature is wasted.

Recommendation

Estimate the CMS size at prepare and refuse with INVALID_ARGUMENT when it will not fit.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-signing)

In signature_value mode for PAdES, prepare (and complete, for symmetry) computes a lower bound of the CMS DSS will build: data-to-sign length + signature value length (RSA modulus bytes; a small bound for ECDSA) + DER length of the signing certificate and of the chain certificates that are not trust anchors (DSS leaves trust anchors out) + 64 bytes of CMS framing, and refuses INVALID_ARGUMENT when it exceeds pades.content_size ('pades.content_size is N bytes, but the CMS DSS builds around the signature value will be at least M (...): raise it, or leave the default 9472'). Remaining: the level-T signature timestamp inside the CMS is TSA-dependent and not part of the estimate, so a content_size that fits the B-level CMS but not the timestamp still fails at complete. cms mode is unchanged (the signer's CMS size is unknown at prepare; complete already checks before DSS).

After review: Same Javadoc handoff as F-025 (INVALID_ARGUMENT for a content_size the CMS cannot fit): already applied.

After review: The estimate now counts exactly the certificates DSS embeds: ExternalSigning.estimatedCmsSize runs DSS's own BaselineBCertificateSelector(parameters.getSigningCertificate(), parameters.getCertificateChain()).setTrustedCertificateSource(verifier.getTrustedCertSources()).setTrustAnchorBPPolicy(parameters.bLevel().isTrustAnchorBPPolicy()).getCertificates() (the same call CMSBuilder makes at complete), so the chain is walked from the signing certificate and stops at the first trust anchor, and certificates above it or off the path are not counted. The rest of the bound (data-to-sign length, RSA modulus bytes / small ECDSA bound, 64 bytes framing) is unchanged; assertContentSizeFits now takes the PAdESSignatureParameters. Verified against the pre-fix code: with chain [root (trusted), TL-signer (off path, untrusted)] the real CMS is 2255 bytes and the old estimate said 3269, so content_size 2255 was refused; it is accepted now. Still partial for the reason the earlier note gave: the level-T signature timestamp is outside the estimate (its size depends on the TSA), so at T the CMS can still fail to fit at complete (SIGNING_FAILED from DSS). Test: SigningTest#theContentSizeEstimateCountsOnlyTheCertificatesDssEmbeds (signs once generously, measures the DER CMS from /Contents, signs again with content_size equal to that length and validates; content_size reduced by the off-path certificate's length is INVALID_ARGUMENT at prepare). The fixture PKI has no trusted intermediate and TestPki is outside this package's ownership, so the reviewer's [signer, intermediate(trusted), root(untrusted)] shape is pinned through the equivalent off-path case instead (both go through the same selector path).

After review: Late handoff: nothing to change in the code. INVALID_ARGUMENT already exits 2 through the generic error path. The --content-size help now says that less than the estimated CMS needs is refused as INVALID_ARGUMENT (exit 2), by prepare and complete alike.

After review: Late handoff (java-signing): /sign/prepare and /sign/complete descriptions, the BadRequest response, the pades.content_size property and server.md's 'Signing' bullet and 400 row say that in mode signature_value a content_size the CMS cannot fit is INVALID_ARGUMENT (from prepare already, before the signer is asked), while a CMS that does not fit for a reason outside the estimate (the level-T timestamp) stays SIGNING_FAILED. No mapping change: INVALID_ARGUMENT was already 400.

After review: openapi.yaml /extend description: 'every signature is already at a higher level than the target' (was 'a signature is already at a higher level'); a B-level signature extended to LT needs the TSA too (it gets a timestamp first); a TSA that cannot be reached or answers badly is TSA_FAILED.

Test: SigningTest#aContentSizeTheCmsCannotFitIsRefusedAtPrepare (500 refused at prepare; 4000 signs and validates)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Confirmed from the code paths, without needing to re-run the harness.

  1. prepare has no size check in signature_value mode. java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:124-128 is just ToBeSigned tbs = ... padesService().getDataToSign(doc, padesParameters(o, visible)) ...; return new PreparedSignature(...). padesParameters (line 401) sets p.setContentSize(o.contentSizeOrDefault()) but nothing compares that number with anything. The only parsing constraint is SigningOptions.java:226-228: if (size < 1 || size > MAX_CONTENT_SIZE) throw p.error("'content_size' must be between 1 and ..."), so 500 is accepted.
  1. DSS itself only checks at sign time. In the extracted DSS 6.5.1 sources (the version in java/pom.xml:43), assertContentSizeSufficient (dss-pades AbstractPDFSignatureService.java:1045-1053, message "The signature size [%s] is too small for the signature value with a length [%s]") is called from exactly one place: PdfBoxSignatureService.signDocument at line 172. The digest path used by getDataToSign (computeDigest, lines 135-158, via PAdESService.getDataToSign lines 176-185 -> computeDocumentDigest -> messageDigest) never reaches it; it signs with DSSUtils.EMPTY_BYTE_ARRAY and returns the digest. So prepare succeeds with content_size 500, and only complete (ExternalSigning.java:149 service.signDocument(doc, parameters, value)) throws the IllegalArgumentException, which DssEngine.signingCall (DssEngine.java:376-386) maps to SIGNING_FAILED "DSS could not create the signature: ... too small ...". That matches the harness observation exactly.
  1. Not already handled, and not a documented decision for this mode. The explicit early check exists only in "cms" mode (ExternalSigning.java:169-174, tested by aCmsLargerThanTheReservedSpaceIsRefused in SigningTest.java:420-424), and there it runs at complete because the CMS size is unknowable at prepare. docs/DECISIONS.md:707-712 acknowledges the hazard ("The size is fixed at prepare, and a CMS that does not fit is lost along with the signature spent on it") and, for signature_value mode, relies on "DSS builds the CMS and its default (9,472 bytes) fits". That reasoning covers the default but not a caller-supplied smaller content_size, and in signature_value mode prepare already holds everything needed to estimate the CMS (signing certificate, chain, level-B attributes, signature length from the key), so an INVALID_ARGUMENT at prepare is feasible, unlike in cms mode. The prepare javadoc in DssEngine.java:331-336 even states the design goal "so that no external signature is spent on a document that cannot be completed", which this case violates.

Severity stays low: it needs the caller to explicitly override pades.content_size with a value below what the CMS needs; the default path is fine, and the failure is reported clearly (SIGNING_FAILED with DSS's message naming both sizes), just one step too late.

For CAdES in "cms" mode, prepare's signing_time is not what the signature claims and complete neither requires nor checks it, contrary to README and DECISIONS

The claimed time comes from the signer's signing-time attribute, which is never compared with the options. complete does not require signing_time for CAdES/cms.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Harness: prepare with 2026-01-01 and a CMS with signing-time=now validated using the signer's time.

Evidence

README.md:364-365 'the signing_time the signature will claim'; ExternalSigning.java:131-136; :266-273 presence-only check

Impact

Applications record the wrong signing time.

Recommendation

Document the CAdES/cms behaviour, or compare the attribute with signing_time within a tolerance.

Remediation: Not fixed (package java-signing)

Classified by the orchestrator as skipped (kept by decision): the implementer re-checked the claim and kept the behaviour, the reviewer confirmed the reason holds, and the documentation now states it. Implementer note: Re-checked: for CAdES in cms mode the claimed time is the signer's signing-time attribute and complete neither requires nor compares the options' signing_time (it is not part of the content digest). Comparing within a tolerance would be arbitrary (signers set it when they sign, minutes after prepare), so the behaviour is kept and documented; what changed in code is that the certificate validity is now checked at the attribute's time (F-025) and the attribute must have exactly one value (F-026). Documentation text handed to docs (README sign section and DECISIONS) and rust-dss (types.rs comment on PreparedSignature.signing_time).

Test: SigningTest#cmsModeChecksTheCertificateValidityAtTheSigningTime (CAdES case uses the attribute's time)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.92

Confirmed by reading the code and the project's own tests; the behaviour is intentional in code but undocumented, so this is a real documentation defect, low severity.

  1. The README makes the general claim. README.md:364-365: "dss_sign_prepare(document, options_json) returns the digest to send to the signer, and the signing_time the signature will claim." README.md:370: "complete also needs signing_time as prepare returned it." README.md:387 (options): "signing_time": ... // prepare: default now; complete: required. docs/DECISIONS.md:677-678 repeats it: "prepare picks it ... and returns it; complete requires it." rust/dss/src/types.rs:109-111 says the same for the Rust API ("The signing time the signature claims: set SignOptions::signing_time to it for complete"). None of these documents a CAdES/cms exception.
  1. complete does not require it for CAdES/cms. java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:133-136: if (o.signingTime == null && (format == Format.PADES || o.mode == Mode.SIGNATURE_VALUE)) { throw new DssError(... "'signing_time' is required to complete" ...) The condition explicitly exempts CAdES + Mode.CMS.
  1. complete never compares the signer's time with the option. cadesFromCms (ExternalSigning.java:182-205) never reads o.signingTime; it only calls checkedCms(...) and then possibly extendDocument. checkedCms at lines 266-273 is presence-only: boolean signingTime = signed.get(PKCSObjectIdentifiers.pkcs_9_at_signingTime) != null; ... if (format == Format.CADES && !signingTime) throw failed("the CMS has no signing-time attribute, which CAdES-BASELINE-B requires");. The only places o.signingTime reaches a signature are lines 397 and 424 (p.bLevel().setSigningDate(Date.from(o.signingTime))), inside padesParameters/cadesParameters, which are used only for PAdES and for signature_value mode. In cms mode the signer builds the signed attributes, so the claimed time is whatever it put in the signing-time attribute; prepare's digest for CAdES is just DSSUtils.digest(digestAlgorithm, document) (line 121), independent of the time, so a mismatch cannot even be detected via the digest check.
  1. The project's own test exercises exactly this scenario and passes. SigningTest.java:281-289 (cadesFromACmsExtendsToLtAndLta): options("{\"mode\":\"cms\",\"level\":\"LT\"}") (no signing_time; options() at line 108-110 is a plain SigningOptions.fromJson), prepare, then the test signer builds the CMS with Cms.SIGNING_TIME, which in testsupport/ExternalSigner.java:126-128 is new Attribute(pkcs_9_at_signingTime, new DERSet(new Time(new Date()))) i.e. the signer's own "now", then Thread.sleep(1100) and engine.completeSignature(text, lt, cms) succeeds. So complete accepts a CMS whose signing-time differs from prepare's returned time, with no signing_time option at all.

Why not refuted: the code's exemption is deliberate (the condition at line 133 is explicit) and reasonable for the mode, but DECISIONS.md:677-678 and README.md:364-370/387 state the opposite without the exception, so the finding's documentation claim stands. Impact is modest: an application that records prepare's signing_time as "the time the signature claims" would be wrong for CAdES/cms by however long the signer took, and the "complete: required" statement is simply inaccurate for that quadrant. Fix is documentation (note the CAdES/cms exception in README, DECISIONS and the Rust doc comment) or an optional tolerance comparison in checkedCms.

F-031LowcorrectnessFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java:102

Visible-appearance Flate streams depend on the host zlib: zlib-ng deflates the fixture's image to different bytes than zlib/Apple libz, so prepare on one host and complete on the other fails with SIGNING_FAILED

The visible appearance's Flate streams are produced by java.util.zip, which on Linux uses the system libz. Running prepare and complete under different zlib implementations (zlib-ng, Apple) can produce different bytes, and the signature then fails to verify.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Invisible signatures are not affected. CI covers only classic zlib.

Evidence

SignatureImage.java:101-115 'new Deflater(Deflater.BEST_COMPRESSION)'; README.md:472 'the same bytes on every platform and in both calls'; DECISIONS.md:539 links -lz

Impact

SIGNING_FAILED in split-host deployments, after the signature has been spent.

Recommendation

Document the same-build/same-zlib requirement, or use deterministic pure-Java compression or a statically linked zlib. Add a CI job on a zlib-ng image.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

Incoming handoff from java-visible (CI side): the compat job's fedora:44 legs (zlib-ng-compat asserted with rpm -q) on linux-x64 and linux-aarch64 replay all committed signing fixtures with the packaged dss-cli sign complete, which only succeeds when the digest equals the one recorded on the JVM, so a deflate difference fails the release.

Files: .github/workflows/ci.yml, scripts/ci/package-smoke.sh

Test: package-smoke.sh verified locally on macOS (all 6 fixtures complete; a wrong .sig fails).

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.85

The defect is real as described, with one correction (Apple's libz is not a divergent implementation in practice; zlib-ng is) and one scope widening (not only the image stream).

Code path, confirmed by reading:

  • SignatureImage.java:100-102: /** A fixed level, so that prepare and complete compress the same samples to the same bytes. */ ... Deflater deflater = new Deflater(Deflater.BEST_COMPRESSION); — a PNG's samples and alpha are Flate-compressed here at parse time (line 59-61), and the result becomes the XObject stream in toXObject() (lines 86-96, COSName.FLATE_DECODE).
  • ExternalSigning.java:109-131 (prepare) and 133-160 (complete): both call visible(document, o) and rebuild the appearance from the original PDF; complete does not reuse any bytes from prepare. In cms mode, padesFromCms (163-176) recomputes the digest via service.getMessageDigest(doc, padesParameters(o, visible)) and checkedCms (216-262) throws failed(...) = SIGNING_FAILED when !MessageDigest.isEqual(signedDigest, digest) ("the CMS signs the digest X, not this document's Y: prepare and complete need the same document and options"). The image stream is inside the ByteRange, so a different deflate output changes the digest. The authors already guard the analogous split-host hazard for time zones (ExternalSigning.java:398-400: "or prepare and complete on hosts in different zones build different PDFs and the signature does not match"), but nothing guards or documents the zlib implementation.
  • The native library really uses the host zlib: otool -L build/native/macos-aarch64/libdssnative.dylib lists /usr/lib/libz.1.dylib (current version 1.2.12); DECISIONS.md:539 "native-image links with -lz" and :593 "validating a PDF loads libdssnative, libc, libz" confirm the same on Linux.
  • Documentation claims platform independence: README.md:472 "the same bytes on every platform and in both calls"; DECISIONS.md:794 "the image and ICC streams are compressed at a fixed level". No doc mentions a same-zlib requirement (grep for zlib/Flate in README and docs/).

Experiment (scratchpad /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/zlibcmp.py and Def.java): I decoded the actual PNG from testdata/fixtures/signing/pades-visible-cms.json (160x80 RGBA, 38400 RGB sample bytes + 12800 alpha bytes) and ran compress2 at level 9 (same windowBits/memLevel/strategy as java.util.zip.Deflater) through three implementations present on this machine:

  • Apple libz 1.2.12 (/usr/lib/libz.1.dylib, what libdssnative links): 35716 bytes, sha256 bf2c34ae…
  • JDK-bundled vanilla zlib (GraalVM CE 25's libzip.dylib has a local _deflate symbol; run via java Def.java): 35716 bytes, sha256 bf2c34ae… (identical to Apple)
  • zlib-ng 2.3.3 compat (/opt/homebrew/Cellar/zlib-ng-compat/2.3.3_1/lib/libz.1.dylib): 35728 bytes, sha256 71c823d1… (different) Also different for the PNG file bytes, README text and random data; identical only for trivially compressible inputs (zeros, alpha mask, gradient). So a deployment that prepares on a zlib-ng host (Fedora 40+/RHEL 10 ship zlib-ng-compat as libz.so.1; Homebrew zlib-ng-compat) and completes on a classic-zlib/macOS host, or vice versa, produces a different image stream and SIGNING_FAILED after the external signer has been used.

Corrections to the finding:

  1. Apple's libz is not a divergent implementation for this path: its output was byte-identical to vanilla zlib on the fixture samples, and CI (ci.yml:66-70, macos-15 and ubuntu-24.04 runners) completes the same vanilla-recorded fixture on both, so "CI covers only classic zlib" is slightly off — it covers classic zlib and Apple's, but not zlib-ng.
  2. Scope is wider than SignatureImage: PDFBox 3.0.8's FlateFilter.encode also uses java.util.zip.Deflater (javap confirmed), and the drawer compresses the sRGB output-intent ICC stream through it (AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.java:377-378, new PDStream(document, ..., COSName.FLATE_DECODE)), as it does for the font subset and content stream; so JPEG appearances are exposed too, through the ICC stream on any PDF without an output intent. (Unverified side note: PDFBox's PDFXRefStream also writes xref streams with FLATE_DECODE, which could expose even invisible signatures on xref-stream PDFs; not tested.)

Severity stays medium: it needs a split-host deployment with mismatched zlib implementations, and the failure is loud and explained, but it is wasted after the signature has been spent and contradicts the documented contract. Fix options in the finding (document the requirement, or a deterministic pure-Java/Rust deflate, or static zlib) are sound.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

Premise confirmed, impact narrowed. SignatureImage.java:101-115 compresses PNG samples and the alpha mask with new Deflater(Deflater.BEST_COMPRESSION) (used at :61-62), with the comment "A fixed level, so that prepare and complete compress the same samples to the same bytes": a fixed level only pins the output within one deflate implementation. The shipped native library really does use the host's libz: otool -L build/native/macos-aarch64/libdssnative.dylib shows /usr/lib/libz.1.dylib (current version 1.2.12), docs/native-library.md:25 requires libz.so.1 on Linux, and DECISIONS.md:539 records native-image linking with -lz. The design explicitly allows the two calls on different processes and hosts: README.md:362 "so they may run minutes or processes apart", DECISIONS.md:671-674 "Two stateless steps ... may run in different processes", and DECISIONS.md:681 already reasons about "prepare and complete on hosts in different zones". So a prepare on a classic-zlib host and a complete on a zlib-ng-compat host (Fedora 40+, RHEL 10; README.md:204 lists "RHEL 9+" as supported) can produce a different Flate stream, hence a different ByteRange digest. Impact is bounded: complete detects it cleanly before building anything (README.md:371 and DECISIONS.md:704-705: SIGNING_FAILED "not this document's digest", "not as a broken PDF"), so there is no invalid signature and no security consequence; the cost is a wasted external-signer transaction (OTP/HSM operation) in a heterogeneous fleet, which is an unusual deployment (the server.md sidecar is one container image). The finding's "Apple" claim is refuted by existing tests: testdata/fixtures/signing/pades-visible-cms.json carries a PNG (Flate path) and a recorded CMS; rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:294-333 and the CLI/C smoke tests replay it through the native library on ubuntu-24.04 (zlib 1.3) and macos-15 (Apple libz), matching a digest made on the macOS JVM (DECISIONS.md:683, 802-803), so Apple libz and classic zlib already agree for this path. Only zlib-ng remains, which I could not test on this machine (no zlib-ng installed), but zlib-ng publicly documents that its output is not identical to zlib's. What is real and actionable: README.md:472 "the same bytes on every platform and in both calls" and DECISIONS.md:792-794 overclaim determinism, and nowhere is a same-libz (or same build) requirement stated for split-host deployments. Severity low: narrow deployment, detected failure, documentation fix suffices.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

The finding is accurate. SignatureImage.java:101-115 Flate-compresses decoded PNG samples and alpha (called at lines 61-62) with new Deflater(Deflater.BEST_COMPRESSION). The only thing keeping the output stable is the fixed level ("A fixed level, so that prepare and complete compress the same samples to the same bytes", line 100). DECISIONS.md:794 says the same thing: "the image and ICC streams are compressed at a fixed level". I confirmed the library links the system zlib dynamically: otool -L build/native/macos-aarch64/libdssnative.dylib shows /usr/lib/libz.1.dylib (... current version 1.2.12), and DECISIONS.md:539 records -lz on Linux. A fixed level does not give identical bytes across zlib implementations. zlib-ng, which is the system libz on Fedora 40+ through zlib-ng-compat, and other optimised forks emit different but valid deflate streams. Cross-host prepare/complete is a supported case. DECISIONS.md:673-682 says "the two steps may run in different processes" and fixes the host time zone for exactly that reason. README.md:472 promises "the same bytes on every platform and in both calls". The mechanism is real, the file and line are correct, and a maintainer can act on it.

The finding overstates the severity, so I lower it from medium to low:

  • It only affects visible signatures that use a PNG image. JPEG goes in as DCTDecode unchanged, and text-only signatures have no Flate image here. The ICC stream may also be affected.
  • It needs prepare and complete to run on hosts with different zlib implementations. Apple's libz and Ubuntu's classic zlib already agree, because the CI fixtures prepared on the Mac complete on Linux. That leaves mainly zlib-ng distros such as Fedora 40+, which README:204 does not list (it lists Ubuntu, Debian and RHEL 9, all classic zlib).
  • The failure is detected, not silent. ExternalSigning.java:283-285 and :368 throw SIGNING_FAILED when the CMS or the signature value does not verify over the recomputed document, so no invalid PDF is produced.

The impact is availability only: one external-signer authorisation (OTP or HSM call) is wasted and the user has to re-sign. There is no attacker vector and no integrity or confidentiality impact. The recommendation to document a same-zlib requirement, or switch to pure-Java or statically linked deflate, is reasonable.
