F-033LowcorrectnessFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java:130

JPEG Exif orientation (APP1) is neither applied nor refused nor documented, so tagged phone photos embed rotated or mirrored

JPEGs are embedded as-is using the SOF dimensions. PDF viewers ignore EXIF orientation 2-8.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Jpeg.header reads only the SOF segment.

Evidence

SignatureImage.java:55-57; :130-178

Impact

The signed PDF shows the image rotated, and fixing it means signing again.

Recommendation

Parse the EXIF orientation and either refuse non-1 values or honour them. Document the behaviour.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-visible)

SignatureImage.Jpeg.header now parses the APP1 Exif segment (both byte orders, bounds-checked) and refuses a JPEG whose Orientation tag is 2-8 with 'the JPEG has Exif orientation N (it is stored rotated or mirrored); PDF viewers ignore it, so save the image with the rotation applied (orientation 1) first'. Orientation 1, a malformed Exif and non-Exif APP1 segments are ignored as before. Refusing rather than honouring keeps the embedded JPEG byte-identical and the layout code unchanged.

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java, java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImageTest.java

Test: SignatureImageTest.jpegExifOrientationIsRefusedUnlessUpright

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The behaviour is exactly as described. java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java:55-57 does Jpeg.Header h = Jpeg.header(bytes); return new SignatureImage(h.width(), h.height(), h.components() == 1, bytes, true, null); and Jpeg.header (:130-178) walks the marker segments only to find SOF0-2 and read precision/height/width/components; every other segment, including APP1/Exif, is skipped with i += 2 + length (:175). toXObject (:88-91) then embeds the untouched file as DCTDecode with those SOF dimensions. A repo-wide grep for "exif"/"orientation" over java, rust and md finds no handling anywhere (the only "rotation" code is the page /Rotate logic in Placement.java and AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.java, unrelated to image metadata). The README (:460-461) documents "A JPEG goes into the PDF as it is" but says nothing about orientation, so a caller is not warned that a phone photo tagged with Exif orientation 2-8 will appear rotated or mirrored; the layout also sizes the image box from the SOF width/height (README :457-458, aspect ratio preserved), so a portrait photo stored landscape+orientation 6 lands sideways. The tests do not cover it: SignatureImageTest.java:89-95 asserts only the header fields and that the bytes are unchanged, and the lone fixture testdata/fixtures/content/stamp.jpg has no APP1/Exif segment (segments: APP0 JFIF, DQT, SOF0, DHT, SOS). Mitigating context, which keeps the severity low: this matches DSS's own ImageIO-based drawer (ImageIO also ignores Exif orientation) and most PDF tooling; the caller can normalise the image first; the result is cosmetically wrong, not invalid. The honest fix is the one recommended: parse APP1 orientation and either refuse non-1 values or document that JPEGs are embedded without applying Exif orientation. The root is in Jpeg.header at :130, though the cited :57 is where the unrotated dimensions are committed.

No veraPDF check is run.

PDF/A archives can be produced non-conforming.

Verified through the engine.

Silent empty signatures.

Reject blank text after expansion when no image is given.

VisibleSignature.appearance() refuses a rendered text that is blank once its placeholders are filled in (INVALID_ARGUMENT: "'text' is blank once its placeholders are filled in (the value they stand for is empty); give a text or leave it out for an image alone"), with or without an image, consistent with the parse-time rule that an empty 'text' must be left out for an image alone.

Effect verified in smoke.c: a second pthread calling dss_version with the main thread's handle, which used to return {"ok":true,...}, now stops with 'Fatal error: A call from native code to Java code provided a JNI environment or IsolateThread that is either corrupt or belongs to a different OS thread' (SIGABRT). docs/native-library.md 'Threads' rule gained 'A wrong handle stops the process' with the three cases (NULL: exit 2 'Failed to enter the specified IsolateThread context'; torn-down isolate / detached thread: SIGSEGV or fatal error; foreign thread: fatal error), the correction that only direct C hosts are exposed (Rust keeps the handles internal, PHP talks HTTP), and that these are Native Image preconditions, not library results. smoke.c handle_misuse_checks runs the three deterministic cases (NULL, foreign thread, torn-down isolate) in forked children and fails if a child returns a result (exits 0) or hangs; the after-detach case is documented but not tested because reading a freed thread structure is not deterministic.

No handle can be NULL (attach failure returns Err(Error::Isolate(rc)) at :459-460), cross a thread, or outlive the isolate. The "silently accepted foreign-thread handle" probe is just the standard Native Image contract (the thread-local isolate state is keyed by the handle, so the call succeeds and is UB only in the formal sense); it is not a defect of this library.

Residual value: a one-line clarification that the "Errors" guarantee presupposes a valid handle of the calling thread would be a harmless docs polish. That is low/info severity, not medium, and not the "crash or corrupt silently" impact claimed.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

The facts in the finding hold up. docs/native-library.md:85-86 says: "Results always carry "ok". No Java exception ever reaches C. NULL is returned only if not even an error result could be built". The Rules section, docs/native-library.md:76-79, says what a handle must be: "Every call takes the *calling thread's* graal_isolatethread_t*", and other threads must call graal_attach_thread/graal_detach_thread. Nowhere does it say what happens if you pass a NULL, torn-down, detached or another thread's handle. The build sets no -H:+CheckIsolateThreadAtEntry: java/pom.xml:299-314 and the jar's native-image.properties carry only --features, the locale -D flags, AddAllCharsets, -march=compatibility and ReportExceptionStackTraces. So a foreign-thread handle is not checked at entry, and bad handles fault in GraalVM's entry stubs, before any Java code runs. That part is a real documentation gap, and a maintainer can act on it.

The finding overstates two things. First, the Errors bullet is about Java exceptions and result building. It does not promise to tolerate invalid C arguments, and the Threads rule already states the required handle use. These failures are caller contract violations, the usual undefined-behaviour case in any C API (compare passing a freed pointer to libc). They are not a defect in the library's error path. Second, the impact needs a host that is already misusing the API. Nobody can reach it remotely, an attacker cannot trigger it with document input, and the Rust crate manages handles itself. Only hand-written C or PHP hosts with bugs are exposed.

The fix is documentation, plus optionally the CheckIsolateThreadAtEntry flag for debug builds. I rate it low, not medium.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The leak repeats on retries in dss_extend, sign_complete and tl_export_snapshot.

Evidence

DssLib.java:265-271; :166-168 'catch (Throwable t) { return WordFactory.nullPointer(); }'

Impact

A native leak exactly when memory is short, and the caller loses the error.

Allocate the document first or free the JSON on failure, and return an error JSON.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-ffi)

DssLib.toC(DocumentResult, out, outLen) now mallocs and fills the document first (the large allocation; if it fails nothing has been allocated), then the result JSON; if the JSON's malloc (or the small Java allocation of the ByteBuffer view) throws, the document buffer is freed before rethrowing, and the out-parameters are only written once both exist. The rethrown Throwable reaches the entry point's catch, which now returns an INTERNAL_ERROR result (F-227) instead of NULL. No offline test can force a document-sized malloc to fail inside a full engine; verified by code reading and the existing extend/sign_complete/export_snapshot smoke paths still passing.

Then :268 CCharPointer out = UnmanagedMemory.malloc(WordFactory.unsigned(Math.max(1, document.length))); allocates the document, which can be up to MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES (:67, ~2 GB). Nothing between :265 and :273 frees json on a failure path; there is no try/finally.

The document malloc really throws, as an ordinary Java throw. javap of org/graalvm/nativeimage/UnmanagedMemory.malloc(UnsignedWord) from ~/.m2/.../nativeimage-25.4.4.1.1.jar: after UnmanagedMemorySupport.malloc, invokeinterface PointerBase.isNull; ifeq 34; new java/lang/OutOfMemoryError; ldc "malloc of unmanaged memory"; athrow. So when libc malloc returns NULL, an OutOfMemoryError propagates out of toC(DocumentResult,...) into the entry point.
  1. The entry points swallow it without cleanup: :166-168 (dss_extend), :214-216 (dss_sign_complete) and :125-127 (dss_tl_export_snapshot) all read catch (Throwable t) { return WordFactory.nullPointer(); }. The malloc'd json pointer is a local of the callee frame and is simply dropped, so it leaks. The class comment (:46-47) says results are "encoded to UTF-8 straight into malloc'd memory", confirming there is no other owner that could free it. The DECISIONS.md note at :277-282 about Native Image unwinding heap-allocation OOMs past the local catch does not apply here (this is an explicit athrow, not a GC slow-path), and even if it did unwind to the C stub the process would abort, so the catch-and-NULL path is the live one.

The sidecar never reaches the expect sites from a request. rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:151 'e.validate_json(&document, &options)', :165 'e.extend_json', :179 'e.prepare_signature_json', :193 'e.complete_signature_json' are the only engine calls in handlers, and their options are built from client JSON (Value::Object(options).to_string(), lib.rs:150/164/178/190), which is UTF-8 by construction and contains no PathBuf. lib.rs:384-393 add_detached additionally rejects any client 'detached_contents[].path' ("detached_contents[].path is not accepted over HTTP"). So "server handler panics" is false. The server's only expect is EngineBuilder::new via Engine::builder at main.rs:241 inside engine_builder(), i.e. at startup with operator-typed argv: a startup failure with a panic message, not a runtime crash.
  1. Every PathBuf involved is operator/host-chosen (oj_keystore.path, trust_store.path, extra_trusted_certificates, tl_snapshot in rust/dss/src/config.rs:44-73,102; DetachedContent::path at config.rs:173). Untrusted documents enter as &[u8]. dss-cli's batch_line takes case: &[String] (main.rs:527-529), so those paths are already UTF-8. No untrusted party can supply a non-UTF-8 path.
  1. The library cannot honour such a path even with a Result: the C ABI converts every argument with CTypeConversion.utf8ToJavaString (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/ffi/DssLib.java:281 'return s.isNull() ? null : CTypeConversion.utf8ToJavaString(s);'). The only possible change is panic-vs-Err(InvalidArgument) for an input that must be rejected anyway, which is an API-hygiene nit, not a correctness or security impact.
  1. Platform reach is narrow: README.md:204 targets Linux and macOS; macOS filesystems only allow UTF-8 names, so only a Linux host deliberately passing a legacy-encoded path triggers it. The cache_dir lossy case is self-evident to the operator (the CLI's create_dir_all at main.rs:560/server main.rs:216 creates the raw-bytes dir while Java uses the visibly different '...\u{FFFD}' dir), and it is operator-only misconfiguration.

Residual: a Rust host application embedding the crate on Linux that forwards a user-picked non-UTF-8 detached path into Engine::validate gets a panic in its calling thread instead of an error. That is a real but negligible robustness issue (host-controlled input, no security consequence, trivially fixed with map_err). Not documented in docs/DECISIONS.md, but the impact as stated (server handler panic, different cache dir in normal operation) is overstated; medium is not warranted. Calibrated severity: low, and through the impact lens the finding is refuted as described.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The mechanism is described correctly. rust/dss/src/engine.rs:36 is serde_json::to_string(config).expect("Config always serializes"), and :151, :178, :209 and :238 use the same .expect(...) on Options, ExtendOptions and SignOptions. Those structs are #[derive(Serialize)] with plain PathBuf fields and no custom serializer: config.rs:44 extra_trusted_certificates: Vec<PathBuf>, :55 tl_snapshot: Option<PathBuf>, :73 OjKeystore path: PathBuf, :102 TrustStore path: PathBuf, :173 DetachedContent path: Option<PathBuf>. serde's impl Serialize for Path returns Err("path contains invalid UTF-8 characters") when to_str() fails, so a non-UTF-8 path panics instead of returning an Err. engine.rs:346 CString::new(b.cache_dir.to_string_lossy().as_bytes()) replaces invalid bytes with U+FFFD, so the native library gets a different directory name, silently.

Severity is lower than claimed. The server impact the finding implies does not hold. dss-server/src/lib.rs:382-391 rejects any detached_contents[].path sent over HTTP ("detached_contents[].path is not accepted over HTTP"). In both dss-server and dss-cli, paths come only from operator-supplied startup arguments (main.rs:55 cache_dir, :62 oj_keystore, :71 trusted_certificates). No remote or unprivileged input can reach the panic. The only way to trigger it is a local operator or library caller using a non-UTF-8 filesystem path, which is rare on macOS (APFS requires UTF-8 names) and uncommon on Linux. The panic happens at startup or in the caller's own thread: it is a crash rather than memory unsafety, and it can be reproduced. The lossy cache_dir is a correctness wart: a different directory may be created or used, but there is no security consequence. The finding is real and actionable (return an InvalidArgument error instead of expect, and use OsStr bytes or reject non-UTF-8 for cache_dir), but it rates low, not medium.

F-048Lowapi-designFixedrust/dss/src/error.rs:43

Unknown library error codes lose their original string in Rust and are re-emitted by dss-server as 'UNKNOWN' / 500 (only under library/binary version skew)

#[serde(other)] Unknown discards the code string, and dss-server serialises the enum back, so new library codes reach clients as UNKNOWN/500.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Java says new codes will be added.

Evidence

error.rs:42-44 '#[serde(other)] Unknown'; dss-server lib.rs:497-500 'serde_json::to_value(code)'

Impact

Version skew hides specific error codes from clients.

Recommendation

Keep the raw code string in Error::Api and forward it.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-dss)

ErrorCode::Unknown is now Unknown(&'static str) holding the wire name (interned once per distinct name so the enum stays Copy/Eq/Hash; the library emits a finite set). Custom Serialize/Deserialize map wire names both ways, so dss-server's existing serde_json::to_value(code) forwards BRAND_NEW_CODE unchanged with no server change (status stays 500 for unknown codes). ErrorCode::from_wire/as_str added.

After review: The interned set of unknown wire names is bounded: MAX_INTERNED = 256 distinct names are kept (a private intern() over a Mutex<Vec<&'static str>>); past that, from_wire/Deserialize return ErrorCode::Unknown("UNKNOWN") and keep nothing, and check_ok (the library path) prepends the real name to the Error::Api message when the code could not keep it. check_ok now also maps an empty code to Error::Protocol itself (ApiError.code is deserialised as a String). Documented on from_wire/Unknown. Test unknown_names_are_interned_up_to_a_bound uses a private set so the process-wide one stays as other tests expect.

After review: Already applied: Error::Nul | Error::Argument map to 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT; Error::Thread and the rest to 500 INTERNAL_ERROR; Error::Closed to 503 NOT_INITIALIZED; library codes are passed through as code.as_str().

After review: RefreshScheduler: stop() aborts at once and a refresh in flight finishes unpublished; dropping the handle publishes the outcome, then the channel closes. Documented in README ('Refresh schedule'), DECISIONS (Rust crates) and the CHANGELOG. Checked against schedule.rs:50-60,168-170.

Files: CHANGELOG.md, README.md, docs/DECISIONS.md, rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss/src/engine.rs, rust/dss/src/error.rs

Test: cargo test -p dss --lib unknown_codes_keep_their_wire_name check_ok_reads_the_envelope

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.88

Reproduced. (1) rust/dss/src/error.rs:42-44: /// A code this version of the crate does not know. #[serde(other)] Unknown — serde's other discards the string. (2) rust/dss/src/engine.rs:677-693: struct ApiError { code: ErrorCode, message: String } and check_ok builds Error::Api { code: e.code, message: e.message }; nothing keeps the raw code string. (3) rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:496-501: Error::Api { code, message } => { let name = match serde_json::to_value(code) { Ok(Value::String(name)) => name, _ => format!("{code:?}") }; ApiError::new(status_of(code), &name, message) } and lib.rs:489 _ => StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. A scratch program in the scratchpad (f048/src/main.rs) linking the real dss and dss-server crates and calling exactly this From<Error> for ApiError + IntoResponse path printed: dss::ErrorCode from "BRAND_NEW_CODE" = Unknown and HTTP 500 Internal Server Error body={"error":{"code":"UNKNOWN","message":"library said something new"},"ok":false}. Reachability: at commit 7e697c9 the Java DssError.Code enum (java/.../engine/DssError.java:13-50) and the Rust enum hold the same 12 codes, so the defect only appears under version skew; skew is a real deployment scenario because the library is dynamically linked (rust/dss-sys/build.rs:28 rustc-link-lib=dylib=dssnative; rust/dss-server/build.rs rpath @executable_path/../lib for the release package) and the Java side explicitly plans for additions (DssError.java:12 "Rust maps these 1:1, so only ever add to this list"; docs/openapi.yaml:467 "New codes may be added"). Not a documented decision for the server: docs/DECISIONS.md:371 only justifies Unknown for typed result enums ("newer libraries stay readable"), docs/server.md:102 promises "the library's code" in the body, and UNKNOWN is listed in no status table, README.md:534-536, or openapi.yaml. Mitigating: the message string is forwarded intact, the HTTP status is still an error, and this is a forward-compatibility edge case, hence low severity. Note the recommendation would cost Copy on ErrorCode/Error::code(); a cheaper fix is a separate raw-string field in Error::Api.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The mechanism is real as described, for the public library API. rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:43 pub fn spawn(engine: Arc<Engine>, every: Duration, refresh_on_start: bool) passes every unchecked into the spawned task at :52 let mut ticker = tokio::time::interval_at(first, every);, and the pinned tokio 1.54.1 (rust/Cargo.lock:748-749) asserts at src/time/interval.rs:109 assert!(period > Duration::new(0, 0), "period must be non-zero.");. The JoinHandle at :37/:75 is only ever abort()ed (:91), never joined, and the doc comment (:41-42) does not state a non-zero requirement.

I reproduced it with a scratchpad crate that mirrors schedule.rs:44-82 verbatim against tokio =1.54.1 (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f050/src/main.rs). With Duration::ZERO: refreshes run: 0, refresh_now() -> false (try_send on a closed mpsc, which :79 documents as "one is already pending"), subscribe().changed() -> Err("channel closed"), task.is_finished() -> true, join is_panic=true. So the "silently dead scheduler whose refresh_now() misreports" part holds.

Two corrections to the finding. (1) The impact "Trusted lists are never refreshed and no error is reported" is unreachable in the shipped server: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:45 takes refresh_hours: u64 (whole hours) and :128 let refresh_every = (args.refresh_hours > 0).then(|| Duration::from_secs(args.refresh_hours * 3600)); with :154 refresh_every.map(|every| RefreshScheduler::spawn(...)), so 0 means no scheduler at all (documented in docs/server.md:40) and the smallest possible period is 3600 s. With no scheduler, lib.rs:219-225 tl_refresh falls back to spawn_blocking(... engine.refresh_trusted_lists()) and works. The existing tests (rust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs:31, :48) use 300 ms and 3600 s, so no test covers zero. (2) "No error is reported" is overstated: the default panic hook prints "period must be non-zero." to stderr (seen in the repro), and dss-server's outcome logger (main.rs:157-161) would exit its loop on the closed watch channel. Nothing is surfaced through the API, though.

Net: a genuine but minor API-hygiene defect in a public library function (a caller passing zero gets a dead scheduler and a misleading refresh_now()), with no path to it from the repository's own binaries. Low severity; a one-line validation in spawn (or documenting the precondition) resolves it.

Still partial for the same reason as before: no automated test holds a refresh in flight at SIGTERM.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.65

Aborting drops the outer future (and with it the publish watch sender), but a spawn_blocking closure cannot be cancelled, so the clone lives until the refresh returns. Reproduction (scratchpad test, stop() called while trusted_list_status().refresh_in_progress was true): immediately after stop(), Arc::strong_count == 2 and refresh_in_progress == true; outcomes.changed() returned Err("channel closed") after 51 ms and the in-flight outcome was never published (watch still None); the clone was released 2.48 s later when the library's response timeout fired. (1) The sub-claim that drop-without-stop is a problem is not: dropping the scheduler drops trigger, requests.recv() yields None (schedule.rs:57) and the loop breaks after the current refresh; the reproduction showed the in-flight outcome IS published on drop (Ok), then the channel closes and the clone is released. Undocumented, but benign. (2) The concrete effect is in dss-server: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:84-91 documents shutdown as "Blocking: dropping the last reference to the engine waits for queued work and a running online refresh", and main.rs:172-178 relies on it (spawn_blocking(move || state.shutdown()).await then returns from main). When a scheduled refresh is in flight, s.stop() leaves the blocking closure holding an Arc, so drop(self.engine.into_inner()) is not the last reference, Engine::drop (engine.rs:428-440, which joins the refresh thread and tears down the isolate) never runs on that path, and the process exits with the refresh still running. The stop() doc ("A refresh already running finishes in the background", schedule.rs:89) documents the scheduler side, and docs/DECISIONS.md:373-375 says nothing about shutdown, so this is a documented limitation rather than an oversight, but the server's shutdown promise does not hold for it. Severity low: only process exit during a (rare, ~15 s) refresh is affected; validations and the schedule itself are unaffected, and existing tests (rust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs) only call stop() after outcomes arrive, so they do not cover the case.

F-061LowtestingFixedrust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs:30

Scheduler tests assert only that outcomes arrive; refresh_on_start, period, manual-refresh reset, refresh_now() back-pressure, stop() and the Err path are unasserted

scheduler.rs:48-55

Impact

Schedule regressions pass CI.

Recommendation

Use tokio::time::pause and assert timing and stop behaviour.

Scheduler tests now assert timing with real time and wide margins (period 1 s): refresh_on_start fires within the period and the next two outcomes are a period apart; without it nothing fires within 250 ms and the first outcome comes after about a period; refresh_now runs at once and the next scheduled refresh is a full period after the manual one (reset); requests during a running refresh are Started/AlreadyPending, never Stopped, and produce no second refresh; stop() ends the schedule and closes the outcome channel; invalid periods are refused; an outcome carries the engine's RefreshInProgress error when a refresh started elsewhere is running. tokio::time::pause was not used: refreshes run on spawn_blocking against the real library, where auto-advance would skip ticks, and the tests need the multi_thread flavour.

Files: rust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs

Test: cargo test -p dss --all-features --test scheduler (8 passed, 7.1 s)

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Confirmed by reading the cited test against the implementation; the scheduler's distinguishing behaviours are not asserted anywhere.

What the implementation promises (rust/dss/src/schedule.rs): refresh_on_start selects the first tick (let first = if refresh_on_start { Instant::now() } else { Instant::now() + every }, lines 47-52); the period is interval_at(first, every) with MissedTickBehavior::Delay (52-53); after every refresh ticker.reset() so "A manual refresh restarts the period" (68-69, also a documented decision in docs/DECISIONS.md:373-375); refresh_now() returns false when a request is already pending (self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok(), line 81); a panicked blocking task maps to Err(Error::Closed) (60-63); stop() aborts the task (90-92).

What the tests assert (rust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs):

  • refreshes_periodically (29-44): spawns with every = 300ms, refresh_on_start = true, then three times waits up to 10 s for outcomes.changed() and checks record.mode == "online" and record.completed. No Instant is captured, so nothing checks that outcomes are ~300 ms apart; a scheduler that ignored every (ticked continuously) or ignored refresh_on_start (first tick at 300 ms) still passes within the 10 s timeout.
  • refresh_now_does_not_wait_for_the_period (46-57): spawns with every = 3600s, refresh_on_start = false, calls refresh_now() and waits for one outcome. Because an outcome is requested explicitly, a buggy refresh_on_start = false that fired immediately would also pass; the false return of refresh_now() when a request is pending is never exercised; and whether ticker.reset() actually restarts the period is unobservable with a 1-hour period.
  • stop() is called at lines 43 and 56 only as teardown; no test asserts that no further outcome arrives after it or that the task is aborted.
  • Both tests unwrap() an Ok result (lines 39, 55); the Err outcome branch and Error::Closed path are never produced.

Severity stays low: a testing gap with no production defect identified.

Only stdout tolerates BrokenPipe. eprintln! panics when stderr is closed.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Reproduced: validate --out-dir, sign prepare and error paths exit with 101.

Evidence

main.rs:408 'eprintln!("error: {e}");'; :763; :936

Impact

Scripts read 101 instead of 0, 1 or 2.

Recommendation

Route stderr through a helper that ignores BrokenPipe, and extend the test.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-cli)

Every eprintln! is replaced by an err! macro that writes to stderr and ignores write errors, including BrokenPipe. A closed stderr no longer panics (exit 101), and the remaining --out-dir reports are still written. The module doc and --help say stdout or stderr.

Files: rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs, rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs

Test: tests/cli.rs closed_stderr_keeps_the_exit_status_and_the_reports: validate --report detailed --out-dir with stderr a closed pipe exits 0 and writes both XML files; an error path exits 2, not 101.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.95

Confirmed by reading and by a read-only experiment against the built binary.

Code: rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:19 documents "Output to a closed pipe (| head) is dropped; the exit status is the same." The BrokenPipe tolerance exists only for stdout: the out! macro (main.rs:36-47) wraps writeln!(io::stdout().lock(), ...) and maps ErrorKind::BrokenPipe to Ok(()). Stderr goes through plain eprintln!, which panics on any write error: main.rs:408 eprintln!("error: {e}"); (the exit-2 error path in main), main.rs:763 eprintln!( (the "digest to sign ... request written to" message in sign prepare), main.rs:936 eprintln!("wrote {}", path.display()); (inside the write closure of write_reports, used by validate --out-dir), plus :671, :752, :851. Rust ignores SIGPIPE, so a write to a pipe whose reader exited returns EPIPE, and eprintln! turns that into a panic (exit 101). The existing test (rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs:33-56, closed_stdout_keeps_the_exit_status) only closes stdout; docs/DECISIONS.md:610-617 likewise only describes stdout, so stderr was never covered.

Reproduction (offline flags as in tests/cli.rs, scratch cache dir, no TL refresh), with 2>&1 >/dev/null | true so stderr is a closed pipe:

  • validate /nonexistent.pdf: stderr open -> "error: No such file or directory", exit=2; stderr closed pipe -> exit=101.
  • validate testdata/fixtures/pades/b-lta.pdf --out-dir <dir>: stderr open -> exit=0; stderr closed pipe -> exit=101.
  • validate b-lta.pdf without --out-dir, stderr closed pipe -> exit=0 (only stdout is written, so the out! guard holds).
  • 2>&- (closed fd rather than closed pipe) -> exit=2, since Rust treats EBADF on stdio as success; the defect is specific to a broken pipe.

Additional consequence not in the original finding: with --out-dir <dir> --report detailed --report etsi and stderr a closed pipe, only b-lta.pdf.simple.xml was written; the panic at main.rs:936 after the first file aborts write_reports (main.rs:940-945), so the detailed and etsi reports are never written and the exit is 101.

Severity stays low: it needs stderr to be a pipe whose reader has already exited (e.g. 2>&1 | head), an unusual invocation, and the fix is small (route stderr through the same BrokenPipe-ignoring helper and extend the test to close stderr).

With --config set, it rejects any of these: tl_snapshot, oj_keystore, a non-empty countries, offline_revocation, a non-empty trusted_certificates, allow_without_trusted_lists, tsa_url, tsa_user, tsa_password_file (new) and tl_threads. The rejection goes through clap's own Cli::command().error(ArgumentConflict, ...).exit(), so it exits 2 with clap's layout: "the argument '--config <CONFIG>' cannot be used with --country: the config file replaces it". Flags with an environment variable are named as e.g. "--tl-snapshot (or DSS_TL_SNAPSHOT)". conflicts_with_all is kept for --help. Related fix: clap's requires on global args wrongly fails when the dependent option comes from its environment variable and the required one is a flag before the subcommand (reproduced: DSS_TSA_USER=alice dss-cli --tsa-url https://x tl status gave 'required arguments were not provided: --tsa-url'). So requires was removed from --tsa-user and --tsa-password-file, and usage_problem checks both (MissingRequiredArgument, exit 2). Behaviour change: an empty DSS_* variable now counts as unset (drop_empty_dss_variables, mirrored from dss-server). DSS_TSA_URL= together with --config therefore no longer conflicts.

After review: README and CHANGELOG: the --config conflicts are enforced wherever the flag is placed, also after the subcommand (main.rs config_conflict/usage_problem).

The user who passes --config supplies a complete config_json, including its own trust settings, so the engine runs on an explicit, user-provided configuration rather than an attacker-chosen one. F-065LowreliabilityFixedrust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:677

extend/sign complete -o overwrite the target with non-atomic std::fs::write; in-place use loses the original on a crash or partial write

extend -o, sign complete -o, --request and tl snapshot -o truncate the target and then write it. There is no temp-file-and-rename, no input==output check and no overwrite guard.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

extend inplace.pdf -o inplace.pdf works, but an interruption during the write loses the original.

Evidence

main.rs:450, :677, :758, :858 'std::fs::write(...)'

Impact

Irreplaceable signed originals can be lost.

Recommendation

Write to a temp file in the same directory, fsync, rename, and refuse input==output without --force.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-cli)

New OutFile type. It creates .<name>.<pid>.tmp next to the target (create_new, after removing a stale one); commit writes, copies the existing target's permissions, fsyncs, renames over the target and best-effort fsyncs the directory. On drop an uncommitted temporary file is removed. A symlinked target is resolved, so the link is kept. Used by extend -o, sign complete -o, sign prepare --request, tl snapshot -o and the --out-dir reports. Because the target is replaced only by the complete result, in-place use (extend x.pdf -o x.pdf) is safe and allowed. No --force guard was added: the data-loss risk is gone and input==output is a legitimate PDF incremental-update use. Only a SIGKILL during the engine call can leave a hidden .tmp file.

After review: Both regressions are fixed. (1) An existing regular target must be writable. OutFile::create first opens it with OpenOptions::new().write(true), with no truncate and no create, and drops it at once. A 0444 file is refused with '<path>: Permission denied' (exit 2) before the engine runs. Content and mode are unchanged and no .tmp file is left. (2) A target that exists and is not a regular file, or any path under /dev or /proc, is opened up front with write+truncate and written directly in commit: no temp file, rename or sync. This covers FIFOs, /dev/stdout, /dev/fd/N from process substitution and /dev/null. Checked by hand: -o >(cat > piped.pdf) gives exit 0 and a full PDF; -o /dev/stdout > f writes f; chmod 444 gives exit 2 and the file is untouched. OutFile.tmp is now Option<PathBuf> (None means direct mode). A failed rename also removes the temp file.

After review: README dss-cli: an existing write-protected output is refused (exit 2, '<path>: Permission denied'). A FIFO, /dev/stdout, a process substitution or any path under /dev or /proc is opened before the engine runs, truncated and written directly, not atomically; regular files are still replaced atomically. CHANGELOG Changed updated. Checked against main.rs:925-960.

Nothing in docs/DECISIONS.md records a decision on it, but no decision was needed: the impact is negligible given the demo role, the required explicit -o, the documented distinct-output usage, and the success-only write. Calibrated severity: low (informational hardening suggestion); the "medium / irreplaceable originals" framing is refuted.

F-071LowcorrectnessFixedrust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:152

validate-batch reports an invalid --validation-time per line and still exits 0

The invalid global option is detected per case instead of up front.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

run -> per-line InvalidArgument, exit 0

Impact

Scripts see success.

Recommendation

Validate the option up front and exit 2.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-cli)

validate-batch checks --validation-time once before any document, with the library's own parser. It sends a 1-byte non-document with {"validation_time": T}. The library parses options before reading the document, so INVALID_ARGUMENT can only come from the options; UNSUPPORTED_DOCUMENT or TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED means the time is fine. An invalid instant exits 2 with '--validation-time "x": INVALID_ARGUMENT: ...' and prints no lines.

Files: rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs, rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs

Test: tests/cli.rs validate_batch_lines_and_validation_time: 'yesterday' exits 2 with empty stdout; a valid instant gives 3 ordered lines with exit 0.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.95

Reproduced exactly as stated, by code reading and by running the built CLI.

Code path: rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:150-152 declares the option with no value parser: #[arg(long)] validation_time: Option<String>. validate_batch (main.rs:503-525) never inspects it; it is forwarded verbatim per case at main.rs:516 (batch_line(engine, case, args.validation_time.as_deref())) into Options { validation_time: validation_time.map(str::to_owned), .. } (main.rs:531), and the function unconditionally ends with Ok(ExitCode::SUCCESS) (main.rs:524). Any engine error is folded into the per-line JSON at main.rs:549-553 ("ok": false, "error": {...}), so the exit status cannot reflect it. The only parser of the value is on the Java side, java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ValidationOptions.java:91-96 (Instant.parse(vt) -> throw f.error("'validation_time' must be ISO-8601 UTC, ...")), which is INVALID_ARGUMENT (DssJsonApiTest.java:132 asserts that), and it runs once per document, not once up front.

Experiment (debug binary rust/target/debug/dss-cli, offline engine as in tests/cli.rs, two-case file): validate-batch --cases F --validation-time yesterday printed, for every case, {"error":{"code":"InvalidArgument","message":"InvalidArgument: options: 'validation_time' must be ISO-8601 UTC, e.g. 2026-01-31T12:00:00Z"},"file":...,"ok":false}, nothing on stderr, and EXIT=0. The control run with 2026-01-31T12:00:00Z produced ok:true lines, also EXIT=0, so a script keyed on the exit status cannot tell the two apart.

Not a documented decision: the function's own doc comment (main.rs:501-502) says "Exit status 2 only if the batch itself cannot run; per-document failures are reported in their line", and a malformed global option is a batch-level failure, not a per-document one, so the behaviour contradicts the stated contract rather than implementing it. docs/DECISIONS.md:444-445 only introduces the subcommand and says nothing about this. No test in rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs exercises validate-batch at all.

Severity stays low: the only consumer in the repo, scripts/diff-vs-jvm.sh:41-42, passes the same value to the Java side (DiffVsNative.java:42 Instant.parse(...)), which would then fail noisily, and every output line plainly says ok:false, so a human notices; the cost is wasted engine start-up and a misleading exit status for scripts. Fix is trivial (a clap value_parser or an up-front check returning Err -> exit 2).

F-074Lowapi-designFixedrust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:835

--chain/--cert reject a multi-certificate PEM bundle that --trust accepts

The PEM is passed through unchanged, and the library requires one certificate per entry.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

main.rs:837-839; SigningOptions.java:246-248

Impact

Avoidable usage failure.

Recommendation

Split bundles in the CLI.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-cli)

New certificates()/pem_certificates() helpers split PEM text into one entry per CERTIFICATE block. A block without an END line is an error naming the file. DER files are base64-encoded as before. A bundle given as --cert supplies the signer first; the rest are prepended to the chain. A bundle given as --chain adds every certificate. Help texts updated.

Files: rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs, rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs

Test: Unit test pem_bundles_are_split_one_certificate_per_entry. tests/cli.rs sign_signature_value_and_cades: --cert <signer+issuer bundle> gives the same digest as --cert signer.der --chain issuer.der, with 1 chain entry; --chain <bundle> gives 2 entries (was INVALID_ARGUMENT, exit 2).

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.95

Reproduced as described. The CLI helper at rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:835-841 passes PEM through unchanged: Ok(text) if text.contains("-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----") => text.to_owned(), and main.rs:727-728 map --cert/--chain through it one file per entry (options.certificate_chain = args.chain.iter().map(|p| certificate(p)).collect…). On the Java side, SigningOptions.java:243-250 parses each entry with DssEngine.readCertificates (which does return every CERTIFICATE block, DssEngine.java:178-191) and then rejects it: if (certs.size() != 1) { throw f.error("'" + key + "' entries must hold one certificate each, got " + certs.size()); }.

Experiment (offline, no TL refresh): concatenated testdata/fixtures/pki/root-ca.pem twice into a 2-block bundle and ran dss-cli --allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation sign prepare --mode cms --level b --chain bundle.pem …. Result: error: InvalidArgument: options: 'certificate_chain' entries must hold one certificate each, got 2, exit 2. The same command with the single-cert file succeeds (prints the digest and writes the request). By contrast the sibling option --trust ("Extra trusted certificate, PEM or DER (repeatable)") accepts bundles because DssEngine.java:166-170 loops over readCertificates(...) and adds every token; the bundle passed via --trust was accepted without error. So the CLI is inconsistent between --trust and --chain/--cert, and the --chain help text at main.rs:211-213 ("Issuer certificate, PEM or DER (repeatable)") does not say one certificate per file. docs/DECISIONS.md has no entry documenting the one-per-entry choice for chain entries.

Severity stays low: the failure is immediate, the error message names the exact cause and count, and the library-level contract (one certificate per JSON array entry, rust/dss/src/config.rs:398-401, README.md:390) is coherent; it is a CLI convenience gap, not a correctness or security issue. The fix the finding suggests (split PEM bundles into entries in certificate() for --chain, and error clearly for --cert) is cheap and local.

  • rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs:20: cli-cache-{pid}; :111 cli-request-{pid}.json; :178-184 cli-visible-{id}.png, cli-visible-request-{id}.json, cli-visible-signed-{id}.pdf; :267 cli-snapshot-{pid}.

F-078LowreliabilityFixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:303

/health goes through the same 512-thread spawn_blocking pool as engine calls; once >512 requests are parked waiting for engine workers, health checks queue FIFO behind them and the binary's --health-check times out

Every endpoint, /health included, uses spawn_blocking. Once 512 requests are queued, health checks and scheduled refreshes wait FIFO.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Measured: N=2500 made /health take 23.53 s against a 3 s/5 s health-check timeout. A container that is busy but healthy gets restarted.

Evidence

lib.rs:303-311; lib.rs:256; schedule.rs:60; Dockerfile:39

Impact

False unhealthy signals kill busy sidecars and drop queued work.

Recommendation

Answer /health from cached state, use async replies (oneshot), and bound admission.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

Engine calls can no longer flood tokio's 512-thread blocking pool: a document request only reaches spawn_blocking with an admission permit, and --max-in-flight is capped at 256, so /health, /tl/status, /version and the scheduler's refresh always find a free blocking thread. /health still asks the engine (trusted_list_status is a cheap control-thread call) and so reports the truth rather than a cached copy.

Files: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs, docs/server.md

Test: http.rs admission_control_refuses_the_request_over_the_limit (the over-limit request never enters the pool; /health answers alongside); no 2500-request flood test

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.9

Code path confirmed. rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-268 health() calls run(engine, |e| e.trusted_list_status()), and run() at lib.rs:303-311 is tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || call(&engine)).await for every endpoint, with the doc comment "The engine's own workers do the work; this thread waits." Each validate request's blocking thread then parks in rust/dss/src/engine.rs:155-163 (self.submit(Job::Validate{..}); result.recv()) on an unbounded std mpsc job queue (engine.rs mpsc::channel::<Job>()) served by N workers (main.rs:238-241: default = available_parallelism). The runtime is #[tokio::main] (main.rs:94) with no max_blocking_threads, so tokio 1.54.1's default of 512 applies (tokio/src/runtime/builder.rs:324 max_blocking_threads: 512) and the overflow queue is FIFO (blocking/pool.rs:624 push_back, :657 pop_front). trusted_list_status itself is cheap (engine.rs:305-307, a control-thread call that "Never waits for a running refresh"), but it cannot run until a blocking thread frees up. Nothing bounds admission: no ConcurrencyLimit/Semaphore layer in the router (lib.rs:103-121, only DefaultBodyLimit). Experiment (release build of 7e697c9 source, offline engine in the scratchpad, --allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation --refresh-hours 0): with --workers 2 and 2500 concurrent POST /validate of testdata/fixtures/pades/b-lta.pdf, the server grew to 536 threads, an in-flight GET /health took 9.56 s (curl: 5.59 s), and dss-server --health-check --listen 127.0.0.1:18731 (main.rs:177-196, 3 s read timeout) exited 1 after exactly 3.00 s, i.e. the false-unhealthy signal the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:39, --timeout=5s) would see. With the default 15 workers and the tiny b-b.pdf the same burst only delayed /health by 0.60 s, so magnitude depends on worker count and document cost; the 23.5 s figure is configuration-specific but the mechanism is real. Below the threshold (N=400) /health stayed at 0 ms. Not a documented decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:879-880 only tested "400 validations from 32 parallel clients", and docs/server.md:42 documents queueing of requests but not that /health queues with them. Corrections: (1) Docker's HEALTHCHECK needs 3 consecutive failures at 10 s interval, so flipping to unhealthy needs ~30 s of sustained saturation, and plain Docker does not restart on unhealthy (Compose depends_on / Swarm / Kubernetes do), so "gets restarted" is orchestrator-dependent; (2) the scheduler claim (dss/src/schedule.rs:60 also uses spawn_blocking for refreshes) is correct in kind, but a late refresh is far less harmful than a failed health probe. Severity medium: real under overload (>512 queued engine calls) and it turns a healthy, merely busy sidecar into a failing probe, but it needs a sustained burst well above the documented load.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Mechanism confirmed in code. health (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-268) does match run(engine, |e| e.trusted_list_status()).await, and run (lib.rs:303-311) is tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || call(&engine)). main.rs uses plain #[tokio::main] with no runtime builder, so tokio's default cap of 512 blocking threads applies. The engine's job queue is unbounded (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:395 mpsc::channel::<Job>(); submit at 267-270 just sends), and every validate/extend/sign call blocks its blocking thread on result.recv(), so once 512 engine calls are in flight, new spawn_blocking tasks (health included, and the scheduler's refresh at rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:60) queue FIFO behind them. trusted_list_status itself is a cheap control_call on the control thread (engine.rs:305-307, 339-343), so the delay is purely the pool, not the engine. The PHP client's default $timeoutSeconds = 120 (php/DssClient.php:26) lets a backlog accumulate, and a dropped request future does not cancel its spawn_blocking task, so a client timeout does not drain it. Nothing in docs/DECISIONS.md or docs/server.md documents this as a trade-off; the only related statements are --workers ... more wait in a queue (server.md:42) and the Dockerfile's intent Healthy once the engine is up (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:38), which the implementation drifts from: readiness is already a synchronous state.engine() OnceLock check (lib.rs:252), so answering /health without the blocking hop is a small, actionable fix.

Impact is narrower than claimed, hence low rather than medium. (1) The trigger is a trusted client (token, private network per DECISIONS.md:856-857) sending more than 512 simultaneous requests and sustaining that overload: the Docker HEALTHCHECK is --interval=10s --timeout=5s with default retries=3, so three consecutive 5 s timeouts (~30 s of stall) are needed; the finding's one-shot N=2500 giving 23.5 s would fail about two probes, not three. (2) The documented deployment is Compose with depends_on: condition: service_healthy (server.md:186-213), which only gates the app's start; Docker and Compose do not restart an unhealthy container, so "kill busy sidecars" happens only under Swarm or a Kubernetes livenessProbe pointed at /health, which the docs do not describe. (3) The delayed scheduled refresh is negligible against a 6-hour period. Still real: under sustained overload the container shows unhealthy, monitoring pages, and an orchestrator that does act on it drops the whole in-flight backlog on restart, so the finding stands as a low-severity reliability gap with the corrected scope.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

The mechanism is real. In rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, the health handler starts at line 251, not 307. It calls run(engine, |e| e.trusted_list_status()).await (lib.rs:256). run (lib.rs:303-311) is tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || call(&engine)). That blocking thread then waits in control_call (dss/src/engine.rs:339-343: self.control.send(...), then result.recv()).

Every engine endpoint uses the same run helper. main.rs:94 is a plain #[tokio::main] with no max_blocking_threads, so the default cap of 512 blocking threads applies. A request thread sits blocked for the whole duration of its engine call, and the engine's worker count is small (default 1, engine.rs:45). So under a burst, all 512 blocking threads are occupied and new spawn_blocking tasks, the health probe included, wait in tokio's FIFO queue. The only limit on incoming requests is a body-size cap (DefaultBodyLimit, lib.rs:120); nothing bounds concurrency.

The scheduled refresh has the same problem: it also uses spawn_blocking (dss/src/schedule.rs:60). The health check client in main.rs:189 uses a 3 s timeout, and the Dockerfile sets HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s --timeout=5s (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:39). So a long queue does produce unhealthy results. The status call itself is cheap because the control thread answers it, which means the delay comes entirely from the queue. I did not re-run the 23.53 s measurement, but it is consistent with this code.

Severity corrections:

  1. Plain Docker HEALTHCHECK only marks the container unhealthy. It does not restart it. A restart, and the lost queued work, happens only under an orchestrator that acts on health status. "Gets restarted" is therefore conditional.
  2. The trigger needs more than 512 concurrent in-flight engine requests to a sidecar. That is unlikely in normal use. When it does happen, every client is already seeing very long latency, so the main defect is the missing admission control, and the false-unhealthy signal is a symptom of it.
  3. Availability is the only impact, and it needs network access (plus the bearer token if one is configured).

That makes this low rather than medium. The finding is precise enough for a maintainer to act on, because the fix sites are clear:

  • answer /health without spawn_blocking, or from cached state;
  • bound admission, for example with a semaphore or tower ConcurrencyLimit;
  • or reply asynchronously so engine calls do not each hold a blocking thread.

F-079LowreliabilityFixedrust/dss-server/src/main.rs:172

No read/idle timeout or shutdown bound: one stalled connection blocks graceful shutdown indefinitely on the private-network sidecar (orchestrator SIGKILL is the only backstop)

axum::serve sets no timer, so hyper's 30 s header timeout is disabled, and there is no body or request timeout.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Verified: a connection with incomplete headers was still open after 45 s, and a trickling body got no answer.

Evidence

main.rs:172; hyper time.rs:75-79 'has default, but no timer set'

Impact

Cheap slowloris DoS, and SIGTERM ends in SIGKILL.

Recommendation

Set a timer and header_read_timeout, add a TimeoutLayer and a connection cap, and bound shutdown.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

main.rs now runs its own accept loop on hyper's http1::Builder with a TokioTimer and header_read_timeout(30 s) (also closes idle keep-alive connections), a --max-connections semaphore on accept (default 1024), and axum-style graceful shutdown per connection (watch channel + Connection::graceful_shutdown). --request-timeout (DSS_REQUEST_TIMEOUT, default 300 s, 0 = none) is a middleware deadline over body upload + engine call answering 504 TIMEOUT, so a stalled upload no longer holds the drain: SIGTERM finishes in-flight requests within that bound. hyper 1.12.0 and hyper-util 0.1.21 (already in Cargo.lock as axum's own stack) became direct dependencies; tower 'util' moved from dev to normal dependencies.

Files: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs, rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss-server/Cargo.toml, docs/server.md

Test: process.rs graceful_stop_is_bounded_by_the_request_timeout (stalled multipart upload, SIGTERM, client gets 504 TIMEOUT, server exits 0 within the bound); the 30 s header timeout itself is not waited for by a test

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.88

Confirmed by reading the source and the locked dependency code. (1) main.rs:172 axum::serve(listener, app).with_graceful_shutdown(stop_signal()).await? sets no builder options. axum 0.8.9 serve/mod.rs:391 uses Builder::new(TokioExecutor::new()); hyper-util 0.1.21 Builder::new installs no timer. hyper 1.12.0 defaults h1_header_read_timeout to 30s (server/conn/http1.rs:253) but common/time.rs:74-80 returns None with warn!(\"timeout 'header_read_timeout' has default, but no timer set\") when the timer is Time::Empty, so the header timeout is disabled — incomplete-header connections have no deadline. (2) lib.rs:104-121 applies only DefaultBodyLimit::max(...) (a size cap); there is no TimeoutLayer and tower-http is not a dependency, so a trickling body is never timed out. (3) Shutdown: axum serve/mod.rs:407-409 only calls graceful_shutdown()→hyper disable_keep_alive() (server/conn/http1.rs:139-141); dispatch.rs:91-99 closes a connection on shutdown only when is_write_closed() or has_initial_read_write_state(), the latter needing an empty read buffer (conn.rs:201-204). A connection with buffered partial headers is kept open, and with no header timer never completes; axum run() awaits close_tx.closed().await (serve/mod.rs:303) for all connection tasks, so main.rs:172 .await? never returns, 'dss-server: stopping' and state.shutdown() (lines 173-177) never run, and the process hangs until SIGKILL. The SIGTERM test (tests/process.rs:73-117) uses only Connection: close requests and never exercises this. Severity medium: default bind is 127.0.0.1 (main.rs:37), but the project ships a container image documented to bind 0.0.0.0 (DECISIONS.md:870-878) with no connection cap, and the shutdown hang applies to every deployment. The line cite (main.rs:172) is exact.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

Code: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:172 axum::serve(listener, app).with_graceful_shutdown(stop_signal()).await?; sets no timer or timeout; rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120 adds only DefaultBodyLimit. hyper 1.12.0 src/common/time.rs:75-79 confirms the 30 s header default is dropped without a timer (warn!("timeout {} has default, but no timer set", name); None). axum 0.8.9 src/serve/mod.rs:296-303 waits unboundedly on close_tx.closed().await for every connection task. Experiment with rust/target/release/dss-server (offline engine, same flags as tests/process.rs): a connection with incomplete headers and, separately, one with a partial multipart body each kept the process alive for the full 15 s after SIGTERM and were never closed by the server; it printed dss-server: stopping and exited 0 only once the client closed its socket. So the shutdown impact is real as described and docs/server.md:27-28 promises the opposite ("stops accepting connections, finishes the requests in progress ... then exits with status 0"); nothing in docs/DECISIONS.md or server.md documents the missing timeouts as a trade-off. Impact calibration, which lowers severity to low: docs/server.md:216-217 and DECISIONS.md place the sidecar on the same host or a private network, never public, and a peer there can already exhaust the server with legitimate 100 MiB uploads (no cap on concurrent body buffering, only on engine workers), so "cheap slowloris DoS" adds little attack surface; the shutdown hang is bounded by the documented Compose deployment, where docker stop SIGKILLs after 10 s and only in-flight requests are lost. The realistic operational case is a half-open TCP connection from a dead peer or partition, which with no timeout and no keepalive lingers forever and turns every later graceful stop into a SIGKILL. Actionable (a timer plus header/idle timeout via hyper-util's builder, or a bounded wait after the signal), but a reliability nuisance rather than a medium security finding.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

The mechanism is described correctly. rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:172 is axum::serve(listener, app).with_graceful_shutdown(stop_signal()).await?;, with no timer, timeout or connection-limit configuration. axum 0.8.9 (src/serve/mod.rs:391) builds Builder::new(TokioExecutor::new()) and never sets a timer. hyper 1.12.0 sets h1_header_read_timeout: Dur::Default(Some(Duration::from_secs(30))) (server/conn/http1.rs:253). Its time.rs check then logs "timeout {} has default, but no timer set" and returns None, so the 30 s header timeout is silently dropped. The router in rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120 only adds DefaultBodyLimit::max(...), and a grep for timeout, Timeout or ConcurrencyLimit in src/ finds nothing on the server side; the only timeouts belong to the --health-check client (main.rs:189-193). axum's graceful shutdown calls conn.graceful_shutdown() and waits for every connection to close. A connection stuck mid-headers or mid-body therefore keeps serve from returning, and the orchestrator's SIGTERM ends in SIGKILL. That also skips state.shutdown() at main.rs:176-178.

I calibrate the severity down from medium to low. docs/server.md (Security section) says the sidecar runs with no TLS and only on the same host or a private network ("never expose it publicly"), and the Compose example tells users not to publish the port. The attack vector is therefore adjacent or local network, not internet. The attack does not need the token, because headers are read before auth. The impact is availability only, through fd/memory exhaustion from many idle connections, plus an unclean stop that docker or k8s resolves with SIGKILL after the grace period. No data is exposed and integrity is not affected. In normal use with a well-behaved PHP client, the shutdown symptom shows up only with keep-alive or stuck clients. The fix is concrete and actionable: serve through hyper_util with .timer(TokioTimer) and header_read_timeout, add a tower-http TimeoutLayer or RequestBodyTimeoutLayer and a connection cap, and wrap the graceful shutdown in a bounded tokio::time::timeout.

F-081LowsecurityPartially fixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:213

POST /tl/refresh shares the single API token, has no cooldown beyond the one-at-a-time guard, and logs no caller

It uses the same token as validation, has no rate limit, and does not log the caller.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

lib.rs:114; :218-227

Impact

Resource abuse and traffic to EU hosts.

Recommendation

Rate-limit it, consider an admin token, and log the peer.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package rust-server)

The caller of POST /tl/refresh is logged ('online trusted-list refresh requested by <peer>'): the accept loop inserts ConnectInfo(peer) into every request, read by the handler as Option<Extension<ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>>>. No rate limit and no admin token: with request_refresh() a request made while a refresh runs is coalesced into it and the engine serialises refreshes, so the refresh rate is bounded by the refresh duration; documented in server.md ('who asked for a refresh' is logged). A separate admin token was not added (one client, one token, by design in DECISIONS.md).

Files: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs, docs/server.md, docs/openapi.yaml

Test: http.rs tl_refresh_with_a_scheduler / tl_refresh_without_a_scheduler cover the handler; the log line is checked by hand only

(1) Same token: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:113 .route("/tl/refresh", post(tl_refresh)) is inside the one .route_layer(middleware::from_fn_with_state(Arc::clone(&state), authorize)) at :114; authorize (:278-295) checks the single state.token: Option<String> (:62), so any holder of the validation token may trigger a refresh; there is no admin token or role. (2) No rate limit: tl_refresh (:213-233) only refuses with 409 while refresh_in_progress is true, and the scheduler's refresh_now (rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:80, self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok() on a capacity-1 channel at :45) refuses a second pending request. Concurrency is bounded to one refresh at a time (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:276 self.refreshing.swap(true, Ordering::AcqRel); java TrustedListManager.java:267 refreshLock.tryLock()), but nothing imposes a cooldown: a client can start the next refresh as soon as the previous one ends, each one re-downloading LOTL + 31 TLs by default (README.md:274 "online_cache_expiration_ms": 0, // 0 = re-download on every online refresh, about 10 s each per DECISIONS.md:887-889). (3) No caller logging: no ConnectInfo, TraceLayer or tracing anywhere in rust/dss-server (grep empty); the only output is the outcome line via describe_refresh (main.rs:160, lib.rs:223) and 5xx errors (lib.rs:525). Severity stays low: the documented deployment is a sidecar on the same host or private network with the port unpublished and the token held only by the app (docs/server.md:212-218, DECISIONS.md:855-857), concurrent refreshes cannot stack, and online_cache_expiration_ms lets an operator cap EU traffic; a token holder could equally hammer /validate. But no document records rate limiting or a separate admin token as a deliberate decision, so the finding stands as described, at low severity.

F-082LowsecurityPartially fixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:278

Tokenless dss-server has no Origin/Host check: cross-site form POSTs from any web page reach /validate, /extend, /sign/* and /tl/refresh

Multipart and form POSTs need no preflight, and neither Origin nor Host is checked.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

main.rs:37, :40-41; lib.rs:279

Impact

A drive-by page can trigger refreshes and submissions.

Recommendation

Reject requests with an Origin header or an unexpected Host, and recommend the token everywhere.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package rust-server)

Without a token, any request carrying an Origin header (browsers add it to every cross-site POST and fetch) is refused 403 FORBIDDEN by the authorize middleware; with a token, the token decides. The Host check was not added: the sidecar cannot know its legitimate Host names (Compose service names, proxies), so a Host allow-list would break documented deployments. server.md recommends the token wherever a browser can reach the server.

Files: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, docs/server.md, docs/openapi.yaml

Test: http.rs requests_from_web_pages_need_a_token (GET and multipart POST with Origin -> 403 tokenless; 401 then 200 with the token)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.9

Reproduced; the claim is accurate as described, with the defect better anchored in lib.rs than main.rs.

Code evidence:

  • rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:37-41: default_value = "127.0.0.1:8484" and token_file: Option<PathBuf> — loopback by default, token optional.
  • rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:105-122 (router): the only layers are route_layer(middleware::from_fn_with_state(.., authorize)) and DefaultBodyLimit. No CORS, Host or Origin layer anywhere; grep -rniE 'origin|host|csrf' over rust/dss-server/src matches nothing.
  • lib.rs:278-295 (authorize): if let Some(token) = &state.token { ... } then next.run(request).await — with no token every request passes untouched; headers other than Authorization are never inspected.
  • lib.rs:213 (tl_refresh) takes only State — no body, no content-type requirement — so a plain <form method=POST action="http://127.0.0.1:8484/tl/refresh"> triggers an online refresh without any preflight. /validate, /extend, /sign/* take Multipart, which an HTML form with enctype=multipart/form-data produces (a "simple" request, no preflight).

Experiment (read-only, offline; the scratch server used --refresh-hours 0, a scratchpad cache dir and --allow-without-trusted-lists; /tl/refresh was never called): started rust/target/debug/dss-server --listen 127.0.0.1:26561 with no --token-file, then:

  • GET /tl/status with Origin: https://evil.example and Host: evil.example -> 200.
  • POST /validate multipart with Origin: https://evil.example, Referer: https://evil.example/attack.html, Host: evil.example, Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site and no Authorization -> 200 in 50 ms.
  • POST /extend ({"level":"LT"}) with the same foreign Origin -> 200.
  • A urlencoded body to /validate is refused (400 "Invalid boundary for multipart/form-data"), but that does not help: forms can set the multipart enctype, and /tl/refresh needs no body.

Not a documented decision: docs/server.md "Security" (lines 214-218) and docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857 only discuss network exposure ("never expose it publicly", "the token stops other containers on the same network") and keep the token optional; the browser/CSRF/DNS-rebinding vector is never mentioned, and the default developer setup (loopback, no token) is exactly the exposed configuration. The test token_guards_everything_but_health (tests/http.rs:439) covers only the token path.

Severity calibrated to low, as the finding says: without CORS headers a cross-site page cannot read responses (DNS rebinding could, since Host is unchecked, but the server holds no secrets — it only processes the attacker's own documents, and detached_contents[].path is already refused at lib.rs:384-393). The real effects are nuisance/DoS: unsolicited online trusted-list refreshes (rate-limited by the 409 REFRESH_IN_PROGRESS path), CPU/memory from up to --max-request-mb (100 MiB) bodies, and, where a TSA with paid credentials is configured, consuming timestamps via /extend or /sign/* at T/LTA. Modern Chrome's Local Network Access gating further reduces exploitability, while Firefox/Safari do not. Recommendation in the finding (reject requests carrying an Origin header or an unexpected Host, and advise the token even on loopback) is sound.

F-084LowcorrectnessFixedrust/dss-server/src/main.rs:131

--max-request-mb overflows silently in release builds: a large value makes every request 413

usize multiplication wraps around.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Verified with 2^44.

Evidence

main.rs:131 'args.max_request_mb * 1024 * 1024'

Impact

A server that looks healthy but refuses every document.

Recommendation

Use checked_mul or a bounded value_parser.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

--max-request-mb is u64 with clap value_parser!(u64).range(1..=1_048_576); the byte count is computed with checked_mul and usize::try_from, failing with 'too large for this platform' instead of wrapping. --refresh-hours has range(0..=1_000_000) and checked_mul(3600); --workers, --max-in-flight, --max-connections, --request-timeout, --tl-threads have ranges too.

After review: start_failures_name_their_cause now sends --max-request-mb 0, --max-request-mb 17592186044416, --max-in-flight 300 and --refresh-hours 1000001: each exits 2 with clap's usage error naming the option and the value, and the server never reaches 'listening on'. A later removal of a value_parser range is caught.

Files: docs/server.md, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs, rust/dss-server/tests/process.rs

Test: clap-enforced ranges; no explicit test of an out-of-range value

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.9

Confirmed as stated. rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:48 declares max_request_mb: usize with a plain clap #[arg(long, env = "DSS_MAX_REQUEST_MB", default_value_t = 100)] and no bounded value_parser; main.rs:131 does router(Arc::clone(&state), args.max_request_mb * 1024 * 1024) with unchecked multiplication. The result goes straight into .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_request_bytes)) at rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:120 with no clamping or validation in between. rust/Cargo.toml has no [profile] section and no overflow-checks, so the release profile uses Rust's default (wrapping, no checks). Reproduced in the scratchpad: a one-line program doing mb * 1024 * 1024 with mb = 17592186044416 (2^44) prints 0 when compiled with rustc -O and panics with "attempt to multiply with overflow" in a debug build. A limit of 0 bytes makes every multipart request fail the body limit, and tests/http.rs:296-304 shows that path yields 413 REQUEST_TOO_LARGE, so a release server started with --max-request-mb 17592186044416 (or any value >= 2^44) would listen and answer /health normally while 413-ing every document. Severity stays low: the wrap only occurs for values >= 2^44 MiB (16 EiB), which no operator would set except by typo or misconfiguration, and the fix is trivial (checked_mul or value_parser!(u64).range(1..=N)).

F-086Lowsupply-chainFixeddocker/dss-server/Dockerfile:10

Dockerfile verifies none of its inputs: base image unpinned, release tarball extracted without checking the .sha256 that package.sh/CI produce, image never built or smoke-tested in CI

debian:trixie-slim is not pinned by digest. The tarball is extracted with no checksum or provenance check, and CI never builds the image.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

package.sh produces .sha256 files, but they are ignored. TARGETARCH requires BuildKit. No signatures or attestations exist.

Evidence

Dockerfile:10 'FROM debian:trixie-slim'; :21-26 'COPY ... tar -xzf'; package.sh:67

Impact

A tampered package or base image goes undetected, and builds are not reproducible.

Recommendation

Pin the base by digest, run sha256sum -c before extracting, and add a CI build plus health-check job.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

Dockerfile: base pinned to debian:trixie-slim@sha256:a72b4433de1c...; the package is read through RUN --mount=type=bind and verified with sha256sum -c against its .sha256 (now required in the build context) before extraction; VERSION build-arg required. New CI job 'docker' builds the image from the linux-x64 package, waits for the image's own HEALTHCHECK (offline, DSS_REFRESH_HOURS=0, DSS_ALLOW_WITHOUT_TRUSTED_LISTS=true), checks UID 10001 and runs package-smoke.sh inside the image (scripts/ci/docker-smoke.sh). release-assets needs it. Signatures/attestations: see F-112.

After review: server.md Docker section now says the build context must hold dss-native-<VERSION>-linux-<x64|aarch64>.tar.gz AND its .sha256, that the build verifies the checksum and stops without the file, that --build-arg VERSION is required and BuildKit (default since Docker 23) is needed.

Files: .github/workflows/ci.yml, docker/dss-server/Dockerfile, docs/server.md, scripts/ci/docker-smoke.sh

Test: Local Docker (BuildKit 29.9.2, arm64) with a stand-in linux-aarch64 package: build succeeds, a tampered .sha256 fails the build, container reaches 'healthy', id = uid=10001(dss); docker-smoke.sh reached 'container healthy' (package checks then fail only because the stand-in has no dss-cli).

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.9

Reproduced every factual claim by reading the code.

  1. Unpinned base: docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:10 is exactly FROM debian:trixie-slim, no @sha256: digest. This is inconsistent with the project's own stated policy in docs/DECISIONS.md:502-509 ("Pinned inputs": GraalVM checked against SHA-256 values in the script, Maven wrapper checksum, GitHub actions pinned to commit SHAs), so it is a gap, not a documented decision.
  1. Tarball not checked: Dockerfile:21 COPY dss-native-${VERSION}-linux-*.tar.gz /tmp/ and :25 tar -xzf "/tmp/dss-native-${VERSION}-linux-${arch}.tar.gz" ... with no sha256sum/shasum anywhere in the file. scripts/package.sh:67-68 does write "$name.tar.gz.sha256", and .github/workflows/ci.yml:113-115 uploads dist/*.tar.gz and dist/*.sha256 to the release, but the Dockerfile never consumes it. A scratchpad glob test confirmed the COPY pattern dss-native-1.2.0-linux-*.tar.gz matches only the tarball, not the .tar.gz.sha256 file, so the checksum is not even copied into the build context layer.
  1. Never built in CI: .github/workflows/ci.yml has no docker/buildx step at all (grep for "docker" in .github/ returned nothing). docs/DECISIONS.md:893-894 explicitly says "Not verified yet. The Docker image built from a real Linux package: only its layout was checked, with a stand-in package." So the authors acknowledge the image is unverified; this is a known gap, not a reasoned decision to skip it.
  1. No signatures/attestations: grep for cosign/slsa/attestation/provenance/sigstore across .github, scripts, docs returned nothing.
  1. TARGETARCH/BuildKit: Dockerfile:13 ARG TARGETARCH with no default; :23 case "${TARGETARCH}" in ... *) echo "no package for ${TARGETARCH}" >&2; exit 1. Under the legacy builder TARGETARCH is empty and the build fails loudly ("no package for "), so this is a usability nit rather than a silent defect; Docker 23+ defaults to BuildKit.

Severity calibration: low is correct. One mitigating point the finding does not mention: the Dockerfile builds from a local context the operator controls (docs/server.md:176-180: dist/ after package.sh, or release assets they downloaded), and a .sha256 sitting beside the tarball in the same directory shares its trust boundary, so sha256sum -c would catch corruption/mix-ups but not a tampered download unless the expected digest were pinned or passed as a build-arg. The gap is real as described but is a hardening/reproducibility issue with no runtime behaviour change.

F-089LowcorrectnessFixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:473
