from_body pairs any status that is not 413 with INVALID_ARGUMENT, so a stream read failure becomes a 500 server error.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Reproduced: 'dss-server: 500 INVALID_ARGUMENT: failed to read stream'.

Evidence

lib.rs:469-475

Impact

Operators get paged for client disconnects, and the response contradicts the docs.

Recommendation

Map by status, and treat a stream failure as 400 without logging it as a server error.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

ApiError::from_body maps by status: 413 stays REQUEST_TOO_LARGE; any other client status keeps axum's message as 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT; a server status (axum's 500 for a broken body stream) becomes 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT 'the request body could not be read: ...' and is therefore not logged as a 5xx.

Files: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, docs/server.md

Test: http.rs request_errors (a BrokenBody http_body::Body that yields one frame then ConnectionReset -> 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.9

Confirmed by code reading and a scratchpad reproduction.

Code path: Parts::read at rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:327/336 uses ? on multipart.next_field().await and field.bytes().await, so a MultipartError reaches impl From<MultipartError> for ApiError (lib.rs:516-519), which calls ApiError::from_body(e.status(), e.body_text()). from_body (lib.rs:469-475) is:

if status == StatusCode::PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE { Self::new(status, "REQUEST_TOO_LARGE", message) }
else { Self::new(status, "INVALID_ARGUMENT", message) }

It keeps whatever status axum chose but hard-codes the code to INVALID_ARGUMENT for every non-413 status. In axum 0.8.9 (~/.cargo/registry/src/*/axum-0.8.9/src/extract/multipart.rs:261-293) status_code_from_multer_error returns StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR for multer::Error::StreamReadFailed when the inner error is neither a multer error nor a LengthLimitError (i.e. a hyper/IO body error such as a client reset), and also for the _ => catch-all. multer-3.1.0 renders that variant as "failed to read stream" (multer src/error.rs:92). Then impl IntoResponse for ApiError (lib.rs:522-529) does if self.status.is_server_error() { eprintln!("dss-server: {} {}: {}", ...) }, producing exactly dss-server: 500 INVALID_ARGUMENT: failed to read stream.

Reproduction: a scratchpad axum 0.8.9 app with a multipart handler fed a body stream whose second frame is an io::Error(ConnectionReset) printed status=500 Internal Server Error body=failed to read stream, so the server's from_body would tag it INVALID_ARGUMENT at status 500.

This contradicts the documented contract in docs/server.md:102-110, where INVALID_ARGUMENT appears only at 400 and 500 carries only INVALID_CONFIG / INTERNAL_ERROR (same in docs/openapi.yaml). No test in rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs covers a mid-body stream error.

Severity calibrated to low rather than medium: when the client actually aborted, the 500 response is never delivered, so the observable effect is a misleading stderr line and an undocumented status/code pairing; "operators get paged" is speculative (the server only writes to stderr). The recommendation stands: map by status (400 -> INVALID_ARGUMENT, 413 -> REQUEST_TOO_LARGE, other -> a client-side disconnect code or INTERNAL_ERROR without the server-error log for stream read failures).

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Mechanism confirmed from code, not just the finding: axum 0.8.9 status_code_from_multer_error (~/.cargo/registry/.../axum-0.8.9/src/extract/multipart.rs:261-291) returns INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR for StreamReadFailed unless the inner error is a LengthLimitError; multer's Display for that variant is "failed to read stream" (multer-3.1.0/src/error.rs:92). ApiError::from_body (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:469-475) then does if status == PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE { REQUEST_TOO_LARGE } else { INVALID_ARGUMENT }, so the pair becomes 500/INVALID_ARGUMENT, and IntoResponse (lib.rs:523-526) runs eprintln!("dss-server: {} {}: {}", ...) for any is_server_error(). No test covers a failing body stream (tests/http.rs request_errors only exercises malformed parts, non-multipart, 413 and 404), and neither docs/DECISIONS.md (the dss-server section, lines 819-881) nor docs/server.md documents this as intended; on the contrary server.md:102-110 lists INVALID_ARGUMENT only under 400 and only INVALID_CONFIG/INTERNAL_ERROR under 500, so the pair contradicts the published contract.

Impact, corrected: (1) When the client truly aborted, the response is never delivered, so the only effect is the stderr line. server.md:29 tells operators that stderr carries "every 5xx error", which makes a spurious "500" line for a client disconnect a false signal in the one channel the docs point them at. There is, however, no alerting in this server; "operators get paged" depends entirely on the operator's log pipeline, and in the documented deployment (a sidecar on a trusted network with one Laravel/Octane host app, DECISIONS.md:819-821) client aborts are rare (PHP timeouts, deploy restarts). (2) When the client is still connected, e.g. a malformed chunked body, it receives 500 with code INVALID_ARGUMENT; php/DssClient.php throws DssException with that status/code either way (server.md:171), so the host app still fails the request, merely with an inconsistent status. Fix is trivial (map by status, or treat stream read failure as 400 and skip the log). Real, but a low-severity log-noise and contract-consistency issue, not a medium correctness problem.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

The mechanism is real and described accurately. At rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:469-475, from_body maps 413 to "REQUEST_TOO_LARGE" and passes every other status through unchanged with the code "INVALID_ARGUMENT": else { Self::new(status, "INVALID_ARGUMENT", message) }. Both From<MultipartRejection> (lib.rs:512) and From<MultipartError> (lib.rs:518) pass in the status that axum reports. In axum 0.8.9 (src/extract/multipart.rs:276-290), multer::Error::StreamReadFailed returns StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR unless the inner error is a multer error or a LengthLimitError. A hyper body error from an aborted upload therefore becomes a 500 with the code INVALID_ARGUMENT. IntoResponse (lib.rs:524-525) then logs it with if self.status.is_server_error() { eprintln!("dss-server: {} {}: {}", ...) }, which matches the reproduced log line. This also contradicts docs/server.md:110, where 500 covers only INVALID_CONFIG and INTERNAL_ERROR. So it is a real code/status mismatch and a docs inconsistency.

I lowered the severity from medium to low. The client that aborted never receives the response. The only server-side effect is one misleading stderr line per aborted upload, with no crash, no leaked state and no security impact. "Operators get paged" overstates it: nothing in the repo sends these lines to alerting, though they can add noise to 5xx metrics. A client can trigger it at will, but the most it can do is spam the logs, and any access log has that same exposure. The fix is simple and cheap: map by status, or treat StreamReadFailed as 400 or 499 and skip the server-error log.

The method exists in the axum 0.8 version in use (axum routing/mod.rs:374, pub fn method_not_allowed_fallback). The error table there lists 400, 401, 404, 409, 413, 422 and 500, with no 405. A grep finds no "405" in docs/openapi.yaml. The test at rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:464 mentions 405 only in a comment and never checks a 405 body.

Correction to the mechanism: authorize is applied with route_layer, so when a token is configured, an unauthenticated wrong-method request probably gets the JSON 401 first. The empty 405 then appears only for authenticated callers, or when the server runs without a token.

Why low: it only happens when a caller uses the wrong HTTP method, which is a programming error and not normal use. The status code and the Allow header still say what went wrong. There is no security or data-integrity impact; this is an API consistency and documentation gap. The fix is cheap: add a JSON method_not_allowed_fallback (for example code METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED) at lib.rs:119, and add the row to server.md and openapi.yaml.

F-092LowreliabilityFixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:214

/tl/refresh: non-atomic in-progress check; status lags the 202 by several thread hand-offs

Between the 202 and the engine's refreshing flag, /tl/status shows no refresh. Concurrent POSTs race, and 409 can be returned for a refresh that is only queued.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

lib.rs:215-227; schedule.rs:80-82

Impact

Pollers return stale data, and 409s are spurious.

Recommendation

Track queued state atomically and return a started_at token.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

With a scheduler the handler calls request_refresh(): Started -> 202, AlreadyPending -> 409 (accurate: a request is queued and will run), Stopped/other -> 500 INTERNAL_ERROR 'the refresh schedule has stopped: restart the server' (logged), so a dead task no longer reads as 'already running' forever. Without a scheduler a server-side AtomicBool set before spawn_blocking makes the 409 atomic instead of reading the engine's lagging flag. The few-millisecond lag of /tl/status after the 202 remains and is now documented (openapi.yaml, server.md); no started_at token was added (the 202 body is unchanged).

After review: tl_refresh_with_a_scheduler no longer assumes the closed-port refresh outlives two sequential POSTs: after the first 202 it fires three concurrent POSTs (tokio::join!) and repeats that until a 409 is seen (30 s bound), asserting every answer is 202 or 409; a refresh the rebuilt library refuses by policy at once cannot make it flaky. The outcome wait and the dead-scheduler part are unchanged.

Files: docs/openapi.yaml, docs/server.md, rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs

Test: http.rs tl_refresh_without_a_scheduler (202 then 409 then 202 again), tl_refresh_with_a_scheduler (202, 409 among the next two, outcome observed, dead scheduler -> 500)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

The structure the finding describes is real, but its impact is overstated; I rate it low, not medium.

What the code does (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:212-235): the handler first asks the library for status, let running = run(..., |e| e.trusted_list_status()).await?.refresh_in_progress; (214-217), then, only if !running, either scheduler.refresh_now() or spawn_blocking(move || engine.refresh_trusted_lists()) (218-227), and answers 202. refresh_now is self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok() on an mpsc::channel::<()>(1) (rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:44, 80-82). The refresh_in_progress flag it checks is not the engine's Rust AtomicBool but Java's onlineRefreshStartedAt, set only once onlineRefresh() takes refreshLock (java/.../TrustedListManager.java:265-279, status at 463-465). So after the 202 the flag becomes true only after: scheduler task recv -> spawn_blocking (schedule.rs:57-60) -> Engine::refresh_trusted_lists swaps the AtomicBool (engine.rs:276) and sends a RefreshJob over a std mpsc to the dss-refresh thread (engine.rs:290-295, 667-668) -> Graal call -> Java tryLock. That is four or five thread hand-offs, i.e. a window of microseconds to a few milliseconds, during which GET /tl/status reports refresh_in_progress: false and the previous last_online_refresh. A client that follows the documented contract (openapi.yaml:280-283: "answers at once. /tl/status shows the progress") and polls immediately can therefore see no refresh at all. Confirmed by reading; not run, because exercising POST /tl/refresh needs the real LOTL (http.rs never calls it, only /tl/status at line 426).

Concurrent POSTs: two requests can both read running == false. Scheduler path: first try_send fills the 1-slot channel; the second either fails (409 "an online refresh is already running" while the refresh is only queued, schedule.rs:80-82) or, if the loop already drained the slot, succeeds and queues a second back-to-back refresh. No-scheduler path (--refresh-hours 0, main.rs:154-169): both get 202, the second refresh_trusted_lists fails with RefreshInProgress (engine.rs:276-280) and is only eprintln!ed (lib.rs:223), so that client got a 202 for a refresh that never ran, though one is running anyway.

Why low: every window is a few scheduler hops wide; in every outcome a refresh is running or queued, so the client's intent is met; the status already carries refresh_started_at and last_online_refresh timestamps (TrustedListManager.java:464-467) that a poller can compare, which covers much of the "started_at token" recommendation; and DECISIONS.md:849-851 and :889-890 document the 202-then-poll design and the hand-checked "409 when called again while that refresh ran". The finding's "spurious 409" and double-refresh cases need two POSTs within milliseconds of each other on an admin endpoint. A tighter fix would be to decide on Engine::refresh_trusted_lists's own result (its AtomicBool is atomic) or to make the scheduler expose a "pending or running" state, but the current behaviour is a minor polish item, not a reliability defect.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The code reads as the finding says (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:215-227: a status read, then scheduler.refresh_now() which is self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok() on an mpsc::channel::<()>(1), rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:44,80-82), but the claimed impact does not hold up in this system.

  1. The window is in-process and milliseconds wide. After the 202, the scheduler loop's requests.recv() wakes at once, spawn_blocking runs e.refresh_trusted_lists() (schedule.rs:60), which synchronously does self.refreshing.swap(true, ...) and sends a RefreshJob to the engine's refresh thread (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:276-294), which calls the Java job that sets the refresh_in_progress reported by /tl/status. No I/O happens in that chain. A poller that lands inside it sees the previous status once more; it does not get wrong data, because /tl/status already carries refresh_started_at and last_online_refresh.{started_at,finished_at} (rust/dss/src/types.rs:173-182, 205-209), which is precisely the "started_at token" the recommendation asks for. Comparing finished_at with the POST time makes the poll robust; the OpenAPI text (docs/openapi.yaml:280-283) already tells clients that /tl/status shows progress and outcome.
  1. Concurrent POSTs do not produce a wrong outcome. Both may read refresh_in_progress=false, but the bounded channel admits exactly one trigger: one caller gets 202, the other 409 (schedule.rs:80-82). The 409's wording "already running" is inaccurate by a few milliseconds (the refresh is queued, about to run), but the semantic a client acts on, "one refresh is pending, do not start another, watch /tl/status", is correct. The worst case, a third POST after the trigger was drained but before the Java flag flips, queues one more refresh that the loop runs sequentially afterwards (the loop awaits the spawn_blocking before recv'ing again), costing one extra ~15 s download on an admin endpoint. In the --refresh-hours 0 path (lib.rs:222-226) a losing concurrent call's RefreshInProgress is only logged while the client got 202, but a refresh is in fact running, so the client's intent is met.
  1. Context neutralises the rest. The sidecar is placed on a trusted host or private network with an optional bearer token (docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857), refreshes also run every 6 hours automatically (DECISIONS.md:849), validations keep serving the previous lists during any refresh by design (docs/server.md:25-26, README.md:254), and the 202/409 behaviour is documented and was exercised against the real LOTL (DECISIONS.md:850-851, 890: "/tl/refresh answered 202, and 409 when called again while that refresh ran"). "Pollers return stale data" and "409s are spurious" therefore describe, at most, one extra poll iteration or one redundant sequential refresh, with no effect on validation, extension or signing results.

Residual: a cosmetic improvement would be to word the 409 as "a refresh is running or queued". That is low/informational, not a medium reliability defect.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

The mechanism is real, but the impact is smaller than claimed.

Code: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:213-228 reads trusted_list_status().refresh_in_progress and then, as a separate step, calls scheduler.refresh_now(). In rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:80-82, refresh_now is self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok() on an mpsc::channel::<()>(1) (line 44). The engine's refreshing flag (engine.rs:276, self.refreshing.swap(true, ...)) is set only after the scheduler loop has called requests.recv() and spawn_blocking has started (schedule.rs:57-60). Confirmed consequences: (1) After a 202, there is a short window (task scheduling plus spawn_blocking startup, usually well under a millisecond) in which /tl/status still reports refresh_in_progress: false. A poller that checks immediately could take that as "finished". (2) Two POSTs that arrive inside the window both see running=false. The first try_send succeeds and the second fails, so the second gets 409 "an online refresh is already running" while the refresh is only queued. Refusing is correct here because a refresh really is pending; only the wording is imprecise. So the 409 is not "spurious" as the finding says. (3) If a POST lands after the loop has dequeued but before the engine flag is set, it enqueues a second refresh that runs right after the first. The result is a redundant refresh, not a failure. (4) The finding misses one case: the no-scheduler path (lib.rs:221-225). Two concurrent POSTs can both get 202 and both spawn refresh_trusted_lists. The engine guard then rejects the second, and that error appears only in stderr via eprintln!. Even so, the engine keeps at most one refresh running at a time (DECISIONS.md: "One online refresh at a time"), so no data is corrupted.

Severity: the endpoint is an admin/ops endpoint, the race window is tiny, and the worst outcomes are one redundant LOTL refresh, a misleading 409 message, or a poller reading the old status once. There is no security or integrity impact. That puts it at low, not medium. The finding is precise enough to act on: the file and line are right (the handler starts at 213, the check is at 215), and the schedule.rs:80-82 citation is accurate.

On the Rust side, rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:488 maps ErrorCode::TlRefreshFailed => StatusCode::BAD_GATEWAY, and that mapping can never be reached. The POST /tl/refresh handler (lib.rs:215-235) starts the refresh on spawn_blocking or the scheduler and returns StatusCode::ACCEPTED, {"ok": true} right away. The outcome only goes to eprintln through describe_refresh (lib.rs:127).

There is no security impact, and nothing is lost silently, because the published lists stay as they were. A client that waits for a 502 would never get one, but the async 202 design makes that expectation unlikely. I rate it low, not medium. The fix is to remove the code from the docs, or to document that failures appear as last_online_refresh.completed=false.

F-095LowcorrectnessFixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:284

Bearer scheme is matched case-sensitively (and only with a single space), contrary to RFC 7235

strip_prefix('Bearer ') rejects 'bearer'.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

RFC 7235 makes the scheme case-insensitive.

Evidence

lib.rs:284; curl with 'bearer' -> 401

Impact

Spurious 401s.

Recommendation

Compare the scheme with eq_ignore_ascii_case.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

bearer_token() splits the scheme at the first space or tab, compares it with eq_ignore_ascii_case("bearer") and trims the token, so 'bearer', 'BEARER', several spaces and a tab are accepted (RFC 7235).

Files: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs

Test: http.rs token_guards_everything_but_health

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.9

Confirmed by reading the code. rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:280-284 extracts the token with .and_then(|v| v.strip_prefix("Bearer ")); str::strip_prefix is a byte-exact match, so an Authorization: bearer <token> (or BEARER, or Bearer followed by more than one space, which RFC 7235's 1*SP permits) yields None and line 285 if !given.is_some_and(...) returns 401 UNAUTHORIZED "missing or wrong bearer token". RFC 7235 section 2.1 makes auth-scheme case-insensitive. The only test, token_guards_everything_but_health at rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:448, covers None, "Bearer wrong!", "Bearer s3cre" and "s3cret" but never a lowercase scheme, so it neither tests nor contradicts the claim. docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857 documents only that the token is read from a file and compared in constant time; docs/openapi.yaml:363-369 declares scheme: bearer, so no documented decision makes case-sensitive matching intentional. Severity stays low: practically every real client sends the canonical "Bearer", so the effect is a spurious 401 only for unusual-but-conformant clients; no security impact. Fix: split on the first whitespace run and compare the scheme with eq_ignore_ascii_case.

F-099LowoperationsFixeddocs/server.md:138

Documented Laravel config snippet silently turns a missing or unreadable DSS_TOKEN_FILE into "no token" (null), which config:cache then freezes

file_get_contents inside the config file is evaluated at config:cache. The token is then cached as null when built at image build time, or cached in plaintext otherwise.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

An unreadable file also silently becomes null.

Evidence

server.md:138 "'token' => is_readable(...) ? trim(file_get_contents($file)) : null"

Impact

Permanent 401s, or a token persisted on disk.

Recommendation

Store only the path and read it lazily, throwing when it cannot be read.

Remediation: Fixed (package php)

New constructor parameter DssClient(tokenFile:) holds only the path. The client reads the file on every request (cheap, and it follows rotation). A missing, unreadable or empty file throws DssException TOKEN_FILE_UNREADABLE with status 0 and sends no request; before, it silently meant no token. '' or null means no token, matching the server's rule that an empty variable is the same as an unset one. Passing both token and tokenFile is refused with InvalidArgumentException. In the docs/server.md Laravel section, config/services.php now stores 'token_file' => env('DSS_TOKEN_FILE'), the provider passes tokenFile:, and a paragraph explains why config:cache must never see the token.

After review: php handoff. DECISIONS records that the token is configured as a file path, read on each request and never cached by config:cache, and that an unreadable or empty file is TOKEN_FILE_UNREADABLE. CHANGELOG has the PHP client entry. The docs/server.md section was already done by the php package, which owns it, so no change was needed there.

Files: CHANGELOG.md, docs/DECISIONS.md, docs/server.md, php/DssClient.php

Test: php/tests/DssClientTest.php: test_token_file_is_read_lazily, test_missing_token_file_throws, test_empty_token_file_throws, test_empty_token_file_setting_means_no_token, test_token_and_token_file_together_are_refused

'dss' => [ 'url' => env('DSS_URL', 'http://dss:8484'), // The same file as the server's --token-file; null when the server runs without one. 'token' => is_readable($file = env('DSS_TOKEN_FILE', '')) ? trim(file_get_contents($file)) : null, ],

  2. The second branch, the token cached in plaintext on disk, is standard Laravel behaviour. Every secret read through env() or config (APP_KEY, DB_PASSWORD) is cached the same way, so it is not a defect specific to this snippet. The cached file is local to the app container, and the token is already in a plaintext file there.

F-100LowreliabilityFixedphp/DssClient.php:138

PHP client: a 2xx without a parsable Dss-Result header (misconfigured URL or header-stripping proxy) throws JsonException instead of DssException

json_decode('') with THROW raises an exception outside the documented exception types.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Reproduced with Http::fake. The Content-Type is not checked either.

Evidence

DssClient.php:138

Impact

The signed document is lost and DssException handlers do not catch the error.

Recommendation

Check the header and throw DssException BAD_RESPONSE.

Remediation: Fixed (package php)

document() (used by extend and completeSignature) now checks the Dss-Result header. If it is missing, is not JSON, is not an object, or has ok=false, the client throws DssException BAD_RESPONSE with the HTTP status and a truncated body excerpt (DssException::badResponse) instead of \JsonException. result() now also requires a 2xx status.

After review: badResponse() quotes the body only when the Content-Type is textual (text/*, */json, */xml, *+json, *+xml). Otherwise it reports 'a <type> body of <N> bytes', so no PDF or CMS bytes reach messages or logs. excerpt() now reads at most MAX_BODY_IN_MESSAGE+1 bytes from the PSR stream instead of loading the whole body or sink.

After review: BAD_RESPONSE no longer quotes non-textual bodies: it gives the Content-Type and size instead (CHANGELOG Changed, DECISIONS PHP client codes). Checked against DssException::badResponse.

In that case the body is not a signed document, so nothing is "lost"; a misconfiguration surfaces as JsonException instead of DssException('HTTP_200'). docs/server.md:171-172 promises only "Every {"ok":false} answer throws DssException ... A connection that fails throws Laravel's ConnectionException"; a foreign 200 answer is neither, so no documented contract is broken. Deployment is a sidecar on the same host/private network (DECISIONS.md:852-853, Compose with depends_on: service_healthy, server.md:189-199).

That is a consistency/robustness nicety for misconfigured deployments, not a medium reliability defect, and not-checking Content-Type is likewise immaterial on a trusted link to a server that always sets it.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The mechanism is real and the finding points at the right place. php/DssClient.php:132-139 document() checks only $response->successful() and then returns [$response->body(), json_decode($response->header('Dss-Result'), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR)]. When the header is absent, Laravel's Response::header() returns '' and json_decode('') with JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR throws JsonException ("Syntax error"). That exception is not a DssException, and DssException.php documents DssException as the error type of the client ("Every {"ok":false} answer throws DssException"). The Content-Type is not checked either. So handlers that catch only DssException miss this error, and the document bytes in the body are discarded.

Likelihood in normal use is low, though. The server always sets the header on success: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:415-436 document_response builds an ASCII-escaped value and returns (header::HeaderName::from_static(RESULT_HEADER), value) together with the body. If building that value fails, it returns ApiError::internal, which is a non-2xx response and is already turned into a DssException by the successful() check. The bad path is reached only when something outside dss-server returns 2xx without the header. Examples: a reverse proxy or API gateway that strips unknown response headers, a wrong baseUrl pointing at another service, or Http::fake in tests. A proxy that rejects an oversized header usually answers 502, and that is already a DssException.

"Signed document is lost" is overstated. The client still holds the input document and the signature, so /sign/complete or /extend can be called again, and nothing is corrupted or silently accepted: the error is loud.

No attacker vector and no integrity or confidentiality impact. This is a robustness and API-contract issue (wrong exception type in a misconfigured deployment), so low rather than medium. The fix is easy to act on: check that the header is present and decodes to an array, and otherwise throw DssException('BAD_RESPONSE', ...).

F-102LowperformanceFixedphp/DssClient.php:138

PHP client holds request and response documents whole in memory (no sink/stream option, no memory_limit guidance); 60 MB extend exhausts the 128M default

A 50 MB response doubled peak memory, close to PHP's 128M default.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

measured 'extend 50MB response: peak 106 MB'

Impact

Fatal out-of-memory errors in FPM workers.

Recommendation

Accept streams, offer a sink, and document memory_limit.

Remediation: Fixed (package php)

Documents (validate, extend, prepareSignature, completeSignature, and detached values) now also accept a stream resource or a PSR-7 StreamInterface, which Guzzle sends without reading it into memory. extend() and completeSignature() take an optional $sink (a file path or a readable+writable resource) that receives the returned document through Laravel's sink(). The first tuple element is then null. A write-only resource is refused, because error bodies are read back from the sink. On any DssException the sink is cleaned: a path sink is unlinked; a resource sink is truncated back to its starting position. docs/server.md has a new 'Memory' paragraph: about 2x the document size at peak, 60 MB exhausts the 128M memory_limit, use streams and a sink.

After review: The caller's resources are never handed to Guzzle. (1) A resource document is wrapped in a non-owning PSR-7 decorator: an anonymous class using StreamDecoratorTrait whose close() and __destruct() only detach. (2) Guzzle's sink is now the client's own: a php://temp stream for a resource sink, or a random '<sink>.<hex>.part' file next to a path sink. The client copies the answer into the caller's resource only after it has checked the status and the Dss-Result header, or for a path sink renames the .part file over the target; on any failure, connection errors included, the .part is unlinked in a finally. Results: an error answer never reaches the sink. A resource sink's earlier content is untouched, and the server's code (EXTENSION_FAILED) is kept because the error is parsed from the response body. A path sink is written whole or not at all, and an existing file stays as it was on error. Behaviour changes: a write-only ('wb') resource sink is now accepted, and a read-only one ('r'/'rb') is refused up front with InvalidArgumentException (writable = mode contains w/a/x/c/+). The document is appended at the resource's current position. A failed write throws the new DssException SINK_FAILED (status 0) and cuts the resource back to where it started. The whole flow also works under Laravel's fake, which is used by the fake tests. New php/tests/RealHandlerTest.php starts tests/fixtures/router.php under php -S on 127.0.0.1 and runs Guzzle's real handler. It checks that after extend() with a resource sink and a resource document, followed by gc_collect_cycles(), both handles are still open and the sink holds the document; that validate() with a resource leaves it open; that an error keeps EXTENSION_FAILED with the earlier sink content intact; and that a path sink is whole or untouched with no .part left behind. Negative check: with the wrapper removed, 2 of these 6 tests fail.

After review: PHP sink semantics are documented in the CHANGELOG (Changed) and in a new DECISIONS bullet 'Sinks never leave a partial document': the atomic '<path>.<hex>.part' rename, a writable directory, the existing file left untouched on error, a resource sink only needing to be writable and receiving the document only on success, and resources never closed. SINK_FAILED (status 0) is listed. Checked against DssClient.php:532,562,597.

Public releases can be broken or have no assets.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

ci.yml now triggers on tag push v* (plus workflow_dispatch) instead of release:published. The release is created by the release-assets job only after build, compat, docker and online all passed: gh release create --draft --verify-tag, upload, then gh release edit --draft=false (prerelease for versions with '-'). A release made by hand beforehand is filled with --clobber and a warning. This changes the decision recorded in DECISIONS.md Phase 6 (see decisions).

After review: Reviewer's smaller point fixed. When the release already exists (a hand-made release, or the draft left by an earlier failed attempt of release-assets), the job now uploads with --clobber and then runs gh release edit --draft=false if gh release view --json isDraft says it is still a draft.

After review: Covered by the 'Release gates' rewrite (warm caches for all release platforms, schedule) described under F-127.

Files: .github/workflows/ci.yml, docs/DECISIONS.md

Test: YAML parsed (ruby YAML); actionlint could not be run here (running an externally built binary was denied); not executed on GitHub.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Reproduced from the code, with two corrections.

  1. Trigger ordering is as claimed. /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/.github/workflows/ci.yml:21-24 reads on: release: types: [published] plus workflow_dispatch. There is no push: tags: trigger and no created/prereleased type, so the only automatic path to a release with assets is: the release is published first (non-draft, visible to everyone with repo access), then plan validates the tag (ci.yml:47-58), then ~25 min/platform of JVM/native/Rust/differential tests run (ci.yml:86-108). A draft release does not fire published, so draft-gating is impossible with this workflow as written. The header comment (ci.yml:10-12) and docs/DECISIONS.md:479-485 describe exactly this sequence, so it is intended, but the decision's recorded rationale (DECISIONS.md:492-498) is cost on a private repo, i.e. why not to run on pushes/PRs; it gives no reason for release: published over a v* tag push that creates a draft release after the gates, which would cost the same minutes.
  1. Asset upload is gated on every job, including the live-LOTL job. ci.yml:183-189: release-assets: if: github.event_name == 'release', needs: [build, online], with no if: always()/!cancelled(). build uses fail-fast: false (ci.yml:64) but the aggregate job still fails if any of the three platform legs fails, and online (ci.yml:130-181) runs ./mvnw -B test -Pintegration, smoke-test-c.sh --online, test-rust.sh --online and dss-cli ... tl refresh against the real EU LOTL (ci.yml:157-171). Any failure there, including a transient network/EU-service failure, skips release-assets, so the already-published release has zero assets until someone re-runs the failed jobs (the only mitigation: ci.yml:205 # --clobber: a re-run replaces the assets it uploaded before). The three platform packages, already built and uploaded as workflow artifacts (ci.yml:110-116), are not published even though they do not depend on the online job; the seed cache is a deliverable, but the coupling of packages to it is avoidable. A consumer such as docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:4-7 expects dss-native-<VERSION>-linux-*.tar.gz from "the GitHub release's assets".

Corrections to the finding: (a) "public" overstates it. docs/DECISIONS.md:492 states "gsguglielmo/dss-rust is private", so a broken or empty release is visible only to collaborators, which is why I rate this low rather than medium; it becomes medium if the repository is ever made public. (b) The ordering is a documented design (ci.yml:6-13, DECISIONS.md:479, README.md:189-195) and a manual workflow_dispatch run can pre-validate a commit (ci.yml:13, README.md:189-191), but nothing enforces that before publishing. The finding is therefore real as described, with the impact reduced by the repo being private.

The code reads as the finding says (.github/workflows/ci.yml:21-23 on: release: types: [published]; :185-186 release-assets ... needs: [build, online]), but the claimed impact does not hold up in this system.

  1. Intentional, documented, trade-off stated. ci.yml:6-8: "Runs only when a GitHub release is published, or when started by hand. Pushes and pull requests run nothing: a full run takes about 25 minutes per platform, and private repositories pay for minutes beyond the plan's allowance, macOS counting 10x." docs/DECISIONS.md:479 and :492-497 repeat this: "gsguglielmo/dss-rust is private ... a 3-platform run uses roughly 300 included minutes. Hence CI runs on releases only (and by hand), never on pushes or pull requests." README.md:189-195 documents the same for users. The release event was chosen deliberately as the only billed trigger.
  1. "Public releases can be broken" is false. release-assets runs only if build (all three platforms: JVM tests, native tests, C smoke, clippy, Rust tests, differential test, package) and online succeed (ci.yml:186). A failing test therefore never attaches a binary to the release; the worst outcome is a release page with only the auto-generated source tarballs. No consumer can download a broken package from this pipeline.
  1. "No assets" is a transient, recoverable state with a designed recovery path. ci.yml:205 "--clobber: a re-run replaces the assets it uploaded before" shows re-runs are the intended fix; GitHub's "Re-run failed jobs" keeps the run's artifacts, so a flaky online job (linux-x64 only, the cheap one) re-runs alone and release-assets then uploads the already-built packages. The owner can also delete the release. Additionally, workflow_dispatch (ci.yml:24-29, README.md:189-190, with -f online=true) lets the owner run the full suite on the same commit before publishing a release, which is the pre-publish quality gate the finding asks for, just manual.
  1. The online dependency is a legitimate deliverable coupling, not an accident: the online job builds the seed trusted-list cache snapshot that release-assets uploads (ci.yml:165-181, :200-203; DECISIONS.md:484-485). Uploading platform packages without the seed cache would produce an incomplete release.
  1. The recommendation is marginal. A tag-push trigger leaves the tag just as public before tests run; only the release object's creation moves after the build. Draft releases do not fire published and GitHub does not run workflows for draft created events, so "use draft releases" alone would not give a pre-publish gate. Today the repository is private (DECISIONS.md:492), has no tags (git tag -l is empty) and the workflow "has not run on GitHub yet" (DECISIONS.md:521), so no one has been affected.

Net: a release-ordering nicety with no security or correctness consequence, fully recoverable by re-run, and the trigger choice is a documented cost decision. Severity low; refuted under the impact lens.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The finding describes the code correctly. In .github/workflows/ci.yml:21-23 the trigger is on: release: types: [published]. The only other trigger is workflow_dispatch, which uploads nothing. Lines 6-12 say so directly: "Runs only when a GitHub release is published", and the assets "are uploaded to that release". So every quality gate runs after the release and its tag are already public. The plan job (lines 47-58) checks the tag format only after publication. release-assets (lines 183-212) has if: github.event_name == 'release' and needs: [build, online]. The online job (lines 130-181) runs -Pintegration, smoke-test-c.sh --online, test-rust.sh --online and a full dss-cli tl refresh against the live EU LOTL. A failing platform build, a test failure, or an outage or flake on an external EU trusted-list endpoint therefore skips release-assets, and the published release has no packages. The mechanism is real as described.

Calibration: docs/DECISIONS.md:479-498 documents running CI only on release or by hand. The reason given is cost: a private repo, with macOS minutes counted 10x. That is a deliberate and reasonable choice. The documentation does not address the side effect that releases go public untested, and the release-only trigger does not require it. A draft release, or a workflow_dispatch that builds and then creates or publishes the release, would cost the same number of minutes. So the recommendation can be acted on without giving up the documented cost goal. Still, impact is limited. It is not a security issue: no attacker vector, no privilege change. The repository is private and has one maintainer. The failure mode is a visible release with missing or stale assets, not corrupted or unverified assets: uploads happen only after every job passes, and a re-run uses --clobber (line 205). The maintainer can re-run the jobs or delete the release. The one real risk is that the live-LOTL dependency makes asset publication depend on a third-party service. That is an availability and process problem, not data integrity. Medium overstates it, so I rate it low.

Precision: the trigger line is 22 (release:) and 23 (types: [published]), so the cited line 22 is close enough to act on.

  • /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/scripts/package.sh:66-68 is the only checksum producer: tar -czf ... ; sha256sum "$name.tar.gz" > "$name.tar.gz.sha256". It runs in the same build job on the same runner that produced the tarball, so it attests integrity in transit only, not origin.
  • The loose oj-keystore.p12 asset is copied in at ci.yml:211 with no accompanying checksum file at all. The keystore's SHA-256 is documented only in /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/trust/README.md:15 (98a76fbc...e6), which is not attached to the release, and that hash is not pinned anywhere in Rust or Java code (grep for it hits only trust/README.md).

Not a documented decision: /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/docs/DECISIONS.md:475-520 ("Phase 6: CI and packaging") describes the release-assets job and lists "Pinned inputs" (GraalVM SHA-256, Maven wrapper checksum, SHA-pinned actions) but says nothing about signing, provenance or an SBOM for the outputs. The parenthetical at line 485 "(only GITHUB_TOKEN, no third-party action)" is about the upload mechanism, not a decision to forgo attestation (actions/attest-build-provenance is first-party anyway).

An unlocked cargo metadata --offline on the stamped copy changed exactly the four workspace-member version lines (diff output) and no third-party crate.   • No build or test command passes --locked:
  • scripts/package.sh:23: cargo build -q --release -p dss-cli -p dss-server ...
  • scripts/test-rust.sh:22: cargo test --workspace ...
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:99 (clippy) and :167 (cargo build)
  • The only --locked is in scripts/collect-rust-licenses.py:41, which runs cargo metadata ... --locked.
  • Note: the finding's paths are slightly off. The scripts are scripts/package.sh and scripts/test-rust.sh, not scripts/ci/.

Experiment: I copied the rust workspace to the scratchpad and applied the same sed to stamp version 1.2.3.

  • cargo metadata --locked --offline failed with "cannot update the lock file ... because --locked was passed".
  • Without --locked, the regenerated lock differed from the original only in the 4 workspace-member version lines (diff at lines 234, 246, 257, 272). No third-party crate changed.

What is overstated: "drift is re-resolved at release time" and "shipped binaries may contain crate versions that were never reviewed". Cargo keeps the existing lock pins for third-party crates and only adds or changes entries whose Cargo.toml requirements no longer match. Unreviewed crates could ship only if someone committed a Cargo.toml dependency change without a matching Cargo.lock update. The missing --locked would then hide that mismatch instead of failing CI. That is a real but narrow hygiene gap: it needs a maintainer mistake, an attacker gains no new vector, and every resolved crate still comes from crates.io with checksums.

There is no release breakage either. Release CI runs clippy and the tests (which rewrite the lock for the member versions) before package.sh, so the later cargo metadata --locked in collect-rust-licenses.py succeeds.

The recommendation is still actionable and correct: update the lock in set-version.sh (for example with cargo update --workspace --offline) and add --locked to the CI cargo commands.

Calibrated severity: low, not medium.

There is no --strict-checksums, no lockfile and no PGP verification, and restore-keys allows old .m2 contents into release builds.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Only the Maven distribution itself is pinned.

Evidence

only java/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties exists; action.yml:45-46 restore-keys

Impact

A tampered artifact could be compiled into libdssnative undetected.

Recommendation

Add --strict-checksums, a lockfile or pgpverify step, and drop prefix restore for releases.

java/.mvn/maven.config sets --strict-checksums for every mvnw run (a checksum mismatch or missing checksum now fails the download); the Maven cache key includes it; tag (release) builds restore ~/.m2 only on an exact key hit (setup action input release: true removes restore-keys). Remaining: no PGP signature verification and no dependency lockfile (checksums come from the same repository, so this protects transport integrity only).

Files: java/.mvn/maven.config, .github/actions/setup/action.yml, .github/workflows/ci.yml

Test: Online ./mvnw -Pnative dependency:resolve cyclonedx:makeBom@sbom with strict checksums resolved the new artifacts; offline ./mvnw -o -q test unaffected.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Every factual component of the finding reproduces, but its impact is overstated, so I calibrate it low rather than medium.

Confirmed facts:

  1. No strict checksum policy anywhere. java/.mvn/ contains only wrapper/ (no maven.config, jvm.config, extensions.xml), and a repo-wide grep for strict-checksums|strictChecksums|checksumPolicy|pgpverify|lockfile|dependency-lock matches nothing outside fixtures and the wrapper script itself. Every Maven invocation is plain ./mvnw -B ... (scripts/build-native.sh:21 ./mvnw -B -Pnative ... package; .github/workflows/ci.yml:157 ./mvnw -B test -Pintegration; scripts/test-rust.sh:15, scripts/smoke-test-c.sh:45, scripts/audit-reflection.sh:14). Maven 3.10's default checksum policy is "warn".
  2. No lockfile and no PGP/signature verification plugin in java/pom.xml. The only plugin executed outside pluginManagement is maven-enforcer-plugin with requireMavenVersion [3.9,) and requireJavaVersion [21,) (pom.xml:230-236), nothing about artifact integrity.
  3. Only the toolchain is hash-pinned. docs/DECISIONS.md:502-509 "Pinned inputs" lists GraalVM (SHA-256 in scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh:16-20), the Maven wrapper distribution (distributionSha256Sum in java/.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties), the Rust toolchain, and GitHub actions pinned to SHAs. Maven dependencies and plugins are absent from that list, so this is a gap, not a documented decision.
  4. .github/actions/setup/action.yml:45-46: key: maven-${{ inputs.platform }}-${{ hashFiles('java/pom.xml', ...) }} with restore-keys: maven-${{ inputs.platform }}-, so a pom change restores an older ~/.m2 by prefix, including in the release-triggered build (ci.yml:73-77, 139-143).

Why only low, and corrections to the finding's framing:

  • "plugins are not pinned" is wrong as written: every dependency version comes from the junit/dss BOM imports and every plugin has an explicit version property (pom.xml:59-67, 150-215). No version ranges or SNAPSHOTs exist in dependencies (the only [x,) ranges are the enforcer rules); no extra <repositories> are declared, so resolution is Central over HTTPS only. The accurate claim is "pinned by version, not by hash".
  • --strict-checksums only turns a transfer-corruption warning into a failure using the .sha1 served from the same repository; it does not defend against a tampered artifact on Central or a compromised mirror, so it addresses little of the stated impact. Only a lockfile with hashes or PGP verification would.
  • The restore-keys concern is weak: Maven resolves by exact GAV, so stale entries in a restored cache cannot substitute a different version; poisoning requires a prior run with write access to the repository's cache, and CI never runs on pushes or PRs (ci.yml:21-24, DECISIONS.md:494-498), removing the fork-PR cache-poisoning vector.

Net: a real but ordinary hardening gap in an otherwise carefully pinned build (toolchain, actions, wrapper all hash-verified), with no positive evidence of an exploitable path. The recommendation (pgpverify-maven-plugin or a Maven lockfile; exact-key-only cache for release builds) is reasonable but low priority.

The finding is accurate but overstated. The real fix belongs in the CI action, not in pom.xml line 72, which is only the </properties>/<dependencyManagement> boundary.

Confirmed facts:

  • java/.mvn/ contains only wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties. That file pins the Maven distribution with distributionSha256Sum=1f6d99.... There is no maven.config (so no --strict-checksums / -C), no lockfile and no pgpverify plugin. A grep over .github, scripts and pom.xml finds no checksum or pgp setting.
  • .github/actions/setup/action.yml:41-46 caches ~/.m2/repository with key maven-<platform>-hashFiles(pom.xml, wrapper props) and restore-keys: maven-${{ inputs.platform }}-. Older .m2 contents can therefore be restored into a build.

  • Artifacts come from Maven Central over HTTPS, and published releases there are immutable.
  • ci.yml:6 says the workflow "Runs only when a GitHub release is published, or when started by hand. Pushes and pull requests run nothing". Fork PRs therefore cannot write a poisoned cache entry. Poisoning the cache needs write access to the repo, or a compromised Central or TLS.

Severity calibration: the attack vector is network or upstream supply chain, it needs high privileges or a compromise of Central or TLS, and likelihood is low. The impact would be high because the code is compiled into the signing library. This is a defense-in-depth hardening item, so I rate it low rather than medium. It is real as described in mechanism, and a maintainer can act on it.

F-116Lowbuild-ciFixedscripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh:32

Cached GraalVM dir is reused without a version check, and the cache key is a second hard-coded copy of the pinned version (drift footgun, not a practical poisoning vector)

Any existing graalvm-community-* directory is trusted without verification. The cache key hard-codes 25.4.4.1.1, so bumping the script keeps using the old toolchain.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

A poisoned or stale cache entry becomes the compiler for every release.

Evidence

install-graalvm.sh:31-34 'existing=...; exit 0'; action.yml:17 'key: graalvm-ce-25.4.4.1.1-...'

Impact

A silent toolchain mismatch or substitution.

Recommendation

Cache the tarball and verify its SHA on every run, derive the key from hashFiles(script), and check the version of an existing install.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

install-graalvm.sh no longer trusts any graalvm-community-* folder: CI caches only <dir>/download/ (the tarball), whose SHA-256 is re-checked on every run (a mismatching cached file is deleted and re-downloaded; other files in download/ dropped); the JDK is always extracted afresh into <dir>/<release>/ and its release file must say IMPLEMENTOR=GraalVM Community and the pinned GRAALVM_VERSION. The cache key is graalvm-ce-<platform>-hashFiles('scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh').

Files: scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh, .github/actions/setup/action.yml

Test: test-scripts.sh with a curl stub: a fake graalvm-community-openjdk-99.9.9 folder with an executable native-image is not used (script fails, prints nothing); a cached tarball with the wrong SHA-256 is refused and deleted; the action's cache key hashes the script.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

Mechanics confirmed. scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh:31-35 reads existing="$(find "$dest" -maxdepth 1 -type d -name 'graalvm-community-*' | head -1)"; if [[ -n "$existing" && -x "$(home_of "$existing")/bin/native-image" ]]; then home_of "$existing"; exit 0; fi. The glob matches any version and the only test is that bin/native-image is executable; the SHA-256 check (lines 41-42) and the pinned release="graal-25.4.4.1.1" (line 12) are never consulted on that path. Experiment in the scratchpad: a directory graalvm-community-openjdk-99.9.9+0.0/Contents/Home/bin/native-image containing a one-line shell stub was accepted, the script printed that path and exited 0, and the stubbed curl was never invoked; with an empty dest the download path was reached. The key is decoupled: .github/actions/setup/action.yml:17 key: graalvm-ce-25.4.4.1.1-${{ inputs.platform }} is a literal, not hashFiles('scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh'), so bumping release/asset_version/the SHAs in the script without editing action.yml keeps restoring the old toolchain wherever a cache exists. docs/DECISIONS.md:503 states the intent ("downloaded by scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh and checked against SHA-256 values written in the script") and does not mention the cache bypass, so this is not a documented decision.

Severity corrected from medium to low because the "poisoned cache becomes the compiler for every release" impact is overstated by the actual workflow: ci.yml:21-32 triggers only on release: published and workflow_dispatch (no pull_request/pull_request_target), with permissions: contents: read; GitHub Actions caches are branch-scoped (a run reads only its own ref's and the default branch's caches), there are no restore-keys (exact match only), and the only writer of ~/graalvm is this same script after a successful SHA check. Poisoning the cache therefore already requires code execution in a run on the default branch or the release tag, i.e. a prior full compromise. The realistic defect is version drift between two hand-maintained literals with no release-file check on the restored directory; it is also partly observable, since scripts/build-native.sh:19 prints native-image --version and scripts/package.sh:30 stamps GRAALVM_VERSION from the installed release file into the package's SOURCE, but nothing fails on a mismatch. The recommendation (hashFiles on the script, or compare the cached dir's release GRAALVM_VERSION to the pinned value) is cheap and correct.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

The code reads as the finding says: scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh:31-35 returns any existing graalvm-community-* directory with an executable bin/native-image without re-hashing, and .github/actions/setup/action.yml:17 hard-codes key: graalvm-ce-25.4.4.1.1-${{ inputs.platform }}. But neither claimed impact holds up in this system.

  1. "Poisoned cache entry becomes the compiler for every release" has no attacker. The Actions cache is written only by workflow runs of this repository, and ci.yml:6-8 / docs/DECISIONS.md:479 state that CI runs only on release: published and workflow_dispatch; "Pushes and pull requests run nothing." So no fork/PR-triggered job ever writes to the cache; the only writers are release/manual runs started by someone with write rights on the private repo (DECISIONS.md:492 "gsguglielmo/dss-rust is private"). Such a person can already edit the script and its pinned SHAs, so the cache shortcut does not cross any trust boundary. The entry that is restored was itself produced by install-graalvm.sh:40-43, i.e. after the SHA-256 check at line 42, using actions/cache pinned to a commit SHA (action.yml:14). GitHub also evicts entries unused for 7 days, so "every release" is at most "a release within a week of the previous run".
  1. "Silent toolchain mismatch" is not silent. scripts/build-native.sh:19 runs "$JAVA_HOME/bin/native-image" --version | head -1 at the top of every build, so the log shows the real version; scripts/package.sh:30 reads GRAALVM_VERSION from the installed JDK's own release file (copied by build-native.sh:61) and writes it into the package's SOURCE file at package.sh:47 ("GraalVM Community Edition $graal_version: ...graal-$graal_version"). A stale cached toolchain after a version bump would therefore be visible in the build log and in every shipped package. It is also a self-inflicted maintainer slip that already has three places to keep in sync (script line 12-13, action.yml:17, java/pom.xml:46-47 graalvm.sdk.version "Must match the GraalVM CE release used to build"), and a wrong Maven SDK version would bite the compile first.

What remains is a hygiene nit: deriving the cache key from hashFiles('scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh') would remove one manual sync point, and checking the cached install's release file against the pinned version would make the mismatch fatal rather than merely visible. Reasonable to do, but not a medium security finding: no substitution path exists for anyone without repo write access, and no mismatch is silent. Severity low; the finding's impact statement is refuted.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

The finding is accurate about the code. scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh:31-35 reads existing="$(find "$dest" -maxdepth 1 -type d -name 'graalvm-community-*' | head -1)" and, if $(home_of "$existing")/bin/native-image is executable, prints that home and runs exit 0. The SHA-256 check (lines 41-42) runs only on the download path, so a restored cache is never verified and its version is never compared with release="graal-25.4.4.1.1" (line 12). .github/actions/setup/action.yml:17 hard-codes key: graalvm-ce-25.4.4.1.1-${{ inputs.platform }} and has no hashFiles of the script. If someone bumps release/asset_version/the SHAs in the script and forgets action.yml, the old cached toolchain is reused with no error. The action's own description (action.yml:5, "GraalVM CE (pinned, checksum-verified)") overstates the guarantee on a cache hit.

Why I rate it lower than medium: (1) Poisoning has a small attack surface. ci.yml:21-29 triggers only on release: published and workflow_dispatch, with top-level permissions: contents: read. DECISIONS.md, Phase 6, says "Pushes and pull requests run nothing", and the repository is private. Writing a cache entry that a release run would restore requires running a workflow in this repository, which takes write access. Anyone with that access could also change the script or the workflow directly. There is no fork-PR or pull_request_target path that could plant an entry. The cache is a defense-in-depth gap, not a remotely exploitable one. (2) The realistic impact is the stale-toolchain case: a maintainer bumps the version and silently keeps building with 25.4.4.1.1. That is a reproducibility and correctness hazard, and it is self-limiting, because the version appears in build logs and the cache entry expires after 7 days without access.

Correction to the title: "decoupled from the pinned version" is correct. "Every release" overstates the reach, since only an actor who already has repository write access can poison the cache. The recommendation still holds: derive the key from hashFiles('scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh'), and check release against the existing install, for example its release file or java -version. Severity: low.

F-117Lowbuild-ciFixed.github/actions/setup/action.yml:21

install-graalvm.sh exit status is masked by echo "$(...)"; a checksum failure leaves JAVA_HOME empty and the setup step green

The script runs inside $(...) as an argument to echo, so its exit status is ignored and JAVA_HOME is written empty.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

run: echo "JAVA_HOME=$(scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh ...)" >> $GITHUB_ENV

Impact

A confusing failure shows up later instead of at the checksum.

Recommendation

Assign to a variable first, then write it.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

The setup step assigns home="$(scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh ...)" first (exit status propagates under bash -e), checks it is non-empty with an executable native-image, then writes JAVA_HOME.

Files: .github/actions/setup/action.yml

Test: test-scripts.sh extracts the step's run block from action.yml and runs it with GitHub's 'bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail' and a failing installer stub: the step fails and nothing is written to GITHUB_ENV (the old one-liner exits 0 with JAVA_HOME= empty, as the verifier reproduced).

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.95

Confirmed by reading and by a reproduction with GitHub's exact bash invocation.

Cited code, /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/.github/actions/setup/action.yml:21: run: echo "JAVA_HOME=$(scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh "$HOME/graalvm")" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

The script /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh uses set -euo pipefail (line 11) and on a checksum mismatch does echo "SHA-256 mismatch for $file: $actual" >&2; exit 1 (line 42) before tar -xzf (line 43). That exit status only propagates if the substitution result is used as a bare assignment; here it is an argument to echo, so the step's status is echo's (0). GitHub runs shell: bash as bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail, and -e does not react to a failed command substitution inside a successful simple command.

Reproduction in the scratchpad with a stub that prints the mismatch message and exits 1: bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail step.sh where step.sh contains the action's exact line -> step exit=0 and the env file contains JAVA_HOME= (empty). The variant home="$(./fail.sh ...)"; echo "JAVA_HOME=$home" >> env -> step exit=1, nothing written. Note the script's own header (install-graalvm.sh:7) documents the assignment form JAVA_HOME="$(scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh <install_dir>)", which the action deviates from.

Impact is as stated: the setup step goes green, JAVA_HOME is exported empty, and the job fails later in scripts/build-native.sh / ./mvnw (ci.yml:85, 152) with an unrelated-looking error instead of at the checksum line. No security impact: the script exits before extraction, so a tampered tarball is never installed, and the job still fails. Hence low severity, diagnostics only.

Test: Package built in scratchpad: SOURCE says 'https://github.com/codingducksrl/dss-rust'.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Reproduced as stated. scripts/package.sh:42-49 writes the SOURCE file with, at line 44: Source and build scripts (LGPL-2.1-or-later, see LICENSING.md): $(git -C "$root" remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null || echo "this repository"). On this machine git remote -v gives https://github.com/gsguglielmo/dss-rust.git, and both existing packages confirm it: dist/dss-native-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT-macos-aarch64/SOURCE and dist/dss-native-0.0.0-dev-macos-aarch64/SOURCE both contain https://github.com/gsguglielmo/dss-rust.git. docs/DECISIONS.md:492 states gsguglielmo/dss-rust is private. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml:108) runs scripts/package.sh on actions/checkout, whose origin is also the gsguglielmo/dss-rust URL, so release packages carry the same private pointer. No decision in docs/DECISIONS.md or LICENSING.md documents using origin deliberately; LICENSING.md:41 only promises the source is "published in this repository". So the inconsistency is real. Severity lowered to low: DECISIONS.md:896 frames the current state as "licensing review before going public", nothing has been distributed publicly yet, anyone who can download a release from the private repo can also reach that repo, and a GitHub rename/transfer to codingduck/dss-native would both redirect the old URL and change the CI checkout's origin. It remains a trivial fix (one constant shared with the manifests) worth doing before publication.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.62

The code reads as the finding says. scripts/package.sh:44 writes Source and build scripts (...): $(git -C "$root" remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null || echo "this repository"); git remote -v on this machine is https://github.com/gsguglielmo/dss-rust.git, and both local packages in dist/ (dist/dss-native-0.0.0-dev-macos-aarch64/SOURCE, dist/dss-native-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT-macos-aarch64/SOURCE) carry that URL, while rust/Cargo.toml:10 (repository = "https://github.com/codingduck/dss-native"), java/pom.xml:19 and :34-35, docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:18 and docs/openapi.yaml:8 name codingduck/dss-native. The package ships no other repository URL: README.md's only GitHub link is esig/dss (line 3) and LICENSING.md:41 says only "published in this repository". So the kernel is real: the sole LGPL source pointer in a tarball is machine-dependent.

The claimed impact ("Recipients cannot follow the source offer") does not materialise in this system as documented, though:

  1. Nothing has been distributed. docs/DECISIONS.md:492 states "gsguglielmo/dss-rust is private", DECISIONS.md:520 "nothing was pushed: commits and pushes are left to the owner", and the whole section at DECISIONS.md:896 is titled "licensing review before going public (2026-11-06)": the inconsistency is a transitional state of a private pre-release repository whose intended public name (codingduck/dss-native) is already written into the manifests. LGPL-2.1 section 6 obligations attach on distribution; today there are no recipients.
  2. The documented release path neutralises the machine dependence. README.md:189-194 and .github/workflows/ci.yml:6-12 say packages are built only by the release workflow; its checkouts (ci.yml:43, :73, :139, actions/checkout v7.0.1) set origin to ${server_url}/${github.repository}, i.e. the repository on which the release is published, so a release package's SOURCE always names the repository its recipients downloaded it from. If that repository is still private, its release assets are visible only to collaborators, who by construction can also read the source. If it is public (codingduck/dss-native), SOURCE matches the manifests automatically. The git remote choice is also arguably better than a hard-coded constant for forks, which must point to their own modified source under the LGPL.
  3. The residual exposure is narrow and procedural: a tarball built on the developer's machine (like the ones in dist/) handed to a third party before the repository is public, or the public repository being created as a fresh push instead of a transfer (GitHub redirects old URLs on transfer), or a Docker image built from such a tarball and pushed to a public registry while the repository stays private. Each requires the owner to distribute before completing the "going public" step the docs already plan.

Net: a real but low-severity release-hygiene inconsistency, not the medium licensing defect described. The "medium / recipients cannot follow the offer" framing assumes a distribution that has not happened and a build path (local, pre-publication) that the documented release process does not use. A one-line fix (a canonical URL constant, or a check that origin matches Cargo.toml's repository) is reasonable as a pre-publication chore, which is why I state the corrected title rather than confirming the finding as filed.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

The finding is accurate and specific enough for a maintainer to act on, so it is not refuted. I am lowering the severity from medium to low.

Mechanism confirmed

  • scripts/package.sh:44 writes the source pointer from the build machine's git config: Source and build scripts (LGPL-2.1-or-later, see LICENSING.md): $(git -C "$root" remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null || echo "this repository").
  • The local remote is https://github.com/gsguglielmo/dss-rust.git.
  • The built dist/dss-native-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT-macos-aarch64/SOURCE contains exactly that URL.

Other files name a different repository

  • rust/Cargo.toml:10: repository = "https://github.com/codingduck/dss-native"
  • java/pom.xml:19, java/pom.xml:34 and java/pom.xml:35 (scm) name codingduck/dss-native.
  • docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:18: org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/codingduck/dss-native".
  • docs/openapi.yaml:8 also names codingduck/dss-native.
  • docs/DECISIONS.md:492 states that gsguglielmo/dss-rust is private.

Correction to the evidence path: the finding cites Dockerfile:18; the file is docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:18.

Why the severity is lower

  • The project does not seem to have published anything publicly yet. CI runs only on releases or by hand in the private repository (DECISIONS.md around line 480; the .github/workflows/ci.yml header).
  • Release assets are uploaded to that private repository's own releases. Today's recipients can therefore reach the source.
  • The URL depends on the clone, so a fork or a mirror would print its own remote (or "this repository"). This is a correctness and consistency defect, not an exploitable one.
  • LICENSING.md:41 and LICENSING.md:54 promise that the source is published "in this repository". Once the packages are shared outside the private repository, the SOURCE pointer would lead to a 404, and codingduck/dss-native may not exist either. That is a real LGPL hygiene gap, but it is latent.
  • There is no security impact. The fix is cheap: use one canonical URL constant.

F-120LowoperationsFixeddocker/dss-server/Dockerfile:36

Container runs as a named, unpinned UID (USER dss; useradd --system without --uid)

USER dss is not numeric, so runAsNonRoot fails, and the UID can change between builds.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

Dockerfile 'useradd --system ... dss'; 'USER dss'

Impact

Fails on hardened Kubernetes, and cache volumes can break.

Recommendation

Use a fixed UID such as 10001.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

groupadd/useradd --system with fixed --uid/--gid 10001, cache chowned 10001:10001, USER 10001:10001 (numeric, so Kubernetes runAsNonRoot can verify it). Existing named volumes created by the old image are owned by the previously allocated system UID and need a one-time chown (docs update).

After review: server.md Docker section: change the listening address with DSS_LISTEN (default 0.0.0.0:8484), not a --listen argument in command:, because the HEALTHCHECK runs a separate dss-server --health-check that sees only the environment and would keep probing 8484.

Files: docker/dss-server/Dockerfile, docs/server.md

Test: docker run --entrypoint id on the test image: uid=10001(dss) gid=10001(dss); docker-smoke.sh asserts UID 10001 in CI.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Reproduced by reading the cited file. docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:27 creates the user with useradd --system --home-dir /var/lib/dss --create-home dss; with no --uid, line 29 does chown dss: /var/lib/dss/cache, line 35 declares VOLUME /var/lib/dss/cache, and line 36 is USER dss (a name, not a number). Nothing else in the repository sets a UID: grep -rn -i 'uid|runAsUser|10001' over docs/, README.md and the Dockerfile finds no mention, and docker/ contains only this Dockerfile. So both halves of the claim hold as stated: (1) with a non-numeric USER, Kubernetes' kubelet cannot verify runAsNonRoot: true and refuses to start the container unless the pod spec also sets runAsUser (the well-known "image has non-numeric user (dss), cannot verify user is non-root" error); (2) the UID is whatever shadow's useradd --system allocates from the free system range (typically 999 on a fresh debian:*-slim) and is not pinned, so a base-image change that adds a system user could shift it, and a named volume (line 35) populated under the old UID would then be unwritable by the new one. Severity is low rather than anything higher: the documented deployment is a Compose sidecar next to a Laravel app (docs/server.md:174-212, "Next to a Laravel app in Compose"), Kubernetes is not a claimed target anywhere, docs/server.md:183 only promises "It runs as a non-root user", and DECISIONS.md:893 already records the image as "Not verified yet". It is not a documented decision to leave the UID unpinned, and the fix is a one-token change (useradd --system --uid 10001 ... dss plus USER 10001), so the finding stands as a minor operations hardening item. Not refuted; no correction to file or line needed.

(panic-location/debug strings from dependency crates). Files: scripts/build-native.sh, scripts/ci/collect-native-licenses.sh

Test: test-scripts.sh: an earlier build's licenses/java/commons-io-2.21.0 is gone after collection; two stax2-api versions make the script fail.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Confirmed by reading the code and a scratchpad reproduction of the script's licence section.

  1. Stale folders are never removed. scripts/build-native.sh:21 builds with (cd "$root/java" && ./mvnw -B -Pnative ${skip[@]+"${skip[@]}"} package): no clean goal. java/pom.xml only pins maven-clean-plugin in pluginManagement (line 192) and binds no clean execution; the third-party-licenses execution (pom lines 329-341) is unpack-dependencies with useSubDirectoryPerArtifact=true into the fixed ${project.build.directory}/third-party-licenses, which that goal populates incrementally and never empties (the java/target/dependency-maven-plugin-markers/*-<version>.marker files present in the tree are its skip-markers). So after a version bump, e.g. commons-io-2.22.0 -> 2.23.0, both folders remain under java/target/third-party-licenses. Lines 52-56 then copy every folder unconditionally: for jar in "$t/third-party-licenses"/*/; do name="$(basename "$jar")"; mkdir -p "$lic/java/$name"; cp "$jar"META-INF/* "$lic/java/$name/"; done. scripts/package.sh:40 copies that directory verbatim (cp -R "$lib/licenses" "$out/licenses") into the release tarball, so the stale inventory is what ships from a local package.sh run. The script only cleans its own output (rm -rf "$out", line 34), not Maven's.
  1. The stax2 glob does break with two versions, but it fails loudly rather than shipping. Reproduction in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f126/run.sh with stax2-api-4.2.1 and stax2-api-4.2.2 folders: the loop copied all three folders (commons-io-2.22.0 stax2-api-4.2.1 stax2-api-4.2.2), then line 57 cp "$root/third-party/stax2-api.txt" "$lic/java/stax2-api-"*/ expanded to two directories and cp exited 1 ("stax2-api-4.2.1/ is a directory (not copied)"), aborting under set -euo pipefail. So a stax2 bump makes the script fail on a dirty target (a local-only nuisance), while a bump of any other jar silently ships both the old and new licence folders.

Scope/severity: CI jobs (.github/workflows/ci.yml:87,153) run on fresh checkouts, so release artifacts from CI are unaffected; this only bites local reruns without mvn clean, which the project expects (scripts/package.sh:22 says "run scripts/build-native.sh again"). The consequence is an over-inclusive, not under-inclusive, licence set, plus a confusing failure in the stax2 case. Real as described with the correction above; low severity.

Still, this is a documented decision (docs/DECISIONS.md:908-915) that matches near-universal practice for GraalVM native-image distributions, the source is public and pinned by exact commit, enforcement risk is negligible, and the fix is a one-line §3(b) offer in SOURCE/LICENSING.md or attaching the oracle/graal + labs-openjdk source archives at those commits to each release.
