confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

Code reads as the finding says. scripts/package.sh:43-50 writes the SOURCE file with only pointers: "GraalVM Community Edition $graal_version: https://github.com/graalvm/graalvm-ce-builds/releases/tag/graal-$graal_version" and "source commit of each component: licenses/graalvm/release (GraalVM's own components: https://github.com/oracle/graal)". scripts/build-native.sh:59-60 copies the release file with the comment "release records the source commit of every GraalVM component (SOURCE=...): the corresponding source of the GPL-licensed runtime in the library" - i.e. the author treats commit ids as the corresponding source. A grep over README.md, LICENSING.md, docs/ and scripts/ for "written offer|three years|corresponding source" hits only that comment: there is no §3(b) offer anywhere.

Impact is real but small in this system:

  • Distribution does happen: .github/workflows/ci.yml:183-212 uploads the packages to every published GitHub release ("gh release upload "$TAG" release/*"), README.md:192-193 documents it, and docs/DECISIONS.md:895 is headed "licensing review before going public". The library contains the Substrate VM runtime and JDK 25 class library under "GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0" (LICENSING.md components table). The Classpath Exception relieves the GPL from spreading to the rest of the library (LICENSING.md: "linking the GraalVM runtime into the library does not extend the GPL to the rest of the library") but it does not remove the distributor's §3 obligation for the GPL code itself. GPLv2 §3 (licenses/graalvm/LICENSE.txt:144-176) allows (a) accompanying source, (b) a written offer, (c) passing on an offer received (noncommercial only), or "offering equivalent access to copy the source code from the same place". A link to github.com/oracle/graal is a different place from the project's release page, and Oracle gives no written offer with CE builds, so (c) is unavailable. The gap also propagates: LICENSING.md tells embedding applications to "point to this repository's source and build instructions, or ship them", which carries the same pointer-only approach downstream.
  • Not a documented trade-off: docs/DECISIONS.md:902-919 covers notices and licence compatibility and says "SOURCE names the full commit, the DSS source tag and the GraalVM CE release", but never discusses §3 source provisioning; the build-native.sh comment shows the question was answered by equating a commit list with source, not weighed.
  • Additional correction: the release file's SOURCE line also lists "labsjdk-builder:f0467471911a..." (the JDK class library actually compiled into the image), but package.sh's SOURCE names only oracle/graal, so even the pointer is incomplete for the JDK part.

Severity calibrated to low rather than medium: no functional or security effect; the exact source is publicly available at the recorded commits; enforcement risk for GraalVM CE native images is remote and the practice is widespread; and the fix is trivial and actionable (a one-paragraph written offer in SOURCE/LICENSING.md, or attaching a graal+labs-openjdk source tarball to the release via the existing release-assets job). Confidence 0.6 because the "same place" reading of GPLv2 §3 is a strict FSF interpretation rather than settled law, and the finding's phrasing about "Oracle's written offer" is slightly off (there is no Oracle offer at all).

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.65

The finding describes the code accurately. scripts/package.sh:42-49 writes a SOURCE file into the release tarball. That file gives only upstream URLs for the GraalVM runtime: line 47 reads "GraalVM Community Edition $graal_version: https://github.com/graalvm/graalvm-ce-builds/releases/tag/graal-$graal_version", and line 48 adds "source commit of each component: licenses/graalvm/release (GraalVM's own components: https://github.com/oracle/graal)".

Nothing in package.sh copies GraalVM/JDK source into dist/, and nothing in it writes a written offer. The cp -R "$lib/licenses" step ships only notices: LICENSE.txt, THIRD_PARTY_LICENSE.txt, legal/ and release, as confirmed by ls on build/native/macos-aarch64/licenses/graalvm.

LICENSING.md:72 confirms that the library contains "GraalVM Community Edition 25.4.4.1.1 runtime (Substrate VM, JDK 25 class library)" under "GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0". LICENSING.md:74-75 relies on the Classpath Exception. That exception only stops the GPL from reaching the rest of the library. It does not remove the GPLv2 §3 duty to provide source for the GPL'd runtime object code itself.

GPLv2 §3 offers three options:

  • (a) ship the source with the binary;
  • (b) give a written offer valid for 3 years;
  • (c) pass on an offer you received, which is allowed only for noncommercial distribution.

A link to a third party's repository is not strictly any of these, so the mechanism is described correctly.

I rate it low, not medium:

  • It has no security or functional impact.
  • Pointing to the exact upstream release tag and component commits, as the release file does, is common practice, and the corresponding source can actually be obtained.
  • Enforcement by Oracle or the OpenJDK copyright holders against an unmodified-CE redistributor is unlikely.

README.md:242, :243 and :250 describe these three functions only in prose ("Builds the engine; loads TLs…", "Downloads and validates LOTL + TLs", "Library and DSS versions"). grep -rn "initial_load\|trusted_lists_loaded\|completed\|\"runtime\"" README.md docs/ finds none of these key names for the C API; the only hits are docs/server.md:81-82, which document the HTTP sidecar's /version and /health endpoints, not dss_init/dss_version. The Rust crate does document this (rust/dss/src/types.rs:177 /// False only if the refresh could not run at all; per-list problems are in the status.), but that does not reach C/Java/JSON integrators, and docs/DECISIONS.md records no decision to leave these shapes undocumented.

Real as described; documentation-only, so severity stays low. Suggested sharper title: the README also lists TL_REFRESH_FAILED as an error code that the code never produces.

Each entity's key, serial number and certificate signature, including the ECDSA nonce, come from a per-entity seeded SHA1PRNG (the new public helper TestPki.deterministicRandom). The validity is fixed: PKI_NOT_BEFORE = 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z, 20x365 days, which matches the committed PKI. Keys and certificates come out identical on every run with the same JDK. F-159LowtestingFixedrust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:498

openapi_document_matches_the_router cannot detect a wrong HTTP method on a guarded route: the token guard answers 401 before the 405

The auth check returns 401 before method dispatch.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

GET /validate without a token gives 401; with a token gives 405

Impact

Method drift ships undetected.

Recommendation

Also test with a token and assert the status is not 405.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

openapi_document_matches_the_router sends every operation a second time with the token and asserts the status is neither 404 nor 405, so a wrong method on a guarded route is detected. That engine uses a closed-port LOTL URL so the POST /tl/refresh it now reaches fails at once offline.

Files: rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs

Test: http.rs openapi_document_matches_the_router

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.93

Confirmed as described.

Code path: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:105-121 builds the guarded sub-router and attaches the auth middleware with .route_layer(middleware::from_fn_with_state(Arc::clone(&state), authorize)) (line 114). axum's route_layer wraps each matched route's MethodRouter as a whole, including its method-not-allowed fallback, so for any path that exists in the guarded router the authorize function (lib.rs:278-295) runs first and returns 401 UNAUTHORIZED when the token is missing, regardless of whether the method is routed. Only a path the router lacks entirely falls through to .fallback(not_found) (404), which route_layer does not wrap.

The test at rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:466-499 parses docs/openapi.yaml, builds each (path, method) request with no Authorization header, and asserts only expected = if open { 200 } else { 401 } (lines 497-498). For the 7 guarded operations (openapi.yaml lines 39-309: POST /validate, /extend, /sign/prepare, /sign/complete, /tl/refresh; GET /tl/status, /version) a wrong method in the document would still produce 401 and the assertion would pass. The doc comment at lines 464-465 ("one the router lacks 404 or 405") is only true for a wrong path (404) or for a wrong method on the two open routes; it does not hold for a wrong method on a guarded path.

Experiment (read-only, offline): started the built rust/target/debug/dss-server on a random local port with a token file, --refresh-hours 0, --offline-revocation, --allow-without-trusted-lists, and probed with curl:

  • GET /validate, no token -> 401 {"code":"UNAUTHORIZED"}
  • GET /validate, Bearer s3cret -> 405
  • POST /version, no token -> 401
  • POST /version, Bearer s3cret -> 405
  • GET /nonexistent, no token -> 404 {"code":"NOT_FOUND"}

This matches the finding's evidence exactly: unauthenticated, a wrong method on a guarded path is indistinguishable from a right one.

Severity stays low: the other tests in http.rs exercise every guarded route with its real method (e.g. POST /validate, GET /tl/status, GET /version), so a method change in the router itself would break those; the gap is only that the OpenAPI document's method could drift from the router without this consistency test noticing. The recommendation (also send each guarded operation with the token and assert the status is not 405) is cheap and would close the gap.

F-160LowdocumentationFixeddocs/server.md:188

Compose example in server.md has no restart policy, although DECISIONS.md says the server exits 2 and relies on the orchestrator to restart it

Compose's default is no restart.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

server.md:187-196

Impact

The sidecar stays down after a failure.

Recommendation

Add restart: unless-stopped.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

The Compose example has restart: unless-stopped with a comment, and the 'Starting' bullet says the server relies on its supervisor to restart it after exit 2.

Files: docs/server.md

Test: documentation

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Confirmed as described. The server really does exit non-zero on failure and the design delegates recovery to the orchestrator: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:104-109 returns ExitCode::from(2) when serve() errors, and fail() at main.rs:201-204 calls std::process::exit(2). docs/DECISIONS.md:846-848 states the intent explicitly: "If the engine fails to start, the process exits with status 2 and the orchestrator restarts it." docs/server.md:18-19 and :24 repeat that the server "exits with status 2". Yet the only orchestrator example the docs give, the Compose snippet at docs/server.md:186-208 (fence at 186, dss: service at 188), contains no restart: key (only image, environment, volumes, secrets), and grep -rn restart docker/ README.md docs/*.md finds nothing outside DECISIONS.md and a Dockerfile comment about the cache surviving restarts. Docker Compose's default restart policy is no, and a Compose HEALTHCHECK (Dockerfile:39) never restarts an unhealthy container; depends_on: condition: service_healthy only gates the app's start. So in the documented deployment the "orchestrator restarts it" assumption does not hold: after any exit-2 the sidecar stays down. Impact is modest (an engine-start failure is usually a configuration error a restart loop would not fix, and this is a docs example, not code), so severity stays low; the fix is a one-line restart: unless-stopped on the dss service and ideally a sentence in server.md noting that the design relies on the supervisor restarting the process.

On a Linux host (the only target the image is built for, Dockerfile:10/23) a bind mount keeps the host inode's uid and mode, and a 0600 file owned by uid 1000 is unreadable by uid 999: a direct check in alpine (chown 1000:1000; chmod 600; su nobody -c cat) gives Permission denied. Severity low: operational/documentation gap with a loud, immediate failure, no security impact.

"TOTAL_PASSED/-" ...), lines 55-60) are identical for every refresh. confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.85

Reproduced by reading the full path. A detached part of N bytes (N = 50 MB; base64 = 1.33N = 67 MB) is materialised this many times:

Rust (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss/src/engine.rs):

  1. lib.rs:336 let bytes = field.bytes().await?; — the raw part, N.
  2. lib.rs:404 let base64 = base64::engine::general_purpose::STANDARD.encode(&bytes); — 1.33N String.
  3. lib.rs:405 entries.push(json!({"name": name, "base64": base64})); — serde_json 1.0.154 macros.rs:279 expands a value expression to $crate::to_value(&$other).unwrap(), i.e. by reference, so the 1.33N String is cloned into the Value and the original dropped.
  4. lib.rs:150 let options = Value::Object(options).to_string(); — the whole options document serialised again, 1.33N.
  5. engine.rs:156 let options = CString::new(options_json).map_err(|_| Error::Nul)?; — another 1.33N copy; the lib.rs String stays alive in the move closure until the call returns, so both are resident during the FFI call.

Java (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/...): 6-7. ffi/DssLib.java:141 fromC(optionsJson) → :281 CTypeConversion.utf8ToJavaString(s); GraalVM 25.4 svm.src.zip CTypeConversionSupportImpl.java:119-123 does byte[] bytes = new byte[length] byte-by-byte then new String(bytes, charset) — two 1.33N allocations. 8-9. engine/Json.java:184-186 readString() accumulates into a StringBuilder (doubling growth, final buffer 1.33N–2.66N, with the intermediate growth copies) and returns sb.toString() — another 1.33N.

  1. engine/ValidationOptions.java:82 Base64.getMimeDecoder().decode(d.requiredString("base64")) — the JDK Decoder.decode(String) first does src.getBytes(ISO_8859_1) (1.33N), then
  2. the decoded byte[], N. InMemoryDocument(bytes, name) (dss-model 6.5.1 sources, line 81-83) stores the array without copying.

Cumulative transient allocation ≈ 2N + 8×1.33N + StringBuilder growth ≈ 700–800 MB for N = 50 MB, so the finding's "about 10 times / ~600 MB" is accurate, if anything slightly conservative. Peak resident is lower but still large: ~134 MB native (copies 4+5) plus ~260 MB Java heap during Json.parse (input String + StringBuilder + toString).

Reachability: default --max-request-mb is 100 (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:47-48), so a 50 MB detached part plus a small .p7s is accepted. The path is exercised by rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:196 validate_takes_detached_content_as_parts.

Not already handled: docs/DECISIONS.md:625-626 and :837-838 explicitly reject base64 for the *output* document because it "would make it a third larger and add a second copy inside the JSON string", and :731 rejects base64 for the signature input for the same reason, but :840-841 routes detached input through base64 anyway, with only the path security rationale and no discussion of the copy cost. So this is not a reasoned trade-off on this point. The recommendation (a binary buffer through the C API, as dss_sign_complete already does for the signature) is consistent with the project's own design rules.

Severity calibration: medium, not high. The impact is bounded by the request cap, the detached-CAdES path is a minority use, and a Java OOM inside DssJsonApi.validate (DssJsonApi.java:90-96 call(...)) is turned into INTERNAL_ERROR per DECISIONS.md:284 and rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:522. One caveat outside this lens: fromC(optionsJson) at DssLib.java:141 allocates the 1.33N byte[]/String inside the entry frame, which DECISIONS.md:279 says must be avoided, so an OOM there might not be caught; that is a separate matter and not needed to confirm this finding.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

The copy chain is real. For a detached part of D bytes: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:343 field.bytes() (D); :404 STANDARD.encode(&bytes) (1.33D); :405 json!({"name": name, "base64": base64}) — serde_json's json! calls to_value(&expr), so the String is cloned into the Value (1.33D); :150 Value::Object(options).to_string() (1.33D); rust/dss/src/engine.rs:156 CString::new(options_json) (1.33D). Engine side: java/.../ffi/DssLib.java:281 CTypeConversion.utf8ToJavaString(s) (a Java String, with a transient CharBuffer); java/.../engine/Json.java:184-191 readString() appends char by char into a StringBuilder then sb.toString() (two more); java/.../engine/ValidationOptions.java:82 Base64.getMimeDecoder().decode(d.requiredString("base64")) (decoder's Latin-1 byte[] plus the D-byte output). Roughly 10-12D cumulative allocations and ~3D peak live on each side, so the "~600 MB for 50 MB" estimate is in the right range.

Impact, however, is smaller than "OOM": (1) the request is capped by --max-request-mb (default 100, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:47) and the engine heap by --max-heap; (2) running out of heap in the engine is handled: docs/DECISIONS.md:277-284 "a 128 MB document on a 64 MB heap returns INTERNAL_ERROR and the isolate keeps working", and docs/server.md:110 maps that to a 500 — a failed request, not a crash of the sidecar; (3) the sidecar is documented for the same host/private network behind a token (docs/server.md:216-218, DECISIONS.md:856-857), so this is not an amplification vector reachable by untrusted parties, and realistic detached contents (.p7s over contracts/invoices) are MB-scale, where 10x of a few MB is negligible; (4) base64 for detached parts is a stated decision (DECISIONS.md:840-841, to refuse path over HTTP), and the authors evidently know the base64 cost since they avoided it for responses (DECISIONS.md:836-838).

What remains real and actionable: docs/server.md:221 tells operators "A request is held in memory whole, and the engine copies it into its own heap. --max-request-mb and --max-heap bound both", which understates the engine-side need for detached parts by several times, so a heap sized from that sentence can yield INTERNAL_ERROR on large detached validations. Cheap fixes exist without a new C API (move the String into Value::String instead of json!, build the JSON directly into the CString buffer, decode base64 in Java without the StringBuilder round trip) or document the multiplier. Severity low: inefficiency plus a sizing-guidance gap, bounded by configuration and gracefully failing.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

The mechanism is real and the cited locations are correct, but "10 times" overstates it and the severity is too high.

The path, traced in the code:

  1. The multipart part is held as Bytes (lib.rs:345-346).
  2. add_detached (lib.rs:403-405) runs let base64 = base64::engine::general_purpose::STANDARD.encode(&bytes); and pushes it into the options map. That is about 1.33x the file. The Bytes is dropped after each iteration.
  3. validate (lib.rs:150) runs let options = Value::Object(options).to_string();. That is another 1.33x, and the map is freed once the statement ends.
  4. engine.rs:156 runs CString::new(options_json), which copies again (1.33x) while the closure still owns the String.
  5. On the Java side, DssLib.java:281 calls CTypeConversion.utf8ToJavaString(s) (1.33x or more).
  6. Json.java:184 readString appends each char to a StringBuilder. Because it grows by doubling, it can reach about 2x the string, and then sb.toString() makes another 1.33x.
  7. ValidationOptions.java:82 runs Base64.getMimeDecoder().decode(d.requiredString("base64")), which yields 1x as a byte[].

For a 50 MB file that is roughly 450-550 MB allocated in total. The peak resident set is much lower: about 135 MB on the Rust side, and about 250-300 MB of Java heap at the worst moment, since earlier buffers become garbage. So the factual core is right, the count is roughly 7-8 copies rather than 10, and "600 MB" is total allocation, not peak.

Severity calibration:

  • The whole request is capped by DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_request_bytes) (lib.rs:120), with a default of 100 MiB (main.rs:47 default_value_t = 100).
  • The /validate route sits behind the authorize middleware (lib.rs:114), so only authenticated callers can trigger it.
  • Memory therefore grows linearly, at a constant factor, and is bounded per request. The realistic risk is that concurrent large detached validations, multiplied by the worker count, exhaust the native-image heap. That is a resource-efficiency issue, not an unbounded DoS.
  • DECISIONS.md:625-626 already rejects base64-in-JSON for the large output ("Base64 would make it a third larger and add a second copy inside the JSON string"). Applying the same treatment to detached input is a reasonable improvement.

The finding can be acted on as written: pass detached contents as binary buffers through the C API. Low is the more accurate severity, not medium.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

InputNormalizer.java:67, :91

Impact

Extra CPU and garbage.

Recommendation

Scan the bytes without allocating.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

InputNormalizer.decodeText scans and compacts the bytes themselves (returns null at the first non-base64, non-whitespace byte, so binary content is rejected without any copy); only PEM-armoured input goes through a String. Also runs for the leaf content of nested envelopes.

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/InputNormalizer.java

Test: InputNormalizerTest.binaryInputIsRejectedWithoutDecoding, InputNormalizerTest.decodesBase64Variants/decodesPemArmour (existing)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The core claim reproduces. java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/InputNormalizer.java:66-67 static byte[] decodeText(byte[] b) { String text = new String(b, StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); allocates a full copy of the input before the character scan at :78-87 that returns null on the first non-base64, non-whitespace char. For bytes >= 0x80 the JDK US_ASCII constructor takes the UTF-16 path (2n bytes plus a per-byte loop), so a binary payload costs 2x its size in garbage before being rejected at its first high byte. Measured with a verbatim copy of the method (scratchpad Bench.java, GraalVM 25): 10 MB ZIP-like binary: decodeText 30.7 ms vs byte scan ~0; 10 MB ASCII XML: 0.8 ms (compact-string fast path); 13.5 MB MIME base64: 73 ms vs 10 ms for Base64.getMimeDecoder, of which String.replaceAll("\\s+","") at :91 alone is 14.6 ms.

Reachability: normalize() (:32-48) only calls decodeText when sniff() returns UNKNOWN, i.e. the bytes are neither 0x30-prefixed CMS nor a PDF with %PDF- in the first 1024 bytes. Callers: DssEngine.validate :218 and extend :300 (top-level; an UNKNOWN result is thrown as UNSUPPORTED_DOCUMENT right after, so the copy only precedes a rejection), ExternalSigning :217 and :332 (small signer outputs), and DssEngine.signedContentIfCms :434 InputNormalizer.normalize(content) on the enveloped content of an attached CAdES signature, run when options.unwrapNested (default on per docs/DECISIONS.md:122-124 'unwrap_nested: false disables this'). For a .pdf.p7m the inner bytes sniff as PDF and decodeText never runs; for .xml.p7m it runs on the ASCII fast path (~1 ms/10 MB); for .docx.p7m / .zip.p7m / image payloads it takes the 2x UTF-16 path and discards the copy at byte 2-4.

Corrections to the finding's summary: (1) it does not run 'for every nested CMS payload'; nested payloads that are CMS short-circuit in sniff(), so it runs at most once per validate, on the leaf content; (2) the regex replaceAll at :91 is only reached when the whole input passes the scan, i.e. for genuine base64 text, never for binary data. Severity stays low: ~30 ms and ~20 MB of short-lived garbage per 10 MB binary leaf payload is dwarfed by DSS's own parsing/validation (DSSUtils.toByteArray at :433 already copies the same content), and there is no correctness impact. The byte-level scan the finding recommends is trivial and would remove the cost entirely; using Base64.getMimeDecoder for the standard alphabet would also replace the regex.

The mechanism is described correctly. In DssError.java:29-41 the javadoc for EXTENSION_FAILED lists "invalid signature, revoked or expired certificate, missing revocation data, already at a higher level, no TSA configured or the TSA failed". SIGNING_FAILED likewise covers a wrong digest or signer, an expired certificate, and "no TSA configured, the TSA failed, revocation data missing". In rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:481-485, status_of maps both codes to 422: "| ErrorCode::ExtensionFailed | ErrorCode::SigningFailed => StatusCode::UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY". So a server-side misconfiguration (no tsa.url) and a transient TSA or network outage come back as 422 with the same code as a client-side refusal. TL_REFRESH_FAILED, by contrast, gets 502 (lib.rs:488). The only machine-readable signal is therefore wrong for retry decisions, and a client can only tell the cases apart by parsing the free-text message. The citations are accurate enough for a maintainer to act on.

README.md:347-354 lists TSA failure under EXTENSION_FAILED. A documented choice does not make the coarseness any less real for HTTP clients, though. The signing flow is stateless (README: "Two steps, with nothing kept in between"; complete takes the same document, options and signing_time). The real harm is a client that treats every 422 as permanent and gives up, or one that retries permanent failures. (3) The issue needs no attacker. Its only effect is retry logic and availability for the integrator, and confidentiality and integrity are not affected.

I am lowering the severity from medium to low: (1) This is not a security issue. There is no attacker vector, and a mismatch needs a deployment mistake. (2) If an exported symbol is removed or renamed, the dynamic loader fails at load time. F-207LowsecurityPartially fixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:472

OCSP requests carry no nonce and out-of-window responses are accepted silently (this matches DSS upstream and demo defaults, not a deviation); a replayed stale 'good' response is accepted by an on-path attacker over plain-HTTP OCSP

certificateVerifier() builds OnlineOCSPSource with only a data loader. nonceSource stays null and alertOnInvalidUpdateTime stays SilentOnStatusAlert, while the default policy's RevocationFreshness is IGNORE, so OCSP responses are not bound to the request and stale ones are not flagged.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

DssEngine.certificateVerifier() does new OnlineOCSPSource(); ocsp.setDataLoader(ocspLoader); verifier.setOcspSource(ocsp); and nothing else. In DSS 6.5.1 a null nonceSource means no RFC 6960 nonce extension is sent and the nonce comparison is skipped. The fallback assertUpdateTimeValid uses SilentOnStatusAlert, so out-of-window responses are accepted without even a log line. The bundled constraint.xml sets RevocationFreshness Level=IGNORE throughout. OCSP normally travels over plain http. DSS ships SecureRandomNonceSource (the DSS demo uses it), and a responder that ignores nonces only produces a WARN, so enabling it does not break validation. README says defaults follow the DSS demo; this deviation is not noted.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:472-474 `OnlineOCSPSource ocsp = new OnlineOCSPSource(); ocsp.setDataLoader(ocspLoader); verifier.setOcspSource(ocsp);`. dss-service OnlineOCSPSource.java:239-241 `byte[] nonce = null; if (nonceSource != null) {...}`; :111 `private StatusAlert alertOnInvalidUpdateTime = new SilentOnStatusAlert();`. constraint.xml:94 `<RevocationFreshness Level="IGNORE" Unit="DAYS" Value="0" />`.

Impact

With online revocation (validate, and extend/sign at LT/LTA), an on-path party can replay a captured 'good' OCSP response for a revoked signing, TSA or responder certificate. The signature then validates TOTAL_PASSED and the result gives no hint.

Recommendation

Call ocsp.setNonceSource(new SecureRandomNonceSource()) and ocsp.setAlertOnInvalidUpdateTime(new ExceptionOnStatusAlert()) (or at least a WARN LogOnStatusAlert). Record the decision in DECISIONS.md and add an OCSP responder to the test PKI so the nonce round trip is exercised.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package java-engine)

OnlineOCSPSource now gets setNonceSource(new SecureRandomNonceSource()) (responses bound to the request; a responder ignoring nonces only warns, as DSS does) and setAlertOnInvalidUpdateTime(LogOnStatusAlert(WARN)) so an out-of-window response is logged instead of accepted silently. Not an exception alert: DSS's revocation loading strategy would turn a responder/host clock skew into an exception path with no OCSP responder in the test PKI to prove it safe. Not directly tested (no OCSP responder in the fixture PKI; the test PKI cannot be regenerated without invalidating the committed fixtures).

(3) In-window replay is inherent to nonce-less OCSP as used by every mainstream client; the only substantive delta is that the replay window is unbounded instead of ending at the responder's nextUpdate. It is actionable and safe: ocsp.setAlertOnInvalidUpdateTime(new ExceptionOnStatusAlert()) (plus setNextUpdateTolerancePeriod for clock skew) makes the fetch loop wrap the AlertException into DSSExternalResourceException (a DSSException, OnlineOCSPSource.java:273-276), which RevocationDataLoadingStrategy.checkOCSP catches (catch (DSSException e)) and falls back to CRL. The DSS 6.5.1 sources (dss-service-6.5.1-sources.jar, OnlineOCSPSource.java) confirm the rest:

  • :82 private NonceSource nonceSource; stays null.
  • :239-241 byte[] nonce = null; if (nonceSource != null) {...} means no nonce is sent.
  • :111 private StatusAlert alertOnInvalidUpdateTime = new SilentOnStatusAlert();, and the setter javadoc says "Default : SilentOnStatusAlert (skips the check validation)".
  • :104 shows that a responder sending no nonce only produces LogOnStatusAlert(Level.WARN), so turning nonces on would not break responders that ignore them.

The policy is DSS's own default policy/constraint.xml (dss-policy-jaxb 6.5.1), and line 94 and every other context have <RevocationFreshness Level="IGNORE" Unit="DAYS" Value="0" />. DECISIONS.md:125-132 records the choice of OnlineOCSPSource and OCSPDataLoader but says nothing about nonces or freshness, so this is not a documented decision. The DSS demonstrations do wire in SecureRandomNonceSource.

Imprecision: the claim that "README says defaults follow the DSS demo" is overstated. The demo-alignment remarks are in DECISIONS.md (lines 40, 53, 56, 59) and cover specific items, not revocation hardening. This does not stop a maintainer from acting on the finding.

Why I rate it low rather than medium:

  1. This is the DSS library's own default behaviour, not a weakening the project introduced.
  2. Exploiting it needs an active on-path attacker on the OCSP HTTP channel, plus a validly signed 'good' response captured before the certificate was revoked. Responses are CA-signed, so they cannot be forged.
  3. Many EU QTSP responders serve pre-produced responses and ignore nonces, so in practice the nonce gives limited protection. The update-time check alone still allows replay within each response's validity window.
  4. Online CRL is also configured, but it is only a fallback, so it does not mitigate this.

Net effect: a real but narrow hardening gap (AV:N, AC:H, high integrity impact on validation results only under MITM). The recommended fix (setNonceSource(new SecureRandomNonceSource()) plus a WARN or exception alert on invalid update time) is cheap and correct.

reported by: java-security, threat-model · round 2 · auditor confidence 0.6 · reported as Medium, calibrated to Low · status: confirmed

F-211LowperformanceFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:239

CMS validation CPU cost grows linearly with embedded certificate count (~0.2 ms per extra EC cert measured; ~40x baseline at 4,000 certs) and nothing caps the count

A small signed CMS can carry thousands of unrelated certificates. DSS builds a CertificateToken for each, and BouncyCastle validates each new RSA modulus, so cost scales with certificate count and the engine applies no limit.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Measured on the JVM with an offline engine:

  • Baseline CMS (2.1 KB): 11 ms.
  • 4,000 extra EC certificates (1.15 MB): 832 ms.
  • 1,000 RSA-2048 certificates with distinct moduli (680 KB): 1,812 ms, but only 71 ms on a re-run and 82 ms with one shared modulus.

With online AIA each certificate whose issuer is missing also triggers a fetch (F-001). There is no admission control (F-052).

Evidence

Probe: `baseline (1 cert): 2136 bytes, validate 11 ms` / `4000 extra EC P-256 certs: 1154105 bytes, validate 832 ms` / `1000 extra RSA-2048 certs, distinct moduli: 679789 bytes, validate 1812 ms`. DssEngine.java:239 `new CMSDocumentValidator(doc)` with no count check.

Impact

Sub-MB uploads can keep an engine worker busy for seconds each. Growth is linear, so this is a nuisance rather than a knock-out.

Recommendation

Reject a CMS whose certificates set exceeds a configurable count (a few hundred) before validation, and pair the request body limit with concurrency limiting in dss-server.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

F-218LowsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:237

cms mode checks SignerInfo.digestAlgorithm but never signatureAlgorithm: SHA-1 and even MD5 (RSA/ECDSA) signatures are accepted at B, extended to LT, and validate INDETERMINATE

checkedCms compares only signer.getDigestAlgOID() with the options. A CMS whose digestAlgorithm is SHA-256 but whose signatureAlgorithm is sha1WithRSAEncryption or ecdsa-with-SHA1 passes every check and is built into the document.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

BouncyCastle derives the JCA algorithm from the signature OID, so a SHA1withRSA signature verifies. DSS reports it as RSA/SHA1 and its policy grades it CRYPTO_CONSTRAINTS_FAILURE_NO_POE. MD5 is refused only by accident. README's list of checks ('the digest algorithm of the options') does not hold for the signature hash. At LT the TSA and revocation fetches are spent before the problem shows.

Evidence

ExternalSigning.java:237-241 `if (!o.digestAlgorithm.getOid().equals(signer.getDigestAlgOID()))`. Probe: `sha1-sig-pades-cms complete OK: level=PAdES-BASELINE-B ... validate: INDETERMINATE/CRYPTO_CONSTRAINTS_FAILURE_NO_POE`; `sha1-sig-cades-cms-LT complete OK: level=CAdES-BASELINE-LT`; `ecdsa-sha1 ... complete OK`; control sha256 → TOTAL_PASSED.

Impact

Legacy signers produce documents that complete reports as baseline B/T/LT but that every eIDAS validator grades INDETERMINATE.

Recommendation

Derive the effective signature algorithm the way DSS does. Require its digest to match the options and its key type to match the certificate. Refuse algorithms DSS's default constraints reject (SHA-1, MD5, PSS with SHA-1). Add a SigningTest case.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-signing)

ExternalCms.checkSignatureAlgorithm derives the effective algorithm the way DSS does (CAdESSignature.getEncryptionAlgorithm/getDigestAlgorithm, PSS parameters included; a bare rsaEncryption signatureAlgorithm falls back to the SignerInfo digestAlgorithm as RFC 5652 allows) and requires its digest to equal the options' digest_algorithm (so SHA-1 and MD5 are refused, since options allow only SHA-256/384/512) and its key family to match the signer certificate's key (EncryptionAlgorithm.isEquivalent). Messages: 'the CMS signature algorithm is RSA with SHA1, the options say SHA256 ...' / '... but the signer's certificate holds a X key'.

Probe: `signature_value with the ROOT CA certificate ... complete OK: level=PAdES-BASELINE-B ... validate: TOTAL_PASSED`; `keyEncipherment-only ... LT complete OK ... warnings=[The signing certificate does not have an expected key-usage!]`; `TSA certificate at LT ... level=PAdES-BASELINE-LT ... validate format=PAdES-BASELINE-T`. DssEngine.java:333-336 javadoc.

Impact

Pointing the signer at the wrong key yields a success result. Strict relying parties reject the documents, and CA-key misuse is a compliance issue.

Recommendation

Before any external signature is spent, refuse with SIGNING_FAILED: basicConstraints CA=true; keyUsage without digitalSignature or nonRepudiation; an EKU limited to timeStamping or serverAuth. Report the level actually reached. Add tests.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-signing)

SigningCertificateCheck.assertSuitable refuses (SIGNING_FAILED) a certificate with basicConstraints cA=true, a keyUsage extension without digitalSignature or nonRepudiation, or an extendedKeyUsage that lacks anyExtendedKeyUsage and consists only of timeStamping/serverAuth/OCSPSigning. It runs at prepare in both modes when signing_certificate is given (before the signer is asked anything) and at complete on the given certificate and on the CMS's signer certificate, before any TSA or revocation request. The 'reported LT while the document is T' side effect disappears with the TSA-certificate case refused; reached() otherwise still reports the requested level, which DSS produces or fails.

Legitimate licensed fonts are refused late with a misleading message (HTTP 422, CLI exit 1). Damaged fonts give HTTP 500 with raw exception names, which clients may retry.

DECISIONS.md (the "Checked before anything is signed" bullet) says option mistakes are INVALID_ARGUMENT at prepare, so the code breaks that promise.

  • Both prepare and complete fail, so no external signature is used up.
  • Nothing is corrupted or leaked.
  • The failures are deterministic, so a retry after a 500 just fails again harmlessly.
  • Fonts that forbid subsetting are uncommon in practice.

What goes wrong is the error classification: a 422 or 500 with misleading wording instead of INVALID_ARGUMENT. That is a real deviation from a documented contract, but a small one.

I rate it low rather than medium: it needs a form whose signature widget was already marked Hidden/NoView (unusual outside a deliberately prepared form), the signature itself is valid and the appearance stream is present (a viewer that lists signatures still shows it), and the fix is a one-line flag check next to the existing empty-rectangle check.

confirmedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Impact lens. The impact is real in this system, though smaller than "medium".

Not documented as a decision. README.md:468-470 lists exactly what pades.visible refuses for an existing field: "a field that does not exist, is not a signature field or is already signed". docs/DECISIONS.md ("After Phase 6: visible signatures") says "the page, box and field are resolved against the PDF before DSS runs ... so mistakes are INVALID_ARGUMENT with the caller's terms" and lists what is "Not done" (preview rendering, CMYK, interlaced PNG, ...). Neither mentions widget /F flags, so keeping Hidden/NoView is not a stated trade-off.

Contrary to intent. Placement.java:115-117 already rejects the other way a field can be invisible: if (r.getWidth() <= 0 || r.getHeight() <= 0) { throw invalid("... has an empty rectangle: it is an invisible field"); }. A widget with Hidden or NoView set is invisible in exactly the same sense for the caller, and the fix is a one-line check beside that one (widget.isHidden() || widget.isNoView()), so the finding is actionable.

No mitigation at another layer. DSS 6.5.1 PdfBoxSignatureService.findExistingSignatureField (sources jar, lines 270-291) checks only existence, instanceof PDSignatureField and getSignature() != null. PDFBox 3.0.8 PDDocument.addSignature (sources, lines 402-406) says "The /F key's Print flag bit shall be set to 1 and its Hidden, Invisible and NoView flag bits shall be set to 0" and then does only firstWidget.setPrinted(true); with a TODO about not overwriting the field's settings. So the flags survive, which matches the finding's evidence (/F=134 = Print|Hidden|Locked? at least Hidden+Print). The library offers no preview ("Not done. Preview rendering" in DECISIONS.md), so a host application cannot notice through this library that the appearance it paid for is not shown. The only test of existing fields (VisibleSignatureTest.anExistingEmptySignatureField, line 208-216) asserts the rectangle, not visibility.

Why low rather than medium: the signature stays cryptographically valid and binding, so a form author who sets Hidden gains nothing beyond suppressing the signer's stamp; this is a correctness gap in the visible-signature contract (plus a PDF/A-1 conformance nit, since Hidden must be 0 there), not a security or integrity issue, and it needs a form prepared with a Hidden signature field, which is uncommon. Correction: the fix belongs beside the empty-rectangle check at Placement.java:115, and clearing the flags vs. rejecting is a product choice the finding leaves open.

The mechanism is described correctly. Placement.java:90 existingField rejects a field that does not exist (93-98), is not a signature field (99-101), is already signed (102-104), has no widget or rectangle (105-108), is on no page (110-113), or has an empty rectangle (114-117, "it is an invisible field"). It never reads the widget's /F annotation flags, and grep finds no isHidden, setNoView or getAnnotationFlags anywhere in java/src/main/java.

Downstream, PDFBox 3.0.8 does not clear those bits. PDDocument.java:399-405 says "Hidden, Invisible and NoView flag bits shall be set to 0" for PDF/A, but the only call is firstWidget.setPrinted(true);. In DSS 6.5.1, the only setHidden call is in PdfBoxDocumentReader.changeVisibility (~line 406), which belongs to the validation and comparison code, not the signing path. So a pre-existing widget with Hidden (2) or NoView (32) keeps it, and /F=134 = Locked + Print + Hidden is a plausible result. docs/DECISIONS.md (~764, 782) describes filling an existing field without saying anything about its flags, so this is not a documented decision. The file and line are accurate and a maintainer can act on it: clear or reject Hidden/NoView/Invisible in existingField, or document the behavior.

Severity is lower than medium:

  • Attack vector: only the document's form author can set Hidden or NoView on an unsigned signature field.
  • Privileges: no signer action is needed. The signer is simply not warned.
  • Impact: only the visual appearance is missing. The signature is still cryptographically valid, and viewers still list it in the signature panel. Nothing is forged and nothing is lost.

This is a quiet usability and correctness gap with no security or integrity impact, so low.

F-227LowcorrectnessFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/ffi/DssLib.java:281

String arguments (options_json/config_json/cache_dir) are UTF-8-decoded in the C entry frame, outside DssJsonApi's guard: a string larger than the heap returns NULL while the isolate stays usable, contradicting the documented NULL contract

fromC(...) runs inside the @CEntryPoint method, outside DssJsonApi.call's Throwable-to-JSON handling. An OOM while decoding UTF-8 returns nullPointer(), although the isolate is still usable.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Documents are deliberately copied inside the guarded call, but string parameters are not. dss-server sends detached content as base64 inside options_json, bounded only by --max-request-mb. Rust maps NULL to Error::NoResult ('out of memory'), and dss-server answers 500 with that text. docs/native-library.md:85-86 and the DssLib javadoc are therefore wrong.

Evidence

DssLib.java:136-144 `return toC(DssJsonApi.validate(view(bytes, len), fromC(optionsJson)));} catch (Throwable t) { return WordFactory.nullPointer(); }`. Probe (-Xmx64m): `big options: NULL` then `still usable: {"ok":true,...}`; `big cache_dir: NULL`.

Impact

Hosts lose the error code and are sent chasing process-level memory exhaustion that did not happen.

Recommendation

Decode the strings inside DssJsonApi's guarded call. In the entry-point catch, try to build a small INTERNAL_ERROR result before falling back to NULL. Fix the docs, and add a smoke.c case.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-ffi)

Every entry point's catch (Throwable) now calls DssLib.failure(t), which writes the same {"ok":false,"error":{"code":...,"message":...}} DssJsonApi.error would build (INTERNAL_ERROR with '<class>: <message>', or the DssError's own code) straight into malloc'd memory from strings that already exist (Enum.name, Class.getName, Throwable.getMessage), JSON-escaped exactly as Json.write does, with no Java-heap allocation, so it can be produced when the heap is exhausted and cannot itself trip Native Image's 'OOM skips the allocating frame's handler' behaviour. NULL is returned only if even that malloc throws. String decoding (fromC) stays in the entry frame (DssJsonApi is owned by java-engine, and the outcome is identical: an OOM while decoding becomes INTERNAL_ERROR, isolate kept). toC(String) was refactored onto the same measure/write helper, byte-for-byte unchanged output. Docs: native-library.md 'Errors' rule and the DssLib class comment rewritten (NULL = not even an error result could be malloc'd).

After review: Reviewer's two non-blocking items done. (1) DssLib class comment: first paragraph reworded to the suggested text (the class decodes arguments strictly, encodes results into malloc'd memory and turns what escapes DssJsonApi into an error result via failure); the 'thin by design / all behaviour lives in DssJsonApi' claim is gone. (2) DssLib.failure(t) now logs 'Unexpected failure' through LoggerFactory.getLogger(DssLib.class).error(...) for non-DssError throwables, strictly after errorToC has produced the malloc'd result, inside its own try/catch(Throwable), so the result cannot be lost to an allocation failure while logging; DssError results (INVALID_ARGUMENT from fromC) are still not logged, as in DssJsonApi. Compiles and the JVM suite passes; the logging path reaches the native library only after scripts/build-native.sh.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

The finding is accurate, but its severity should be low, not medium.

The mechanism is real. DssLib.java:141 is return toC(DssJsonApi.validate(view(bytes, len), fromC(optionsJson)));. fromC (DssLib.java:280-282) is CTypeConversion.utf8ToJavaString(s), so it builds a heap String inside the @CEntryPoint frame, before DssJsonApi's guarded call. The only catch around it is catch (Throwable t) { return WordFactory.nullPointer(); }. The same pattern appears in:

  • dss_init: fromC(cacheDir), fromC(configJson) at line 82
  • dss_extend: line 165
  • dss_sign_prepare: line 183
  • dss_sign_complete: line 212

The class javadoc (DssLib.java:40-45) says the entry points "allocate nothing large themselves", and documents are handed over as a ByteBuffer view and copied "inside DssJsonApi's error handling". Option strings break that rule. docs/native-library.md says NULL is returned only when "the Java heap and native memory are both exhausted", and the DssLib javadoc says "A NULL return means ... (out of memory)". Both overstate the guarantee.

The downstream path is as described. rust/dss/src/engine.rs:469-470 maps a NULL return to Err(Error::NoResult), whose message (error.rs:54) is "libdssnative returned no result (out of memory)". dss-server puts detached contents into options_json as base64 (lib.rs:382-401). The size is capped only by --max-request-mb, which defaults to 100 (main.rs:46-48), and --max-heap is optional (main.rs:81-83).

Severity is low:

  • The isolate stays usable. The finding's probe shows a later call returning ok. I did not rerun the probe; the code path supports it.
  • A request this large would usually exhaust the heap inside DssJsonApi anyway. The client sees an HTTP 500 either way, so only the error code and message are lost.
  • It needs a heap configured smaller than roughly the request size. With the default heap, which grows with physical memory, and 100 MB requests, normal use is unlikely to hit it.
  • There is no integrity, confidentiality or availability loss beyond one failed request.

One caveat on the mechanism. The class javadoc says an OutOfMemoryError raised in the entry frame itself unwinds to the C stub and aborts the process. If utf8ToJavaString were inlined there, the result could be a crash rather than NULL. The finding's probe observed NULL, and either outcome confirms that string decoding is outside the guarded call.

The cited file and line (DssLib.java:141) are correct and actionable. The fix is to move string decoding into DssJsonApi's guarded call and correct the docs.

EngineBuilder::max_heap pushes "-Xmx{size}" and isolate_arg pushes any string. Typos produce an engine with an unintended heap limit and no diagnostic.

Tokens such as -xmx512m, --foo, foo and '-Xmx 64m' return rc=0 and are ignored. With -Xmx512 (what --max-heap 512 becomes), 4 MB inputs work and inputs of 6 MB or more fail INTERNAL_ERROR OOM, while /health stays 200. The help text shows units, but nothing enforces them.

engine.rs:58-61. Probe: `arg -xmx512m rc=0 ... 300 MB zeros: UNSUPPORTED_DOCUMENT (no cap)`; `arg -Xmx512 rc=0: 4 MB ok; 6 MB -> INTERNAL_ERROR OutOfMemoryError`.

Impact

DSS_MAX_HEAP=512 yields a sidecar that fails every document over ~5 MB. A mistyped flag silently runs with no limit.

Recommendation

Validate max_heap against ^[0-9]+[kKmMgG]$ (or treat a bare number as MB). Reject isolate_arg tokens not starting with -X, -XX: or -D. Add a test that --max-heap 512 is refused.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-cli)

Incoming handoff: --max-heap 512 (no unit) is now refused at build() with Error::Argument, which the CLI reports with exit 2. Test added.

After review: max_heap now splits on a char boundary: size.strip_suffix(['k','K','m','M','g','G','t','T']) plus an all-ASCII-digit check on the rest, so "512é", "é", "5€" and "２m" are refused by build() as Error::Argument instead of panicking. builder_refuses_bad_arguments_before_touching_the_library asserts those four multi-byte tails (and that "2G" is accepted).

Test: tests/cli.rs engine_flags_are_checked: --max-heap 512 exits 2, stderr mentions max_heap.

Callers forward user input verbatim: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:82-83 #[arg(long, env = "DSS_MAX_HEAP")] max_heap: Option<String> -> :248-249 builder.max_heap(heap); rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:97-102 likewise, plus the hidden --isolate-arg with allow_hyphen_values = true. F-230LowcorrectnessFixedrust/dss/src/types.rs:177

RefreshRecord.duration_ms is u64 but Java computes it from two wall-clock Instant.now() reads: a backwards clock step larger than the refresh's elapsed time makes build(), trusted_list_status(), refresh_trusted_lists() and export_tl_snapshot() fail with Error::Protocol until the next refresh or restart (the exported-snapshot poisoning path is not reachable through the Rust API, which fails the export instead)

Java computes finishedAt - startedAt from Instant.now(). A negative value fails serde's u64 decode, so the whole call fails. The record is sticky and is copied into snapshot headers.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The record lives in InitInfo, TrustedListStatus and TlSnapshotInfo. In dss-server, /health goes through trusted_list_status() and answers 500, so the orchestrator restarts a healthy sidecar. A failure at the initial load makes build() fail. A snapshot exported afterwards poisons every Rust engine that loads it. trusted_list_status_json is unaffected, which makes the failure inconsistent.

Evidence

types.rs:177 `pub duration_ms: u64,`; TrustedListManager.java:103 `m.put("duration_ms", finishedAt.toEpochMilli() - startedAt.toEpochMilli());`. Scratch: `invalid value: integer `-5000`, expected u64` for RefreshRecord, TrustedListStatus and InitInfo.

Impact

An NTP step or VM restore during a minutes-long refresh breaks status and health until the next refresh, and can poison exported snapshots.

Recommendation

Use i64 or a clamping deserializer. Compute the duration with System.nanoTime(). Add decode tests, and review the other non-Option numeric fields.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-dss)

RefreshRecord.duration_ms keeps the u64 type but is decoded with a clamping deserializer (i64, negative -> 0), so a backwards clock step no longer fails build(), trusted_list_status(), refresh_trusted_lists() or export_tl_snapshot(); unit tests decode -5000/-1 inside RefreshRecord, TrustedListStatus and InitInfo. The other non-Option numeric fields are counts (never negative). Computing the duration with System.nanoTime() on the Java side is a handoff to java-trust.

After review: RefreshRecord gained a seventh component durationMs measured on the monotonic clock: run() and importSnapshot take System.nanoTime() at start and pass elapsedMs(startNanos) to every record (published, keepPrevious, snapshot); started_at/finished_at stay wall-clock Instants. The compact constructor clamps durationMs at 0, and the previous 6-arg constructor is kept (used by DssJsonApiTest) computing the clamped wall-clock difference, so a backwards clock step can no longer produce a negative duration_ms in the stored record, the status, or a snapshot header's lists_loaded.

After review: java-trust late handoff, docs part. README refresh records: duration_ms is measured on a monotonic clock and is never negative; started_at/finished_at are wall-clock times and may then appear out of order. Checked against RefreshRecord (TrustedListManager.java:120-146, System.nanoTime). DECISIONS 'Durations from wall-clock reads are clamped' notes that the Rust clamp now only matters for older libraries. CHANGELOG entry added.

After review: Docs of RefreshRecord.duration_ms / clamped_ms now state the monotonic measurement (never negative; a pre-change library's negative value is read as 0) and that started_at/finished_at are wall clock and may appear out of order after a clock step. The decode clamp and its unit tests stay.

After review: openapi.yaml RefreshRecord.duration_ms: minimum 0 and the note that it is measured on a monotonic clock (never negative even if the clock steps back; started_at/finished_at are wall-clock and may then appear out of order); the same sentence in server.md's /tl/status row.

After review: README: RefreshRecord.duration_ms is measured on a monotonic clock and never negative, while started_at/finished_at are wall-clock and may be out of order after a clock step (Rust types paragraph; already in the status section). CHANGELOG already had the monotonic-clock entry.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

The core defect is real as described, with one overstated consequence.

Evidence:

  • rust/dss/src/types.rs:177 pub duration_ms: u64, inside RefreshRecord, which is embedded in InitInfo (types.rs:187 initial_load: RefreshRecord), TrustedListStatus (types.rs:207-208 last_offline_refresh / last_online_refresh: Option<RefreshRecord>) and TlSnapshotInfo (types.rs:288 lists_loaded: Option<RefreshRecord>).
  • java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:103 m.put("duration_ms", finishedAt.toEpochMilli() - startedAt.toEpochMilli());. Both instants come from the wall clock: line 282 Instant start = Instant.now(); and lines 289/292 new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), ...), and the same pattern for snapshot import at lines 306/326. There is no Clock injection, no System.nanoTime(), no clamping (grep for Clock/nanoTime in main sources finds nothing).
  • rust/dss/src/engine.rs:699-703 decode() runs serde_json::from_value(value).map_err(|e| Error::Protocol(e.to_string())). It is used by build() (engine.rs:390 engine.init = decode(&init_json)?;), trusted_list_status() (engine.rs:306), refresh_trusted_lists() (engine.rs:301) and export_tl_snapshot() (engine.rs:330). trusted_list_status_json() (engine.rs:310-313) only runs check_ok, so it is unaffected, which produces the inconsistency the finding describes: dss-server's /tl/status (lib.rs:208) keeps working while /health (lib.rs:256 run(engine, |e| e.trusted_list_status()) -> Err(e) => e.into_response()) fails, and dss-server --health-check requires HTTP/1.1 200 (main.rs:198), so a container health probe fails.
  • Reproduced in the scratchpad (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f230) with the project's pinned serde 1.0.229 / serde_json 1.0.154: the exact struct shape with "duration_ms":-5000 yields Err(Error("invalid value: integer -5000, expected u64")), both direct and via the Value round-trip that decode() uses. No Rust test exercises duration_ms decoding (grep finds no test fixture with that field).

Corrections to the finding:

  1. "A snapshot exported afterwards poisons every Rust engine that loads it" is not reachable through the Rust crate or dss-cli: export_tl_snapshot() decodes the result JSON into TlSnapshotInfo (engine.rs:330), whose lists_loaded carries the same negative record (TrustedListManager.java:429-430 copies loadedBy().toMap() into the header), so the export fails with Error::Protocol and the bytes are dropped rather than written. dss-cli's export goes through that same call (dss-cli/src/main.rs:449). Only a direct FFI/Java caller that ignores the result JSON could write such a file.
  2. The impact is bounded and self-healing: a restart re-runs the initial load with fresh timestamps, so an orchestrator restart fixes the engine rather than looping (unless the clock steps again); the record is only sticky until the next refresh of the same mode. The trigger also requires a backwards step larger than the refresh's elapsed time, which is rare outside VM restores or large NTP steps.

Severity: low rather than medium. It is a genuine serde/type mismatch with a trivial fix (i64 or a clamping deserializer on the Rust side, or System.nanoTime() on the Java side), it can make a successful refresh look like a protocol failure and fail build() during a clock step at startup, but it is rare, transient and recovers on restart.

Mechanism confirmed. TrustedListManager.java:282/289/292/326 take Instant start = Instant.now() and Instant.now() again for finishedAt; toMap() at line 103 emits finishedAt.toEpochMilli() - startedAt.toEpochMilli() unclamped. rust/dss/src/types.rs:177 declares pub duration_ms: u64, and decode() at engine.rs:699-703 maps any serde failure to Error::Protocol. A scratch program reproducing the Value round-trip gives invalid value: integer -5000, expected u64. Consumers that fail: build() (engine.rs:387 engine.init = decode(&init_json)?, InitInfo.initial_load), trusted_list_status() (engine.rs:308), refresh_trusted_lists() (engine.rs:294-298), export_tl_snapshot() (engine.rs:328). dss-server /health runs trusted_list_status() (lib.rs:256) and non-API errors become 500 (lib.rs:489); POST /tl/refresh also calls trusted_list_status() first (lib.rs:215), so the HTTP route to clear the record is blocked; /tl/status uses trusted_list_status_json (lib.rs:208) and is unaffected. Dockerfile:39 probes /health every 10 s; a build() failure exits the server (main.rs:140). No clock/monotonic mention in docs/DECISIONS.md, README.md or sources, so it is not a documented decision.

Impact is real but smaller than claimed: (1) the "poisons every Rust engine that loads it" part is largely unreachable, because export_tl_snapshot() itself fails on the Rust side before returning bytes (engine.rs:328) and dss-cli exports only through it (dss-cli/src/main.rs:449); CacheSeeder does not export snapshots. (2) The bad record is in memory only and self-heals: the next refresh replaces lastOnline/lastOffline and publishes with tlSnapshot=null (TrustedListManager.java:294), and the scheduler calls engine.refresh_trusted_lists() directly (main.rs:155), bypassing /tl/refresh; a restart also heals since the disk cache is untouched. Validations and /tl/status keep working throughout. (3) The trigger requires a backward wall-clock step larger than the refresh's elapsed time during the refresh; NTP slews by default and VM restores usually jump forward, so the realistic case is a boot-time chrony step coinciding with the initial load (main.rs:134 says the load takes seconds). Net effect: one spurious restart or /health answering 500 for at most one refresh period, no incorrect validation results, no security impact. Actionable with a one-token fix (i64 or clamp, nanoTime on the Java side), so not stylistic; kept as a low-severity robustness defect.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The finding is accurate. Every claim below was checked against the code.

Rust side

  • rust/dss/src/types.rs:177 declares pub duration_ms: u64, in RefreshRecord.
  • RefreshRecord is used in four places:
  • InitInfo.initial_load (types.rs:187)
  • TrustedListStatus.last_offline_refresh and last_online_refresh (types.rs:207-208)
  • TrustedListStatus.tl_snapshot, which is an Option<TlSnapshotInfo>
  • TlSnapshotInfo.lists_loaded (types.rs:288)

Java side

  • TrustedListManager.java:103 computes m.put("duration_ms", finishedAt.toEpochMilli() - startedAt.toEpochMilli());.
  • Both ends come from Instant.now(), for example Instant start = Instant.now(); at :282 and :306, and new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), ...) at :289, :292 and :326.
  • This is wall-clock time, not monotonic. If the clock steps backwards during a refresh, the value is negative and serde's u64 decode fails.

How the failure spreads

  • status() (:466-467) always includes lastOffline and lastOnline, and they stay until the next refresh replaces them. The failure is therefore sticky until then.
  • dss-server's /health (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:256) calls e.trusted_list_status() and returns Err(e) => e.into_response(), so health fails instead of answering 200.
  • engine.rs:385 engine.init = decode(&init_json)?; makes build() fail if the initial load's record is negative.
  • The export header keeps the original lists_loaded (:429, "Exporting again keeps it"). So a bad record carried in an exported snapshot reaches every engine that loads it, through TlSnapshotInfo inside TrustedListStatus.tl_snapshot. The poisoning claim holds.

Severity calibration I rate this lower than the reported medium.

  • It is not reachable by an attacker. It needs the host's wall clock to step backwards inside the refresh window. Offline and snapshot loads take milliseconds to seconds; online refreshes take longer.
  • NTP normally slews small offsets and only steps large ones, typically at boot or after a VM resume or restore. In normal operation this is rare.
  • The impact is availability and observability only. Validation and signing results are not wrong.
  • The status and health breakage heals at the next refresh, or on restart for the initial-load case.
  • The most durable effect is a poisoned exported snapshot, which also requires the rare clock event during that particular load.

Recommendation The suggested fix is sound and easy to act on:

  • Use System.nanoTime() for the duration in Java.
  • Use i64 or a clamping deserializer in Rust.

File and line are correct, so no correction is needed.

F-232LowtestingPartially fixedrust/dss/tests/engine.rs:613

Engine Drop with queued jobs or a running refresh is untested; Error::Closed/NoResult/Protocol never produced in tests (check_ok/decode have no unit tests)

Every test that drops an engine joins its callers or refresher first. The Drop ordering that keeps dss_shutdown from racing dss_tl_refresh_online (F-042) is unverified, and Error::Closed, NoResult and Protocol are never produced.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

engines_are_independent_and_drop_cleanly drops idle engines. validation_keeps_working_during_a_refresh joins the refresher before dropping. A regression in Drop ordering would strand the Java latch or abort the isolate while the suite stays green.

Evidence

engine.rs:81 doc and :428-442. tests/engine.rs:547-558, :614 `refresher.join().unwrap().unwrap();`. grep Closed|NoResult|Protocol in tests → none.

Impact

A shutdown hang on SIGTERM could regress unnoticed.

Recommendation

Add tests: drop with queued jobs (assert all Ok); drop during a refresh blocked on the never-answering server; check_ok/decode on malformed results.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package rust-dss)

Added drop_with_calls_in_flight_completes_them (last Arc dropped while 8 validations are queued on 2 workers: all Ok, drop completes within 60 s) and drop_during_a_blocked_refresh_waits_for_it (main handle dropped while a refresh is stuck on a never-answering server; the engine is torn down right after the refresh returns, promptly). Note: by construction (&self methods) Engine::drop can never run while a call is in flight, so the Java-side race (F-042) is unreachable from Rust; the tests cover the shutdown ordering that follows in-flight work. check_ok/decode on malformed results are unit-tested (Protocol for not-JSON, ok:false without error, missing fields; the library error wins over a wrong shape). Error::Closed is only produced by a panicked/absent thread and cannot be triggered offline.

Files: rust/dss/tests/engine.rs, rust/dss/src/engine.rs

Test: cargo test -p dss --test engine drop_; cargo test -p dss --lib check_ok_reads_the_envelope decode_reports_malformed_results_as_protocol_errors

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.82

The finding is accurate as stated: it is a genuine test-coverage gap, not a code defect, and low severity is the right calibration.

Drop ordering is load-bearing and documented. rust/dss/src/engine.rs:428-442:

fn drop(&mut self) {
    // Closing the queues lets workers finish what they have and detach; the refresh thread finishes a
    // running refresh first. Only then may the isolate be torn down.
    self.jobs.take();
    self.refresh.take();
    for t in self.threads.drain(..) { let _ = t.join(); }
    let _ = self.control.send(Control::TearDown);
    ...

The control thread then runs dss_shutdown + graal_tear_down_isolate (engine.rs:593-594), and docs/DECISIONS.md:360-361 states the guarantee ("Drop closes the queues, joins workers and the refresh thread (so it waits for a running refresh), then the control thread calls dss_shutdown"). The server relies on it: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:84-91 shutdown() drops the engine after stopping the scheduler, invoked from main.rs:174-177 on SIGTERM.

No test exercises Drop with work in flight. Every test in rust/dss/tests/engine.rs that drops an engine first quiesces it:

  • engines_are_independent_and_drop_cleanly (tests/engine.rs:547-558) calls a.validate(...) synchronously, then drop(a) on an idle engine.
  • validation_keeps_working_during_a_refresh (560-621) does refresher.join().unwrap().unwrap(); at :613, so the refresh is finished before the engine is dropped.
  • extensions_and_validations_from_many_threads and concurrent_validations_from_many_threads join all handles (:437, :516) before the engine goes out of scope.
  • rust/dss-server/tests/process.rs:74-118 serves_until_sigterm starts the server with --refresh-hours 0 (process.rs:25), waits for /health ready, runs two health-checks, then sends SIGTERM with nothing in flight.

No #[cfg(test)] module exists in rust/dss/src (only rust/dss-sys/src/lib.rs:16), so nothing exercises Drop at the unit level either. A regression that, e.g., sent TearDown before joining threads would keep this suite green.

Closed/NoResult/Protocol are never produced in any test. grep -rn "Closed\|NoResult\|Protocol" rust/*/tests returns nothing; the only occurrences are in src (error.rs:55,58,64; engine.rs:163-422 and 470, 688-702; schedule.rs:62; dss-server/src/lib.rs:504 mapping Closed to 503). check_ok and decode (engine.rs:681-703) are private pure functions and could be unit-tested cheaply on malformed JSON as the finding recommends; Error::Closed is reachable from the public API only if a worker thread died (engine.rs:268-269 self.jobs.as_ref().ok_or(Error::Closed) is always Some until Drop), and NoResult only on a NULL return (engine.rs:469-471), so those two are hard to reach without a fake library, which somewhat limits the practical recommendation, but the Drop-under-load tests (drop with queued jobs; drop while the never-answering-server refresh from test :560 is still running) are cheap and would use existing test infrastructure.

Impact is correctly modest: the current Drop implementation is correct on reading, so this is a missing regression guard, not a present bug.

F-233LowreliabilityFixedrust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:307

dss-server has no request deadline or cancellation: an engine job whose client has gone still runs to completion and keeps its worker

run() awaits spawn_blocking with no timeout, and the engine call blocks on an untimed recv(). A disconnected client detaches the task but the job keeps its worker. No request timeout is documented.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

PHP gives up after 120 s and may retry, which enqueues a second copy. Slow revocation fetches or expensive documents (F-001/F-002) pin workers for minutes. The --workers default is the CPU count, and the queue is unbounded (F-052).

Evidence

lib.rs:303-311 `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || call(&engine)).await`; engine.rs:163 `result.recv()`; php/DssClient.php:26 `$timeoutSeconds = 120`. grep timeout|cancel|deadline in server.md, openapi.yaml and lib.rs → none.

Impact

A burst of slow documents fills the workers with abandoned jobs, and retries double the backlog.

Recommendation

Add a per-request deadline (e.g. --request-timeout, answering 504 TIMEOUT). Add a cancellation flag that workers check before entering the isolate. Document both.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

--request-timeout (default 300 s) answers 504 TIMEOUT when a request exceeds it (upload included); the blocking closure checks the deadline before calling the engine, so a request that waited past it in the pool is skipped; the admission permit stays with the engine call until it returns, so an abandoned job cannot let a new one in. Cancelling a job already queued or running inside the engine needs a flag the workers check (handoff to rust-dss). Documented in server.md 'Sizing' and openapi.yaml (do not retry a timed-out upload at once).

After review: Per-call cancellation: dss::CancelToken (Clone, shared AtomicBool; cancel()/is_cancelled()) and Engine::cancellable(&self, &CancelToken) -> Cancellable<'_>, a Copy view with validate/validate_json/extend/extend_json/prepare_signature/prepare_signature_json/complete_signature/complete_signature_json. Jobs carry the token; worker_main checks it before entering the isolate and answers a cancelled job with the new Error::Cancelled without running it (a call already running completes and returns its result). Engine's own methods delegate to an uncancellable view, so their behaviour is unchanged. Tests: unit (token sharing, Work::reply_cancelled) and integration cancelled_calls_are_skipped_while_queued (one worker blocked ~2 s on a never-answering TSA; a queued validate cancelled meanwhile returns Cancelled when the worker takes it; a fresh token changes nothing; a pre-cancelled token skips all four call kinds at once). dss-server must set the token from its deadline middleware to benefit (handoff to rust-server).

After review: Every engine call of dss-server is now bound to a dss::CancelToken: run() creates one per request and holds a CancelOnDrop guard in the handler future, so the token is cancelled whenever the request is abandoned before its answer: when the --request-timeout layer drops the handler future (deadline), and when hyper drops it on the client's mid-request EOF (disconnect). The four document handlers call engine.cancellable(&token).<validate_with_contents_json|extend_json|prepare_signature_json|complete_signature_json>(...) inside spawn_blocking; the blocking closure also skips the call when the token is already cancelled or the deadline passed. A queued call whose caller is gone is therefore skipped by the worker (Error::Cancelled, mapped to a never-sent 504 TIMEOUT, not logged as a 5xx); a running call still completes and keeps its admission slot. Documented in server.md (Sizing, --request-timeout; Errors 504 row), openapi.yaml (info description, Timeout response), the --request-timeout help text and the Settings::request_timeout doc.

After review: README has a new 'Cancelling queued calls' paragraph (CancelToken, Engine::cancellable, Error::Cancelled; running calls complete), and the HTTP sidecar paragraph says abandoned requests are skipped. DECISIONS has a new sidecar bullet 'Abandoned requests are skipped, not run for nobody' next to admission control: the deadline or a client disconnect cancels the token, a queued call is skipped, a running one keeps its slot. It names the two timing-based tests, tests/http.rs abandoned_requests_are_skipped_by_the_engine and tests/process.rs clients_that_disconnect_do_not_keep_the_engine_busy. A Rust crates bullet 'Queued calls can be abandoned' and CHANGELOG entries were added too.

Mitigation that lowers severity: each revocation/AIA/TSA fetch inside a job is bounded by the library's own http.connect_timeout_ms (30 s) / response_timeout_ms (60 s) (README.md:276, DECISIONS.md:134), typical validation is ~30 ms (DECISIONS.md cold-start table), the server is meant for a same-host/private network with a bearer token (DECISIONS.md "There is no TLS: the server is meant for the same host or a private network"), and a job already inside the isolate could not be interrupted even with a flag, so the fix would only shed queued-but-unstarted jobs. The defect is real as a reliability gap (no backpressure, no deadline, abandoned work not shed), but it is self-healing once the queue drains and not reachable by unauthenticated parties, so I rate it low rather than medium.

  1. Deployment model: docs/server.md:212-217 and docs/DECISIONS.md:856 place the sidecar on the same host or a private Compose network, token-protected, serving one trusted host application. Clients are not adversaries; the untrusted input is the document, and the cost of a slow document (bounded per fetch by README.md:276 connect_timeout_ms: 30000, response_timeout_ms: 60000) is incurred regardless of any disconnect handling. That is a separate concern (the finding's own F-001/F-002), not a consequence of missing cancellation. Queueing beyond --workers is documented (server.md:42 "more wait in a queue"), and normal validations take tens of milliseconds (docs/native-library.md:179).

What remains is a minor, optional hardening (drop queued jobs on client disconnect; document that no server-side timeout exists), severity low.

The only timeout in dss-server is the 3 s healthcheck at main.rs:189. docs/server.md describes no request deadline. php/DssClient.php:26 does set $timeoutSeconds = 120. The file and line (lib.rs:307) are correct, and a maintainer could act on this.

Corrections that lower the severity: (1) The shipped PHP client does not retry. grep for retry in php/*.php finds nothing, and line 100 uses only ->timeout(...). So "retries double the backlog" requires the application to add its own retry. It is not default behaviour. (2) Engine network I/O is already time-bounded per fetch. EngineConfig.java:114-115 sets connect_timeout_ms 30_000 and response_timeout_ms 60_000, and DssEngine.java:122-146 applies them to the CRL, OCSP, TL and TSA loaders (DECISIONS.md:134: "All share the http timeouts"). A job therefore cannot hang forever on a slow fetch. It can still take minutes when several fetches or expensive documents add up. (3) The service is an internal sidecar, optionally behind a bearer token. The effect is slower responses for other requests and wasted CPU, not data exposure or a crash. Exploiting it on purpose takes network access to the sidecar, plus the token if one is configured. A caller like that could flood the server anyway.

Overall the issue is real but it is a robustness and hardening gap. The impact in normal use is limited, so I rate it low rather than medium.

F-234LowcorrectnessFixedrust/dss/src/schedule.rs:50

--refresh-hours is unbounded: with a warm cache, a value >= 2.56e15 panics the scheduler task at schedule.rs:50 (Instant + Duration overflow) and POST /tl/refresh then answers 409 REFRESH_IN_PROGRESS forever; the debug multiply overflow at main.rs:128 aborts startup instead

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

This reaches the dead-scheduler state that F-050 recorded as unreachable from dss-server. The 409 mislabel applies to any way the scheduler can die.
