main.rs:128 `Duration::from_secs(args.refresh_hours * 3600)`; debug run: `attempt to multiply with overflow`; schedule.rs:50, :80-82; lib.rs:218-233.

Impact

A typo in DSS_REFRESH_HOURS gives either a crash loop or a server that never refreshes and refuses manual refreshes with a misleading 409.

Recommendation

Give the flag a clap range and use checked_mul. Distinguish a closed channel (500/503 plus a log line) from a full one (409). Use checked_add in the scheduler.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-dss)

Scheduler side: try_spawn refuses a period for which now + 2*every overflows (Error::Argument("... too long to schedule")), the task uses checked_add, and request_refresh() returns Stopped for a closed channel vs AlreadyPending for a full one. The clap range / checked_mul for --refresh-hours and mapping Stopped to 503 instead of 409 are in dss-server (handoff).

After review: Already applied and re-verified against the current rust-dss: POST /tl/refresh uses scheduler.request_refresh() (Started -> 202, AlreadyPending -> 409 REFRESH_IN_PROGRESS, Stopped -> 500 INTERNAL_ERROR 'the refresh schedule has stopped: restart the server' plus the eprintln of every 5xx); test tl_refresh_with_a_scheduler's dead-scheduler part.

Files: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs, rust/dss/src/schedule.rs, rust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs

Test: cargo test -p dss --all-features --test scheduler invalid_periods_are_refused_before_the_task_starts

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Code read at commit 7e697c9. rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:45 declares refresh_hours: u64 with no clap value_parser range, and main.rs:128 computes Duration::from_secs(args.refresh_hours * 3600) unchecked; rust/Cargo.toml and the crate manifests set no [profile]/overflow-checks, so release wraps and debug panics. rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:47-51 does Instant::now() + every when refresh_on_start is false, and tokio 1.54.1 (rust/Cargo.lock) implements that as Instant::from_std(self.std + other) (tokio src/time/instant.rs:157-163), which panics on overflow. The scheduler task is a tokio::spawn (schedule.rs:46) so its panic does not stop the server; it drops requests, and schedule.rs:80-82 refresh_now() is self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok(), which conflates Closed with Full. rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:218-234 maps !started to 409 REFRESH_IN_PROGRESS / "an online refresh is already running", while lib.rs:215-217 reads refresh_in_progress from the engine (false), so /tl/status and /tl/refresh contradict each other.

Reproduced in the scratchpad (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f234, a copy of the spawn() body against tokio =1.54.1): hours=3000000000000000 with refresh_on_start=false, debug and release: thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked at .../tokio-1.54.1/src/time/instant.rs:161:27: overflow when adding duration to instant, then try_send -> Err("channel closed"), i.e. refresh_now() false -> 409 forever. Threshold confirmed at exactly i64::MAX/3600 = 2562047788015215 hours (panics at that value too, since now > 0). hours=6 behaves normally.

Corrections to the finding as stated: (1) The debug multiply overflow at main.rs:128 does not "panic the scheduler task": serve() runs on the main task before TcpListener::bind (main.rs:128 vs :132), so hours=6000000000000000 in debug gives thread 'main' panicked ... attempt to multiply with overflow and the process exits before listening; that is a loud startup failure, not a dead scheduler. In release the product wraps to an arbitrary period (6e15 -> 3153255926290448384 s) and the server runs with a silently wrong schedule. (2) The dead-scheduler path needs refresh_on_start == false, i.e. a cache that is already loaded (main.rs:154 passes !loaded); with an empty cache tokio's Interval survived the same period in the experiment (ticks and manual refreshes kept working across two try_sends). (3) The panic is printed on stderr by the default panic hook, so it is not fully silent, but nothing in dss-server observes the JoinHandle and the HTTP surface stays wrong. (4) "A typo in DSS_REFRESH_HOURS" overstates reachability: the value must be a 16-19 digit number (>= 2.56e15); realistic typos (60, 600, 60000) are harmless. The only test touching the flag is rust/dss-server/tests/process.rs:25 with --refresh-hours 0. The defect is real but needs an absurd input, hence low severity; the 409-on-closed-channel mislabel is the part worth fixing (distinguish Closed from Full in refresh_now, bound the flag with clap, use checked_add at schedule.rs:50).

The token is the only barrier on the Compose network, and there is no lockout or rate limit.

main.rs:114-126; grep 'openssl rand|generate.*token|random' in docs → none.

Memorable or weak tokens are brute-forceable from any container on the same network.

read_token refuses tokens shorter than 16 bytes after trimming ('the token is N bytes long, at least 16 are needed (e.g. openssl rand -base64 32)'); server.md documents the generation command, the minimum and that there is no lockout.

Files: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs, docs/server.md

Test: process.rs start_failures_name_their_cause (6-byte token exits 2), token_file_and_environment_variables (a 19-byte token works)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

Reproduced from the code; the finding is accurate as stated, and its own "low" rating is right.

There is no length, entropy or character-set check anywhere between there and AppState::new(token) (lib.rs:67-71), so a one-byte token file is accepted and becomes the server's bearer token.
  1. No lockout or rate limit. authorize in rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:278-294 does a constant-time compare (same, lib.rs:297-300) and returns 401 on mismatch; there is no counter, delay or limiter. A grep of rust/dss-server/src and Cargo.toml for rate/limit/governor/lockout/delay/sleep finds nothing relevant (only the body-size limit).
  1. No generation guidance in the docs. docs/server.md:39, 193-218 and docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857 describe the token only as "read from a file", "compared in constant time", and that it "stops other containers on the same network from using it". A grep for openssl rand|generate.*token|random|urandom|pwgen across docs/, README.md, docker/ and scripts/ returns nothing. The Compose example points at ./secrets/dss_token without saying how to fill it.
  1. Tests do not cover length. rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:439 (token_guards_everything_but_health) builds the router via AppState::new(token) directly and only checks that a token is required; nothing exercises a short token or the main.rs file-reading path for length.

Calibration: the threat model is narrow by design (DECISIONS.md:855-857: no TLS, private network, same host), the compare is already constant-time, and brute-forcing requires an attacker already on the Compose network. This is a hardening/documentation gap, not an exploitable flaw in itself, so low is correct. The recommendation (minimum length plus a documented openssl rand -base64 32) is cheap and reasonable. No online experiment was run: starting the binary with an empty cache would trigger a trusted-list refresh, and the code path is unambiguous without it.

F-238LowreliabilityFixedrust/dss-server/src/main.rs:206

A second SIGTERM or Ctrl-C during the graceful drain is silently swallowed: a stalled client keeps the server alive until SIGKILL

stop_signal() consumes one signal. Tokio's handlers stay installed after the future is dropped, so later SIGTERM and SIGINT are ignored while with_graceful_shutdown waits on a stalled upload.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Distinct from F-079 (no drain deadline): even with a deadline, the usual escape hatch of a second signal forcing exit is missing. Reproduced with the release binary.

Evidence

main.rs:206-212; `after 1st TERM alive? yes` / `after 2nd TERM alive? yes` / `after INT alive? yes` / exits only when the stalled connection closes.

Impact

Interactive operators must kill -9. Orchestrated stops take the full grace period while health checks already fail.

Recommendation

After the first signal, keep listening and exit immediately on a second one. Document this in server.md.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-server)

watch_signals keeps listening after the first SIGTERM/SIGINT (which logs 'stop requested, finishing the requests in progress (N connection(s) open)' and starts the graceful drain); a second signal logs 'stopping now, N connection(s) dropped' and exits 0 at once. Documented in server.md.

After review: Both Signal handles are registered in serve() before anything runs (a failure is 'cannot install the SIGTERM/SIGINT handler: ...', exit 2) and handed to watch_signals, whose task never ends, so the stop channel's sender lives for the life of the process; the accept loop's select arms additionally match only Ok(_) from wait_for and a connection task only calls graceful_shutdown on Ok, so a dropped sender could never read as a stop. No automated test: a signal registration failure cannot be provoked from a test; serves_until_sigterm, graceful_stop_is_bounded_by_the_request_timeout and a_second_signal_stops_at_once cover the signal path.

Files: docs/server.md, rust/dss-server/src/main.rs

Test: process.rs a_second_signal_stops_at_once (stalled upload, --request-timeout 0, two SIGTERMs)

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.95

Confirmed by reading the code and by a live reproduction with the release binary.

Code: /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:206-212 is the only signal handling in the server:

async fn stop_signal() {
    let mut term = signal(SignalKind::terminate()).expect("SIGTERM handler");
    tokio::select! {
        _ = term.recv() => {}
        _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c() => {}
    }
}

It resolves after the first SIGTERM or SIGINT and is passed to axum::serve(listener, app).with_graceful_shutdown(stop_signal()) (main.rs:172). Nothing else listens for signals afterwards, and there is no drain deadline: the router (lib.rs:104-121) only adds DefaultBodyLimit, no timeout layer. The vendored tokio 1.54.1 (rust/Cargo.lock:748-749) documents why later signals are swallowed rather than killing the process, in src/signal/unix.rs:328-333: "The first time that a Signal instance is registered for a particular signal kind, an OS signal-handler is installed which replaces the default platform behavior when that signal is received, for the duration of the entire process." So after stop_signal() returns and its Signal is dropped, SIGTERM and SIGINT are still caught by tokio's handler and simply discarded.

Reproduction (script at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f238/repro.py, run against rust/target/release/dss-server with the same offline options as tests/process.rs, no trusted-list refresh): after /health returned 200, a client opened a POST /validate with Content-Length: 1000000 and sent only the first bytes, keeping the socket open. Output: after 1st TERM: alive? yes / after 2nd TERM: alive? yes / after INT: alive? yes / after 3rd TERM: alive? yes / new connection accepted after TERM? refused: [Errno 61] Connection refused / then, only after the script closed the stalled socket: dss-server: 500 INVALID_ARGUMENT: failed to read stream / dss-server: stopping / exited with 0. This matches the finding's evidence line for line, and also confirms the impact claim that the listener is already closed (health checks fail) while the process lingers.

Existing coverage does not catch it: tests/process.rs serves_until_sigterm (line 75-118) sends a single kill -TERM with no request in flight. docs/server.md:27-28 documents only "On SIGTERM or Ctrl-C the server stops accepting connections, finishes the requests in progress ... then exits with status 0" and says nothing about a second signal, so this is not a documented decision.

Severity stays low: it needs a stalled in-flight request during shutdown, the workaround is SIGKILL (orchestrators do this after the grace period anyway), and no data is lost. The fix is cheap: keep listening after the first signal and std::process::exit on the second (e.g. spawn a task that awaits another term.recv()/ctrl_c()), or add a drain deadline.

Verified live: the response carries only content-type, content-length and date.

Test coverage, checked by grep over rust/dss-server/ (tests are only tests/http.rs and tests/process.rs; grep -n "cfg(test)\|#\[test\]" rust/dss-server/src/*.rs finds nothing): no test ever puts "filename" in an options JSON; every detached part in http.rs (lines 206, 221-225) is sent with Some("document.txt"), so the detached-N default never runs; the string "detached-1" appears nowhere outside lib.rs. The only filename assertion is http.rs:180-183 (simple_report_xml ... contains("b-lta.pdf")), which covers rule 1's default branch only.

The specific claim that an injection regression in sign/* would go unnoticed also holds: sign_prepare_then_complete (http.rs:361-417) uploads "content/document.pdf" in both steps via Form::document, which sets filename="document.pdf" (http.rs:82-84). The Java side uses exactly that as its fallback when no filename option arrives: java/.../engine/ExternalSigning.java:377 String name = o.filename != null ? o.filename : (format == Format.PADES ? "document.pdf" : "document");. The signing fixtures (testdata/fixtures/signing/*.json) contain no "filename" key, so they were recorded against the default name. If a regression made sign_prepare/sign_complete call default_filename, the injected value "document.pdf" would equal the default, the digest would be unchanged and the recorded .sig fixtures would still complete: the test passes.

That the filename actually matters was verified by experiment with the built CLI (which sets options.filename from the file name, rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:730): preparing the identical PDF with the same --signing-time 2026-10-28T14:01:20Z under names a.pdf, b.pdf and document.pdf gave three different digests (c23HdJ..., BJZkdT..., gnx8ff...). So a server-side filename injection in sign/* is exactly the class of regression the README (README.md:370) warns breaks external signing, and the suite cannot detect it unless the upload name differs between prepare and complete or from "document.pdf".

Severity stays low: the code is correct today and the rule is documented; the gap is only that it is unguarded. The recommended tests (prepare as a.pdf, complete as b.pdf; explicit options.filename overriding the part name on /validate; an unnamed detached part named detached-1) are cheap and would close it.

F-243Lowbuild-ciFixed.github/workflows/ci.yml:166

Release seed TL cache step does not gate on per-list health: up to 3 missing or invalid national TLs can ship without failing the job

The online job runs dss-cli tl refresh, which exits 0 whenever the refresh completed and at least one certificate loaded. Per-list download, signature or expiry failures never fail the release. The project's CacheSeeder gate is unused, and no config sets tl_verify_tls.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

CacheSeeder.java exits 1 on any non-TOTAL_PASSED, download error or expired list. CI does not use it. The default tl_verify_tls=false means the published artifact is built from unauthenticated downloads.

Evidence

ci.yml:166; dss-cli main.rs:482 `Ok(if record.completed && status.loaded {...})`; TrustedListManager.java:86 `loaded() { return source.getNumberOfCertificates() > 0; }`; CacheSeeder.java:48,56; EngineConfig.java:116.

Impact

A release can ship a seed cache that is missing countries or holds bad lists. Deployments started from it give INDETERMINATE results for those countries until an online refresh, which may be hours away (F-090).

Recommendation

Gate the seed step on per-list health, as CacheSeeder does or via a --strict flag. Pass a config with tl_verify_tls true. Fail or warn on alerts.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

New scripts/ci/check-tl-status.py applies CacheSeeder's rule (download error, signature not TOTAL_PASSED, expired, not used for trust) to dss-cli tl status --json and fails the online job (default 0 problems allowed, --max-problems N); alerts become warnings. The tl_verify_tls part was not changed: the verifiers refuted it and DECISIONS keeps TL downloads unverified at the TLS layer because the lists are XML-signed and validated against the OJ keystore.

Files: scripts/ci/check-tl-status.py, .github/workflows/ci.yml

Test: test-scripts.sh: healthy status accepted; download error, expired list, nothing loaded rejected; --max-problems 1 tolerates one.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

Half of the finding reproduces, half misreads a documented decision.

CONFIRMED (per-list gating gap):

  • .github/workflows/ci.yml:166 runs "$cli" --oj-keystore trust/oj-keystore.p12 --cache-dir build/tl-seed tl refresh, then tl status --json and tars build/tl-seed/tl regardless.
  • rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:482-486: Ok(if record.completed && status.loaded { ExitCode::SUCCESS } else { ExitCode::from(1) }). status.loaded is source.getNumberOfCertificates() > 0 (TrustedListManager.java:86). completed is false only when the whole DSS job throws: TrustedListManager.java:283-290 catch (RuntimeException e) { // DSS records per-list failures itself; reaching here means the job could not run at all. So a national TL that fails download, signature or is expired leaves the exit code 0.
  • CacheSeeder.java:41-56 implements exactly the per-list gate (!valid || !downloaded || expired -> exit 1), but grep shows it is only invoked by scripts/seed-tl-cache.sh:25, never by ci.yml. The CLI has no --strict (grep for strict/problems in main.rs: none).

OVERSTATED ("never fail the release"): the same online job first runs ./mvnw -B test -Pintegration (ci.yml:155), and OnlineTrustedListTest.fullLotlLoads asserts tls.size() >= 27, no PKIX download errors, and assertTrue(valid >= tls.size() - 3, "too many invalid TLs") (OnlineTrustedListTest.java:101-108). release-assets has needs: [build, online], so 4+ broken lists do fail the release; only up to 3 can slip through (and on a separate temp cache from a separate run, so the seed itself is not asserted). The per-list status JSON dss-native-tl-cache-$stamp.status.json is also published next to the tarball (ci.yml:167-170), so the defect is visible to consumers.

REFUTED (TLS part): tl_verify_tls defaulting to false is a user-approved, documented decision in docs/DECISIONS.md:192-198: ES and HU TL hosts fail PKIX against the JDK trust store; the loader uses TrustAllStrategy like the DSS demo's tl.loader.trust.all; "TL integrity comes from the XML signature, checked against the OJ keystore (for the LOTL) and the LOTL's pointers (for TLs). Combined with the strict sync, a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one." DssEngine.java:123-128 implements this and TrustedListManager.java:488/495 sets used_for_trust from syncStrategy.canBeSynchronized(tl) with accept_invalid_signature default false (EngineConfig.java:106). So the downloads are not "unauthenticated" and the seed cannot "hold bad lists"; passing tl_verify_tls: true in CI would make the ES/HU lists fail to download (the very reason for the default) and fullLotlLoads explicitly asserts no PKIX errors. Only expired lists are accepted, also by documented decision (accept_expired: true, DECISIONS.md:190-191).

Net: a real but low-severity CI gap — the seed step reproduces CacheSeeder's download/refresh but not its per-list exit-1 gate, so a release seed can be missing up to 3 countries without failing. Impact is bounded by the preceding integration test, the published status JSON, and the fact that deployments refresh online anyway.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

Code reads as the finding says: .github/workflows/ci.yml:166 runs dss-cli ... tl refresh, and rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:482 returns Ok(if record.completed && status.loaded { SUCCESS } else { 1 }), so per-list problems alone do not fail the step. But the claimed impact does not hold up in this system.

  1. "Holds bad lists / built from unauthenticated downloads" is false. TLS-off for TL downloads is a documented decision with the trade-off stated, docs/DECISIONS.md:191-197: "TLS for trusted-list downloads: not verified ... TL integrity comes from the XML signature, checked against the OJ keystore (for the LOTL) and the LOTL's pointers (for TLs). Combined with the strict sync, a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one." The strict sync is real: TrustedListManager.java:185-187 builds ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy with setAcceptInvalidListOfTrustedLists/TrustedList(config.tlAcceptInvalidSignature), default false (EngineConfig.java:103). And the consumer side re-checks: DECISIONS.md:390-391 "Loading from the cache re-validates every list's signature", so a tampered file in the tarball is rejected at dss_init regardless of how it was downloaded. The reason for TLS-off is also stated (ES and HU TL hosts fail PKIX): the finding's recommendation to seed with tl_verify_tls: true would make the seed *more* likely to lack countries, the opposite of its goal.
  1. "Missing countries" is bounded by the same job. The online job runs ./mvnw -B test -Pintegration before the seed step (ci.yml:153-154); OnlineTrustedListTest.fullLotlLoads asserts tls.size() >= 27 and valid >= tls.size() - 3 (lines 103, 109). So a release already fails when more than 3 national TLs are invalid; the residual window (up to 3 bad lists, or a failure between the test and the seed step minutes later) is small and is a deliberate tolerance consistent with accept_expired: true ("a country that is late re-publishing does not break validation", DECISIONS.md:94-95).
  1. The artifact is self-describing and optional. ci.yml:167-168 uploads dss-native-tl-cache-$stamp.status.json next to the tarball with the per-list download/validation outcome; README.md:206 presents the seed as a convenience ("To use the seed cache, extract ... into your cache_dir"). A deployment refreshes online on a schedule (dss-server RefreshScheduler, main.rs:154-167) or POST /tl/refresh; a country missing from the seed is the same state the engine already handles and reports after any failed online refresh (status used_for_trust, alerts). Notably the project's own gate, CacheSeeder.java:19-20 and 56, "exit 1 when some list has a problem (the snapshot is still written)", also does not withhold the artifact, so using it in CI would only change the exit code, not what ships.

Net: no injection path, missing lists bounded by the preceding integration test and visible in the published status JSON, and the TLS default is an intentional documented trade-off. What remains (a --strict/warn flag on the seed step) is a minor hardening nicety, not a medium-severity build-ci defect. Severity low.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

Verdict: the mechanism is real but narrower than the finding says, so I rate it low rather than medium.

What is confirmed

  • ci.yml:171 (the finding says 166, which is the step name) runs "$cli" ... --cache-dir build/tl-seed tl refresh. Nothing checks the health of each list before the cache is tarred, hashed and uploaded as tl-cache-snapshot, and release-assets then publishes it.
  • rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:482 returns success on Ok(if record.completed && status.loaded { .
  • loaded is defined at TrustedListManager.java:86 as source.getNumberOfCertificates() > 0. So one good list is enough for exit 0, even if national TLs failed to download or failed validation.
  • CacheSeeder.java treats any list that is not TOTAL_PASSED, has a download error or is expired as a problem and exits 1. Only scripts/seed-tl-cache.sh:25 uses it; CI does not.

What is overstated

  1. TLS verification. EngineConfig.java:116 does default to tl_verify_tls false, and the CI step passes no config. But docs/DECISIONS.md:190-198 records this as a decision the user made: "TLS for trusted-list downloads: not verified... a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one". The reason given is the ES and HU hosts failing PKIX. List integrity comes from the XML signature, checked against the OJ keystore. So "built from unauthenticated downloads" is wrong. The content is authenticated; only the transport is not, and the worst an attacker can do is the same as a download failure.
  2. "Holds bad lists". With strict sync (DECISIONS.md:192-193), lists with a bad or indeterminate signature "are never used". The real effect is lists missing from the cache, not bad lists loaded from it. One caveat: expired lists are accepted by design (accept_expired: true).

Why low severity

  • Not attacker-controlled for content. A network attacker can at most cause omissions, so the issue is availability or completeness only.
  • Needs a transient national-TL failure during a release build.
  • The impact is INDETERMINATE results for some countries until the next refresh. That fails safe and does not turn into a false PASS.
  • The cache ships with dss-native-tl-cache-$stamp.status.json, which shows per-list status to anyone who checks, though nobody gates on it.
  • The online job also runs the full online suites first, which partly catches a broken LOTL.

Actionable fix: gate the seed step on the per-list statuses in that status JSON, the same way CacheSeeder does (for example with jq), or add a --strict flag to tl refresh.

Only CI's install-graalvm.sh enforces the pinned CE version. Local builds use whatever JAVA_HOME holds, and package.sh hard-codes the vendor string.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The pom enforcer only requires Java [21,). Oracle GraalVM (GFTC) is deliberately not used per DECISIONS.md and LICENSING.md, but local builds do not enforce this. dist/ already holds locally built packages.

build-native.sh:19; pom.xml:46-47, :234; package.sh:47 `GraalVM Community Edition $graal_version: ...`.

Impact

A local package can misstate its licensing (wrong runtime or vendor), and version drift goes unnoticed.

Fail unless $JAVA_HOME/release shows IMPLEMENTOR GraalVM Community and GRAALVM_VERSION equal to the pom's value. Read the vendor from that file.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

build-native.sh calls scripts/ci/check-graalvm.sh: IMPLEMENTOR must be 'GraalVM Community' (always an error otherwise) and GRAALVM_VERSION must equal graalvm.sdk.version (error in CI, warning locally). package.sh reads vendor and version from the build's licenses/graalvm/release through the same script instead of hard-coding the vendor.

Files: scripts/ci/check-graalvm.sh, scripts/build-native.sh, scripts/package.sh

Test: test-scripts.sh: pinned CE accepted, Oracle GraalVM and non-GraalVM refused, other CE release warned locally and refused with CI=true; local JDK 17 refused, local CE 25.4.4.1.1 warned.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

Reproduced by reading the cited paths. scripts/build-native.sh:14 states "# Requires JAVA_HOME = GraalVM Community Edition 25 (see docs/DECISIONS.md)." but the only use of that requirement is line 19, "$JAVA_HOME/bin/native-image" --version | head -1, which prints and never compares; lines 58 and 61 then copy $JAVA_HOME/LICENSE.txt, THIRD_PARTY_LICENSE.txt and release from whatever JAVA_HOME holds. java/pom.xml:234-236 enforces only <requireJavaVersion><version>[21,)</version>; there is no vendor rule (grep for IMPLEMENTOR/java.vendor/requireProperty in pom.xml and the repo finds nothing). scripts/package.sh:47 writes GraalVM Community Edition $graal_version: https://github.com/graalvm/graalvm-ce-builds/releases/tag/graal-$graal_version unconditionally, so an Oracle GraalVM in JAVA_HOME (whose release also carries GRAALVM_VERSION but IMPLEMENTOR="Oracle Corporation") would yield a SOURCE line claiming CE while licenses/graalvm/LICENSE.txt and release say otherwise. The only enforcement is CI: scripts/ci/install-graalvm.sh pins release graal-25.4.4.1.1 with per-platform SHA-256 and .github/actions/setup/action.yml sets JAVA_HOME from it.

Corrections to the finding: (1) "version drift goes unnoticed" is overstated for SOURCE, because package.sh:30 reads graal_version from $lib/licenses/graalvm/release (GRAALVM_VERSION=...), i.e. the real build JDK; only the vendor is hard-coded. Drift does, however, go unnoticed against the static texts: pom.xml:46-47 ("Must match the GraalVM CE release used to build (graal 25.4.4.1.1)") and LICENSING.md:72 ("GraalVM Community Edition 25.4.4.1.1 runtime"), and LICENSING.md is copied into every package by package.sh:39 with no check. (2) Impact is limited: README.md:189-196 and docs/DECISIONS.md:479-491 document that release packages are produced only by CI from the pinned CE install, local/non-release builds report the placeholder 0.0.0-dev, and dist/ is gitignored (.gitignore:20); the local dist/ SOURCE present here (commit cf94a96) does not even contain the GraalVM line. So the defect is real as a missing local guard plus a hard-coded vendor string, but it cannot affect published releases unless someone packages by hand outside CI. Low severity; the recommended release-file check (IMPLEMENTOR="GraalVM Community", GRAALVM_VERSION == pom value) is cheap and the local CE's release file confirms both keys exist.

F-253LowsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:243

validateLevel never calls setSignaturePolicyProvider. Today no fetch happens only because DefaultDocumentAnalyzer reads the null field rather than its lazy NativeHTTPDataLoader getter, which 5.12.1 did call.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

If upstream restores the call, extend and sign-complete as well as validate would open document-chosen URLs. NativeHTTPDataLoader accepts any scheme (file: included), has no timeouts and no size cap. None of the engine's http.* settings reach it. A PoC with a stalling listener confirmed that no request is made today. No fixture carries id-aa-ets-sigPolicyId and no test asserts the absence of fetches.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:243-255 (no setSignaturePolicyProvider); DefaultDocumentAnalyzer.java:876-879; javap: only DefaultDocumentAnalyzer references getSignaturePolicyProvider in 6.5.1; 5.12.1 SignedDocumentValidator `invokevirtual getSignaturePolicyProvider`; NativeHTTPDataLoaderCall.java:210, :158-175.

Impact

No exploit today. After a DSS upgrade, any document could trigger SSRF, file reads or unbounded blocking fetches, with no config to stop them.

Recommendation

Explicitly set a SignaturePolicyProvider with no data loader, or one backed by the engine's configured loader. Add a FakeHttp test asserting zero hits, and record the decision in DECISIONS.md.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-tests)

Handoff from java-engine (with F-254). New SignaturePolicyTest builds an enveloping CAdES-BASELINE-B at test time with CAdESService and a signature policy: OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.2.1, SHA-256 digest of a policy document, SPURI http://policy.dss-native.test/policy.der. FakeHttp is routed to serve the genuine policy document at that URL, so a fetch would succeed and the policy would become identified. The test validates through the online TestEngines engine and asserts: zero FakeHttp hits for the policy URL; signatures[0].policy present with the OID in id, url = the SPURI, identified=false, digest_valid=null; info contains DSS's 'The signature policy is not available!'; indication TOTAL_PASSED. It passes on the current engine (setSignaturePolicyProvider without a data loader), on the JVM and in the native image. The test is in its own class rather than FixtureValidationTest, because that class shares one engine and has no access to FakeHttp hit counts.

After review: Strengthened, as the reviewer suggested. The new SignaturePolicyTest.noLoaderFetchesThePolicyUrl puts the SPURI on a real HttpServer on 127.0.0.1 that serves the genuine policy. It asserts zero server hits, identified=false, the url reported, and TOTAL_PASSED. It catches a SignaturePolicyProvider given any loader of its own (a fresh CommonsDataLoader or DSS's default), which the existing FakeHttp-based test could not see. signWithPolicy now takes the URL as a parameter.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The code reads as the finding says: DssEngine.validateLevel (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:233-255) never calls setSignaturePolicyProvider, and in DSS 6.5.1 DefaultDocumentAnalyzer.extractSignaturePolicyContent reads the raw field (if (signaturePolicyProvider != null) { return signaturePolicyProvider.getSignaturePolicy(...) }, DefaultDocumentAnalyzer.java:872-877), while the lazy getter that would build a NativeHTTPDataLoader (lines 294-300) has no caller in any 6.5.1 jar (byte-scan of every *-6.5.1.jar in ~/.m2 found no reference outside its own declaration; 5.12.1's SignedDocumentValidator does invokevirtual getSignaturePolicyProvider). Through the IMPACT lens the claim does not hold up as a medium security finding:

  1. The finding itself states "No exploit today": with the pinned DSS 6.5.1 (<dss.version>6.5.1</dss.version>, java/pom.xml:43) the fetch path is unreachable. The impact is entirely contingent on a hypothetical future upstream change reversing a direction DSS deliberately took in 6.x (moving to field-only reads). This repository never used 5.12.1 (git log -S"5.12.1" is empty; the 5.12.1 jar in ~/.m2 is a binary-only leftover with no sources); the "regression" is speculative.
  1. Document-chosen URL fetches are already an inherent, default-on property of this engine, so the hypothetical would not open a new class of exposure. With the defaults "revocation": "online" and "aia": true (README.md:280-281; EngineConfig.java:123-129), certificateVerifier wires OnlineCRLSource, OnlineOCSPSource and DefaultAIASource(httpLoader) (DssEngine.java:462-480), which call dataLoader.get(crlUrl) / dataLoader.get(caIssuersUrl) with URLs taken from the untrusted document's certificates (OnlineCRLSource.java:202, DefaultAIASource.java:160). The configured CommonsDataLoader.get even dispatches file: URLs to fileGet → ftpGet → URL.openStream (CommonsDataLoader.java:798-806, 921-923). So "SSRF / file reads driven by the document" is an accepted trait of an online signature validator here; the only delta the finding identifies is that the hypothetical NativeHTTPDataLoader would lack the engine's timeouts (withTimeouts, DssEngine.java:146-150) and a size cap.
  1. The deployment docs already bound the blast radius: docs/server.md:216-217 "No TLS. Run the sidecar on the same host or on a private network ... never expose it publicly", with a bearer token and --max-request-mb/--max-heap limits. Documents from untrusted parties are the expected input, but the same holds for the existing CRL/AIA fetches.
  1. It is not a documented decision (DECISIONS.md:201 "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only" is about the validation policy, not SPURI), and the recommendation (set an explicit provider backed by the configured loader, add a FakeHttp zero-hit test) is cheap and sensible hardening. But as an impact statement, "medium / security" overstates a currently unreachable path whose worst case duplicates behaviour the engine already has by design, minus a timeout. Calibrated: low-severity hardening / future-proofing note, not a present vulnerability.

In java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:243-251, validateLevel calls setCertificateVerifier, setLocale, setEnableEtsiValidationReport, setValidationTime and setDetachedContents, but never setSignaturePolicyProvider. So with the field unset, nothing is fetched today. In dss-validation, SignedDocumentValidator only forwards the setter (:236-237). SignaturePolicyProvider.java:103 fetches through dataLoader.get(url) only when a loader is set.

Severity calibration. There is no reachable attack today. To become exploitable, an upstream release would have to switch to the lazy getter, and the maintainers would then have to bump dss.version (pinned at java/pom.xml:43 as 6.5.1) without noticing. A version bump is a deliberate, reviewable act. The impact would be SSRF, file: reads or a hang, driven by the document. That conflicts with the documented "offline" revocation contract (README:280, :345). Even so, the likelihood is low and the risk is speculative. This is a defence-in-depth gap plus a missing regression test, so low fits better than medium.

Line. DssEngine.java:243 is the setCertificateVerifier line, inside the configuration block where the missing call belongs, so the line reference is precise enough to act on.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.9

Reproduced through code + the shipped DSS default policy; did not craft a JS-injected PDF (avoided weaponizing). Chain: (1) DssEngine.java:255 calls validator.validateDocument() and sets no custom ValidationPolicy anywhere (grep over java/src/main finds no setValidationPolicy/ValidationPolicy), so DSS's bundled default policy is used; object-level modification detection is deliberately on (pdfObjFactory, DssEngine.java:452-463; DECISIONS.md:112-114). (5) ValidationResult.java:33,77-78,90 surfaces modifications only as a flat List<String> warnings via texts(), with no structured modification data and no active-content flag; repo-wide grep finds zero handling of /OpenAction, /AA, /JavaScript, /Launch, /EmbeddedFiles. Thus injected active content yields TOTAL_PASSED with only the generic undefined-modifications warning, identical to a benign undefined edit — indistinguishable, no active-content classification, exactly as stated. Nuance (the finding acknowledges it): a warning IS emitted, so the 'clean pass' is only clean for a caller that branches on indication and ignores warnings; this is DSS's documented eIDAS default-policy behavior faithfully reflected, and the recommendation (fail on undefined modifications, or classify active-content additions as a distinct structured warning) is a hardening enhancement rather than a correctness defect. Hence severity low (borderline low-medium) rather than medium; the factual claims are all confirmed, so not refuted.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

Lens: IMPACT. I accept the mechanics as described (DSS's PdfObjectModificationsFilter routes anything that is not an extension/form-fill/annotation change to addUndefinedChange: dss-pades 6.5.1 PdfObjectModificationsFilter.java:72, and DSS has no /OpenAction, /AA, /JavaScript, /Launch or /EmbeddedFiles classification at all — grep of eu/europa/esig/dss/pdf returns nothing). But the claimed impact, "the library reports a clean pass", does not hold in this system:

  1. The pass is not clean. ValidationResult.summarize (ValidationResult.java:73-78) forwards every simple-report warning verbatim into warnings, which the finding's own evidence shows is non-empty ("The document contains undefined object modifications after the signature revision!"). README.md:316-320 documents warnings as a first-class per-signature field; Rust exposes it as pub warnings: Vec<String> (rust/dss/src/types.rs:75). A host that reads indication and ignores warnings is ignoring documented output.
  1. Structured detail already exists one layer down. DSS's PAdESDiagnosticDataBuilder.java:218-230 writes each undefined change into DiagnosticData as <Undefined action="CREATION" type="...">/Root /OpenAction</Undefined> (value = PdfObjectTree.toString(), the key chain joined with " /", PdfObjectTree.java:93-99; schema DiagnosticData.xsd:441-466). The project exposes that XML per call ("reports": [... "diagnostic"], README.md:296) or by default (config.defaultReports, EngineConfig.java:130; README.md:282), and DssEngine.validateLevel puts it in the result (DssEngine.java:268-270). So a host wanting to flag active-content additions can do so today with an XPath over ObjectModifications/Undefined; the recommendation's "distinct structured warning" is a convenience, not a missing capability.
  1. The WARN level is DSS's own default policy, not a project choice: dss-policy-jaxb 6.5.1 policy/constraint.xml:67 <UndefinedChanges Level="WARN" /> (same at :373 for timestamps), alongside DocMDP/FieldMDP/SigFieldLock also at WARN. The project uses the stock policy (no setValidationPolicy anywhere in java/src/main). Under ETSI EN 319 102-1 the signature indication concerns the signed revision; later incremental updates do not invalidate it, which is why the EU reference implementation warns rather than fails. "Fail on undefined modifications" (the first recommendation) would reject the very common benign case of a viewer re-saving a signed PDF (updates to /Info, /Metadata, viewer prefs all land in Undefined), i.e. a regression against real-world documents from public administrations and signing portals. DECISIONS.md:112-114 records that object-level modification detection stays on while visual comparison is off, and DECISIONS.md:144-147 that errors/warnings are "taken from the simple report so Rust does not need an XML parser for the common case" — i.e. the flat-string summary is a deliberate minimal projection with the XML reports as the full channel.
  1. The threat is misattributed. JavaScript in a PDF runs (or not) in the viewer; the signature neither enables nor sandboxes it, and an attacker who wants a victim to open JS does not need a signed PDF at all. This library does not render or open PDFs (DECISIONS.md: PDFBox rendering disabled; AWT-free) and makes no "document is safe to open" promise anywhere in README.md or docs/DECISIONS.md — its stated hardening concern is "a hostile file attacking the process" (README.md:512). Signature-validity and content-safety are different properties; conflating them is what produces the "weaponised while clean" framing.

Net: real behaviour, overstated impact. The actionable residue is an enhancement (project a typed modifications/undefined_changes list, or an active-content hint, from DiagnosticData into SignatureSummary) — low severity, and arguably an upstream DSS feature. Not a security defect of this library as described.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

The behaviour is real, but the finding points at the wrong place and overstates the severity.

Location. DssEngine.java:442 is the pdfValidator helper (new PDFDocumentValidator(doc); validator.setPdfObjFactory(pdfObjFactory())). Lines 448-458 keep object-level modification detection on and only turn off visual comparison: "Object-level modification detection between revisions stays on". Nothing in the project's Java code decides how modifications are classified. A grep for undefined/modification/policy under java/src/main finds no custom policy and no handling of modifications. The verdict comes from DSS's default constraint.xml. That is a documented decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:201 says "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now."

Warnings are flat strings. ValidationResult.java:78 builds warnings as texts(report.getAdESValidationWarnings(id), ...), and ValidationResult.java:47 outputs them as m.put("warnings", warnings). So the only signal is the generic DSS message. The project adds no structured flag for active content, which matches the finding's claim.

Severity. This is how upstream DSS and the ETSI default policy behave. A JVM DSS run with the default policy gives the same TOTAL_PASSED and the same warning, so this is not a regression introduced by the wrapper.

  • The signed byte range is still intact.
  • A caller who reads the warnings can see that unsigned content was added after the signature.
  • Incremental updates after signing are normal in PAdES (LTA extensions, DSS dictionaries, form fills). Failing on every undefined change would break legitimate files.
  • Attack vector: someone other than the signer modifies a signed file. The JavaScript runs only in a viewer, not in this library.
  • Impact: integrity/UI deception for consumers that look only at the indication.

Overall this is a hardening gap, low severity, not medium.

Recommendation. It is actionable: allow a custom or stricter policy (UndefinedChanges=FAIL), or add a structured warning when /OpenAction, /AA, /JavaScript, /Launch or /EmbeddedFiles appear in a post-signature revision.

I did not reproduce the f_openaction_js run. That part of the evidence is accepted as reported, and it fits DSS default-policy semantics.

F-261LowsecurityFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:97

OnlineTSPSource is built without a NonceSource, so TimeStampReqs carry no nonce and BouncyCastle skips the nonce check on the response

setNonceSource is never called, so every TimeStampReq lacks a nonce and BouncyCastle skips the nonce check. A token with an unrelated nonce was embedded.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The message imprint must still match, which limits exposure to replays for the same imprint and to man-in-the-middle on plain http (F-006).

Evidence

DssEngine.java:96-97; `[nonce] extend pades/b-b.pdf -> LT: OK`; every request is 89 bytes (no nonce).

Impact

Replayed or proxy-cached responses cannot be detected.

Recommendation

Call tspSource.setNonceSource(new SecureRandomNonceSource()) and add a test for a mismatching nonce.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

The OnlineTSPSource is built with setNonceSource(new SecureRandomNonceSource()), so every TimeStampReq carries a nonce and BouncyCastle's response validation compares it; a mismatch is TSA_FAILED.

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java

Test: EngineHardeningTest.tokensWithAWrongClockWeakAlgorithmOrWrongNonceAreRefused (a TSA answering a request with another nonce is refused with a message mentioning the nonce)

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.92

Confirmed as stated. java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:96-97 builds the TSA as new OnlineTSPSource(config.tsaUrl.toString(), tsaLoader != null ? tsaLoader : httpLoader) and nothing else touches it: grep -rn "NonceSource\|setNonceSource" java/src rust docs README.md finds no hit anywhere in the repository, and the word "nonce" does not occur in any project source or doc (docs/DECISIONS.md:640-656 discusses the TSA loader, credentials and the test TSA, but never nonces, so this is not a documented decision). In DSS 6.5.1 (dss-service-6.5.1-sources.jar, OnlineTSPSource.java:168-173) the request is tsqGenerator.generate(asn1ObjectIdentifier, digest) when nonceSource == null, i.e. no nonce; the nonce branch tsqGenerator.generate(..., new BigInteger(nonce)) is only taken when a NonceSource is set. The response is then checked by BouncyCastle TimeStampResponse.validate(request) (bcpkix 1.86, TimeStampResponse.java:193): if (request.getNonce() != null && !request.getNonce().equals(tstInfo.getNonce())) throw ..., so with a nonce-less request the token's nonce is never compared. A jshell experiment against the project's own BC 1.86 jars reproduced it: a nonce-less TimeStampReq (57 bytes with a SHA-256 imprint; the finding's 89 bytes matches a SHA-512 imprint) validated a token whose TSTInfo carried nonce 123456789 ("validate(nonce-less request): ACCEPTED"), whereas the same token was rejected against a request that did carry a different nonce ("response contains wrong nonce value."). The test TSA (TestPki.java:187-188) builds its response from the incoming request, so the existing suite cannot catch this. Severity stays low: the nonce is optional in RFC 3161, the message imprint and the TSA signature are still verified, so an attacker can only replay a genuine TSA token for the same imprint (an older but authentic timestamp) or serve a cached response over an unprotected transport; no forgery is possible. Fix as recommended: tspSource.setNonceSource(new SecureRandomNonceSource()) at DssEngine.java:97.

F-262LowoperationsPartially fixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:319

PAdESLevelBaselineLT adds the T timestamp first and checks revocation afterwards. With revocation offline, or a revocation source that is down, every attempt consumes a billable token and then fails.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

DECISIONS.md documents that T→LT is refused offline, but not that B→LT still contacts the TSA first.

Evidence

`not extended: ExtensionFailed: ... Revocation data is missing ...` / `TSA hits during B->LT: 1`; `B->LTA: 1`.

Impact

Recommendation

Pre-check that revocation is available for the signing chain (or reject B→LT/LTA when revocation is offline) before contacting the TSA. Document the behaviour.

Remediation: Partially fixed (package java-engine)

DssEngine.assertExtensionPossible runs before extendDocument: with revocation offline and a target of LT/LTA, when any signature is below LT it runs DSS's own LT checks (PAdESSignatureRequirementsChecker.assertCertificateChainValidForLTLevel and PDFDocumentAnalyzer.getValidationData with CompleteValidationContextExecutor) on the document's own revocation data and refuses with EXTENSION_FAILED ('Revocation data is missing ... revocation is "offline", so the data cannot be fetched; the timestamp the extension needs was not requested') before any TSA call. Not done: the same pre-check for LT/LTA signing (the new signature's chain can legitimately find its CRL in the PDF's DSS dictionary, so a static refusal would be wrong) and the online-but-down revocation source case (needs a fetch, which is the cost being avoided).

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.95

Reproduced. The ordering lives in DSS 6.5.1 itself: PAdESLevelBaselineLT.extendSignatures (dss-pades-6.5.1-sources.jar) first calls super.extendSignatures(...) (the T level, which runs assertSigningCertificateIsValid and then timestampDocument(...), contacting the TSA) and only afterwards signatureRequirementsChecker.assertCertificateChainValidForLTLevel(signatures), which throws "Revocation data is missing". DssEngine.extend (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:303-319) passes the document straight to service.extendDocument(doc, parameters) with no pre-check of revocation availability; the only pre-checks are empty input and CMS/non-PDF type (lines 296-310).

  • B->LT offline: TSA hits = 1 ; refused: EXTENSION_FAILED ... Revocation data is missing for one or more certificate(s)
  • B->LTA offline: TSA hits = 1 ; same refusal
  • T->LT offline (control, b-t.pdf): TSA hits = 0 ; same refusal

This matches the finding's evidence exactly. The existing test ExtensionTest.missingRevocationDataIsRefused only covers T->LT (b-t.pdf), so the B->LT ordering is untested.

Signing half: ExternalSigning.prepare (ExternalSigning.java:109-129) only computes getDataToSign/getMessageDigest; no revocation availability check, and complete then does signDocument followed by extendDocument (lines 149-201), so an LT/LTA request with revocation unavailable consumes the external signature before DSS refuses. The Javadoc on prepareSignature (DssEngine.java:333-337) shows the project already pre-checks certificate validity "so that no external signature is spent on a document that cannot be completed", but not revocation.

Documentation: docs/DECISIONS.md:638-639 documents only "T→LT is refused" offline; line 646 says "B→LT needs one [timestamp]" without noting that the timestamp is spent before the revocation refusal. So the behaviour is real and undocumented. Severity stays low: the operation fails loudly with the right error code and no incorrect document is produced; the cost is one wasted TSA request (and, for signing, one external signature) per doomed attempt, which is an operational/cost nuisance rather than a correctness or security defect.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Without GrantedOrRecognizedAtNationalLevelTrustAnchorPeriodPredicate, DSS treats trust anchors as always valid. The tl status is identical in every case.

Document the semantics of both settings. Consider renaming the key, or warning when it is false. Add tests covering service history.

README now explains use_sunset_date both ways. true (the default) trusts a CA only for its granted or recognised periods: B and LT signatures turn INDETERMINATE/NO_CERTIFICATE_CHAIN_FOUND_NO_POE after a withdrawal, and LTA with an earlier POE survives. false keeps withdrawn CAs as anchors forever. pivot_support and tl_versions also got comments. Adding service-history tests and a warning for false are code and test changes (java-trust, java-tests) and are not done.

(2) withdrawn 2020-06-01, i.e. before the signatures were made: all four levels, LTA included, are INDETERMINATE/NO_CERTIFICATE_CHAIN_FOUND_NO_POE. (3) use_sunset_date=false against that same earlier-withdrawn list: all four levels TOTAL_PASSED. tl_versions is passed straight to DSS, where it only triggers structure-validation messages. A TL of an unlisted version is still synchronised and trusted, and nothing reports it. [] silently falls back to DSS's default [5,6].

setTLVersions only produces structure-validation messages, which the sync strategy ignores. TLParsingErrorDetection is not registered. The only effect is a per-signature 'structure ... not valid' warning. [] silently means DSS's default [5,6].

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

DECISIONS.md:59 implies other versions are excluded.

Evidence

TrustedListManager.java:158-160, 205-209; probe `tl_versions:[5]` → `loaded=true`, `IT version=6 used=true`, `alerts=[]`, `TOTAL_PASSED`.

Impact

An operator's filter is not enforced and nothing signals it.

Recommendation

Enforce the filter, or add a tl_structure_error alert and status field. Document the [] behaviour, and add a test.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-trust)

DSS's structure messages (version not in tl_versions, schema deviations) are now visible: per-list status field structure_messages, alerts tl_structure_error / lotl_structure_error, and a new tl_sync.accept_structure_errors (default true, DSS's behaviour) which when false excludes such lists from trust (used_for_trust=false) via a SynchronizationStrategy wrapper. tl_versions: [] is normalised to DSS's default [5,6] explicitly (EngineConfig.DSS_DEFAULT_TL_VERSIONS) and recorded as such.

Verification

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The mechanism is real and accurately described.

  • The only use of the setting. TrustedListManager.java:157-158 is the only place config.tlVersions is used: if (!config.tlVersions.isEmpty()) { lotl.setTLVersions(config.tlVersions); }. The finding cites 158-160; the right lines are 157-158.
  • What DSS does with it. In DSS 6.5.1, the value reaches TLSourceBuilder.java:85 and then AbstractParsingTask.verifyTLVersionConformity (lines 171-178). That method only runs TLStructureVerifier and stores the output with result.setStructureValidationMessages(...).
  • The sync strategy ignores it. ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy.isSyncSupported (lines 125-145) checks only nextUpdateDate and validationCacheInfo.isValid(). It never looks at structure messages, so a signature-valid TL of a non-listed version is still synchronised into the trusted source.
  • No alert covers it. The registered TL alerts (TrustedListManager.java:205-209) are only TLSignatureErrorDetection and TLExpirationDetection. Nothing covers structure or parsing errors.
  • The empty-list case. With [], setTLVersions is never called, so the default from TLSource.java:38 applies: DEFAULT_SUPPORTED_TL_VERSIONS = Arrays.asList(5, 6). The finding is right that [] silently means [5,6].
  • Documented intent. DECISIONS.md:59 says the demo "uses TL version 6 only ... Both are adopted as defaults". A reader could fairly take that to mean other versions are excluded. README.md:266 lists "tl_versions": [6] with no explanation.

Severity: low, not medium.

  • This is DSS's own upstream meaning of tl_versions; the reference code (PlainDssReference.java:86-87) does exactly the same. So the problem is a misleading config name and missing docs, not a broken security control.
  • No attacker can exploit it. A TL is only trusted if its XAdES signature validates against certificates announced in an OJ-anchored LOTL. Choosing the TL version does not add any trust beyond what the EU scheme already grants.
  • In normal use, the EU TLs are on v6, so the setting rarely changes the outcome.

The impact is an operator expectation that is not met (and not visible), plus an untested default. That is worth a docs fix or an alert, but it is low severity.

README.md:270 lists "tl_versions": [6] with no semantics; DECISIONS.md:59 only notes the demo's version-6 default; no test covers it (grep in java/src/test finds only PlainDssReference mirroring the pass-through), while the neighbouring countries setting IS a real TL predicate filter, which makes the asymmetry easy to misread. Correction: "nothing reports it" is slightly overstated: the validation reports do carry the WARN; the status and alert channels do not. Severity lowered to low: this is exactly DSS's own (and the DSS demo's) semantics for this setting, the default policy's TLVersion FAIL constraint already covers truly unknown versions in qualification, the realistic case (a v5 list under [6]) still produces a visible report warning, and the fix is small (register TLParsingErrorDetection as a tl_structure_error alert, expose structure messages in describe(), document the pass-through and the [] fallback).

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.72

The code reads as the finding says: TrustedListManager.java:157-158 does if (!config.tlVersions.isEmpty()) { lotl.setTLVersions(config.tlVersions); }, DSS's AbstractParsingTask.verifyTLVersionConformity (dss-tsl-validation 6.5.1, lines 171-176) only calls result.setStructureValidationMessages(...), ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy.isSyncSupported checks only expiry and signature indication, and job.setTLAlerts (TrustedListManager.java:204-208) registers only TLSignatureErrorDetection and TLExpirationDetection, not TLParsingErrorDetection. But through the IMPACT lens the claim "an operator's filter is not enforced" presumes a filter that neither DSS nor this project ever defines. In DSS the setting is a structure-validation input by definition: TLSource.java:59-60 "List of TL Versions accepted for the current TLSource. When defined, an error is returned on structure validation", and TLStructureVerifier.java:79 "an error message will be produces for Trusted Lists with a different version". The project passes DSS's own knob through under DSS's own name, mirroring the demo's tl.loader.lotl.tl.versions=6 (docs/DECISIONS.md:59-60: "The DSS 6.5.1 demo uses TL version 6 only ... Both are adopted as defaults"). Nothing in README.md (line 270 lists "tl_versions": [6] with no comment) or DECISIONS.md promises that unlisted versions are excluded or untrusted; the finding's "implies" is an inference, not a stated contract. Practical impact is negligible: a TL that is referenced by the signed LOTL and whose own XAdES signature validates (the real trust gates, DECISIONS.md "Only signature-valid lists count", TrustedListManager.java:180-186) is a legitimate trust anchor regardless of schema version; excluding v5 lists would reduce coverage, not security. With the default [6] and the current EU lists all at v6 (the finding's own probe: "IT version=6"), the default configuration is self-consistent, so only an operator who sets a non-default list and reads it as a filter is affected, and the status output already reports each list's version (TrustedListManager.java:514 m.put("version", p.getVersion())), so the version actually loaded is observable. The downstream effect is DSS's documented one: the default policy (dss-policy-jaxb constraint.xml:645-649) has TLVersion Level="FAIL" for ids 5,6 and TLStructure Level="WARN", matching the probe's TOTAL_PASSED with a structure warning. The [] behaviour keeps DSS's DEFAULT_SUPPORTED_TL_VERSIONS (TLSource.java:62) instead of DSS's "skip structural validation" path (TLStructureVerifier.java:128-129), which is the safer of the two and harmless. What remains is a documentation/observability nit (say in README that tl_versions is DSS's accepted-versions list for structure validation, not a filter; optionally register TLParsingErrorDetection to surface structure messages as alerts), not a medium correctness defect. No test covers tl_versions (only PlainDssReference.java:86-87 mirrors the same pass-through), but that does not raise the impact.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

In a multi-country list, GR silently drops Greece.

Evidence

EngineConfig.java:93-98; DssEngine.java:419-421; probe `countries:["XX"]` → `completed=true ... trusted_certificates=0`, `alerts=[]`.

Impact

A typo disables validation while the refresh reports success.

Recommendation

Compare the configured codes with the LOTL territories and alert or fail on unmatched ones. Expose the matched set. Fix the error text and document EL/GR.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

Handoff applied: trustSnapshot()'s TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED message is now 'trusted lists not loaded: no list yielded trust anchors (empty cache, a LOTL that could not be used, or countries that match no list: see dss_tl_status, last_*_refresh.error, countries_unmatched and alerts)'.

After review: Late handoff already implemented: trustSnapshot() raises the handoff's exact message (DssEngine.java:623-626), as the failing-then-fixed F-219 test run confirmed verbatim.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The finding is accurate as described, but I'd rate it low rather than medium.

What the code does

  • Only the format is checked. EngineConfig.java:93-98 upper-cases each countries entry and checks only c.matches("[A-Z]{2}"). It never compares the codes against the LOTL.
  • No GR/EL alias. TrustedListManager.java:160-162 passes the codes to TLPredicateFactory.createEUTLCountryCodePredicate. In dss-tsl-validation 6.5.1 (inspected with javap), SchemeTerritoryOtherTSLPointer just checks whether the pointer's {http://uri.etsi.org/02231/v2#}SchemeTerritory is in the set of codes. "GR" therefore never matches Greece's "EL", and "XX" matches nothing.
  • Zero lists still reports success. run() (TrustedListManager.java ~283-296) returns new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), true, null, staging.getNumberOfCertificates()), so completed is true even with 0 certificates. No alert source fires for an unmatched code: the alerts come from DSS's TL/LOTL detections (lines ~35-57, 240).
  • Validation then fails with a misleading message. Snapshot.loaded() is source.getNumberOfCertificates() > 0 (line 86). DssEngine.java:419-421 then throws TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED with "the cache is empty or unreadable; run an online refresh first". For a bad country code that text points at the wrong fix.
  • Not covered by the docs. README.md:265 and DECISIONS.md:32-33 only document ["IT"] and the empty default. Neither mentions EL vs GR or warns about unmatched codes.

Why low, not medium

  • Who can trigger it: only the operator, by a typo in their own config. No attacker can cause it.
  • It fails closed. require_trusted_lists defaults to true (EngineConfig.java:131), so every validation errors out. Nothing is accepted wrongly; this is an availability and diagnosability problem, not a weakened trust decision.
  • Partial typos are not silent losses. If a multi-country list contains GR, Greek-anchored signatures simply find no trust anchor. That is a conservative result, not a security bypass.
  • It shows up quickly. The all-invalid case (for example ["XX"]) appears on the first validation. Only the GR-in-a-list case can go unnoticed for long.

Precision note The finding's wording "every validation fails" holds only when every configured code is unmatched. With a mix of valid and invalid codes, the trusted lists load and only the missing countries' signatures fail.

The finding is actionable as written: check the codes against the LOTL territories, map or document EL/GR, and fix the error text.

reported by: gap-r1-trust-config-semantics · round 2 · auditor confidence 0.85 · reported as Medium, calibrated to Low · status: confirmed

F-269Lowapi-designFixedjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:464

Extra-anchor verdicts are indistinguishable from EU-TL verdicts except via qualification NA and a DSS error string; the gap is undocumented and the status does not report the extra anchors

Extra anchors are merged into the same verifier. A private-CA signer gets TOTAL_PASSED, qualification NA and errors ['Unable to build a certificate chain up to a trusted list!']. Neither the docs nor the status explain this.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The status has no field for extra anchors, and loaded:false even when they are configured.

Evidence

DssEngine.java:463-464; probe `extra+countries DE ... TOTAL_PASSED/null qual=NA ... errors=[Unable to build a certificate chain up to a trusted list!]`.

Impact

Clients cannot tell private-PKI trust from EU trust, and clients that treat any error as failure misread valid results.

Recommendation

Add a per-signature trust_anchor field, document what NA means, report extra anchors in the status, and add a test.

Remediation: Fixed (package java-engine)

Per-signature trust_anchor: 'trusted_list' (the first trusted certificate of the chain has trust services, i.e. came from a TL), 'extra_trusted_certificates' (trusted but from the extra anchors), or 'none'. dss_tl_status gains extra_trusted_certificates (count of anchors loaded from config). With F-250 the qualification message no longer appears under errors. Docs must explain qualification NA for private PKIs.

Files: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ValidationResult.java, java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java

Test: EngineHardeningTest.qualificationErrorsAreNotValidationErrorsAndTheTrustAnchorIsNamed (private PKI → extra_trusted_certificates and status count 1; TL engine → trusted_list; no anchors → none)

Verification

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

The mechanism is described correctly. DssEngine.java:462-468 merges the extra anchors into the same verifier: if (extraTrusted.getNumberOfCertificates() > 0) { verifier.setTrustedCertSources(snapshot.source(), extraTrusted); }. The anchor source is therefore invisible to the AdES indication, as the finding says. The per-signature summary carries only indication, sub_indication, format, qualification, signing_time, best_signature_time, signed_by, errors, warnings (DECISIONS.md:145-146) and has no trust-anchor field. The status reports TL loaded (DssJsonApi.java:50, TrustedListManager.loaded()) and has no field for extra anchors. The docs do not explain what a private-PKI verdict looks like. README.md:284 says only "PEM/DER files trusted in addition to the TLs", and DECISIONS.md:99 says require_trusted_lists:false is "for private PKIs used with extra_trusted_certificates". So the finding is real and a maintainer can act on it. File and line are accurate (DssEngine.java:463-464).

Severity calibration, downgraded from medium to low: (1) This is upstream DSS behaviour, and it is ETSI-correct. A chain to a configured anchor is TOTAL_PASSED for AdES. Qualification NA plus DSS's own "Unable to build a certificate chain up to a trusted list!" message is DSS's standard way to signal non-EU trust. So the signal exists; it is just not documented. (2) Only an operator who deliberately configures extra_trusted_certificates can reach this. No attacker can reach it. (3) The detailed and diagnostic reports, available through options reports, still expose the chain and the trusted source. (4) Clients that decide EU trust from qualification (QESIG/QESEAL/ADESIG etc.) get the right answer, because NA is not EU-qualified. What remains is an API-clarity and documentation gap: no explicit trust_anchor field, NA is not explained, and the status does not report extra anchors. That is a low-severity design issue, not a medium one. The quoted probe output was not re-run here, but it is consistent with the code path.

Reproduced the behaviour (dss-cli, empty cache, --trust testdata/fixtures/pki/root-ca.pem --allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation, pades/b-lta.pdf): indication TOTAL_PASSED, qualification "NA", errors ["Unable to build a certificate chain up to a trusted list!"], exit code 0. The code at java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:463-464 (verifier.setTrustedCertSources(snapshot.source(), extraTrusted)) does merge both sources. But the claimed impact does not hold in this system:

  1. "Clients cannot tell private-PKI trust from EU trust" is false. The API passes DSS's simple report through (ValidationResult.java:71-78, DECISIONS.md:146-147 "taken from the simple report"). qualification is exactly the discriminator: DSS yields NA only when no trusted list is reached (dss-i18n 6.5.1 QUAL_CERT_TRUSTED_LIST_REACHED_ANS=Unable to build a certificate chain up to a trusted list!); any EU-TL-anchored signer gets one of the other 21 SignatureQualification values. The Rust type already documents NA as an expected value (rust/dss/src/types.rs:65 /// e.g. "QESIG", "ADESIG", "NA"). Full provenance is available on request via the documented reports: ["diagnostic"] (README.md:303): the diagnostic XML for the private root shows <Source>TRUSTED_STORE</Source>, <Trusted>true</Trusted> and an empty <TrustedLists/>, so a client that needs "which anchor" can read it.
  1. "Clients that treat any error as failure misread valid results" is a client misuse the docs already steer away from: docs/server.md:89-90 "A failed signature is not an error ... check each signatures[].indication"; openapi.yaml SignatureSummary has required: [id, indication] with indication described as "DSS's outcome". This is not specific to extra anchors: an EU-TL signer with a non-qualified certificate also returns TOTAL_PASSED with qualification errors, so a client keyed on errors is wrong in the EU case too. The CLI itself uses indication for its exit code (observed exit 0 with the error line printed).

What remains is a documentation nicety: README.md:321 shows only "QESIG" as a qualification example and does not spell out that NA means "no EU trusted list reached" or that errors includes DSS qualification errors. The LOTL is then signed by the last signer, announces it, and lists the pivots newest first before the OJ URL in SchemeInformationURI, which is where DSS's PivotSchemeInformationURI looks for them. withFirstPivotSignedBy(ListSigner) forges the first link. serveOn routes the pivots, and pivot(i) returns pivot bytes. (2) Pivots are stored in <cache>/tl, and an offline restart (FakeHttp offline, zero requests) loads 3 certificates through the chain. (3) pivot_support=false: LOTL not TOTAL_PASSED, used_for_trust=false, no pivot downloaded, 0 trusted certificates. (4) A chain whose first pivot is signed by a key outside the OJ keystore: the pivot and LOTL are not TOTAL_PASSED, nothing is trusted, and the forged pivot is not cached.

DSS builds XMLSignature with secureValidation=false and verifies every reference even when the signature fails. XSLT and XPath transforms in an attacker's ds:Signature are evaluated. Native builds are protected only because reflection metadata is missing.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

No file or network access was observed (secure processing is on for XSLT). JVM timings: N=5,000 → 4.1 s, N=10,000 → 15.5 s. Native builds throw MissingReflectionRegistrationError, which escapes catch(Exception) and aborts the analysis.

Impact

Limited in the shipped native build. On the JVM, or after a metadata regeneration, a hostile TL can stall refreshes repeatedly.

Recommendation

Pre-check TL signatures: allow only enveloped-signature and c14n transforms, few references, no Manifest. Record in reflection-audit.md that the XSLTC and XPath-function classes are deliberately absent.

java-trust handoff applied to docs/reflection-audit.md (see F-157).

The project never changes this: grep -rn "secureValidation|setSecureValidation" java/src/main/java is empty, and TrustedListManager.java:182 wires a stock TLValidationJob whose TLValidatorTask (dss-tsl-validation, TLValidatorTask.java:93-102) runs new XMLDocumentValidator(trustedList, ...) .validateDocument(policy) — i.e. full XML-DSig processing of every downloaded/cached list — before the ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy (TrustedListManager.java:185-189) decides trust. TrustedListManager.java:176 itself states "Loading from the cache re-validates every list's XAdES signature", so a hostile list that reached the cache is re-processed at every startup offline refresh. Reproduced with the library's own CLI, offline (no TL refresh): dss-cli validate --allow-without-trusted-lists --offline-revocation --trust root.pem --report diagnostic on the corpus input out/pdfs/lock-p1-signed.pdf gives no lock-related warning, while the library-extended out/signed/lock-p1-signed.ext-T.pdf gives W=['Document contains changes restricted by /FieldMDP dictionary!', 'Document contains changes restricted by /SigFieldLock dictionary!']; certified-p1.ext-T.pdf (DocMDP P=1) gives none. The diagnostic data shows why: the only post-signature changes are ExtensionChange {action: CREATION, fieldName: 'Signature1', type: 'DocTimeStamp'} (the document timestamp field that extend adds), and the signature carries SigFieldLock [Action=ALL, Permissions=NO_CHANGE_PERMITTED] plus FieldMDP [Action=ALL] (the FieldMDP /Reference is written by DSS at signing time, PdfBoxSignatureService.setFieldMDP, lines 395-411, copying the field's /Lock).

Root cause is upstream DSS 6.5.1, not DssEngine: PDFRevisionWrapper.getModifiedFieldNames() (lines 185-195) includes getExtensionChanges(), and AbstractPdfLockDictionaryCheck.process() returns false for case ALL whenever that list is non-empty, so both FieldMDPCheck and SigFieldLockCheck fail; DocMDPCheck.process() by contrast only looks at SignatureOrFormFill/Annotation/Undefined changes and ignores extension changes, hence the inconsistency. Default policy levels are <FieldMDP Level="WARN"/> <SigFieldLock Level="WARN"/> (constraint.xml lines 65-66), so the indication stays TOTAL_PASSED as the finding says; a policy with Level=FAIL would turn the library's own extension into FAILED/FORMAT_FAILURE. The repo's extend (DssEngine.java:318, service.extendDocument(doc, parameters)) delegates straight to PAdESService, and nothing in README.md, docs/DECISIONS.md or java/src/test mentions FieldMDP/SigFieldLock (grep found no hits), so the behaviour is neither handled nor documented.

Corrections: (1) it is upstream DSS behaviour surfaced by the library, not a defect in the extend code itself; (2) the trigger is /Lock /Action /All, not P=1 specifically: the harness shows lock-p2-signed gets the same two warnings (summary.txt lines 125-126), consistent with the case ALL: return false branch being independent of /P. Severity low: warnings only under the default policy, cosmetic/trust-perception impact; the reasonable remediation is a regression test, a doc note, and an upstream report, as the finding recommends.
