F-280Lowbuild-ciFixedscripts/package.sh:63

package.sh names the tarball from version.properties but never checks that the packaged libdssnative and dss-cli report the same version (output of line 63 discarded)

The tarball name comes from java/target/classes/version.properties, the library from build/native/, and dss-cli/dss-server from Cargo.toml. The script runs dss-cli version but discards its output, so a mislabelled package goes undetected.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Any Maven run re-filters version.properties from the current pom, including the ./mvnw test-compile inside scripts/test-rust.sh, smoke-test-c.sh and diff-vs-jvm.sh. Only scripts/build-native.sh replaces build/native/<platform>/libdssnative. Running scripts/ci/set-version.sh 1.2.3, then scripts/test-rust.sh, then scripts/package.sh locally therefore produces dss-native-1.2.3-<platform>.tar.gz. Its dss-cli and dss-server report 1.2.3, while its libdssnative still reports 0.0.0-dev. package.sh:63 already runs the packaged CLI's version command, which prints these values, but sends the output to /dev/null. Release CI runs the steps in the right order, so the risk is in local packaging, which the Dockerfile header explicitly supports.

Evidence

package.sh:27-28  version_file=".../version.properties"; version="$(sed -n 's/^library=//p' "$version_file")"
package.sh:20-21  lib="$root/build/native/$platform" (only existence is checked)
package.sh:63  "$out/bin/dss-cli" ... version >/dev/null
docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:4-5  build context: dist/ after scripts/package.sh

Impact

A locally built package or Docker image can carry a library whose dss_version disagrees with the package name and the binaries. Bug reports and LGPL SOURCE pointers then name the wrong build.

Recommendation

Capture the output of package.sh:63 and fail unless both the dss-cli line and the libdssnative line equal $version. Also check that $version is non-empty, and remove the mktemp cache directory afterwards.

Remediation: Fixed (package scripts-ci)

package.sh checks version.properties exists and both versions are non-empty, captures dss-cli version and requires 'dss-cli <v>', 'libdssnative <v>', 'EU DSS <dss>' lines, and requires dss-server --version == 'dss-server <v>'; the mktemp cache is removed by a trap.

Files: scripts/package.sh

Test: Scratch package with version.properties library=1.2.3 but a 0.0.0-dev build: package.sh stops with 'the packaged dss-cli does not report "dss-cli 1.2.3"' and writes no tarball; matching versions package fine.

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

Every factual claim in F-280 is confirmed by the code.

Three independent sources, no cross-check (scripts/package.sh):

  • line 20-21: lib="$root/build/native/$platform" then [[ -f "$lib/libdssnative.$ext" ]] || ... — only existence is tested; nothing reads the library's version.
  • line 23: cargo build -q --release -p dss-cli -p dss-server — binaries get their version from rust/Cargo.toml [workspace.package] version (currently 0.0.0-dev, line 6), which dss-cli prints via env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:427).
  • line 27-28: version_file="$root/java/target/classes/it/codingduck/dssnative/version.properties"; version="$(sed -n 's/^library=//p' "$version_file")" — the tarball name name="dss-native-$version-$platform" (line 32) comes from the Maven-filtered output file, which maven-resources-plugin re-filters from java/pom.xml <version> on every lifecycle run reaching process-resources (java/pom.xml:184-187 <directory>src/main/resources-filtered</directory><filtering>true</filtering>; source file contains library=${project.version}). scripts/test-rust.sh:15 and scripts/smoke-test-c.sh:45 run ./mvnw -q -B test-compile exec:java, which includes process-resources, so they do refresh that file without rebuilding the library.
  • line 63: "$out/bin/dss-cli" ... version >/dev/null — the one command that prints all three versions (dss-cli {}\nlibdssnative {}\nEU DSS {} at main.rs:426-431) has its output discarded; line 64 does the same for dss-server --version. No [[ -n "$version" ]] check exists either, so an empty/missing version_file would silently produce dss-native--macos-aarch64.

The library's version really can diverge: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/nativeimage/DssFeature.java:80 registers it/codingduck/dssnative/version.properties as a native-image resource and BuildInfo.java:31 reads it via getResourceAsStream, so libdssnative's dss_version is frozen at scripts/build-native.sh time; strings build/native/macos-aarch64/libdssnative.dylib | grep '^library=' prints library=0.0.0-dev embedded in the binary. The scenario in the finding (set-version.sh 1.2.3 -> test-rust.sh -> package.sh) therefore yields a dss-native-1.2.3-*.tar.gz whose dss-cli/dss-server say 1.2.3 and whose libdssnative says 0.0.0-dev, and package.sh:63 passes.

Mitigations that keep this low rather than medium: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs set-version.sh (line 84) before build-native.sh (87), test-rust.sh (102) and package.sh (108), so release artifacts are consistent; scripts/ci/set-version.sh is documented as a CI tool (header: "CI runs it on release builds"). docs/DECISIONS.md:517-518 describes the line-63 run only as proving "the package works on its own", i.e. a smoke test, not a version check, so the missing cross-check is an omission, not a documented decision. The exposure is local packaging, which docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:4-5 explicitly supports ("dist/ after scripts/package.sh"). The impact is a mislabelled package/SOURCE file, not a functional defect. Severity low stands; the recommendation (compare the dss-cli and libdssnative lines of the version output against $version, and assert $version is non-empty) is cheap and well targeted.

(2) On Linux the GLIBC_ symbol-version check is in fact a sound load-time proxy for glibc, since glibc versioned symbols are exactly what ld.so resolves; what it does not cover is libz/libgcc_s or non-glibc behaviour. F-058Infoapi-designFixedrust/dss/src/schedule.rs:81

refresh_now() during a running refresh queues an immediate second full refresh (Engine refuses with RefreshInProgress; dss-server guards its endpoint, direct library users are not guarded)

The capacity-1 trigger is accepted while a refresh is running, so a second full refresh starts immediately afterwards.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

The Engine itself returns RefreshInProgress in the same situation.

Evidence

schedule.rs:79-82 'self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok()'

Impact

A wasted back-to-back download.

Recommendation

Document this, or drain the trigger after each refresh.

Remediation: Fixed (package rust-dss)

After each refresh the task drains the one-slot trigger (while requests.try_recv().is_ok() {}), so a request made while a refresh runs is served by that refresh (as the engine itself would refuse a second one) and no back-to-back download follows; documented on refresh_now/request_refresh. Test requests_during_a_refresh_are_coalesced uses a 2 s blocked refresh and asserts a single outcome.

Files: rust/dss/src/schedule.rs, rust/dss/tests/scheduler.rs

Test: cargo test -p dss --all-features --test scheduler requests_during_a_refresh_are_coalesced

Verification

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Info · confidence 0.95

Confirmed by reading and by a live reproduction.

Code path (rust/dss/src/schedule.rs): the trigger is mpsc::channel::<()>(1) (line 44). The task loop is select! { ticker.tick(), requests.recv() } (lines 55-58) followed by spawn_blocking(move || e.refresh_trusted_lists()).await (line 60). While that await is pending the task is not at recv(), so the one-slot buffer is empty and refresh_now() (self.trigger.try_send(()).is_ok(), line 81) succeeds. When the refresh finishes the loop goes back to select!, requests.recv() resolves at once with the buffered (), and refresh_trusted_lists() runs a second full refresh — its refreshing flag was already reset by the Reset drop guard (engine.rs:275-287), so it does not return RefreshInProgress. ticker.reset() at line 69 only prevents a doubled *scheduled* tick; it does not drain the trigger channel. The doc comment at line 79 ("Returns false if one is already pending") is accurate only for a queued-not-started trigger, not for a running refresh.

Reproduction (scratchpad program at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/f058/src/main.rs, hanging LOTL server with response_timeout_ms=2000, period 3600 s, refresh_on_start=false). Output: refresh_now #1 -> true engine says refresh_in_progress=true engine.refresh_trusted_lists() direct -> Some(RefreshInProgress) refresh_now #2 (during running refresh) -> true refresh_now #3 (during running refresh) -> false [2.01s] outcome #1: ok=true [4.02s] outcome #2: ok=true total outcomes after one trigger during a running refresh: 2 So one refresh_now() during a running refresh produced a second full back-to-back refresh, exactly as the finding states, while the Engine itself refused with RefreshInProgress at the same moment.

Mitigating context (keeps this at info): dss-server's POST /tl/refresh (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:213-227) first checks trusted_list_status().refresh_in_progress and answers 409 REFRESH_IN_PROGRESS before calling scheduler.refresh_now(), so the shipped HTTP path only hits this in a narrow check-then-trigger race. The behaviour is reachable for any direct library user of RefreshScheduler::refresh_now(), and neither docs/DECISIONS.md:373-375 nor the doc comment documents it. Impact is a wasted extra download, no correctness issue; recommendation (document, or drain the trigger / check refresh_in_progress after each refresh) stands.

confirmedReproducecalibrated severity: Info · confidence 0.8

Mechanism confirmed from the code. The composite action .github/actions/setup/action.yml declares three actions/cache steps: GraalVM (lines 13-17, key graalvm-ce-25.4.4.1.1-${{ inputs.platform }}), Maven (lines 41-46, key maven-<platform>-<hash> with restore-keys), Cargo (lines 48-55). It is used only by .github/workflows/ci.yml (build job line 75, online job line 141), whose triggers are exactly release: types: [published] and workflow_dispatch (ci.yml:21-29); the header comment (lines 6-8) and docs/DECISIONS.md:479 ("Pushes and pull requests run nothing") confirm nothing ever runs on push to main. A release event runs on refs/tags/<tag>; GitHub Actions cache isolation lets a run restore only caches created on its own ref or on the default branch, so a cache saved during the v1.0.0 release run cannot be restored by the v1.0.1 release run. Thus caches saved by release runs are indeed never reusable by later releases, as the finding says.

Two corrections to the stated impact: (1) "Every release starts cold" is slightly overstated. A manual gh workflow run ci.yml (README.md:189-190) runs on the chosen ref, by default main, and its caches are default-branch-scoped and therefore restorable by subsequent release runs (if not evicted after 7 days unused). So the cold start is the common case, not a guarantee. (2) The impact is minor: docs/DECISIONS.md:494-496 states a run "takes about 25 minutes per platform, mostly the two native-image builds", which none of these caches cover; the caches save only the GraalVM tarball download, the Maven repository and the Cargo registry, a few minutes at most. The recommendation (populate caches from the default branch, e.g. a cheap push-triggered job that only runs the setup action) is sound but is at odds with the documented cost decision of running nothing on pushes, so it is a reasonable trade-off to leave as is. Real, but info-level.

Recommendations

Prioritised units of work; each links the findings it closes.

P0 · fix before any release

Put an egress policy with size and time bounds in front of every outbound fetch

effort: medium

In DssEngine.certificateVerifier()/withTimeouts() wrap the CRL, OCSP, AIA, TSA and TL data loaders in one DataLoader decorator that allows only http/https, rejects loopback, link-local and private ranges by default (config http.allowed_hosts, http.allow_private_networks), disables or re-validates redirects, caps bytes per fetch (e.g. http.max_response_bytes, ~64 MB for TLs, ~1 MB for TSA) by checking Content-Length and counting while streaming, and enforces a whole-transfer deadline per operation. Call DefaultAIASource.setAcceptedProtocols(HTTP, HTTPS) and setLdapTrustedHostnames(empty). Add a cross-call CRL/OCSP cache. Set SecureRandomNonceSource on both OnlineOCSPSource and OnlineTSPSource and a WARN or exception alert on invalid OCSP update time. Explicitly set a SignaturePolicyProvider with no loader and pin it with a FakeHttp zero-hits test. F-122 F-124 F-127 F-119 F-120 F-162 F-163 F-065 F-066 F-072 F-183 F-062 F-041 F-042 F-077 F-173 F-175

Remediation

What was changed after the audit, by which work package, and what remains open.

The remediation ran on 2026-11-09, after the audit, on the same working tree. Nothing was committed: every change is an uncommitted edit on top of the maintainer's own uncommitted work, which was backed up first and checked line by line at the end (see "Maintainer edits" below).

How the work was organised. The 228 confirmed findings were grouped into 12 work packages with disjoint file ownership, so that several agents could edit one working tree at the same time without touching the same files. Packages ran in three waves: Java first (trusted lists, signing, visible signatures, the C API, then the engine core, which depends on the other four), then the Rust crates, scripts and CI (the CLI and the HTTP sidecar after the dss crate they build on), then documentation, the PHP client and a Java test sweep. Each package agent received its findings with the verifiers' notes, the audit's grouped recommendations, and the handoffs, API changes and decisions recorded by the packages that ran before it; what it could not change in its own files it handed off to the owning package. Handoffs that arrived after a package had finished were applied in later fix-up rounds (13 later review and fix-up rounds in all).

Independent review. Every package was then reviewed by a separate agent that had not written the fixes: it read the diff, re-checked each finding at its cited location, ran the tests the implementer named and the module suite, and reported must-fix issues (a finding reported fixed but not fixed, a security weakening, a broken test, an unrecorded contract change) apart from improvements. A fix-up agent resolved the must-fix issues and, in a second pass, the improvements too. The reviewers also confirmed, line by line, that the maintainer's pre-existing edits survived in substance in the files the packages rewrote.

Verification. After the last round the native library was rebuilt from the final Java sources and a separate agent ran every suite and check on this machine (macOS 27.2, GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1, Rust 1.99.1): the offline JVM suite (300 tests), the native JUnit image (297 tests, 291 passed, 6 skipped by design), the C smoke test, Rust format, lints, tests, docs and cargo deny, the offline Rust script, the script and repository-rule tests, the package script with its own smoke checks (including the packaged keystore lookup), the PHP suite (35 tests), the OpenAPI parse and the Markdown link checks. Every functional check passed in the first round, so no verification fix-up was needed. shellcheck and reuse are not installed locally and were skipped (CI runs them); the repository-rule check reports only audit.html itself, which carries no licence header. The table under "Checks run after the fixes" lists each check with its command and result.

Reading the status. *Fixed* means the defect is removed and a regression test covers it. *Partial* means the behaviour improved but a part of the finding remains, stated in the note (most often infrastructure that does not exist in this repository, or a change the maintainer must decide). *Handed off* means the fix belongs to another package and the handoff was applied there. *Skipped* means the finding was re-checked and not fixed on purpose, with the reason: usually a recorded design decision in docs/DECISIONS.md that the finding did not show to be unsafe, or a choice that is the maintainer's to make (licensing, repository settings). The counts: 204 fixed, 19 partial, 0 handed off, 5 skipped of 228 confirmed findings.

Findings not fully fixed

Partially fixed (19)

  • F-014 Low Trusted-list cache files are truncated and rewritten in place (DSS FileCacheDataLoader, no temp+rename); an interrupted write leaves that list unusable until the next online refresh, and dss-server's shutdown waits for a running refresh with no deadline
    Cache writes are atomic (temp + fsync + rename), so SIGKILL or a full disk cannot leave a torn list in the cache; a garbage cache file is now a per-list download error, not a crash of the load. Not in this package: dss-server's shutdown deadline (rust-server) and DssJsonApi.init closing the previous engine only after creating the new one (java-engine). Shared cache_dir: see F-212.
  • F-035 Low README's unqualified PDF/A-2 claim: DeviceRGB appearance on a PDF whose only output intent is non-RGB (mirrors DSS, but without DSS's warning); no conformance test
    AwtFreeSignatureDrawer now checks the PDF's output intents in init(): when there are intents but none has an /N 3 destination profile (a CMYK print profile only), the appearance stream's resources get /ColorSpace << /DefaultRGB [/ICCBased <our sRGB profile, N 3, Alternate DeviceRGB>] >>, which ISO 19005-2 6.2.4.3 accepts for DeviceRGB content and images; PDFs without an intent still get the sRGB intent, PDFs with an RGB intent are untouched (bytes of the fixtures unchanged). Remaining: no veraPDF/preflight conformance check is run (no such dependency offline), and README's PDF/A claim must be qualified (docs handoff).
  • F-057 Low RefreshScheduler::stop drops the in-flight outcome and leaves an Arc<Engine> clone alive, so dss-server's shutdown does not wait for a scheduled refresh
    AppState::shutdown is now async: it subscribes to the scheduler's outcomes, drops the handle instead of calling stop() (abort), awaits the outcome channel until it closes (the schedule ends after the refresh in flight, whose outcome is still published and logged), then drops the engine on the blocking pool. main.rs awaits it after the accept loop has drained. Partial: no automated test holds a refresh in flight at SIGTERM (a closed-port refresh ends in milliseconds); the drop semantics relied on are the ones the verifier reproduced in rust/dss. After review: Documented on RefreshScheduler (struct docs and stop()): stop() aborts at once and the in-flight refresh's outcome is not published; dropping the handle lets the refresh in flight finish, publishes its outcome to subscribers taken before, then the schedule ends and the outcome channel closes. The reviewer's concern that the watch sender dies with the task does not hold: dropping the tokio JoinHandle detaches the task, which still owns the sender until its loop breaks on the closed trigger channel. New test dropping_the_handle_publishes_the_refresh_in_flight_then_ends proves it (blocked refresh, drop(scheduler), outcome received, channel closes within 2 periods, Arc::strong_count(engine) back to 1), which is exactly the sequence dss-server's AppState::shutdown relies on. After review: tl_refresh's no-scheduler path now captures Arc::downgrade(&state) plus the Arc<Engine> (upgrade only to clear direct_refresh), the connection task drops its pinned connection (and the router clone holding the state) before close_rx and the slot, and the None branch of Arc::into_inner says 'the state is still in use (the engine is starting, or a refresh is running): not waiting for it'. Still partial for the original reason: no automated test holds a refresh in flight at SIGTERM (a closed-port refresh ends in milliseconds). After review: Unchanged code: AppState::shutdown keeps dropping the scheduler handle (not stop()) and awaiting the outcome channel, which rust-dss has now documented as the semantics (the schedule ends after the refresh in flight, whose outcome is still published). Still partial for the same reason as before: no automated test holds a refresh in flight at SIGTERM.
  • F-075 Low CLI exit-status contract is documented only in main.rs module doc and docs/DECISIONS.md, not in README or --help
    --help now ends with an 'Exit status:' block (clap after_help) covering 0/1/2 per command, the validate-batch rule and closed-pipe behaviour. The module doc also points to it. The README section belongs to the docs package (see docs_updates).
  • F-081 Low POST /tl/refresh shares the single API token, has no cooldown beyond the one-at-a-time guard, and logs no caller
    The caller of POST /tl/refresh is logged ('online trusted-list refresh requested by <peer>'): the accept loop inserts ConnectInfo(peer) into every request, read by the handler as Option<Extension<ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>>>. No rate limit and no admin token: with request_refresh() a request made while a refresh runs is coalesced into it and the engine serialises refreshes, so the refresh rate is bounded by the refresh duration; documented in server.md ('who asked for a refresh' is logged). A separate admin token was not added (one client, one token, by design in DECISIONS.md).
  • F-082 Low Tokenless dss-server has no Origin/Host check: cross-site form POSTs from any web page reach /validate, /extend, /sign/* and /tl/refresh
    Without a token, any request carrying an Origin header (browsers add it to every cross-site POST and fetch) is refused 403 FORBIDDEN by the authorize middleware; with a token, the token decides. The Host check was not added: the sidecar cannot know its legitimate Host names (Compose service names, proxies), so a Host allow-list would break documented deployments. server.md recommends the token wherever a browser can reach the server.
  • F-112 Low Release assets carry only same-pipeline .sha256 files; the loose oj-keystore.p12 asset has no checksum, signature, provenance attestation or SBOM
    release-assets writes SHA256SUMS over every asset (packages, seed cache, the loose oj-keystore.p12, source archives) and runs actions/attest-build-provenance v4.2.2 (SHA-pinned) with subject-checksums, giving Sigstore-signed SLSA provenance; CycloneDX SBOMs ship inside every package (F-115). Remaining: GitHub only offers attestations to private repositories on Enterprise Cloud, so the attest step is conditioned on a public repository and does nothing while codingducksrl/dss-rust is private.
  • F-114 Low Maven dependencies/plugins are version-pinned but never hash- or PGP-verified; Maven cache restored by key prefix
    java/.mvn/maven.config sets --strict-checksums for every mvnw run (a checksum mismatch or missing checksum now fails the download); the Maven cache key includes it; tag (release) builds restore ~/.m2 only on an exact key hit (setup action input release: true removes restore-keys). Remaining: no PGP signature verification and no dependency lockfile (checksums come from the same repository, so this protects transport integrity only).
  • F-122 Low Release tarballs and Rust binaries are not reproducible (unsorted tar with real mtimes/owners, $HOME/.cargo paths in dss-cli/dss-server, unpinned apt packages); no reproducibility goal is documented, and the fix also needs the native-image output addressed
    Packages are now reproducible from the same inputs: new scripts/ci/deterministic-tar.sh (sorted entries, numeric owner 0:0 without names, normalised permissions, every mtime = SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, gzip -n, no macOS xattrs/AppleDouble), package.sh defaults SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH to the commit time and builds dss-cli/dss-server with --remap-path-prefix for CARGO_HOME and the repository (via CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS). Remaining: apt packages on the runners are not version-pinned, and native-image's own output was not examined for determinism; no published reproducibility goal (docs handoff).
  • F-124 Low macOS release binaries are only linker ad-hoc signed, not notarized, and the quarantine workaround is undocumented
    Classified by the orchestrator as partial: the signing and notarization step needs an Apple Developer ID certificate and notarytool credentials that do not exist in this repository or its CI; the quarantine workaround is documented in README.md. Implementer note: Signing and notarizing needs an Apple Developer ID certificate and notarytool credentials, which do not exist in this repository or CI. Documentation of the quarantine workaround is in README.md (docs package): handed off.
  • F-141 Low The copy-into-your-app PHP client (DssClient.php, DssException.php) is LGPL-2.1-or-later although it contains no DSS code
    Relicensing the copyright holder's files (to MIT or Apache) is a licensing choice for the maintainer, not a code defect. docs/DECISIONS.md (licensing review, 2026-11-06) records 'The licence stays LGPL-2.1-or-later'. The verifier rated it low, adoption friction only. The LGPL header is kept on all files, new ones included, and composer.json declares LGPL-2.1-or-later. If the maintainer decides to relicense, the change is to the SPDX lines of php/*.php, php/tests/*.php and php/phpunit.xml, the composer.json 'license' field, and a DECISIONS.md note. After review: php handoff. DECISIONS records that the copy-in PHP client stays LGPL-2.1-or-later, and that whether to offer it under a more permissive licence is left to the maintainer. The underlying decision is still open.
  • F-171 Low ConcurrentRefreshTest serves identical trust in every refresh, so it cannot detect stale or mixed trust pools
    ConcurrentRefreshTest now alternates the DE list between listing OTHER_CA and no CA, so consecutive refreshes publish different pools (3 and 2 anchors, asserted per refresh) while the fixtures (all under the IT list) must keep validating TOTAL_PASSED; validator threads also sample trusted_certificates and fail on any value other than 2 or 3. A mixed pool cannot be told apart from a stale one by verdict with the available fixtures, so this detects empty/half-built and foreign pools, not every mix.
  • F-173 Low Commit messages are uninformative ('Phase 6' x4, 'Added signing' x2) on large multi-thousand-line commits; no tags yet because no release has been cut (tag-driven release process documented in docs/DECISIONS.md:479-491)
    Existing commit messages cannot be fixed without rewriting history, and committing is forbidden. CONTRIBUTING.md now sets the convention (one topic per commit, imperative message saying what and why, finding/issue reference) and the release rule (push a v<semver> tag; move CHANGELOG 'Unreleased' under the version). Tags are already the designed release mechanism (DECISIONS 'Release gates').
  • F-203 Low Rust types allow invalid states that are only rejected at run time (DetachedContent path/base64, Level::B for extend)
    DetachedContent is now an enum File { name, path } | Bytes { name, content: Vec<u8> } (untagged serde, bytes travel as base64, Debug prints the byte count): exactly one source by construction, and bytes are bytes like image. Constructors file() (unchanged signature) and bytes(); no external code used the old fields. A dedicated ExtendLevel was not introduced: ExtendOptions.level: Level is built by dss-cli (main.rs:659-664) and changing the type breaks it; documented on Level::B and ExtendOptions::level instead, handoff recorded.
  • F-207 Low OCSP requests carry no nonce and out-of-window responses are accepted silently (this matches DSS upstream and demo defaults, not a deviation); a replayed stale 'good' response is accepted by an on-path attacker over plain-HTTP OCSP
    OnlineOCSPSource now gets setNonceSource(new SecureRandomNonceSource()) (responses bound to the request; a responder ignoring nonces only warns, as DSS does) and setAlertOnInvalidUpdateTime(LogOnStatusAlert(WARN)) so an out-of-window response is logged instead of accepted silently. Not an exception alert: DSS's revocation loading strategy would turn a responder/host clock skew into an exception path with no OCSP responder in the test PKI to prove it safe. Not directly tested (no OCSP responder in the fixture PKI; the test PKI cannot be regenerated without invalidating the committed fixtures).
  • F-219 Medium Timestamp tokens from the configured TSA are embedded without trust/EKU/algorithm/genTime checks: a self-signed rogue TSA yields T/LT/LTA documents that validate TOTAL_PASSED with the timestamp INDETERMINATE
    New CheckedTspSource wraps the OnlineTSPSource for every extend/sign call (built per call with the verifier's trusted sources). Before DSS writes a token it refuses: unparsable token or imprint not over the digest sent; no certificate in the token that verifies the signature; TSA certificate not valid at genTime or without id-kp-timeStamping EKU; MD2/MD5/SHA-1 signature or RSA < 2048 bits; genTime further than tsa.max_clock_skew_ms (default 300,000) from the host clock; and, with tsa.require_trusted (default true), a certificate that does not chain (through the token's certificates and the anchors) to the trusted lists or extra_trusted_certificates. The trust check is skipped with a warning when the engine has no trust anchors at all, keeping the recorded decision that T-level signing needs no trusted lists. All refusals and TSA transport/HTTP errors are the new code TSA_FAILED. Per-timestamp verdicts are now in the result (F-009). After review: Option (b) taken: behaviour unchanged (the no-anchor bypass keeps the recorded 'T-level signing needs no trusted lists' decision), but it is now stated precisely in the CheckedTspSource Javadoc and pinned by a test: an engine with require_trusted_lists:true and tsa.require_trusted:true whose cache is empty refuses to extend (TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED, since extend goes through trustSnapshot()) but signs at cms-T through prepare/complete with the rogue TSA's token embedded unchecked; after refreshTrustedListsOnline() the same engine refuses the same TSA with TSA_FAILED 'does not chain to a trusted certificate' (EngineHardeningTest.tokensFromAnUntrustedTsaAreRefused). Note the reviewer's premise is narrower than stated: only signing at B/T (trustedLists.current()) is affected, not extend. Option (a) (an 'explicit require_trusted' flag that refuses with TSA_FAILED when there are no anchors) was not done: it is a contract change touching EngineConfig (java-trust's file) and needs a docs decision; the README/TSA_FAILED wording is left to docs (docs_updates in notes).
  • F-232 Low Engine Drop with queued jobs or a running refresh is untested; Error::Closed/NoResult/Protocol never produced in tests (check_ok/decode have no unit tests)
    Added drop_with_calls_in_flight_completes_them (last Arc dropped while 8 validations are queued on 2 workers: all Ok, drop completes within 60 s) and drop_during_a_blocked_refresh_waits_for_it (main handle dropped while a refresh is stuck on a never-answering server; the engine is torn down right after the refresh returns, promptly). Note: by construction (&self methods) Engine::drop can never run while a call is in flight, so the Java-side race (F-042) is unreachable from Rust; the tests cover the shutdown ordering that follows in-flight work. check_ok/decode on malformed results are unit-tested (Protocol for not-JSON, ok:false without error, missing fields; the library error wins over a wrong shape). Error::Closed is only produced by a panicked/absent thread and cannot be triggered offline.
  • F-248 Medium PAdES validation time grows super-linearly (~quadratically) with the number of signature revisions because DSS re-copies and re-parses each revision prefix twice; the engine and server add no signature-count cap, per-call deadline or queue admission control
    New DocumentLimits pre-check (one PDFBox parse before DSS) refuses a PDF with more signature revisions (PDDocument.getSignatureDictionaries) than limits.max_pdf_signatures (default 100) for validate, extend, prepare and complete, with the operation's failure code and a message naming the limit. No cooperative per-call deadline: DSS's validation has no cancellation point, so a deadline would need the Rust/server layer (handoff noted for rust-dss as a note only).
  • F-262 Low B→LT/LTA extension (and LT/LTA signing) spends the TSA timestamp / external signature before DSS refuses for missing revocation data; T→LT-only refusal is documented, B→LT ordering is not
    DssEngine.assertExtensionPossible runs before extendDocument: with revocation offline and a target of LT/LTA, when any signature is below LT it runs DSS's own LT checks (PAdESSignatureRequirementsChecker.assertCertificateChainValidForLTLevel and PDFDocumentAnalyzer.getValidationData with CompleteValidationContextExecutor) on the document's own revocation data and refuses with EXTENSION_FAILED ('Revocation data is missing ... revocation is "offline", so the data cannot be fetched; the timestamp the extension needs was not requested') before any TSA call. Not done: the same pre-check for LT/LTA signing (the new signature's chain can legitimately find its CRL in the PDF's DSS dictionary, so a static refusal would be wrong) and the online-but-down revocation source case (needs a fetch, which is the cost being avoided).

Not fixed (5)

  • F-019 Low README validation example shows "sub_indication": null, but Json.write omits null keys so the key is absent in real output
    Not a defect in the tree any more: README's example now comments sub_indication as present only when not TOTAL_PASSED and states 'A key with no value is left out rather than set to null, in this result and every other one'; Json.write's behaviour is deliberate and tested. Remaining: docs/openapi.yaml declares these fields as [string, 'null'] (misleading, not wrong) — docs handoff recorded.
  • F-030 Low For CAdES in "cms" mode, prepare's signing_time is not what the signature claims and complete neither requires nor checks it, contrary to README and DECISIONS
    Classified by the orchestrator as skipped (kept by decision): the implementer re-checked the claim and kept the behaviour, the reviewer confirmed the reason holds, and the documentation now states it. Implementer note: Re-checked: for CAdES in cms mode the claimed time is the signer's signing-time attribute and complete neither requires nor compares the options' signing_time (it is not part of the content digest). Comparing within a tolerance would be arbitrary (signers set it when they sign, minutes after prepare), so the behaviour is kept and documented; what changed in code is that the certificate validity is now checked at the attribute's time (F-025) and the attribute must have exactly one value (F-026). Documentation text handed to docs (README sign section and DECISIONS) and rust-dss (types.rs comment on PreparedSignature.signing_time).
  • F-131 Low JAXB runtime 3.0.2 / jakarta.xml.bind-api 3.0.1 (last released Jul 2021) inherited from DSS's Java 8 pin; project targets Java 21 and records no accepted-risk decision
    Kept DSS 6.5.1's JAXB pin (jaxb-runtime 3.0.2, jakarta.xml.bind-api 3.0.1). Overriding to 4.x would change the classes compiled into the image while the reachability metadata is recorded exactly for JAXB 3.0.2 (docs/DECISIONS.md, reflection metadata 'exact'), and DSS 6.5.1 is built and tested against 3.0.x. Recorded as an accepted risk (decisions), with osv-scanner now watching these transitive versions weekly so a published advisory fails the security workflow.
  • F-199 Low Rust result fields sub_indication, qualification, level, packaging and mode are String although the library emits closed DSS enum values and the crate already types Indication
    Typing sub_indication/qualification/mode/packaging as enums changes the field types, and dss-cli reads them as strings (r.mode == "snapshot", r.mode.as_str(), signed.packaging.to_lowercase(), s.qualification.as_deref()), so the change would break a crate I do not own and the workspace with it. The value sets are now documented on each field instead. Recommend doing it in one coordinated change with rust-cli (handoff recorded with the exact sites); level/format should stay String (DSS SignatureLevel has dozens of variants that change between DSS versions).
  • F-275 Low README says PAdES level T at signing adds a document timestamp for both modes; in signature_value mode DSS puts a signature-time-stamp inside the new CMS and adds no DocTimeStamp
    Classified by the orchestrator as skipped (kept by decision): the implementer re-checked the claim and kept the behaviour, the reviewer confirmed the reason holds, and the documentation now states it. Implementer note: Re-checked and kept: in signature_value mode PAdESService puts a signature-time-stamp inside the new CMS and adds no DocTimeStamp at T; in cms mode PAdESWithExternalCMSService extends the document with a DocTimeStamp that also covers the PDF's other signatures. Aligning signature_value mode (sign at B, then extend to T) would make it re-check the PDF's other signatures (F-274) and change existing output, so the modes stay as they are and the difference is documented (text in docs_updates for README and DECISIONS). The requested assertion on the timestamp kind was added as a test.

  • (1) Running python3 -I -m py_compile scripts/*.py as specified writes __pycache__ into the tree, because -I ignores PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX. What is done well

  • Strict trusted-list synchronisation with immutable publication ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy with accept_invalid_signature=false replaces DSS's AcceptAllStrategy (TrustedListManager.java:183-189), so a tampered cache or MITM cannot inject anchors without the OJ-rooted signature chain; the pool is published as an immutable copy under refreshLock through a volatile, status() never blocks on a refresh, and ConcurrentRefreshTest plus a probe of 389 validations across 5 re-inits found zero failures.
  • Snapshot deserialisation is defended in depth TlSnapshotFile.java:113-115 and 310-329 install an ObjectInputFilter with a class and package allow-list, depth, reference and array limits, certificates are re-parsed from DER, the header pins DSS version, settings and the OJ keystore digest, and TlSnapshotTest's canary proves a foreign class is refused before its readObject runs. DssFeature's serialization registrations mirror the allow-list exactly.
  • The FFI boundary catches every exception and uses one allocator Every @CEntryPoint in DssLib.java catches Throwable, nulls out-parameters before any work and copies the document inside the guarded call; results are encoded straight into UnmanagedMemory.malloc so dss_free is correct for strings and documents alike, apart from the OOM-path leak and NULL return in F-043/F-227. C probes with NULL, oversized, pre-init and post-shutdown inputs all returned structured errors, and an OOM at the document copy is an INTERNAL_ERROR with a usable isolate at -Xmx8m, 64m and 512m.
  • Sound Rust thread and ownership model Attached holds a raw pointer so it is !Send, Isolate's unsafe impl Send is justified in a comment, user threads never attach, and Engine::drop closes queues, joins workers and the refresh thread, then runs dss_shutdown and graal_tear_down_isolate on the control thread (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:428-442, 549-599). The GraalVM 25.4 first-isolate hang is worked around once per process with a documented reproduction (DECISIONS.md:358-366).
  • External signing binds the signer's output to this exact preparation complete recomputes the digest from the document and options and compares it with MessageDigest.isEqual (ExternalSigning.java:257); signature_value mode verifies the value over rebuilt data before signDocument (lines 147, 154); prepare is deterministic (whole-second UTC signing time, VisibleImageParameters.toString() as a SHA-256 fingerprint replacing DSS's identity-hash seed). Probes with wrong keys, shifted times, malformed ECDSA and PSS-for-PKCS1 values all ended as SIGNING_FAILED, and JVM and native digests matched byte for byte.
  • Image and text parsers survive malformed bytes PngDecoder bounds chunk lengths by the file, verifies CRCs, checks dimensions before allocating and bounds the inflater by declared size (a 50 MB zlib bomb for a 1x1 image decodes in 66 ms); 30,000 random PNG and 30,000 JPEG mutations produced no crash or hang. checkFont refuses most malformed fonts in the 45-font hostile corpus (truncations, missing tables, bad loca format, TTC collections, CFF outlines) with INVALID_ARGUMENT, the exceptions being the resource-cost cases in F-222 and F-259. checkGlyphs refuses CJK, U+0000, U+202E and 5000-character signer names at prepare so nothing fails only at complete; text goes through PDType0Font hex strings so no content-stream injection is possible.
  • XXE, entity expansion and signature-policy fetches are closed by the DSS wiring TL and report XML go through DSS's hardened factories (disallow-doctype-decl, external entities off, ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/SCHEMA empty); a DOCTYPE with a loopback external entity got 0 connections, billion-laughs was refused, a 200,000-level document was rejected by the depth cap, and external ds:Reference URIs have no resolver, although ds:Reference transforms in TL signatures are still evaluated (F-273). Five SPURI-bearing CAdES files (stalling listener, file:///etc/hosts, redirect) validated with zero requests on both JVM and native.
  • The sidecar's security basics are right Bearer token read from a file, trimmed, refused when empty and compared in constant time (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:298-300); the guard runs before any body is read; detached_contents[].path is refused with a test (lib.rs:384-393); every error path except axum's default 405 (F-091) yields the documented {ok:false,error:{code,message}} JSON; the Dss-Result header carries only server-generated keys with non-ASCII escaped; and openapi_document_matches_the_router asserts the auth status of every documented operation (tests/http.rs:466-504).
  • A genuinely offline, multi-layer test estate 152 JVM tests and the same suite as a native image (150 passed, 2 @DisabledInNativeImage, under Throw, Exit and Warn reporting modes and under it_IT.UTF-8), 44 Rust tests including the seeded synthetic snapshot cases, and a C smoke test with 80 concurrent validations on 4 threads all pass without network: synthetic LOTL and national TLs signed against a synthetic OJ keystore are served by FakeHttp, ports are ephemeral, and PlainDssParityTest plus the JVM-vs-native differential guard the native path.
  • Supply-chain pins that were independently verified All four GitHub Actions are pinned to commit SHAs that git ls-remote matched to their tags; install-graalvm.sh pins per-platform SHA-256 values that match GraalVM's published checksums; the Maven wrapper's distributionSha256Sum matches the real 3.10.0 zip; Rust is pinned to 1.99.1; the workflow token is contents: read except in release-assets, and the tag reaches shell only through env after regex validation. Release binaries carry only @executable_path rpaths.
  • Dependencies are current and clean DSS 6.5.1, BouncyCastle 1.86, PDFBox 3.0.8, HttpClient 5.6.5, xmlsec 3.0.6 and all 87 crates.io packages are at the newest release of their line, none yanked; an OSV batch over all 121 resolved coordinates and cargo deny check advisories (RustSec DB 2026-11-05) report nothing; Cargo.lock has no duplicate versions and axum is trimmed to http1, tokio and multipart.
  • Licensing and design governance beyond the project's age LICENSE is byte-identical to the FSF LGPL-2.1 text; all 25 non-DSS runtime jars have LICENSE and NOTICE collected into licenses/java/; collect-rust-licenses.py matches cargo tree exactly and fails closed when a crate lacks a licence file; the sRGB profile is generated in code and fixtures are synthetic. docs/DECISIONS.md (11,145 words) records every deviation from DSS defaults with its rationale, and trust/README.md documents the keystore's provenance, digest and update procedure.
  • Contract consistency across layers The 12 error codes are identical in README.md:534-536, DssError.Code and rust/dss/src/error.rs; the config_json/options_json keys and defaults in README, openapi.yaml, the Java allowOnly sets and the Rust structs match exactly (except tl_threads, F-049); the C function table, generated header and DssLib.java agree on all 11 functions; the README Rust snippet compiles; the OpenAPI document is embedded, version-stamped and served without a token.
  • Performance architecture that keeps the hot path cheap Trusted-list snapshots cut cold start from 6.5 s to 0.63 s; empty-cache start-up measured at 59 ms and 42 MB RSS; refreshes run on a dedicated thread so a 15 s refresh never occupies a validation worker; the server returns documents as raw bodies with the result JSON in a header, avoiding base64 inflation; the costliest DSS stage (visual page rendering) is disabled via setMaximalPagesAmountForVisualComparison(0).

Architecture and trust boundaries

Pieces. java/ holds the engine (engine/: DssEngine, TrustedListManager, ExternalSigning, EngineConfig, the hand-written Json layer and the allow-listed option parsers), the AWT-free visible-signature drawer (visible/), the C entry points (ffi/DssLib) and the Native Image feature (nativeimage/DssFeature). Every call crosses the C boundary as UTF-8 JSON strings plus pointer/length buffers; results are {ok, error:{code,message}} envelopes or a JSON-plus-document pair, all freed with one dss_free. rust/dss-sys binds the generated header; rust/dss owns the isolate on a control thread, attaches N worker threads once each and a dedicated refresh thread, and exposes typed and raw-JSON APIs plus an optional tokio RefreshScheduler; dss-cli and dss-server (axum, HTTP/1.1, multipart) are thin consumers. php/DssClient.php talks to the sidecar. Trust inputs live in trust/oj-keystore.p12 (the LOTL signing certificates), the cache directory (<cache_dir>/tl/*) and optional snapshot files.

Trust boundaries. Document submitters are untrusted and reach DSS through the host application or the sidecar's multipart boundary; the host application is trusted and controls config_json and options_json (including validation_time, detached_contents[].path, which the server refuses, and fonts and images for visible signatures). The sidecar network is semi-trusted: loopback by default, 0.0.0.0 in Docker, one optional bearer token for every endpoint, no TLS. TL hosts are authenticated only by XML signatures rooted in the OJ keystore (TLS verification is off by default); CRL/OCSP/AIA responders are reached at URLs chosen by the submitted document; the TSA is operator-configured. Whoever can write cache_dir, the snapshot file or the keystore controls trust. The external signer never sees more than a digest or signed attributes, and no private key enters the engine.

Validation flow. The host (or dss-server after buffering the multipart body) passes the document bytes and options to dss_validate; InputNormalizer sniffs and strips base64/PEM and nested .p7m layers; DssEngine.validateLevel builds a DSS validator with the published, immutable TrustedListsCertificateSource snapshot, DSS's default constraint.xml policy and, by default, online CRL/OCSP/AIA loaders; ValidationResult.summarize flattens the simple report into signatures[] (indication, sub-indication, qualification, errors, warnings, nested[]) and attaches the requested XML reports. The Rust layer decodes the JSON into typed results; the server maps error codes to HTTP statuses in one table.

Signing flow. dss_sign_prepare builds the PAdES or CAdES signed attributes for the given options (signing time truncated to whole seconds, UTC /M, deterministic appearance fingerprint as DSS's encryption seed), returns the digest and data_to_sign; the external signer produces a CMS (cms mode) or a bare signature value (signature_value mode); dss_sign_complete recomputes the digest from the document and the same options, compares it with MessageDigest.isEqual, checks the signer's attributes and signature, then lets DSS embed it and, for T/LT/LTA, contact the TSA and revocation sources. Extension (dss_extend) follows the same TSA and revocation path. Trusted-list refreshes run on their own thread, download through a FileCacheDataLoader into the same cache the offline loader reads, and publish a new immutable snapshot under a lock.

Method and coverage

The audit ran as an orchestrated workflow of independent subagents over commit 7e697c9. Each audit dimension had its own finder with a brief naming the files to read and the risks to look for; the model and reasoning effort were chosen per dimension. Raw findings were merged (same root cause = one finding) and every merged finding was then handed to independent verifiers who were told to refute it: medium and higher findings got three lenses (reproduce, impact, severity calibration) and survived only if at least two did not refute; low and info findings got the reproduce lens alone. A finding with exactly one supporting vote out of three is listed as plausible, not confirmed. After each round a completeness critic listed what was not examined and proposed gap probes for the next round, together with a re-run of the deep dimensions that was told what had already been found. Test suites, lints and metrics were collected on this machine in parallel. A synthesis step wrote the summary, scorecard and recommendations from the confirmed findings only.

Process notes

  • The first run hit the account usage limit during round 2 verification. 17 findings (F-265, F-267, F-269 to F-283) had their missing verification lenses re-run in a follow-up workflow with the same prompts and models; the synthesis was produced in a second follow-up.
  • Round 3 was cut short by the same limit: 9 of its 10 deep re-probe finders (all but build-ci-supply-chain) and the round 2 completeness critic did not run, so no gap probes were generated for round 3. The deep dimensions therefore had two rounds instead of three.
  • The synthesis was checked mechanically (every cited finding id exists and is not refuted; every confirmed high and medium finding is covered by a recommendation; scorecard areas and counts) and by an independent reviewer agent, which returned "revise" with 26 issues (19 must-fix). A revision pass then applied the fixes. The final mechanical checks were clean.
  • The repository changed after the audit: its git history was re-initialised on 2026-11-06 at 23:35 (HEAD is now bbc99be "Init"; commit 7e697c9 no longer exists in the history), and as of 2026-11-09 thirteen tracked files carry uncommitted edits (126 insertions, 90 deletions): README.md, docker/dss-server/Dockerfile, docs/DECISIONS.md, docs/native-library.md, docs/openapi.yaml, docs/reflection-audit.md, docs/server.md, java/pom.xml, java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/RuntimeDefaults.java, rust/Cargo.toml, rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs, scripts/run-agent.sh and testdata/fixtures/README.md, mostly repository-URL and documentation updates. File and line references in this report refer to the tree as it was audited.

Not covered

  • Round 3 was cut short by the account usage limit: 9 of its 10 deep re-probe finders (all but build-ci-supply-chain) and the round-2 completeness critic did not run, so no round-3 gap probes exist and the nine deep dimensions other than build/CI (Java security, Java correctness, signing, visible signatures, FFI, Rust core, server security, server correctness, threat model) had two rounds instead of three. The remaining 11 dimensions (Rust CLI, PHP client, dependencies, licensing, two documentation lenses, tests, repository hygiene, configuration/operations, performance, API design) had a single finder round, supplemented only where a round-2 gap probe touched them.
  • Round 2 verification was interrupted by the same limit; 17 late findings, 14 of which are now confirmed (F-265, F-267, F-269 to F-278, F-280, F-282) and 3 refuted, had their missing verification lenses re-run in a follow-up workflow with the same prompts and models, and the synthesis was produced in a second follow-up.
  • Nothing online was exercised: the real EU LOTL and national trusted lists, real TSA, OCSP and CRL responders, OnlineTrustedListTest, the -Pintegration profile, scripts/diff-vs-jvm.sh, scripts/seed-tl-cache.sh and every --online flag were off limits. Behaviour against the real lists (pivot handling, sunset dates, cache-load cost and memory with real list sizes, OJ rotation) is unassessed; all trusted-list findings rest on synthetic lists served by FakeHttp or on code reading.
  • Linux was never tested: no Linux native library or release package exists on this host, so the .so, the glibc 2.34 floor, the Docker image build, its HEALTHCHECK and Native Image heap behaviour under cgroup limits were not run. macOS 14 (the documented floor) was never tested either; the audit ran on macOS 27.2 arm64 only.
  • Native-image behaviour of several findings was reasoned rather than observed: F-032, F-222, F-259 and F-224 were reproduced on the JVM, and crafted fonts were also run through the native dss-cli, but the process-abort path for F-032/F-222/F-259/F-224 was not observed natively (F-186 was reproduced through the native library with a C probe); the native JUnit image was built once and passed (150 of 152) but the shared library itself was not rebuilt, so the prebuilt build/native/macos-aarch64/libdssnative.dylib of 2026-11-06 was used throughout.
  • The PHP client was never run against a live dss-server (only a harness with Laravel Http::fake and a stub php -S server), no Laravel exists in CI, and Octane/FrankenPHP concurrency was not examined.
  • Several claims were not demonstrated end to end: no proof-of-concept certificate with a file:// or internal AIA URL was run against the engine (F-001 and F-002 rest on DSS source reading plus the SPURI probe); the two-process torn-cache race (F-212) was not run; the zlib-ng byte difference (F-031) is inferred from dynamic libz linkage; the cwd keystore attack (F-064) was not shown with a forged LOTL; the scheduler-death-to-409 path (F-234) was established by code reading.
  • Algorithmic-cost coverage is partial: CMS inputs with thousands of certificates, hundreds of signers or CRLs beyond F-211, deeply nested object trees, and extend/sign cost on the adversarial PDFs were not generated or timed; all performance measurements are single-run on one Apple-silicon host.
  • Tooling absent on the machine: cargo-audit (cargo-deny covered RustSec), shellcheck and actionlint (shell and workflow lint skipped), PyYAML and yq (openapi.yaml parsed with Ruby's Psych instead), OpenAPI linters (redocly, spectral, openapi-spec-validator), veraPDF (no PDF/A conformance check), cloc (raw wc -l line counts). cargo deny check licenses fails only because no deny.toml exists, not from a concrete licence problem.
  • The CI workflow has never run on GitHub (per DECISIONS.md), so its real behaviour, the Linux-only steps, caching and the release-assets upload are unverified; round 3 could not re-check the action SHAs against their tags offline (round 1 did, via git ls-remote). GitHub repository settings (branch protection, whether the repo is public or private, signed-commit enforcement) and the trust status of the commit signatures (%G? reports G) were not examined.
  • Not exercised in signing: RSASSA-PSS and EdDSA keys in signature_value mode (no test keys), linearized PDFs (no qpdf or mutool), CAdES over the PDF edge corpus, TSA responses with GRANTED_WITH_MODS or policy mismatch, Digest/NTLM/SPNEGO challenges and proxies, real-viewer rendering of NoRotate widgets and EXIF-oriented JPEGs, and RTL or complex-script layout beyond glyph presence.
  • Bit-for-bit reproducibility of the native-image output, Maven 3.10's default checksum policy, whether github.com/codingduck/dss-native is public, whether esig/dss uses the tag 6.5.1, and the upstream licence header of the GraalVM SDK sources could not be checked offline. The licensing conclusions (LGPL §4 versus §6, GPLv2 §3) are an engineering reading, not legal advice.
  • Dynamic checks skipped by design: scripts/build-native.sh --with-tests, run-native-tests.sh as a CI step, diff-vs-jvm.sh and package.sh were not run by the checks runner; the metrics are approximations (Java class counts are file counts, unsafe/synchronized counts are line greps).

Measurements, all offline, with the release dss-cli and dss-server against the prebuilt libdssnative, a scratch cache and test-PKI-signed synthetic inputs in the scratchpad:

  • Empty-cache start-up: 59 ms, 42 MB RSS.
  • b-lta.pdf validation: 0.11 s, 99 MB RSS.
  • 37 MB attached CMS (made with openssl from the test PKI): 0.65 s, 390 MB RSS. Its 50 MB base64 form: 1.15 s, 616 MB RSS.
  • Heap sweeps on that CMS reproduced a process abort (rc=134, 'Reference processing and cleaners must handle all potential exceptions') at 128m, 144m and 176m.
  • dss-server with 2 workers: 12 concurrent 37 MB uploads raised RSS from 42 MB to 1.74 GB at peak, with 1.56 GB retained afterwards; vmmap showed 424 MB of empty malloc-large regions still resident.
  • A 194 KB 25 MP 16-bit PNG in /sign/prepare: 578 MB peak, 4 concurrent requests 1.42 GB, and OOM with --max-heap 256m.
  • A 256m-heap server running 6 concurrent 37 MB validations: 4 requests failed with OOM and the server survived on that run.
  • All test servers were killed afterwards. No repository files were modified and no network refresh was triggered.

threat-model round 1

Threat model. Assets: the trust pool (LOTL + national TLs, derived from trust/oj-keystore.p12 and the on-disk cache or a snapshot), validation verdicts, documents being signed or extended, the external signer's keys (never in-process), TSA credentials, the bearer token, the cache directory and snapshot files, the release packages. Actors and boundaries: (1) document submitters (end users of the host app) are untrusted and reach the engine through the host app and the sidecar; (2) the host application is trusted and controls options_json (validation_time, reports, unwrap_nested) and the config; (3) the sidecar network: other containers/hosts, trusted only if the optional token is set; (4) the EC (OJ keystore, LOTL), national TL hosts, TSA, CRL/OCSP/AIA responders: reached over HTTPS, but TL hosts without TLS verification by default, and revocation URLs chosen by the submitted document; (5) whoever writes cache_dir/tl, the snapshot file or the OJ keystore has full control of trust; (6) the release pipeline (GitHub Actions on release events, caches, release assets, Docker build context). Trust decisions reviewed: strict signature sync with accept_expired=true; TrustAll TLS for TL downloads; same directory for online and offline TL cache; unauthenticated snapshot import with header/CRC/settings checks; OJ keystore from the DSS demo, located relative to the executable or CWD; external CMS accepted after attribute and signature checks but with unsigned attributes trusted; sidecar with one optional token for all endpoints, no TLS, listening on 0.0.0.0 in Docker; online revocation with DSS's CommonsDataLoader. Residual gaps found: trust-list channel integrity/availability (eviction and cache poisoning, rollback, silent staleness), SSRF/file read via document-controlled URLs, unauthenticated sidecar in the shipped image, unverified external timestamp, no aggregate verdict for non-Rust clients, root-of-trust discoverability and update process, snapshot pinning, release artefact verification. Not found: a way for a document to force TOTAL_PASSED (the base64/PEM normaliser and the nested unwrapping only re-run the same validator with the same verifier; the only client-side lever is validation_time, which the trusted host controls). Files read in full: README.md, docs/DECISIONS.md, docs/native-library.md, docs/server.md, trust/README.md, engine/TrustedListManager.java, EngineConfig.java, TlSnapshotFile.java, DssEngine.java, ExternalSigning.java, SigningOptions.java, ValidationOptions.java, ValidationResult.java, InputNormalizer.java, DssJsonApi.java, rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs and main.rs, rust/dss/src/schedule.rs, parts of rust/dss/src/types.rs and engine.rs and rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs, php/DssClient.php, .github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/actions/setup/action.yml, scripts/package.sh, build-native.sh, ci/install-graalvm.sh, ci/set-version.sh, seed-tl-cache.sh, docker/dss-server/Dockerfile, parts of java/pom.xml, docs/openapi.yaml and TrustedListTest.java. DSS 6.5.1 behaviour was verified from the sources jars in ~/.m2 (extracted into the scratchpad): ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy, TrustedListCertificateSourceSynchronizer, TrustedListsCertificateSource, FileCacheDataLoader, CommonsDataLoader, OnlineCRLSource, OnlineOCSPSource, DefaultAIASource, TSLSequenceNumberErrorDetection, PAdESWithExternalCMSService, CAdESLevelBaselineT/PAdESLevelBaselineT, DefaultAdvancedSignature, and the default policy constraint.xml from dss-policy-jaxb. Commands run (all read-only): keytool -list on trust/oj-keystore.p12, shasum of the keystore (matches the README pin), git ls-files, greps. Nothing was built or executed from the project; no test suite was run and no network access occurred, so the good-then-bad refresh transition, the cache overwrite and the file:/ldap: fetch paths are established from code reading, not reproduced. Not assessed: DSS's validation policy internals and revocation freshness windows beyond the TL constraints quoted, the visible-signature parsers (PNG/TTF from caller input), Native Image reachability of JNDI (grep found no jndi metadata, so ldap: likely fails natively; untested), memory/DoS behaviour under large CRL responses (CommonsDataLoader has no size cap; not pursued), and the correctness of the Rust FFI layer, which other dimensions cover. Minor nits not reported as findings: cargo build in package.sh/ci.yml lacks --locked (mentioned in the cache finding); the constant-time token compare short-circuits on length, leaking only the token length.

threat-model round 2

THREAT MODEL. Assets: (1) the trust pool (OJ keystore → LOTL → national TLs → published TrustedListsCertificateSource; snapshots and the file cache are its persisted forms); (2) validation verdicts consumed by host applications; (3) documents being extended/signed and the external signer's key; (4) TSA credentials and TSA budget; (5) engine availability (CPU/heap of the single sidecar process). Actors and boundaries: document submitters (untrusted; cross the HTTP multipart boundary, then the C/JSON boundary into DSS); the host application (trusted, holds the bearer token, supplies options incl. validation_time/signing_time); the sidecar network (semi-trusted: no TLS, optional token); TL hosts/EC (authenticated only by XML signatures; TLS unauthenticated by default); CRL/OCSP/AIA responders (reached at document-controlled URLs, TLS verified when https, OCSP mostly http); the TSA (operator-configured, Basic auth); whoever writes cache_dir, the snapshot file or the OJ keystore (effectively root of trust); the release pipeline (ships the keystore and the library). Round 2 focused on interactions and unmeasured costs: adversarial-but-valid inputs, network-attacker effects on the refresh path, config combinations (countries, accept_expired+snapshot, nonce-less OCSP + default policy), and multi-process operation.

FILES READ (whole): README.md, docs/DECISIONS.md (all sections incl. TL sync, validation, sidecar, snapshots), docs/native-library.md, docs/server.md, trust/README.md, testdata/fixtures/README.md, java engine: DssEngine, EngineConfig, TrustedListManager, TlSnapshotFile, ExternalSigning, DssJsonApi, ValidationOptions, ValidationResult, SigningOptions, VisibleSignature; rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs and main.rs; scripts/seed-tl-cache.sh; build/diff/real-config.json. DSS 6.5.1 sources (from ~/.m2 source jars, extracted to the scratchpad): DefaultDocumentAnalyzer, SignaturePolicyProvider, NativeHTTPDataLoader(+Call), CommonsDataLoader, CommonsHttpClientResponseHandler, FileCacheDataLoader, DSSUtils.saveToFile, OnlineTSPSource, OnlineOCSPSource, TLValidatorTask, ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy, DocumentBuilderFactoryBuilder/SchemaFactoryBuilder, AbstractPDFSignatureService (revision loop), policy/constraint.xml. Compiled classes of dss-spi/validation/cades/pades/pdfbox/document/cms/tsl-validation/service were scanned (javap and constant-pool grep) to confirm no caller of getSignaturePolicyProvider.

WHAT RAN: release dss-cli against build/native/macos-aarch64/libdssnative.dylib, offline only (cache dir in the scratchpad, --allow-without-trusted-lists, --offline-revocation, test root via --trust): baseline validations of fixtures; a scripted loop signing content/document.pdf 400 times in signature_value mode (dss-cli sign prepare → openssl pkeyutl with the committed test RSA key → sign complete), saving PDFs at 1/10/25/50/100/150/200/300/400 signatures; timed validations of each with /usr/bin/time -l (results in the first finding). No network, no TL refresh, no repository writes.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE (not reported): the SPURI/NativeHTTPDataLoader fetch (dead default in 6.5.1); XML parser hardening; status() never blocks (reads volatile snapshot; DECISIONS 'Status never blocks' holds); same() short-circuits only on length, which leaks token length, not content (DECISIONS:856 'constant time' is acceptable); TSA credentials are scoped to host:port with protocol null (AuthScope in CommonsDataLoader:1359) so they would also be sent to http:// on the same host after a redirect+challenge, but only the TSA operator's own redirect can cause that; TSA requests carry no nonce, but replay needs an identical message imprint, so no finding; a nested/base64 path cannot forge a verdict (the inner envelope is genuinely signed). The OCSP finding's claim that the DSS demo webapp sets SecureRandomNonceSource is from memory of DSSBeanConfig, as the demo sources are not in the Maven cache; the rest of that finding is from DSS 6.5.1 code.

NOT ASSESSED: Linux, Docker image, the native JUnit image, anything online (real LOTL, real TSA/OCSP behaviour), the PHP client at runtime, extend/sign on the many-signature PDFs (same revision loop, expected at least as slow, not timed), CMS-side algorithmic costs (many certificates/countersignatures), and how the OOM from an oversized TL download propagates in the native image (F-186 suggests process abort; not reproduced).

The test metadata lists 22 it.codingduck.dssnative reflection entries, all test classes (OutcomeTest, SigningTest, TestPki and similar), plus TlSnapshotFile$CertificateDer and TlSnapshotTest$Canary with serializable only. CertificateDer is a production class, but DssFeature.registerTlSnapshotClasses registers it through TlSnapshotFile.OTHER_CLASSES and RuntimeSerialization.register, so it does not depend on the test metadata. Production code uses no Class.forName or ServiceLoader on its own types; its only resource lookups are version.properties and the default font. So no production class sits only in test metadata. F-165 is a latent hazard only.
  • Locale: no test sets or inspects a Locale; the tests call the Java engine directly, not DssLib.prologue(). Grep of production code for locale-sensitive String.format, toUpperCase and DateTimeFormatter finds only String.format("\\u%04x") in Json.java:329, which is locale-insensitive. The it_IT native run therefore shows no locale-dependent failure. It also shows that the Locale.US pin is not exercised by the run (the F-167 gap, already reported).

COULD NOT RUN OR ASSESS

  • The build-shared-library execution and the C smoke test (not asked for, and the rules forbid scripts/build-native.sh).
  • Linux native images.
  • The online and integration test groups, which the rules forbid.

No new finding of substance, so the findings list is empty.

gap-r1-doc-claims-and-shared-cache round 2

(1) Holds, with a wording gap. TlSnapshotTest compares two engines in one JVM: one loaded online and one started from the exported snapshot. The assertEquals on Json.write of validate().toMap() uses a fixed validation_time. It does not compare JVM against native. The suite runs in both modes, which is what DECISIONS.md means. ./mvnw -o -q test -Dtest=TlSnapshotTest passed (rc 0). (2) Holds by code reading: status() takes no lock and uses the copy. It does synchronize on the alerts list briefly; that list is not held during a refresh. I did not run the slow-TL timing demo. (3) The sentence is accurate only for input copy. smoke.c uses a 128 MB calloc document and -Xmx64m, and it asserts an OutOfMemoryError result for dss_validate and dss_extend, which fail at the input copy. It does not cover an OOM raised inside DSS, so the sentence 'a document or report that does not fit the heap' overstates it. That is already F-186. (4) See the finding above. (5) I read the FileCacheDataLoader source and the loader setup. I did not run two concurrent refreshes, so torn or missing lists are unconfirmed.
