F-255Mediumsecurityjava/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:255

PDF validation uses DSS's default policy unchanged, so annotations or form fields added after signing can still give TOTAL_PASSED with no modification warning in the summary

A FreeText or Stamp annotation, or an added or filled form field, appended as a post-signing incremental update yields TOTAL_PASSED with errors=[] and only qualification warnings. DSS's default policy keeps PdfAnnotationOverlap, PdfVisualDifference, AnnotationChanges, FormFillChanges and UndefinedChanges at WARN, and the engine installs no custom policy.

Details, evidence and verification

What happens

Tested on b-b.pdf and b-lta.pdf through the engine with synthetic trust. Plain DSS with visual comparison on also gave TOTAL_PASSED, because added annotations are subtracted before the screenshot comparison. This is worse than F-004, which at least carried a warning string.

Evidence

`a_annotation [pades_b-b.pdf] (+577 bytes) ... TOTAL_PASSED/- errors=[] warnings=[The authority info access is not present!, ...qualification]`; `b_formfield ... TOTAL_PASSED`; visual-on: `pades_b-lta.pdf__a_annotation.pdf TOTAL_PASSED/null warnings=[The authority info access is not present!]`; constraint.xml:62-63.

Impact

Anyone holding a signed PDF can overlay fake approval text, amounts or seals, and every consumer sees a clean TOTAL_PASSED.

Recommendation

Install a custom ValidationPolicy that raises these checks to FAIL (or make it configurable). Add a structured 'modified after signing' field derived from ModificationDetection. Document that TOTAL_PASSED does not mean the document is visually unchanged.

Verification

refutedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.65

REPRODUCTION (scratchpad program /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gsguglielmo-Programming-dss-rust/ce66e047-e979-43ad-b05a-45215722e195/scratchpad/repro/Repro.java, run against java/target classes + TestEngines synthetic trust, log in .../scratchpad/repro/stdout.log): appending a FreeText annotation to testdata/fixtures/pades/b-b.pdf and b-lta.pdf as a PDFBox incremental update gives TOTAL_PASSED/null errors=[] warnings=[The authority info access is not present!, The certificate is not qualified ...] (qualification warnings only), while the diagnostic data the engine returns on request records <ModificationDetection><ObjectModifications><AnnotationChange action="CREATION" type="Annot">/Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Kids 4 0 R /Annots 13 0 R</AnnotationChange>. Adding a text field gave TOTAL_PASSED plus "The document contains undefined object modifications after the signature revision!" (only because /NeedAppearances was touched). So the observable behaviour in the finding is real.

WHY IT IS REFUTED AS A DEFECT OF THIS REPOSITORY:

  1. Documented, deliberate decision. docs/DECISIONS.md:201: "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now." and DECISIONS.md:112-114: "PDF visual comparison is off ... Object-level modification detection between revisions stays on (it does not render)." The engine code matches: DssEngine.java:456-462 pdfObjFactory() only sets setMaximalPagesAmountForVisualComparison(0), and DssEngine.java:230-255 (validateLevel) installs no policy, so DSS's stock constraint.xml applies.
  2. The project's contract is parity with plain DSS, not stricter verdicts. README.md:22 "a differential test checks the native path against plain DSS on the JVM"; DECISIONS.md:422 "The reference is plain DSS, not the engine." The finding itself concedes plain DSS (even with visual comparison on) yields TOTAL_PASSED. A custom FAIL policy would make the engine diverge from the reference it is validated against; PAdES/ISO 32000-2 permits annotation and form-fill incremental updates after an approval signature, which is why DSS classifies them as allowed changes (PdfObjectModificationsFilter.java:61-76 routes them to addAnnotCreationChange / addFormFillInAndSignatureCreationChange rather than addUndefinedChange).
  3. The finding misstates the policy. It claims "AnnotationChanges, FormFillChanges and UndefinedChanges at WARN". The default dss-policy-jaxb 6.5.1 policy/constraint.xml (lines 60-67) contains PdfAnnotationOverlap, PdfVisualDifference, DocMDP, FieldMDP, SigFieldLock, UndefinedChanges at WARN; a grep for AnnotationChanges|FormFillChanges returns 0 hits. With a null constraint, dss-validation ChainItem.java:124-128 does if (level == null) { LOG.trace("Check skipped : constraint not defined"); callNext(); } so AnnotationChangesCheck/FormFillChangesCheck are not evaluated at all (not WARN). DocMDPCheck.java:58-66 only acts when the signature carries DocMDP permissions, which these approval-signature fixtures do not.
  4. Already partially handled: the modification detail is exposed through reports: ["diagnostic"] (README.md:282, 325; ValidationOptions.reports; DssEngine.java:269-271 puts getXmlDiagnosticData into the result), so a consumer who cares can read ObjectModifications today.

RESIDUAL (low): the summary JSON (ValidationResult.java:72-79 maps only simple-report indication/errors/warnings) has no structured "modified after signing" field, and README does not state that TOTAL_PASSED asserts signature validity rather than visual integrity. That is a documentation/ergonomics gap, not a security defect in the engine's logic, and the recommendation to raise DSS checks to FAIL conflicts with the stated DSS-parity design.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.65

Observed behaviour is accurate (TOTAL_PASSED, no modification warning), but it is DSS's documented default, intentionally adopted, consistent with PDF/ETSI semantics, and partially mitigated; the claimed high security impact does not hold for this system.

  1. The finding misdescribes the policy, in a way that undercuts its own argument. Default policy/constraint.xml in dss-policy-jaxb 6.5.1 (lines 58-67) defines ByteRange FAIL, PdfSignatureDictionary FAIL, PdfPageDifference FAIL, and PdfAnnotationOverlap, PdfVisualDifference, DocMDP, FieldMDP, SigFieldLock, UndefinedChanges at WARN. AnnotationChanges and FormFillChanges are not present at all. EtsiValidationPolicy.getAnnotationChangesConstraint (line 238) then returns null and ChainItem.execute (dss-validation 6.5.1, line 124-128) does if (level == null) { LOG.trace("Check skipped : constraint not defined"); callNext(); }. So in plain DSS, with any pdfObjFactory and with visual comparison on or off, annotation and form-fill changes after signing never affect the verdict or produce a warning. The finding itself confirms plain DSS with visual comparison on gives TOTAL_PASSED. This is the DSS project's deliberate default, not an engine omission.
  1. The engine's behaviour is a documented, intentional decision. docs/DECISIONS.md:201: "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now." docs/DECISIONS.md:112-113 records visual comparison off and object-level detection on. README.md:209-213 defines the differential test whose reference is plain DSS on the JVM ("Any difference fails it"): the engine is designed to reproduce DSS's verdicts, so changing the policy to FAIL would deliberately break the parity the project tests for.
  1. The semantics are standard, not a trap specific to this library. ISO 32000 incremental updates are how multi-signature, LTA extension and review comments work; DSS classifies post-signing changes as secure / formFillAndSignatureCreation / annotation / undefined (PdfObjectModificationsFilter lines 66-69) precisely because annotation and form-fill changes are permitted after an approval signature (DocMDP P=2/3) and only UndefinedChanges/DocMDP/PdfPageDifference are policed by default. A DocMDP P=1 certification signature that forbids changes IS checked (DocMDP WARN). The recommendation to raise AnnotationChanges to FAIL would make AnnotationChangesCheck return FAILED/FORMAT_FAILURE (lines 65-74 of the check) for every signed contract on which a reviewer later added a sticky note, i.e. false negatives in common legitimate workflows; that trade-off is why DSS leaves it undefined.
  1. Mitigation exists: the modification detection the finding wants is already available to consumers. DiagnosticData.xsd (dss-diagnostic-jaxb 6.5.1) line 358 <ModificationDetection> with <ObjectModifications> (lines 427-441) is in the diagnostic data, which the engine returns on request (reports: ["diagnostic"], README.md options_json; DssEngine.java:264-272 puts diagnostic_data_xml in the result). A host that needs a "changed after signing" signal can read it today.
  1. Threat model: the attacker here already holds a validly signed PDF and adds a visible annotation. The signature verdict is correct (the signed revision is intact); what is missing is a convenience flag in the summary. Viewers render the annotation as a current-revision object and Acrobat likewise keeps the signature valid while noting changes. This is an API-ergonomics/documentation gap, not a bypass.

What remains true and actionable, at low severity: README's "Validation result" section (lines 311-321) does not state that indication covers only the signed revision and that later incremental updates (annotations, form fills) are reported only in the diagnostic data; DECISIONS.md:113 ("object-level modification detection ... stays on") can be misread as influencing the verdict. A doc sentence, and optionally a structured modified_after_signing summary field derived from ModificationDetection, would close it. Raising the policy to FAIL is not recommended.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Medium · confidence 0.65

The core mechanism checks out, but the finding needs a different line, has two errors in its details, and is rated too high.

What holds up

  • DssEngine.java:255 calls dssReports = validator.validateDocument(); and never supplies a custom validation policy.
  • DECISIONS.md:201 records this as a choice: "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now."
  • The bundled dss-policy-jaxb-6.5.1 constraint.xml (lines 61-67) contains PdfPageDifference Level="FAIL", then PdfAnnotationOverlap, PdfVisualDifference, DocMDP, FieldMDP, SigFieldLock and UndefinedChanges, all at Level="WARN".
  • If the signature has no DocMDP restriction, PDF rules allow adding annotations and filling form fields in a later incremental update. DSS's object-level modification detection classifies these as permitted changes. So TOTAL_PASSED with no modification warning is the expected result of DSS's default policy. That matches the reported test output, which I did not re-run.
  • ValidationResult.java:78 copies only the AdES and qualification warnings into the summary, so the modification detail appears only in the diagnostic and detailed XML reports.

Corrections

  • Line: line 456 is pdfObjFactory(), which turns visual comparison off. The finding itself says that setting does not matter here. The actionable place is the validation call at line 255, where no policy is set.
  • Constraint names: AnnotationChanges and FormFillChanges do not exist in the 6.5.1 constraint.xml. The relevant entries are DocMDP, FieldMDP, SigFieldLock and UndefinedChanges.
  • "No warning at all": the change data is still in the diagnostic report (ModificationDetection and object modifications). It just is not surfaced in the summary.

Severity

  • Attack vector: anyone holding a signed PDF can append an incremental update, and no privileges are needed.
  • Impact: integrity in how a document is presented to a reader. The signed revision itself stays cryptographically intact.
  • This is upstream DSS behaviour, and the PDF specification explicitly allows it. The project knowingly adopted DSS's defaults.
  • Mitigation: integrators can request the diagnostic or detailed report.

Overall this is medium rather than high: a real gap worth documenting or making configurable, with low exploit complexity but no break of signature integrity.

F-101Lowoperationsphp/DssClient.php:98

PHP client has no retry or readiness wait, and /health turns 200 before the trusted lists are loaded (first start with an empty cache only)

There is no retry, and the health check goes green before trusted lists are loaded.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

DssClient.php:100; server.md:198-201

Impact

Errors for about 15 s after each cold start.

Recommendation

Add a bounded retry for 503 and connection errors, plus an isRetryable() helper.

Verification

refutedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.6

Literal facts check out: php/DssClient.php:98-103 builds the request with baseUrl/timeout/acceptJson and no ->retry(); result() (121-129) and document() (132-139) throw DssException on the first non-ok answer; no isRetryable() exists. rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-265 returns 200 {"status":"ready","trusted_lists_loaded":s.loaded} as soon as the engine is up, and tests/http.rs:157-160 asserts ready with trusted_lists_loaded == false; --health-check (main.rs:97-98, healthy() at 181) only checks for 200, so Compose service_healthy (server.md:198-201) passes before the first refresh completes.

But the finding does not survive as a defect: (1) NOT_INITIALIZED is already handled — /health is 503 until the engine is up (lib.rs:252-254; DECISIONS.md:845-848 "so a container's health check and the client both see 'starting' rather than 'refused'") and the documented Compose example gates the app on service_healthy, so the client never sees it there. (2) "Errors for about 15 s after each cold start" is false: main.rs:144-158 reads engine.init_info().trusted_lists_loaded, which is true when lists come from the cache, and the start-up refresh runs only when !loaded; the Compose example mounts a persistent dss-cache volume, so only the very first start with an empty cache has the window (DECISIONS.md: a restart from cache was ready in 7.5 s, during which /health is 503). (3) That single window is documented with two mitigations at server.md:20-24 ("Until it finishes, validations fail with TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED. To skip that wait, extract a seed cache ... or start from a trusted-list snapshot"). (4) Tying /health to loaded lists would be worse: a server with --allow-without-trusted-lists or whose first refresh fails (TL_REFRESH_FAILED, offline) would never become healthy and the app would never start; exposing trusted_lists_loaded as a field is a reasonable, tested design. (5) The client is a thin copy-in sample documented to throw on every {"ok":false} (DssClient.php:15, server.md:167-168); a bounded retry is a hardening suggestion, not a correctness bug. Residual value: at most a low/info note that the Compose example's service_healthy does not wait for trusted_lists_loaded on a first empty-cache start, which the docs already address.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The claimed impact ("errors for about 15 s after each cold start") is overstated and the residual case is a documented, intentional trade-off with stated mitigations. (1) The health check does not go green before cached lists are loaded: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:139-144 calls starting.set_engine(engine, scheduler) only after builder.build() returns, and reads engine.init_info().trusted_lists_loaded right there; rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-254 answers /health 503 {"ok":false,"status":"starting"} until then. DECISIONS.md:892 measured "a restart from the cache, which was ready in 7.5 s". (2) The online refresh at start runs only with an empty cache: main.rs:155 RefreshScheduler::spawn(Arc::clone(&engine), every, !loaded) and DECISIONS.md:849 "at start only when nothing was cached". The documented deployment keeps the cache in a volume (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:34-35 "kept across restarts"), so the TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED window exists only on the first start with an empty or wiped cache, not after each restart. (3) That one-time window is documented with its trade-off and two ways to remove it: docs/server.md:20-24 ("With an empty cache, an online refresh starts right away (about 15 s for the full EU list). Until it finishes, validations fail with TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED. To skip that wait, extract a seed cache ... or start from a trusted-list snapshot") and Dockerfile:38 ("Healthy once the engine is up; with an empty cache, loading the EU trusted lists online takes a while longer"). The health body also exposes trusted_lists_loaded (lib.rs:261) for stricter gating. (4) NOT_INITIALIZED never reaches the app in the documented Compose setup: server.md:198-200 gates the app on condition: service_healthy, and tests/process.rs:84-92 and tests/http.rs:143-160 confirm /health is 503 until the engine is up; listen-first is a stated decision (DECISIONS.md:845-848). (5) Only validation and LT/LTA extension/completion need trusted lists; prepare and B/T complete do not (DECISIONS.md:718), narrowing the affected calls further. (6) The PHP client is a copy-into-your-app sample on Laravel's HTTP client (server.md:130-132, DssClient.php:15), whose built-in ->retry() lets a host add bounded retries in one line if its deployment skips the seed cache; the 503 answers carry explicit codes (DssException.php:14-16) so the host can already detect them. Net impact: a narrow, one-time, documented and mitigated window in a sidecar on a trusted network; a retry helper in the sample client would be a nice-to-have, not a defect. Not confirmed as a medium operations issue.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

The finding is real, but its impact is overstated.

What is confirmed in the code:

  • php/DssClient.php has no retry anywhere. request() (lines 98-103) builds $this->http->baseUrl(...)->timeout(...)->acceptJson() with no ->retry().
  • result() throws DssException::fromResponse on any ok that is not true. DssException carries errorCode and status, but there is no isRetryable() helper.
  • rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-266: health() returns 200 "status": "ready" as soon as the engine exists. Whether trusted lists are loaded is only reported in the body field "trusted_lists_loaded": s.loaded.
  • rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:144-172 calls set_engine whatever the value of loaded. So --health-check and Compose service_healthy both pass while trusted lists are still not loaded.
  • docs/server.md:112 lists NOT_INITIALIZED and TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED as 503.

What is overstated:

  • The impact claim ("errors for about 15 s after each cold start") is wrong. docs/server.md:19-22 says the ~15 s TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED window happens only on a first start with an empty cache. With a cached copy, or a seed cache, or tl_snapshot, init_info().trusted_lists_loaded is true when the engine becomes ready. The Compose example also keeps the cache in a volume (dss-cache:/var/lib/dss/cache), so later restarts load it from the cache.
  • The NOT_INITIALIZED window is already covered for the documented deployment. server.md:198-201 has depends_on: condition: service_healthy, and health returns 503 until the engine is up.
  • The failure mode is clean, not silent. The caller gets a typed DssException with code TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED and status 503, and can retry it. Nothing is accepted wrongly and no data is corrupted.
  • An unconditional retry would be wrong for TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED when no refresh is scheduled (main.rs logs "no trusted lists yet and no refresh scheduled"), so the recommendation needs care.

Severity: Low. This is availability and ergonomics only: no attacker angle, no integrity impact, and it occurs once per fresh deployment. The cited line 100 sits inside request(), which starts at line 98, so a maintainer can find it.

SigningResult.java:27-28; ExtensionResult.java:26; ValidationResult.java:40

A confusing contract that requires string parsing.

Recommendation

Use consistent fields before 1.0.

Verification

refutedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The factual observation is accurate but it is a documented, deliberate design that mirrors DSS's own vocabulary, and the claimed impact ("requires string parsing") has no instance in the codebase.

Facts confirmed. Input level is the short enum: SigningOptions.java:45-49 enum Level { B(...), T(...), LT(...), LTA(...) } and fromJson at :156-160 ('level' must be "B", "T", "LT" or "LTA"). Output level is the full DSS name: SigningResult.java:28 m.put("level", level.toString()) and ExtensionResult.java:26, where DSS's SignatureLevel.toString() (dss-enumerations 6.5.1 sources :101-102) is super.toString().replace('_', '-'), giving e.g. PAdES-BASELINE-LT (asserted in rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:172 and rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:325). The validation summary field format is a SignatureLevel: ValidationResult.java:31 SignatureLevel format and :40 m.put("format", ... format.toString()).

Why it is not a defect:

  1. The validation format name is DSS's, not an invention: ValidationResult.java:74 fills it from report.getSignatureFormat(id), and DSS's SimpleReport.xsd (dss-simple-report-jaxb 6.5.1, line 105) defines <xs:attribute name="SignatureFormat" type="SignatureFormat"> whose enumeration values are exactly XAdES-BASELINE-LT-style strings (xsd :299-312). The docstring at :29 says these are "the fields of the simple report that callers and the differential test compare" with the JVM, so keeping DSS's name is the point.
  2. The short input level is a recorded decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:631-633 "options_json names a level, not a format. "level": "T" | "LT" | "LTA", and the format follows the document. CAdES could be added later without changing the contract." The full output level is also deliberate: it reports the level actually reached, which can differ from the one requested (SigningResult.java:18-19 "the requested one, or T when an external CMS asked for at B already carries a signature timestamp"; DECISIONS.md:717 "A timestamped CMS asked for at B is reported as T, the level it has"; README.md:407-410).
  3. All three shapes are documented side by side in README.md: validation "format": "CAdES-BASELINE-B" (:317), extend "level": "LT" in / "level": "PAdES-BASELINE-LT" out (:335, :339), sign "level": "LT" in / "level": "PAdES-BASELINE-LT" out (:384, :404).
  4. Nothing parses the strings. The Rust bindings keep them opaque (Signed.level: String, Extended.level: String, SignatureSummary.format: Option<String> at rust/dss/src/types.rs:63, :89, :129); the CLI only prints them (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:691, :867); the server derives the content type from the separate format field, not from level (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:197-202); grep over rust/ and java/src/main for ends_with/startsWith/split on level strings finds no consumer. The sign result also carries format ("PAdES"/"CAdES") next to level (SigningResult.java:27), so a caller never needs to parse level to learn the format.

What remains is a naming-taste remark (a typed Rust Level could be offered for the outputs), which is at most low/info and is not the "confusing contract that requires string parsing" described.

The only code that branches on these fields is rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:197-202, which matches format ("PAdES"/"CAdES") and packaging for the Content-Type, both closed two-/three-value vocabularies. Tests compare the full strings verbatim (rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:158, :172, :257; rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:325, :403; rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs:77).

The naming mirrors DSS's own vocabulary rather than being invented here: DSS's SimpleReport element is "SignatureFormat" and its value is the SignatureLevel enum, so a caller cross-referencing signatures[].format with the simple_report_xml that is always returned finds the same name and value. The output level as the full ETSI identifier is strictly more informative than the input (it carries format and level, which matters in the documented B-asked/T-reported case).

What remains is a stylistic naming wart (the output level cannot be compared to the input level without a suffix check, and "format" means different things on the sign-input and the validation-output). confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

The finding is accurate. All three cited lines say what it claims. Input: SigningOptions.java:161 and ExtensionOptions.java:50 parse "level" with Level.valueOf(...toUpperCase()), so the input is the short enum (README.md:384 "B", "T", "LT" or "LTA"; README.md:335 "T", "LT" or "LTA").

Output:

  • SigningResult.java:28 m.put("level", level.toString()) and ExtensionResult.java:26 do the same with a DSS SignatureLevel, which gives "PAdES-BASELINE-LT" (README.md:339 and :404 show this).

So the same key names carry different value domains across the contract. A caller who wants to compare the requested level with the reached level has to parse "PAdES-BASELINE-LT" to get "LT".

Mitigations:

  • README documents each output shape exactly.
  • The field names come from DSS: the simple report calls SignatureLevel "format".
  • DECISIONS.md:631 explains why extension takes a level and not a format.
  • Nothing is ambiguous at runtime: each response's shape is fixed and documented.

Severity: medium is too high. This is API ergonomics with no security or correctness impact. Every value is deterministic and documented, and it is only a breaking-change concern before 1.0. I calibrate it as low. The file, lines and mechanism are correct, so a maintainer can act on it.

F-205Lowsecuritydocker/dss-server/Dockerfile:32

Docker image binds 0.0.0.0 without a token by default and the server does not warn (documented optional-token design; adjacent-network exposure only)

Any network peer can spend TSA credits, trigger refreshes and submit documents.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

Dockerfile:32 'DSS_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8484'; main.rs:114-126

Impact

Abuse from co-located containers.

Recommendation

Refuse non-loopback binding without a token unless explicitly allowed.

Verification

refutedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.7

The literal facts hold: docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:32 sets ENV DSS_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8484, the token is optional (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:39-41 token_file: Option<PathBuf>), and serve() (main.rs:114-131) binds args.listen and prints only "listening on ..." with no check or warning when the address is non-loopback and token is None. rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:278-285 enforces the bearer token only if let Some(token) = &state.token.

But the finding describes a documented and reasonable design, not a defect:

  • A container must bind a non-loopback address to be reachable from any other container at all; 127.0.0.1 inside the image would make the sidecar useless. main.rs:36 and docs/server.md:38 both say "Use 0.0.0.0:<port> in a container".
  • The token being optional is an explicit decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857 "Optional bearer token, read from a file ... There is no TLS: the server is meant for the same host or a private network."
  • The exact threat the finding names (co-located containers) is addressed in docs/server.md:212-217: "Do not publish the port: the app reaches the sidecar over the Compose network." / "never expose it publicly. The token stops other containers on the same network from using it." The only Compose example (server.md:184-209) mounts DSS_TOKEN_FILE: /run/secrets/dss_token. The Dockerfile itself cannot bake a token in, since the token must come from a secret file by design (DECISIONS.md:855 rejects env/args because they show in docker inspect).
  • The recommendation (refuse non-loopback without a token) would contradict the documented same-host/private-network-without-token mode and would make the Docker image unusable without a token even on an isolated network.

The one residual kernel is that the server emits no startup warning when bound to a non-loopback address without a token (confirmed by reading main.rs:114-131; the only warn string in the file is the log-level default at line 85). That is a hardening nicety of low severity, not a medium security defect, and the deployment docs already carry the warning. The test at rust/dss-server/tests/process.rs:102-106 exercises 0.0.0.0 only for --health-check, so no test contradicts either side.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.85

The code reads as the finding says: docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:32 sets DSS_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8484, the token is optional (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:39-41 token_file: Option<PathBuf>), and serve() (main.rs:115-131) prints only "listening on ..." with no warning about a non-loopback bind without a token. But through the IMPACT lens the claimed impact does not hold up in this system:

  1. Documented, intentional decision with the trade-off stated. docs/server.md "Security": "No TLS. Run the sidecar on the same host or on a private network, as above, and never expose it publicly. The token stops other containers on the same network from using it." and docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857: "Optional bearer token, read from a file ... There is no TLS: the server is meant for the same host or a private network." The Compose example in server.md:183-209 configures DSS_TOKEN_FILE: /run/secrets/dss_token on both services and says "Do not publish the port: the app reaches the sidecar over the Compose network." The threat model explicitly places the sidecar on a trusted network and gives the token as the mitigation for co-located containers; the finding's "abuse from co-located containers" is exactly the case the docs address.
  1. 0.0.0.0 is the only workable default for the image. A process bound to 127.0.0.1 inside a container is unreachable from any other container, so the image would be unusable out of the box; main.rs:36 and server.md:38 both say "Use 0.0.0.0:<port> in a container". The EXPOSE 8484 at Dockerfile:37 is metadata only; nothing publishes the port to the host, so the reachable set is the Docker network the operator attached, not "any network peer".
  1. Blast radius is small. The server holds no signing key (server.md Security: "Signing keys never reach the server"), refuses detached_contents[].path (DECISIONS.md:840-842), bounds request size and heap (--max-request-mb, --max-heap). "Spend TSA credits" needs the operator to have set DSS_TSA_URL (main.rs:76-78, default none). Refreshes coalesce: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:213-232 answers REFRESH_IN_PROGRESS (409) when one is running, and schedule.rs:79 refresh_now "Returns false if one is already pending", so a peer cannot amplify refreshes beyond one at a time. What remains is CPU use and, with a TSA configured, timestamp requests, from an attacker who already controls another container on the private network and whose operator ignored the documented token.
  1. The recommendation ("refuse non-loopback binding without a token") would break the documented tokenless same-host/private-network deployment that the authors chose on purpose. A startup warning when !args.listen.ip().is_loopback() && token.is_none() would be a reasonable one-line hardening nicety, but it is a stylistic/defence-in-depth improvement, not a security defect in a system whose docs already state the constraint and ship a tokenised Compose example.

Calibrated severity: low (at most an informational hardening suggestion).

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.75

The facts in the finding are right. docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:32 sets ENV DSS_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8484 and does not set DSS_TOKEN_FILE. In rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:39-41 the token is Option<PathBuf> with no default. At main.rs:114-126 the token is only loaded when a file is given; the server errors only when a token file is given but empty. At main.rs:132-133 it binds and prints only "listening on ...". Nothing warns about a non-loopback bind without a token. With no token, /validate, /extend, /sign/prepare, /sign/complete and /tl/refresh (lib.rs:107-113) are open to anyone who can reach the port.

The severity is overstated, so I rate it low rather than medium: (1) Binding 0.0.0.0 is required for a container to be reachable at all. The CLI default stays loopback (main.rs:37 default_value = "127.0.0.1:8484"). (2) The Dockerfile does not publish the port to the host. EXPOSE is only metadata, and docs/server.md:212 says "Do not publish the port". The attacker must already be a peer on the same Docker network (adjacent vector). (3) Running without a token is a documented choice. DECISIONS.md:855 says "Optional bearer token, read from a file... the server is meant for the same host or a private network". The documented Compose example (server.md:193) sets DSS_TOKEN_FILE, and server.md:216-217 says "The token stops other containers on the same network from using it." (4) Impact is bounded. Signing keys never reach the server (server.md:219-220), so no forgery is possible. TSA cost only applies when DSS_TSA_URL is set to a paid TSA. A /tl/refresh flood or document submissions mostly mean wasted resources or DoS, bounded by --max-request-mb and --max-heap.

What is real is a secure-by-default gap: the image ships listening on all interfaces with no token and no startup warning. A one-line warning, or a refusal unless explicitly allowed, is still a fair hardening step.

F-197Infoapi-designrust/dss/src/config.rs:195

Input option enums in config.rs (Level, SignatureFormat, SigningMode, Packaging, DigestAlgorithm, Report, Revocation, Placement, ...) lack #[non_exhaustive]; only matters once the crate is published

Adding a variant is a semver break, and Packaging cannot represent ENVELOPED.

Details, evidence and verification

Evidence

config.rs:193-204, :245-260

Impact

Major version bumps.

Recommendation

Add #[non_exhaustive].

Verification

refutedReproducecalibrated severity: Low · confidence 0.8

The finding has two concrete claims; one misreads the code and the other overstates a deliberate, reasonable design choice.

  1. "Packaging cannot represent ENVELOPED" is a misread. Packaging is an input-only option, scoped to CAdES: rust/dss/src/config.rs:245 "/// CAdES only: whether the content stays apart from the signature or goes inside it." and config.rs:402-404 "/// CAdES only. Default [Packaging::Detached]. ... pub packaging: Option<Packaging>". The Java engine it drives has the identical input enum public enum Packaging { DETACHED, ENVELOPING } (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/SigningOptions.java:66) and rejects any packaging for PAdES: SigningOptions.java:202 "'packaging' must be \"detached\" or \"enveloping\"", :205 and ExternalSigning.java:97-99 "'packaging' applies to CAdES only (a PAdES signature is always inside the PDF)". ENVELOPED exists only as an output value, and the Rust result type carries it as a String: rust/dss/src/types.rs:131-132 "/// \"ENVELOPED\" (PAdES), \"DETACHED\" or \"ENVELOPING\" (CAdES). pub packaging: String", asserted by rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:371 assert_eq!(signed.packaging, "ENVELOPED"). So ENVELOPED is representable where it occurs, and adding it to the input enum would only let callers send a value the engine refuses.
  1. The exhaustive option enums are a deliberate pattern, not an oversight. The crate already applies #[non_exhaustive] exactly where values come back from the library and may grow: rust/dss/src/types.rs:11 (Indication, with a #[serde(other)] Unknown), rust/dss/src/error.rs:9 (ErrorCode, "Stable; new codes may be added") and error.rs:48 (Error). The option enums cited (Level, SignatureFormat, SigningMode, Packaging, DigestAlgorithm, Report, Revocation) derive only Serialize (config.rs:193, 222, 233, 246, 255, 129, 139), i.e. they are constructed by callers and never deserialised, so a new variant only breaks a caller that exhaustively matches on an input enum it builds itself, which is unusual. Splitting non_exhaustive between output and input enums is a common, defensible API design.
  1. The stated impact "Major version bumps" is largely moot: the workspace is publish = false (rust/Cargo.toml:11) with version 0.0.0-dev (rust/Cargo.toml:6); the only in-repo consumer is dss-cli, which maps its own clap enum onto Packaging (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:718-720) and would be updated in the same commit.

Adding #[non_exhaustive] to the input enums would be a harmless style tweak, but as described (semver hazard, missing ENVELOPED) the finding is not a defect. Severity at most low/info.

refutedImpactcalibrated severity: Info · confidence 0.85

Impact is negligible and half the claim misreads the code. (1) The cited enums are input-only option values: config.rs:139/194/222/234/246/255 derive Serialize but not Deserialize; a host builds them and never needs an exhaustive match on them to read library output. The result-side enums a host would match on are already #[non_exhaustive] with an Unknown fallback (types.rs:11 Indication with #[serde(other)] Unknown; error.rs:9 ErrorCode, "Stable; new codes may be added"; error.rs:48 Error), and docs/DECISIONS.md Phase 4 states the intent: "Unknown enum values map to Unknown and unknown fields are ignored, so newer libraries stay readable." So forward compatibility was handled where it matters. (2) The "major version bump" impact has no bite here: rust/Cargo.toml:11 publish = false, version 0.0.0-dev, versions come from the release tag (DECISIONS.md:487-491); the crate is consumed as a path/git dependency alongside the native library it must match anyway, and in-workspace consumers map their own clap enums into the library enums (dss-cli main.rs:619-725, e.g. PackagingArg::Detached => Packaging::Detached), so a new library variant breaks nothing. (3) "Packaging cannot represent ENVELOPED" is wrong: Packaging is a signing input documented "CAdES only" (config.rs:245), mirroring Java enum Packaging { DETACHED, ENVELOPING } (SigningOptions.java:66) which rejects it for PAdES (ExternalSigning.java:97-99: "'packaging' applies to CAdES only (a PAdES signature is always inside the PDF)"). ENVELOPED is only a result value and the result type carries it as a String (types.rs:131-132: /// "ENVELOPED" (PAdES), "DETACHED" or "ENVELOPING" (CAdES). pub packaging: String), asserted in tests/engine.rs:371. Adding #[non_exhaustive] to the input enums would be a harmless stylistic nicety, not a fix for a real problem.

confirmedSeverity and precisioncalibrated severity: Info · confidence 0.6

The narrow fact holds. rust/dss/src/config.rs:195 pub enum Level, :223 SignatureFormat, :235 SigningMode, :247 Packaging, :256 DigestAlgorithm, plus :131 Revocation, :141 Report, :342/:357/:366 Placement/TextAlign/ImagePosition, carry no #[non_exhaustive]. The only enums that have it are types.rs:11 (Indication) and error.rs:9/:48 (ErrorCode, Error).

Two parts of the finding are wrong or overstated: (1) "Packaging cannot represent ENVELOPED" is incorrect. Packaging is an input option and is documented as CAdES-only. config.rs:245 reads "CAdES only: whether the content stays apart from the signature or goes inside it", with variants Detached (.p7s) and Enveloping (.p7m). The README says "packaging": "detached", // CAdES only. ENVELOPED is the PAdES output value. It comes back in a result struct as a free String: types.rs:131-132 has /// "ENVELOPED" (PAdES), "DETACHED" or "ENVELOPING" (CAdES). pub packaging: String. No input ever needs ENVELOPED, so nothing is missing. (2) Semver impact. These enums derive only Serialize. They are inputs that callers build, so adding a variant breaks only callers that match on them exhaustively, which is rare for option enums. The crate is also not released: rust/Cargo.toml has version = "0.0.0-dev" and publish = false. The selective use of #[non_exhaustive] on output/decoded enums (Indication, ErrorCode, Error) looks like a deliberate split between inputs and outputs, not an oversight.

What remains is a minor, forward-looking API hygiene suggestion with no runtime, security or correctness impact today. Severity is info, not medium.
