F-007 Trusted-list snapshots inject trust anchors protected only by a CRC; the library offers no hash pinning java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:303
  • Reproduce: Reproduction of the mechanics confirms the facts: TrustedListManager.importSnapshot (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:303-316) does TlSnapshotFile.header(bytes); checkCompatible(header); TlSnapshotFile.contents(bytes); checkUsable(contents); and then publishes. TlSnapshotFile.header (TlSnapshotFile.java:179-203) checks only magic, format version, CRC-32C and header length; checkCompatible (TrustedListManager.java:341-365) compares the header's dss and settings against the engine's own snapshotSettings. No SHA-256/HMAC/signature verification exists anywhere (grep for sha256/hmac/pinned in java/src/main and rust/ finds only oj_keystore_sha256, the signing digest option and the CLI digest arg); EngineConfig.java:83,146 lists tl_snapshot as the only snapshot key. TlSnapshotTest.java:278-291 even shows a test helper that rewrites the header and recomputes a matching CRC. So anyone who can write the file can inject trust anchors, and status reports a normal mode: "snapshot" load. However, this is not a defect but a recorded, reasoned, user-requested decision, which the audit method classifies as refuted. docs/DECISIONS.md:930-934: "Trust is the application's decision, not the library's (asked; answered). A snapshot holds trust anchors that nothing re-checks against the EU's signatures, so whoever can write one can make any certificate trusted. The user decided the library only exports and imports, and the application that stores and hands over a snapshot vouches for it (read-only deployment, its own hash or signature). No pinned hash or signature verification in the library." DECISIONS.md:936-938 further states the checks are for "Mistakes, not attacks: the CRC catches a damaged file, not a forged one." README.md:508-511 repeats it in bold for integrators: "The library does not decide whether a snapshot can be trusted... Whoever can write the file can make any certificate trusted. The application ... must make sure they are its own, e.g. by shipping them in its read-only deployment, or by checking a hash or signature of its own before naming the file in tl_snapshot." The Javadoc at TrustedListManager.java:299-301 and TlSnapshotFile.java:51-52 say the same. The threat (attacker with write access to the snapshot path) is precisely the one the documentation hands to the application, and the application that holds config_json can compute and check its own digest before naming the path, so the gap is closable outside the library exactly as documented. One detail in the finding is also misleading: "The header settings, including oj_keystore_sha256, are part of the attacker-controlled file" implies the header's hash is a trust input. It is not: checkCompatible compares the header value against snapshotSettings.put("oj_keystore_sha256", certificatesSha256(ojKeystore.getCertificates())) computed by this engine from its own keystore (TrustedListManager.java:147, 215-225), so the header can only cause rejection, never widen trust; it is a settings-compatibility check, never advertised as a trust check. Net: the recommendation (optional tl_snapshot_sha256 in config_json) is a reasonable enhancement request, not a defect in the code as designed and documented. Severity as a finding: info.
F-008 INTERNAL_ERROR conflates input-driven resource exhaustion (OOM/StackOverflow) with library faults and echoes raw exception text plus stack trace java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssJsonApi.java:213
  • Reproduce: The mechanics reproduce: DssJsonApi.java:207-213 catches Throwable, logs "Unexpected failure" at ERROR with the throwable (slf4j-simple prints the stack trace), and returns INTERNAL_ERROR with "<class>: <message>". Running cargo test -p dss --test engine heap_limit_is_an_error_not_a_crash -- --nocapture printed exactly that: "[System-0] ERROR it.codingduck.dssnative.engine.DssJsonApi - Unexpected failure / java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Array allocation too large." plus 9 frames, and the API message is "java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Array allocation too large.". rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:530 and java/src/test/c/smoke.c:368,372 do match on the substring "OutOfMemoryError". dss-server lib.rs:487 maps it to 500 and lib.rs:501,527 forward the message. However the finding is a documented and deliberate decision, and its impact claims are not supported: (1) "Hosts cannot return 413" is false: dss-server already rejects oversized requests with 413 REQUEST_TOO_LARGE before the engine is called (lib.rs:120 DefaultBodyLimit::max, lib.rs:469-472, main.rs:47 DSS_MAX_REQUEST_MB default 100, docs/server.md:108), and any embedder knows the document length before calling. (2) "Oversized uploads flood stderr" is false: over-limit uploads never reach line 208; only a within-limit request that still exhausts the heap does, producing one ~10-line trace per request. (3) "can include file paths" has no positive evidence; the observed OOM message is "Array allocation too large.". (4) The conflation is the documented contract: DssError.java:42-43 "Anything unexpected, including JVM errors.", rust/dss/src/error.rs:36-37 "including running out of heap", docs/native-library.md:112-113, docs/server.md:110 "INTERNAL_ERROR (including an engine out of heap)", docs/DECISIONS.md:277-285 (the OOM-to-INTERNAL_ERROR behaviour was engineered specifically so the process does not abort and the isolate stays usable, which the test confirms). A dedicated RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED code would be an enhancement, not a defect; logging an OOM with its stack trace at ERROR is standard practice and useful for diagnosing where the allocation happened.
F-015 Signing does not apply the base64/PEM normalisation that validate and extend apply java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:92
  • Reproduce: The literal behaviour is reproducible but it is the documented, consistent and (for a signer) correct contract, not a defect. What the code does (confirmed): ExternalSigning.java:92-93 boolean pdf = InputNormalizer.sniff(document) == InputNormalizer.Type.PDF; Format format = options.format != null ? options.format : (pdf ? Format.PADES : Format.CADES); and document() at :376-379 wraps the raw bytes (new InMemoryDocument(document, name)); prepare digests document as given (:121). So a base64 text file with no format is signed as detached CAdES over that text. Only the external signer's output is normalised (:217 InputNormalizer.normalize(external), :332 decodeText(external)). Why this is not a bug: 1. It is the documented contract. README.md:382 and docs/openapi.yaml:545-546 (format: Default PAdES for a PDF, CAdES otherwise); docs/DECISIONS.md:724 "CAdES signs the bytes given.". Every mention of base64/PEM decoding in the signing docs (README.md:388,416-418; DECISIONS.md:706-708; openapi.yaml:216-218) concerns the certificate, the CMS or the signature value, never the document, and the signing results have no transformations field, unlike validate/extend (README.md:314, DECISIONS.md:649). The finding's premise that signing is "supposed" to normalise is an inference from validate/extend, not from any stated intent. 2. The asymmetry is reasonable. validate/extend only accept PDF or CMS, so a base64 wrapper is unambiguous transport encoding. CAdES signing accepts arbitrary content: a file consisting of base64 characters (a .pem, an encoded blob, a text file) is legitimate content, and silently decoding it would sign bytes the caller did not give, which is the actual "wrong bytes" hazard. Refusing base64-looking input with INVALID_ARGUMENT (the recommendation) would break legitimate CAdES use. 3. The caller is not blind: prepare returns format (PreparedSignature.java:31 m.put("format", ...), README.md:400), so an unexpected "CAdES" is visible before any signature is spent, and prepare and complete apply the same sniff, so there is no mismatch between the two steps. The tested behaviour matches: SigningTest.java:470-477 signs a PDF as detached CAdES over its bytes on purpose ("A PDF can be signed as CAdES too: detached, over its bytes"). At most this is a documentation nit (one could state explicitly that the signing document is never base64-decoded). No code defect as described.
F-021 Every concurrent validation serializes on the published TrustedListsCertificateSource monitor java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:448
  • Reproduce: The mechanism cited is real but the claimed impact ("every concurrent validation serializes", "reduced scalability with many workers") is not supported by the code or by measurement. What is true: TrustedListManager.publishSnapshot (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:448-452) copies staging into new TrustedListsCertificateSource() and publishes it via the volatile current (line 122); DssEngine.certificateVerifier (DssEngine.java:464/466) hands that single snapshot.source() to every validation's CommonCertificateVerifier. In DSS 6.5.1 (dss-spi sources from ~/.m2), getTrustServices (TrustedListsCertificateSource.java:126) and getTrustTime (line 156) are synchronized, and isTrusted (214) and isTrustedAtTime (177) call getTrustTime. DSS does call them during validation: DiagnosticDataBuilder.getRelatedTrustServices (dss-validation ...DiagnosticDataBuilder.java:442, 567, 596, 2096) and TrustAnchorVerifier.isTrustedAtTime (TrustAnchorVerifier.java:188) via SignatureValidationContext. Multiple validation workers exist (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:45 default 1, .workers(n) at line 51; docs/DECISIONS.md:355). Why it is refuted as described: (1) Only the lookups serialize, not the validations: each critical section is a HashMap.get on an entity key (lines 127-133, 157-173), nothing is held across I/O, parsing or crypto. (2) Measured: a micro-benchmark (scratchpad/bench/LockBench.java, run on JDK 25, 15-CPU machine) hammering getTrustServices+getTrustTime+isTrusted on one shared source with nothing else in between gave ~125-150 ns/call at 1 thread and a flat aggregate of ~6-7 M calls/s at 4, 8 and 16 threads — the monitor's absolute ceiling. A validation performs on the order of a few hundred such lookups (one per certificate per chain walk) against ~30 ms of other work (docs/DECISIONS.md:400 "One validation (PAdES B-LTA) ~30 ms"), i.e. roughly 50 µs of lock time per validation, ~0.15%. With 16 workers the offered lock utilization is ~2-3%; the lock would only bottleneck at >~20,000 validations/s, two orders of magnitude above what 16 workers at ~33 validations/s each can produce. Queueing at that utilization is negligible, so "reduced scalability" is not observable. (3) The design is documented and reasonable: TrustedListManager.java:69-72 and docs/DECISIONS.md:74 explain the immutable-snapshot copy; a DSS TrustedListsCertificateSource instance is needed because DSS's DiagnosticDataBuilder selects trust info by instanceof TrustPropertiesCertificateSource / TrustedCertificateSourceWithTime (DiagnosticDataBuilder.java:438, 2094). The finding itself rates it info and says "measure first"; the measurement shows no actionable contention, so there is nothing to fix.
F-028 No strength check on the external CMS's key or signature algorithm: an RSA-1024 signer is accepted java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:237
  • Reproduce: The behaviour is real but it is the documented contract, matches DSS's own signing services, and is mis-scoped to the external-CMS path, so I do not count it as a defect. What the code does (confirmed): ExternalSigning.checkedCms (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:216-288) checks: one signer (229), detached (232), digest OID equals the options' algorithm (237: if (!o.digestAlgorithm.getOid().equals(signer.getDigestAlgOID()))), content-type id-data (247), message-digest equals the recomputed digest (257), signing-certificate(-v2) (262), signing-time rules (267/271), signer certificate present and equal to signing_certificate (275-279), and cryptographic verification via new CAdESSignature(cms, signer)...getSignatureCryptographicVerification() (280-286). Nothing reads signer.getEncryptionAlgOID() or the key length of signerCertificate.getPublicKey(). A grep of java/src/main/java for keysize/keyLength/getKeyLength/CryptographicConstraint/isReliable returns nothing. So an RSA-1024 signer is accepted, as the finding says. Why it is not a defect as filed: 1. It is the documented contract, not an oversight. README.md:412-418 ("What complete checks in \"cms\" mode, before building anything") and docs/DECISIONS.md:692-700 enumerate exactly this list; neither promises that the result passes the default validation policy. complete is specified as checking "what came back against this document" (README.md:366-367), i.e. consistency with the prepared digest, not policy conformance. DECISIONS.md:201 also records "Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now." 2. It matches DSS 6.5.1's own behaviour at signing time. In the extracted sources, AbstractSignatureService.assertSigningCertificateValid delegates to SignatureRequirementsChecker.assertSigningCertificateIsValid (dss-document SignatureRequirementsChecker.java:82-87), which only runs assertCertificatesAreYetValid, assertCertificatesAreNotExpired, assertCertificatesAreNotRevoked; and PAdESWithExternalCMSService.isValidCMSSignedData (dss-pades :272-291) only does the cryptographic verification. DSS does not refuse an RSA-1024 key when signing in any mode; the engine mirrors that. 3. The finding is mis-scoped. The same acceptance holds in "signature_value" mode: signatureValue() (ExternalSigning.java:330-354) derives the algorithm from EncryptionAlgorithm.forKey(o.signingCertificate.getPublicKey()) with no size check, and cadesParameters/padesParameters pass the certificate to DSS which, per point 2, does not check it either. "Only the digest OID is constrained" singles out line 237 wrongly: it is a property of the whole signing feature (and of DSS), not of the external-CMS check. 4. The impact statement is overstated: ok:true means the signed document was built from a CMS that is consistent with this document and cryptographically verifies, which is all that is promised; the caller chose the signer and its key. Validation afterwards reports the weak key exactly as it should. If the maintainers want signing to pre-empt the default policy's cryptographic constraints, that is a feature request touching both modes (ExternalSigning.java:275 for the CMS signer certificate, :338 for signing_certificate), not a correctness bug at line 237. No cheap experiment was needed: the absence of any key-size/algorithm check in the engine and in DSS's signing path is established by reading the code.
F-029 signature_value mode cannot use RSASSA-PSS with an RSA key; PSS values are refused with a misleading message java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:343
  • Reproduce: The mechanics described are accurate but the finding is a documented, deliberate scope decision, and the finding itself concedes it ("this is a limitation rather than a bug"). Code path (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java): line 338 encryption = EncryptionAlgorithm.forKey(o.signingCertificate.getPublicKey()), line 343 SignatureAlgorithm algorithm = SignatureAlgorithm.getAlgorithm(encryption, o.digestAlgorithm). In DSS 6.5.1 (java/pom.xml:43), EncryptionAlgorithm.forKey is forName(key.getAlgorithm()) and the enum maps JCE name "RSA" -> RSA("RSA", "1.2.840.113549.1.1.1", "RSA/ECB/PKCS1Padding"), so an ordinary RSA certificate always yields RSA_SHA256 (PKCS#1 v1.5). A PSS-produced value then fails service.isValidSignatureValue(...) at lines 147/154 and assertSignatureValueValid (366-370) throws the generic message "the signature value does not verify with the signing certificate ... the signer must use the signing certificate's key". (Side note: a certificate whose SPKI is id-RSASSA-PSS has JCE name "RSASSA-PSS", which forName maps to RSASSA_PSS and RSA_SSA_PSS_SHA256_MGF1, so that rarer shape is actually accepted; the finding's "an RSA key always means PKCS#1 v1.5" is only true for the common rsaEncryption SPKI.) Why refuted: the limitation is explicitly documented in two places the finding's recommendation asks for. README.md:378 states the signer returns "RSA PKCS#1 v1.5, or ECDSA as DER or r‖s". docs/DECISIONS.md:734-735, under "Not done": "RSASSA-PSS signature values (RSA keys are PKCS#1 v1.5)". So "document the limitation" is already done, and omitting PSS is a recorded design choice consistent with the test matrix in DECISIONS.md (RSA and ECDSA in both encodings). The remaining residue, that the refusal message lists mismatch/signing_time/wrong-key causes and does not mention padding, is an ergonomics nit, not a defect: the message is factually correct (the value genuinely does not verify under the declared algorithm) and the generic text is shared with the real mismatch cases tested in SigningTest (e.g. line 386 "does not verify"). No test or code path shows a wrong result being produced. Calibrated severity: info.
F-034 JPEG metadata (EXIF GPS, device ids, thumbnails, XMP) is embedded verbatim in the signed document java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java:91
  • Reproduce: The mechanism is real but it is a documented, tested, deliberate decision that matches upstream DSS, so the finding does not hold as a defect. What the code does (confirmed): /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImage.java:57 stores the whole file for a JPEG (new SignatureImage(h.width(), h.height(), h.components() == 1, bytes, true, null)), and :90-91 wraps it unchanged: new PDImageXObject(document, new ByteArrayInputStream(data), jpeg ? COSName.DCT_DECODE : COSName.FLATE_DECODE, ...). PDFBox 3.0.8's constructor (pdfbox-3.0.8-sources.jar, PDImageXObject.java:120-132) does super(createRawStream(document, encodedStream), COSName.IMAGE) and only sets Filter/Width/Height/ColorSpace, so APPn/COM segments are indeed copied into the XObject. Jpeg.header() (:130-178) only walks segments to find SOF; it strips nothing. Why it is refuted as a finding: 1. Documented behaviour, exactly what the finding's own recommendation accepts as an alternative ("or document the behaviour"): README.md:461 "A JPEG goes into the PDF as it is."; docs/DECISIONS.md:766 "a JPEG goes in as DCTDecode, with its size and components read from the frame header"; SignatureImage.java:23 Javadoc "A JPEG goes into the PDF as it is ({@code DCTDecode})". 2. Tested as intended behaviour: java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SignatureImageTest.java:95 assertArrayEquals(Fixtures.read("content/stamp.jpg"), jpeg.data(), "a JPEG goes into the PDF unchanged"). 3. Identical to upstream DSS 6.5.1: dss-pades-pdfbox-6.5.1 NativePdfBoxVisibleSignatureDrawer.java:248 and :416 call PDImageXObject.createFromByteArray(doc, bytes, ...), which for JPEG goes to JPEGFactory.createFromByteArray (JPEGFactory.java:96-123) and builds the same new PDImageXObject(document, byteStream, COSName.DCT_DECODE, ...) on the raw bytes. So any DSS-based PAdES visible signature embeds JPEG metadata verbatim; this library is not weaker than the reference implementation. 4. The rationale is sound: the native library has no ImageIO/AWT (DECISIONS.md "Visible signatures"), so a JPEG cannot be re-encoded; the raw bytes also feed the deterministic prepare/complete seed (SignatureImage.java:83-86 "The bytes that identify this image in the signature's deterministic seed"), so the file is kept as the caller supplied it. The image is an input chosen by the integrating application (a signature stamp/logo), which can strip metadata before calling; the library is a signing library, not an image sanitiser. A marker-level APPn/COM strip would be a reasonable hardening enhancement (note APP0/JFIF and APP14/Adobe affect decoding and must be kept), but as filed, "security/low, GDPR leak" overstates a documented and upstream-consistent choice. Calibrated severity: info.
F-046 First-isolate probe caches a transient failure for the lifetime of the process rust/dss/src/engine.rs:536
  • Reproduce: The mechanics are as cited: rust/dss/src/engine.rs:535-547 keeps static FIRST: OnceLock<i32> and control_main (engine.rs:556-559) returns Err(Error::Isolate(rc)) on every later build once the probe failed. However this is a documented, reasoned decision, not a defect. The doc comment at engine.rs:532-534 and docs/DECISIONS.md:363-369 (reproduced in C per docs/native-library.md:92-96) state: "if the *first* graal_create_isolate of a process fails, every later graal_create_isolate in that process hangs, spinning inside the library." After a failed probe there is therefore nothing to retry: not caching the failure would make the next build hang the calling thread instead of returning an error. The cache converts a guaranteed hang into an immediate typed error, which is strictly better. The finding's impact ("cannot obtain an engine again") cannot occur: the probe runs before the first engine (engine.rs:556), so a failed probe means no engine was ever obtained; when the probe succeeds the cached value is 0 and Ok(()) is returned forever. "Transient" is unsupported: the probe passes null params, so a failure is process-level, and under the documented bug the process is already poisoned. The only residual is cosmetic: Error::Isolate's Display string ("GraalVM isolate error {0}", rust/dss/src/error.rs:60-61) does not say the refusal is per-process permanent, while DECISIONS.md already says "OnceLock, once per process". That is an info-level message/doc nit, not an operational defect.
F-047 UTF-8 encoder uses an int write offset, so a result over 2 GiB would write out of bounds java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/ffi/DssLib.java:307
  • Reproduce: The textual mismatch is exactly as quoted: /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/ffi/DssLib.java:291 long size = 0; sizes the buffer, :305 mallocs WordFactory.unsigned(size + 1), then :306 int o = 0; and :315-:327 out.write(o++, (byte) ...) use the write(int, byte) overload (javap of nativeimage-25.4.4.1.1 shows CCharPointer also has write(SignedWord, byte), so a long offset is available). If o wrapped past Integer.MAX_VALUE the next write would land ~2 GiB before the buffer. However, the condition is unreachable through any entry point. s.length() is an int, so UTF-8 size can exceed 2^31-1 only when the string holds >~715M-1.07G non-ASCII chars (ASCII content gives size == len <= Integer.MAX_VALUE, and the final out.write(o, 0) at index len still fits). Every string that reaches toC(String) is result JSON from DssJsonApi (init/status/version/shutdown/validate/prepare/extend/complete, lines 82-234): metadata built from DSS reports, error messages and base64 (ASCII) fields; PreparedSignature.toMap() (engine/PreparedSignature.java:30-40) only emits a base64 digest and the DER signed attributes, not the document. The large payloads, the extended/signed document and the TL snapshot, go through the separate byte[] path at DssLib.java:263-272 (CTypeConversion.asByteBuffer(out, document.length).put(document), bounded by the byte[] limit and MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES at :66). No API path produces a multi-gigabyte, mostly non-ASCII JSON string, and the finding itself states "Not reachable in practice". Per the verification rules an unreachable path is refuted; the one-line hardening (use a long offset with write(WordFactory.signed(o), b)) remains a reasonable tidy-up at info level.
F-056 Blocking semantics of validate/extend/sign and of Drop are not stated for async callers rust/dss/src/engine.rs:149
  • Reproduce: The mechanics are as the finding says, but the documentation claim is largely false. Mechanics confirmed: validate_json/extend_json/prepare_signature_json/complete_signature_json each do result.recv().map_err(|_| Error::Closed)?? (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:163, 194, 222, 262), and Drop does self.jobs.take(); self.refresh.take(); for t in self.threads.drain(..) { let _ = t.join(); } then sends Control::TearDown and joins the control thread (engine.rs:428-441). Documentation, however, already states this. (1) The Drop semantics the finding says are undocumented are documented verbatim on the Engine type: engine.rs:81 "Dropping the engine waits for queued work and for a running online refresh, then tears down the isolate." (2) The same doc comment (engine.rs:77-79) says validate/extend/signing "run on the engine's worker threads, online refreshes on a separate thread ... Status calls never wait for either", and the functions are plain synchronous fn ... -> Result<T> (no futures), which in Rust means blocking by construction. (3) build is labelled "Blocking." (engine.rs:69) and refresh_trusted_lists "Blocking; validations keep running." (engine.rs:272). (4) docs/DECISIONS.md:357 states the design: "Calls are blocking, with a reply channel per call", and DECISIONS.md:373-375 that the core API "stays runtime-agnostic" with the tokio-feature schedule::RefreshScheduler running refreshes "through spawn_blocking"; rust/dss/src/schedule.rs:32-33 repeats "Each refresh runs on tokio's blocking pool" and schedule.rs:60 shows the spawn_blocking pattern in-crate, so third-party async users do have an in-tree example. The only residual gap is that the word "blocking" is not literally repeated on the validate/extend/sign doc comments, which is an info-level wording nit, not a defect; "async runtimes stall" applies to any synchronous call and is not specific to this crate. Refuted as described (Drop is documented, blocking is documented at type level, in DECISIONS.md, and in the scheduler); at most an info-level suggestion to add the word "Blocking." to four doc comments.
F-083 5xx bodies pass internal diagnostics to clients: Java exception class names, panic payloads and library messages rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:505
  • Reproduce: The mechanism described is real at the code level, but it is a documented, deliberate pass-through in a sidecar whose threat model excludes public exposure, and the details are already logged on both sides; so the finding is not a defect as described, at most a hardening suggestion. What the code does (confirmed): - java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssJsonApi.java:213: return error(DssError.Code.INTERNAL_ERROR, t.getClass().getName() + ": " + t.getMessage()); (catch Throwable). Only class name + getMessage(), no stack trace. - rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:497-505: Error::Api { code, message } => ... ApiError::new(status_of(code), &name, message) and lib.rs:545 builds the body {"ok": false, "error": {"code": .., "message": ..}} with that message unchanged. - rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:309: .map_err(|e| ApiError::internal(format!("engine call failed: {e}"))); tokio 1.54.1's JoinError Display (registry src/runtime/task/error.rs:139-145) is task {} panicked with message {:?}, so a panic payload string would be in the body. However Engine methods map worker-thread panics to Error::Closed (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:163,194,222,262,296), which the server turns into 503 NOT_INITIALIZED with the fixed text "engine is shut down" (lib.rs:507). A JoinError needs the spawn_blocking closure itself to panic, i.e. a panic in the dss crate's calling code, which is not a reachable path by request content. Why it is refuted as a defect: 1. Documented design: docs/DECISIONS.md:835-836 "Multipart in, the library's JSON out. ... results pass through verbatim, so README.md's contract is also the HTTP contract"; docs/server.md:99-100 "The body is always {ok:false, error:{code,message}}: the library's code"; server.md:110 "500 | INVALID_CONFIG, INTERNAL_ERROR (including an engine out of heap)". The library test rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:529-530 asserts err.to_string().contains("OutOfMemoryError"), so the Java class name inside the INTERNAL_ERROR message is a contractual, tested part of the library's error text, not an accident. 2. Threat model: docs/DECISIONS.md:856-857 "There is no TLS: the server is meant for the same host or a private network", with an optional constant-time bearer token (lib.rs:285-291); docs/server.md:216 "never expose it publicly". A client that can reach the sidecar is a trusted application. 3. The recommendation's "log the details" is already in place: DssJsonApi.java:208-212 logs "Unexpected failure" with the Throwable (stack trace) and lib.rs:541-543 prints every 5xx (if self.status.is_server_error() { eprintln!(...) }). Only the generic-message-plus-correlation-id part is missing, and in exchange the current design gives the PHP client (php/DssException.php:25 "{$errorCode}: {$message}") an actionable message. 4. Disclosed content has little attack value: exception class names and messages such as java.lang.OutOfMemoryError, no stack traces, no secrets. INVALID_CONFIG messages that include server paths (TrustedListManager.java:132,144) are produced at engine start, which exits the process (DECISIONS.md:847-849), not per request. Net: the behaviour exists exactly as stated, but it is a documented and reasonable decision for a private-network sidecar and is already logged; calibrated as informational hardening, not a security finding.
F-087 Server graceful shutdown has no deadline and AppState::shutdown does not tear the engine down as documented rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:86
  • Reproduce: The finding's central claim ("the orderly exit the docs promise does not happen") is contradicted by the code and by two live reproductions. What the docs promise (docs/server.md:27): "On SIGTERM or Ctrl-C the server stops accepting connections, finishes the requests in progress (and a running refresh), then exits with status 0." Waiting for a running refresh is the documented intent, not a defect. How the code delivers it: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:172-177 awaits graceful shutdown, then Arc::into_inner(state) and spawn_blocking(move || state.shutdown()). AppState::shutdown (lib.rs:86-91) aborts the scheduler task and drops its own Arc<Engine>. The finding is right that this is often not the last reference: the scheduler task (schedule.rs:59 let e = Arc::clone(&engine)) and the in-flight spawn_blocking(move || e.refresh_trusted_lists()) (schedule.rs:60) still hold clones. But that does not lose the teardown: main returns, #[tokio::main] drops the runtime, and tokio 1.54.1 (rust/Cargo.lock:748) documents at src/runtime/runtime.rs:466 "dropping a runtime will block indefinitely for spawned blocking tasks to complete" (BlockingPool::drop -> shutdown(None), pool.rs:343-346). When the blocking refresh returns, its e clone (and the aborted scheduler task's clone, dropped at scheduler shutdown) release the last Arc, so impl Drop for Engine (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:428-441) joins the worker/refresh threads and sends Control::TearDown before the process exits. abort() being asynchronous is irrelevant to this ordering. Reproduction (release binary rust/target/release/dss-server, LOTL URL pointed at a local tarpit socket that accepts and never answers, http.response_timeout_ms=15000): 1. --refresh-hours 0, POST /tl/refresh, /health shows refresh_in_progress:true, SIGTERM after ~2 s: stderr prints "dss-server: stopping" at once, then "[dss-tl-2] ... Read timed out" and "online trusted-list refresh completed in 15020 ms", process exits with status 0 after 12.99 s. 2. --refresh-hours 1 with an empty cache (scheduler's refresh-on-start path, schedule.rs:47-52), SIGTERM after "engine ready": same behaviour, exit status 0 after 12.53 s, after the refresh timed out. Both show exactly the documented behaviour: the refresh is finished, the exit is orderly with status 0, nothing is left mid-write by the server itself. The existing test rust/dss-server/tests/process.rs:75-117 (serves_until_sigterm) also asserts "stopping" plus exit status 0. What remains is not what the finding states: there is no stop deadline, so if an operator sends SIGTERM while a full EU refresh is in progress (measured 9.7 s on first start, docs/DECISIONS.md:889; "about 15 s", docs/server.md:20) and Docker's default 10 s grace expires, the container is SIGKILLed mid-refresh. That is a direct consequence of the documented "finishes a running refresh" decision; docker/dss-server/Dockerfile and docs/server.md do not mention raising stop_grace_period. That is an informational documentation note, not the defect described (the finding claims the opposite: that the server does not wait/tear down). The doc comment on shutdown() (lib.rs:84-85) is also accurate as written: it is conditional on "dropping the last reference", which is exactly what Engine::drop does when the refresh's clone goes away.
F-088 dss-server has no access log, request ids or metrics; only 5xx lines are logged rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:525
  • Reproduce: The factual observations hold, but they describe a documented, deliberate scope rather than a defect. Facts confirmed in the code: - rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:105-121 builds the Router with only route_layer(authorize) and .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(...)); there is no TraceLayer, request-id or metrics layer, and no /metrics route. rust/dss-server/Cargo.toml has no tower-http, tracing or metrics dependency. - rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:522-526: if self.status.is_server_error() { eprintln!("dss-server: {} {}: {}", ...) } — only 5xx ApiErrors are logged, plain stderr, no timestamp. All other process logging is eprintln!("dss-server: ...") (main.rs:107,133,145,160,167,173,202; lib.rs:223). Why it is refuted as a finding: 1. It is a documented decision. docs/server.md:29-30 states: "Logs go to stderr: start-up, each refresh, every 5xx error, and the library's own messages at --log-level." That is exactly the behaviour observed; the finding restates the design as a bug. 2. It is reasonable for the stated deployment. docs/DECISIONS.md:817-870 describes dss-server as a sidecar for one Laravel application "meant for the same host or a private network", shipped as a Docker image (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile). In that setting stderr is captured by the container runtime / journald, which add timestamps, so the "no timestamps" point is handled by the platform; an access log for a single trusted client is optional scope. 3. The "outage floods logs with one line per request" claim is overstated: /health (lib.rs:251-255) returns its 503 "starting" body directly via json_response, not through ApiError::into_response, so orchestrator health probes during the 4-8 s start-up do not log. Only API calls made before the engine is ready (NotInitialized / TrustedListsNotLoaded → 503, lib.rs:486) log one line each, and a client calling the API before /health is green is itself a condition worth a line. 4. Request ids, JSON logs and /metrics are enhancement requests, not a defect: nothing is incorrect, insecure or unreachable. Residual: the point is legitimate as a wish-list item (severity info), and if the operator does want alerting, a /metrics endpoint would need adding. But as stated ("defect") it is refuted by the documented and consistent design.
F-108 PHP client base URL is unvalidated, the bearer token defaults to plain HTTP, and redirects are followed php/DssClient.php:24
  • Reproduce: The three facts in the finding are literally true of php/DssClient.php (line 24 private readonly string $baseUrl = 'http://dss:8484', line 100 $this->http->baseUrl($this->baseUrl)->timeout(...)->acceptJson() with no scheme check and no withoutRedirecting()), but none of them is a defect in this code base. 1. Base URL "unvalidated": the value is operator configuration, not request input. docs/server.md:134-152 shows the only documented wiring: 'url' => env('DSS_URL', 'http://dss:8484') from config/services.php injected via a service-provider singleton. Nothing attacker-controlled flows into $baseUrl; sending the bearer token to the configured server is the client's purpose. There is no meaningful validation the client could do beyond a scheme check, and that check would be wrong, see 2. 2. "Defaults to plain HTTP": dss-server has no TLS at all, by documented decision. docs/server.md:216-217: "No TLS. Run the sidecar on the same host or on a private network, as above, and never expose it publicly. The token stops other containers on the same network from using it." docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857: "There is no TLS: the server is meant for the same host or a private network." The Compose example (server.md:184-212) uses DSS_URL: http://dss:8484 and says "Do not publish the port". An https:// default or an https-only check would make the client unusable against the server it is written for. The default matches the only transport the server offers, and the trusted-network requirement the finding asks to "document" is already documented in server.md's Security section. 3. "Redirects are followed": (a) dss-server never issues one: grep -rn -i "redirect\|Location" rust/dss-server/src/*.rs returns nothing. (b) Even if some intermediate hop redirected, Guzzle's RedirectMiddleware (checked in a local Guzzle 7.16.1 copy, vendor/guzzlehttp/guzzle/src/RedirectMiddleware.php:219-222) removes the header on cross-origin redirects: if (Psr7\UriComparator::isCrossOrigin($request->getUri(), $modify['uri'])) { $modify['remove_headers'][] = 'Authorization'; ... }. So the token cannot be forwarded to a different origin; a same-origin redirect only re-sends it to the already-trusted server. Calling withoutRedirecting() would change nothing in practice. Net: no reachable leak, the configuration model is the documented one, and the "plain HTTP" choice is a deliberate, documented decision for a same-host/private-network sidecar. The finding is at most a hardening note, not a defect.
F-128 collect-rust-licenses.py is run without -I, unlike the project's stated convention scripts/package.sh:41
  • Reproduce: The factual part reproduces: scripts/package.sh:41 is python3 "$root/scripts/collect-rust-licenses.py" "$out/licenses/rust", with no -I, and CI runs it (.github/workflows/ci.yml:108 run: scripts/package.sh). But the premise that this departs from "the project's stated convention" does not hold, and the stated impact is not real in this context. 1. There is no project-wide convention. python3 -I appears in exactly three places, all for one script: README.md:82 (python3 -I scripts/merge-metadata.py), docs/reflection-audit.md:222 (same line), and merge-metadata.py:10 (its own docstring: "Run with python3 -I scripts/merge-metadata.py"). docs/DECISIONS.md has no mention of -I or any Python invocation policy (grep for "python" in DECISIONS.md hits only the SPDX/licensing lines 899/906). There is no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. merge-metadata.py's -I is tied to its purpose: it parses java/target/agent-output JSON produced by the tracing agent (merge-metadata.py:4-10), i.e. generated data, which matches the generic "run Python that reads downloaded/extracted data with -I" advice. collect-rust-licenses.py (lines 17-21, 29-41) imports only stdlib (json, shutil, subprocess, sys, pathlib) and reads rustc -vV / cargo metadata --locked output from the repository's own lockfile. 2. The claimed vector ("the environment and the script directory can affect packaging") is already moot. -I would (a) drop the script's directory from sys.path and (b) ignore PYTHON* env vars and user site-packages. For (a), scripts/ contains only collect-rust-licenses.py, merge-metadata.py, shell scripts, agent/caller-filter.json and ci/*.sh (full find scripts -type f listing); nothing there can shadow json, shutil, subprocess, sys or pathlib, and the directory is committed source, not downloaded data. For (b), package.sh already fully trusts the same environment: it runs cargo build (line 23), git (31, 44), objdump/otool (54, 58) and executes the freshly built binaries (63-64) with whatever PATH/env the caller has. An attacker who controls PYTHONPATH or user site-packages controls PATH and CARGO_HOME too, so adding -I to the one Python line provides no additional boundary. 3. Adding -I would be harmless (the script uses Path(__file__) which still works under -I, and no site packages are needed), so it is at most an optional stylistic tweak, not a defect. Severity: info at most; the finding as titled ("unlike the project's stated convention") misstates the repo's documentation.
F-130 Woodstox 6.5.1 is the runtime StAX implementation; hardening fixes exist only in 7.x java/pom.xml:125
  • Reproduce: The factual chain is confirmed: offline dependency:tree shows dss-tsl-validation:6.5.1 (java/pom.xml:125) -> dss-xades -> dss-xml-utils -> org.apache.santuario:xmlsec:3.0.6 -> com.fasterxml.woodstox:woodstox-core:6.5.1 (runtime) -> stax2-api 4.2.1; the version comes from the imported dss-bom (pom.xml:85-86) and is nowhere declared in the repo. It is registered in the image (reachability-metadata.json:10-13 com.ctc.wstx.sr.Attribute[], com.ctc.wstx.stax.WstxInputFactory; :796 META-INF/services/javax.xml.stream.XMLInputFactory; docs/reflection-audit.md:114) and is genuinely reached with external XML: eu.europa.esig.dss.jaxb.common.AbstractJaxbFacade.avoidXXE does XMLInputFactory.newInstance() (ServiceLoader picks Woodstox), sets javax.xml.stream.supportDTD=false and javax.xml.stream.isSupportingExternalEntities=false, and eu.europa.esig.dss.tsl.parsing.AbstractParsingTask unmarshals trusted lists via TrustedListFacade.unmarshall(InputStream, boolean) through that path (jdeps/javap on the jars; no other classpath jar references XMLInputFactory except xmlsec's own StAX API, which DSS does not use). The defect claim, however, does not hold. Impact "XML DoS limits lag upstream" is contradicted by evidence: javap -constants com.ctc.wstx.api.ReaderConfig gives identical limits in 6.5.1 and 6.7.0 (DEFAULT_MAX_ELEMENT_DEPTH=1000, DEFAULT_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT=100000, DEFAULT_MAX_ENTITY_DEPTH=500, DEFAULT_MAX_DTD_DEPTH=500, DEFAULT_MAX_ATTRIBUTES_PER_ELEMENT=1000, DEFAULT_MAX_ATTRIBUTE_LENGTH=524288), the 6.5.1->6.7.0 class diff is only shaded MSV internals, and the upstream release-notes/VERSION file (fetched) lists no entry from 6.6.0 through 7.3.0 that changes any of those limits; the DTD-depth/stack-overflow fix (CVE-2022-40152) landed in 6.4.0, which 6.5.1 already includes. The only 7.x limit-related entry (#341, P_MAX_TEXT_LENGTH counting skipped text) is moot because mMaxTextLength defaults to 2147483647 in 6.5.1. The 7.x XXE-related entries (#211/#226/#321 SAX layer, #162 ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD, #330 MSV schema factories) do not affect DSS's StAX usage, where DTDs and external entities are already disabled. What remains in 7.x are input-strictness fixes (#291 overlong UTF-8, #293 out-of-range UTF-32) with no CVE, which the finding itself concedes. The recommended 6.7.0 bump would change nothing relevant, and the version follows DSS 6.5.1's own BOM, consistent with docs/DECISIONS.md Phase 0 (dependencies pinned to what DSS 6.5.1 builds against). So the title is at most a generic "dependency is not the newest" note with no demonstrated weakness: severity info, refuted as described.
F-136 Apache-2.0 code statically combined with LGPL-2.1 DSS: the compatibility rationale (via LGPL-3) is undocumented docs/DECISIONS.md:916
  • Reproduce: The finding's premise ("the combination works only under LGPL-3.0") misreads the licences, and its documentation claim ("the docs do not say so") is false on the repository's own text. 1. Premise is wrong for LGPL-2.1. The Apache-2.0/GPLv2 incompatibility arises when Apache code must be relicensed under GPLv2 inside a single GPL'd work. LGPL-2.1 is weak copyleft: §6 lets a work combined with the Library be distributed "under terms of your choice" subject to relinking/source conditions, and §7 permits a combined library with "other library facilities not covered by this License". Here only DSS and the wrapper are LGPL; PDFBox, xmlsec, HttpClient, Commons and Woodstox stay Apache-2.0 with their notices passed on. /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/LICENSING.md states exactly this rationale under "Why LGPL, and how replaceability works": "dss-native meets LGPL-2.1 §6 by giving users everything needed to rebuild the native library against a modified DSS", followed by the four concrete mechanisms (published source, dss.version property, build-native.sh, stable C ABI), and "Applications that embed dss-native must give their users the same ability ... They must also pass on the notices of the components below". The component table lists each Apache-2.0 jar with its licence. 2. The combination is upstream's, not an assumption introduced here. /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/java/pom.xml declares only eu.europa.ec.joinup.sd-dss artifacts (lines 97-147: dss-validation, dss-pades-pdfbox, dss-utils-apache-commons, ...); the Apache-2.0 jars arrive as DSS's own dependencies (~/.m2/.../dss-pades-pdfbox-6.5.1.pom line 37-38: <groupId>org.apache.pdfbox</groupId><artifactId>pdfbox</artifactId>), and DSS's sources carry "either version 2.1 of the License, or (at your option) any later version" (PdfBoxUtils.java header). The European Commission already ships LGPL-2.1-or-later DSS combined with these Apache-2.0 libraries. 3. Even on the finding's own theory, nothing is unstated: the project is LGPL-2.1-or-later everywhere. LICENSING.md: "GNU Lesser General Public License, version 2.1 or (at your option) any later version (LGPL-2.1-or-later)"; README.md:546-547 says the same; every source file carries SPDX-License-Identifier: LGPL-2.1-or-later (e.g. java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/visible/SrgbProfileTest.java:4). A recipient who believes LGPL-3.0 is needed for Apache-2.0 compatibility already has it at their option, and the docs say so. 4. The cited lines docs/DECISIONS.md:916-917 ("Checked: every runtime jar and crate is under a licence compatible with distributing the combined library and executables (Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD-2/3-Clause, EDL, Unlicense, OFL, GPLv2 + Classpath Exception)") are a decision-log summary; the rationale lives in LICENSING.md, which DECISIONS.md:899 and README.md:25/550 point to. The only residual truth is that LICENSING.md does not spell out the Apache-2.0-vs-LGPL-2.1 compatibility argument in licence-theory terms, and "have counsel review" is generic advice applicable to any project. That is at most an informational doc nicety, not a defect in the legal position as the finding describes it.
F-137 SOURCE records HEAD without detecting a modified working tree scripts/package.sh:31
  • Reproduce: The literal observation is correct: scripts/package.sh:31 is commit="$(git -C "$root" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)" and nothing in the script (or anywhere under scripts/ or .github/, grep for porcelain/diff-index/--dirty returns nothing) checks the working tree. But the finding misreads the design and its recommendation would break the release path. 1. The release build is dirty by design. .github/workflows/ci.yml:80-84 runs scripts/ci/set-version.sh "$VERSION" on the checkout before any build, and :107-108 runs scripts/package.sh afterwards. set-version.sh rewrites the committed java/pom.xml and rust/Cargo.toml in place (sed -i.bak ... "$pom", "$cargo"), and its header says "The committed files keep the 0.0.0-dev placeholder: nothing else holds a version." docs/DECISIONS.md:488-491 documents the same. So every official package is produced from a working tree that differs from HEAD by exactly the version stamp. "Mark the package dirty or fail" (the recommendation) would therefore fail or mis-flag every release build; the state the finding calls a defect is the normal, documented state. 2. The commit pointer does match the binary's source in that path. The workflow triggers on release: types: [published] (ci.yml:22-23) and checks out the tag, so git rev-parse HEAD is the tag's commit; the only divergence is the version string, reproducible from the tag name with set-version.sh (README.md:195-196, DECISIONS.md:488-491). That is what SOURCE is for (LICENSING.md:111, "the repository and commit the package was built from" for the LGPL rebuild path). 3. "Record the stamped version" is already done: package.sh:27-28 reads library= from the generated java/target/classes/.../version.properties (the stamped pom version) and :43 writes dss-native $version ($platform), commit $commit into SOURCE, so the package name, SOURCE and the binary all carry the stamped version. 4. The only scenario in which the pointer can mismatch is a developer running package.sh by hand with uncommitted code changes. Such a package reports version 0.0.0-dev (README.md:195-196: "placeholder 0.0.0-dev, which local and non-release builds report"), which already marks it as a non-release build, and DECISIONS.md:496-497 states CI (releases, or manual runs) is the packaging path. No distribution path is affected; the residual risk is an ad-hoc local tarball, which is info-level at most and not the "defect" as described.
F-138 An application that ships only the library (build/native) gets no SOURCE pointer scripts/build-native.sh:48
  • Reproduce: The literal observation holds: grep -n SOURCE scripts/*.sh shows only scripts/package.sh:42: cat > "$out/SOURCE" <<EOF; scripts/build-native.sh (lines 45-62) writes licenses/ only (LGPL, DSS/PT Serif/stax2 notices, per-jar LICENSE/NOTICE, GraalVM LICENSE.txt/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSE.txt/legal/, and release). But the finding mischaracterises this as a licensing defect, and its impact statement does not survive the code: 1. Documented, intentional scope. LICENSING.md's table containing the SOURCE row is explicitly headed "Release packages" (lines 104-116: "A release package (scripts/package.sh), and the Docker image... carries..."). Lines 118-119 then say only that build-native.sh writes "the same licenses/, without rust/... so an application that ships only the library takes its notices from there" - it never claims SOURCE lands in build/native. docs/DECISIONS.md:513 and :915 likewise attribute SOURCE to package.sh ("a SOURCE file with repository and commit, for the LGPL rebuild path"). So the cited evidence (LICENSING.md:118-119) describes exactly the current behaviour; nothing is out of step with its documentation. 2. The recipient of build/native is the builder, not a downstream. build/native/<os>-<arch>/ is never distributed by the project: .github/workflows/ci.yml uploads only dist/*.tar.gz / dist/*.sha256 (lines 111-115) after scripts/package.sh (line 108); build-native.sh is a local step (lines 87, 153). Anyone who has build/native has run scripts/build-native.sh from a checkout, so they already hold the repository, the commit (git rev-parse HEAD, exactly what package.sh writes), and the DSS version pinned in java/pom.xml / java/target/classes/.../version.properties. The LGPL §6 source-offer obligation towards end users is the embedder's, and the embedder has everything SOURCE would tell them. 3. The GPL part is already covered in build/native. The only GPL-licensed code in the library is the GraalVM/Substrate runtime (GPLv2+CPE), and build-native.sh:59-61 copies $JAVA_HOME/release into licenses/graalvm/ precisely for that: the built tree at build/native/macos-aarch64/licenses/graalvm/release line 9 contains SOURCE=".:git:391a5a739cb6+ ... substratevm:95ce1499c8c96ab7d5a6697c5b4bf42160f3b68b ...". So "embedders ship ... GPL code without source information" is false even for the library-only directory. What remains is a convenience suggestion (also emit the repo/commit/DSS-tag pointer in build/native so an embedder can copy it verbatim), not a defect: the behaviour is a documented and reasonable decision and the stated impact is not supported. Severity info.
F-145 Release redistributes EU trusted lists without reuse attribution; Docker image GPL source duties not mentioned LICENSING.md:131
  • Reproduce: Both halves of F-145 fail on the cited text and the code around it. 1. "Source acknowledgement missing" for the seed trusted-list cache. LICENSING.md:131-133 is itself the acknowledgement: "The seed trusted-list cache attached to each release holds the EU List of Trusted Lists and the national trusted lists exactly as the European Commission and the Member States publish them under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS)." It names the publishers, the legal basis, and that the lists are unmodified, which is what a reuse acknowledgement (e.g. Decision 2011/833/EU: source acknowledged, content not distorted) asks for. The origin is also intrinsic to the shipped data: the seed tarball is DSS's FileCacheDataLoader cache (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:165-173, setFileCacheDirectory(tlCache.toFile())), and DSS names every cache file after its publication URL (DSSUtils.getNormalizedString(url) at FileCacheDataLoader.java:220/270/330 in the dss-service 6.5.1 sources jar); the test caches on disk show the pattern, e.g. https___ec_europa_eu_tools_lotl_Final_EU_TSL_UKsigned_xml, http___tl_nbu_gov_sk_kca_tsl_tsl_xml. Each list is the Member State's own signed XML with its scheme operator name. The release pipeline (.github/workflows/ci.yml:165-212) uploads this cache next to packages that carry LICENSING.md. Trusted lists are published under eIDAS Art. 22 for automated consumption by relying parties, and caching them is their intended use (DSS does the same). A more ceremonial "© European Union" line would be a stylistic preference, not a missing obligation. 2. "Docker image GPL source duties not mentioned / Debian source note missing". The project does not distribute a Docker image at all. grep -rln -i docker .github scripts returns nothing: ci.yml has no docker build or registry push, and the release-assets job uploads only packages, the seed cache and the OJ keystore (ci.yml:183-212). docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:4-7 and docs/server.md:176-180 tell the user to build the image themselves from a release package ("docker build -f docker/dss-server/Dockerfile --build-arg VERSION=1.2.0 ... dist/"). GPL §3 source-offer duties for Debian's packages therefore fall on whichever downstream party distributes an image they built, not on this repository. LICENSING.md:121 and Dockerfile:14-15 correctly say where the Debian notices live. A note telling downstream image distributors about Debian source availability would be optional courtesy guidance, outside the project's own licensing obligations, which docs/DECISIONS.md:896-918 shows were reviewed deliberately (every runtime jar/crate notice collected, SOURCE file, GraalVM component commits). No defect in the project's compliance posture; at most a wording preference. Severity info at best, and refuted as described.
F-168 Differential test cannot catch some divergences: rejections compare equal whatever their codes java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/diff/Outcome.java:79
  • Reproduce: The three factual statements in the finding are accurate as code behaviour, but each is a documented, tested and reasonable design decision rather than a defect, and the "coverage is overstated" impact does not hold. 1. Rejections compare equal regardless of code. Confirmed at java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/diff/Outcome.java:79-81: if (e.error != null) { return; // both rejected the document; the messages legitimately differ }. This is asserted as the intended behaviour by OutcomeTest.java:28: assertTrue(Outcome.compare(Outcome.rejected("x"), Outcome.rejected("y")).isEmpty());. The recommended fix ("compare error codes") is not implementable against this reference: the plain-DSS side has no error codes at all. PlainDssReference.java:124-126 produces Outcome.rejected(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()) (a Java exception class), while the native side at DiffVsNative.java:56 stores error.code (e.g. UNSUPPORTED_DOCUMENT). Mapping DSS exception classes to dss-native codes would put engine knowledge into the reference, which docs/DECISIONS.md:422-431 explicitly rejects ("The reference is plain DSS, not the engine ... Only EngineConfig ... is shared"). The one class of masked divergence that matters (a native-only failure such as a missing reflection registration producing a rejection) is caught by a separate mechanism: scripts/diff-vs-jvm.sh:35-45 greps the native stderr for Missing[A-Za-z]*RegistrationError|UnsupportedCharsetException|UnsupportedFeatureError|UnsatisfiedLinkError|NoClassDefFoundError and fails the run, precisely because "the verdicts alone can hide them" (DECISIONS.md:452-457). 2. Non-signature files are fed in. True: diff-vs-jvm.sh:61 find "$fx" -type f ! -path "*/pki/*" ! -name "README.md" includes content/*.pdf, stamp.jpg and signing/*.json. But this was already the case when the documented "24 documents / 25 signatures" result was recorded (6+4+5+4+1 signed fixtures + content/document.txt + content/document.pdf + 2 detached cases = 24), and the report never counts them as signatures: DiffVsNative.java:86-90 counts signatures from the reference outcome and labels rows "rejected" (line 136) or "no signature" (line 145), and the headline separates "N documents, M signatures" (lines 104-105). The parity test includes content/document.txt deliberately and guards every other fixture with assertTrue(!expected.signatures().isEmpty(), "reference found no signature in " + fixture) (PlainDssParityTest.java:82-84). Note also that the signing/*-cms.sig files are real BER CMS (first byte 0x30), so both sides parse them as CAdES and compare them field by field rather than as rejections. 3. Only validation is compared. True, but the differential test is defined as a validation comparison from the outset (DECISIONS.md:411-419, README.md:209-213: "Per signature it compares indication, sub-indication, level, qualification, signing time and signer DN"). Extension has its own JVM tests (java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExtensionTest.java). The absence of an extend differential pass is a scope choice, not a defect anchored at Outcome.java:79. Residual kernel: within the fixture set, the only both-rejected cases are inputs that are neither PDF nor CMS (DssEngine.java:219-222 UNSUPPORTED_DOCUMENT vs plain DSS's fromDocument exception), which carry no signature to compare anyway, so the class of divergence that the shared-rejection shortcut can hide is narrow and already partly covered by the log grep. At most this is an informational note that the comparator is verdict-oriented by design.
F-169 No test pins the qualification result java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/FixtureValidationTest.java:88
  • Reproduce: Literal claim checks out but the conclusion ("regressions go unnoticed") does not, and the gap is a documented limitation. 1. Literal fact: FixtureValidationTest.fixtureHasExpectedVerdict (java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/FixtureValidationTest.java:82-91) asserts container, transformations, verdicts(r) (indication/sub-indication, lines 149-159), format and the SIMPLE report, and never touches SignatureSummary.qualification (ValidationResult.java:31). True. 2. The synthetic fixtures carry no meaningful qualification to pin. docs/DECISIONS.md:470: "Synthetic fixtures do not exercise QES qualification (the test certificates are not qualified), and the fixtures set uses offline revocation. Real-world coverage comes from testdata/private/." TestPki.java:341-346 issues leaf certs with only basicConstraints/keyUsage, no QcStatements. I ran the built CLI against the seeded synthetic cache (rust/target/synthetic-tl) on the fixtures: pades/b-lta.pdf -> ('TOTAL_PASSED', None, 'UNKNOWN'); pades/b-b.pdf and cades/*.p7m -> ('INDETERMINATE', 'CERTIFICATE_CHAIN_GENERAL_FAILURE', 'INDETERMINATE_UNKNOWN'); tampered/pades/b-b.pdf -> ('TOTAL_FAILED', 'HASH_FAILURE', 'NOT_ADES'). The qualification is a trivial function of the already-pinned indication (UNKNOWN / INDETERMINATE_UNKNOWN / NOT_ADES), so pinning it in this test would add essentially no regression signal. 3. Qualification is already guarded in the default (offline) test run: PlainDssParityTest (java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/diff/PlainDssParityTest.java:34-96, not tagged online) validates every fixture through the engine and through plain DSS and asserts Outcome.compare(expected, actual) is empty; Outcome.compare includes field(p + "qualification", es.qualification(), as.qualification(), out) (Outcome.java:95). A wrapper regression in the qualification field therefore fails the normal ./mvnw test, and the native differential run (DiffVsNative.java:102, README.md:212) compares it again against real private documents, which is where qualified certificates actually appear. Net: a documented, reasonable decision with the field already covered by parity tests; at most a cosmetic suggestion, not a coverage hole.
F-170 Timing-dependent assertions in the JVM suite java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TlSnapshotTest.java:210
  • Reproduce: The three cited assertions do depend on wall-clock time, but reading the code and measuring an actual run shows the margins are far too wide to support "flaky releases", and the test design already contains the mitigations the finding asks for. 1. TlSnapshotTest.java:208-215 (listsThatExpiredSinceTheExportAreRejectedWhenExpiredListsAreRefused). built = Instant.now() is taken, then withNextUpdateIn(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).serveOn(t.http), two exportFrom calls, then Thread.sleep(Math.max(0, Duration.between(Instant.now(), built.plusSeconds(6)).toMillis())). The sleep is to an absolute deadline, not a fixed duration, and SyntheticTrustedLists.java:165/181 builds NextUpdate from Instant.now().truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.SECONDS) plus 5 s, so NextUpdate <= built+5s and the deadline built+6s always lies past it: the "expired" side is deterministic. The only timing exposure is that the strict export must load its lists before NextUpdate (~4-5 s after serveOn). Measured: the whole test took 6.495 s with ~6 s of sleep, and a test that does one full exportFrom plus a rejection (unexpectedClassesAreRefusedBeforeTheyAreInstantiated) took 0.059 s. That is roughly a 50x margin against a local FakeHttp with synthetic lists. 2. ConcurrentRefreshTest.java:110 (assertTrue(during >= VALIDATOR_THREADS * REFRESHES) = 24). The test forces the overlap window: t.http.beforeEachRequest(() -> sleep(DOWNLOAD_DELAY_MS)) with DOWNLOAD_DELAY_MS=100 and 3 requests (LOTL + IT + DE) per refresh, so 6 refreshes take >= 1.8 s regardless of machine speed, and validators are never blocked (TrustedListManager.java:72 "Validators only ever read snapshots. Refreshes are serialized", via a volatile Snapshot). Measured output: "Concurrent run: 64 validations, 60 of them while 6 refreshes ran" (60 vs the required 24, 2.5x). The assertion is the test's purpose (proving refreshes do not stall validation) and a latch cannot express "many validations completed while a refresh was in flight" without the same wall-clock element. 3. TrustedListTest.java:111 (assertTrue(ms < 10_000, ...)). The whole startupLoadsFromCacheWithoutNetwork test took 0.062 s, a ~160x margin on a generous sanity bound; the functional assertions (no network hits, loaded, 3 trusted certificates, verdict) do not depend on it. Additional context: docs/DECISIONS.md:479 states CI runs only on published releases or by hand, and TrustedListTest.java:208-209 already uses CountDownLatch where ordering (not duration) is what is tested, so the author distinguishes the two cases. The "overlap counts" and "5 s window" are real timing assumptions, but with 2.5x-160x measured headroom against a loopback fake HTTP server and deadline-based sleeps, there is no positive evidence of flakiness. The finding is at most an observation, not a defect; refuted per the default (claim not confirmable, design reasonable).

  • Reproduce: The observations are factually accurate for this working copy but describe untracked, git-ignored local outputs that the repository already handles, so there is no defect at commit 7e697c9. .gitignore contains rust/target/, /build/, /dist/ and testdata/private/* (with only !testdata/private/README.md re-included); git ls-files dist build rust/target is empty and git status --ignored lists all three as !!. dist/: dist/dss-native-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT-macos-aarch64/SOURCE reads "dss-native 0.1.0-SNAPSHOT (macos-aarch64), commit cf94a96" (cf94a96 = "Phase 5" on main) next to the current 0.0.0-dev package (commit 1d0dd2c; version 0.0.0-dev at java/pom.xml:14 and rust/Cargo.toml:6). scripts/package.sh:33-34 (out="$root/dist/$name"; rm -rf "$out") only replaces the package of the current name, so an older one lingers, but README.md:198 and docs/DECISIONS.md:510 document dist/ as the package output and it is ignored. build/diff: build/diff/private.md, private.cases and private.native.jsonl do carry signer DNs from the three testdata/private PDFs (real names, a tax code), yet README.md:213 ("reports go to build/diff/"), docs/DECISIONS.md:420 and testdata/private/README.md state exactly that; /build/ is ignored; CI cannot produce a private report because testdata/private/* never reaches it; and the packaged tarball (tar tzf dist/dss-native-0.0.0-dev-macos-aarch64.tar.gz) contains only lib/, include/, bin/, share/dss-native/{oj-keystore.p12,README.md}, no diff/private/jsonl entries, so no leak vector exists. rust/target/tmp (907 dirs, 8 MB) is CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR, used by rust/dss/tests/common/mod.rs:29-38 (temp_dir, which only removes a pre-existing dir of the same name before creating it) and rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs:267; cargo's documented convention is that this scratch space accumulates and is removed by cargo clean.   • Reproduce: The raw facts hold: testdata/fixtures/pki/test-pki.p12 is tracked by git (git ls-files), testdata/fixtures/README.md:27 documents the password dss-native-test (verified: openssl pkcs12 -passin pass:dss-native-test lists the root, "Mario Rossi (TEST)", "Giulia Bianchi (TEST)", TSA, LOTL/TL signers and a DE CA), and root-ca.pem has notAfter=Dec 27 2045 with basicConstraints CA:TRUE and no nameConstraints. (2) The impact ("misuse outside tests would let anyone forge trusted signatures") has no reachable path: grep over rust/dss/src, rust/dss-cli/src, rust/dss-server/src, rust/dss-sys/src and java/src/main for fixtures|test-pki|root-ca returns no hits; the root is trusted only when a caller explicitly passes it in extra_trusted_certificates, whose default is [] (README.md:284), as the tests (rust/dss/tests/common/mod.rs:46, rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:39, rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs:27) and scripts/smoke-test-c.sh:32 do deliberately.   • Reproduce: The narrow factual observation is accurate: /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/.gitattributes contains only two rules (testdata/ -text and trust/ -text, lines 3-4, plus a two-line comment explaining they exist because "Line-ending conversion ... rewrites the CRLFs inside text-like PDFs and CMS files"), and git check-attr -a on java/mvnw and scripts/*.sh returns no attributes, so a Windows clone with core.autocrlf=true would convert them to CRLF. F-178 0.0.0-dev placeholder in pom.xml and Cargo.toml relies entirely on CI stamping java/pom.xml:14
  • Reproduce: The observation itself is accurate but it is a documented, deliberate design decision rather than a defect, so under the audit rules it is refuted. What the code does (confirmed): java/pom.xml:14 is <version>0.0.0-dev</version> and rust/Cargo.toml:6 is version = "0.0.0-dev" under [workspace.package]; all four crates use version.workspace = true. The only place a real version comes from is scripts/ci/set-version.sh, which rewrites both files with sed from the release tag (ci.yml:47-58 scripts/ci/set-version.sh "${TAG#v}", repeated per build job at ci.yml:81-84 and 147-150, guarded by if: needs.plan.outputs.version != ''). The library reports it via Maven-filtered java/src/main/resources-filtered/.../version.properties (library=${project.version}), dss-cli via env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:427), and dss-server via env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:52, 243). No git describe, buildnumber-maven-plugin, vergen or similar exists anywhere (grep of pom.xml, build.rs files and src trees found nothing). So a local or workflow_dispatch build does report 0.0.0-dev with no commit identifier. Why it is refuted: this behaviour is explicitly chosen and documented in four places. docs/DECISIONS.md:487-491: "Version: the release tag ... The committed files only hold the placeholder 0.0.0-dev, which every non-release build reports." README.md:194-196: "The repository itself carries only the placeholder 0.0.0-dev, which local and non-release builds report." .github/workflows/ci.yml:15-16: "Manual runs keep the committed 0.0.0-dev placeholder." scripts/ci/set-version.sh:10-11: "The committed files keep the 0.0.0-dev placeholder: nothing else holds a version." The rationale is reasonable: a single source of truth (the tag), reproducible/clean committed manifests, and CI that runs only on published releases or manual dispatch (ci.yml:21-28), so the only artifacts that are distributed carry a real version. The placeholder is also load-bearing: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:47 pins OPENAPI_VERSION_LINE = "\n version: 0.0.0-dev\n" for substitution, and set-version.sh validates that exactly one four-space-indented <version> exists in the pom. Appending git describe for non-release builds would be a nice-to-have for traceability of ad-hoc builds, but no shipped artifact is affected, the finding's own severity is "info", and the behaviour is the documented intent. Severity: info.
