F-182 A rejected tl_snapshot is a fatal start failure, so DSS upgrades or OJ rotations crash-loop snapshot deployments java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:341
  • Reproduce: The mechanics the finding describes are real, but they are an explicitly documented and deliberate design decision, documented for operators in three places and covered by tests, so the finding is not a defect. What the code does (confirmed): - java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:101-102: this.initialLoad = config.tlSnapshot != null ? trustedLists.importSnapshot(config.tlSnapshot) : trustedLists.offlineRefresh(); wrapped in a try that only calls trustedLists.close() and rethrows. There is no branch that falls back to offlineRefresh() when the snapshot is rejected. - java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:341-344 (checkCompatible): if (!Objects.equals(dss, BuildInfo.dss())) { throw TlSnapshotFile.rejected("written with DSS " + dss + "; this library uses DSS " + BuildInfo.dss()); }, and lines 346-363 reject any difference in the trusted-list settings (including oj_keystore_sha256). So a DSS upgrade or an OJ keystore change does make the configured snapshot fail dss_init with TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED. Why it is refuted as a finding: - docs/DECISIONS.md:935-939 records exactly this choice, attributed to the user: "What the library still checks (TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED, failing dss_init, as the user asked for rejected snapshots; no fallback to the cache): layout and CRC-32C, format version, DSS version, and the trusted-list settings the pool depends on (LOTL and OJ URLs, the OJ keystore by a SHA-256 ...)". The recommendation ("add a fallback option") would reverse an explicit user decision. - The DSS-version check is inherent to the chosen format, also documented at docs/DECISIONS.md:943-948: the payload is "Java serialization of DSS's own model ... The price: a snapshot only loads under the DSS version that wrote it." Loading an old serialized DSS model under a new DSS version is not safely possible, so a version mismatch cannot be anything but a rejection. - The OJ keystore check is a security property, not an accident: a snapshot holds unverified trust anchors (README.md:505-511), and a snapshot built against other LOTL signers must not be accepted silently (TlSnapshotTest.java:166-180 tests precisely oj_keystore_sha256 rejection). - Operators are told the consequence and the remedy: README.md:500-504 lists every rejection cause; docs/server.md:21-24: "A snapshot that cannot be used stops the server with status 2, like any other engine start failure." README.md:488-489 says how to make a new one ("Make one from an engine that has lists loaded ... after an online refresh"), and the rejection message itself says "write a new snapshot" (TrustedListManager.java:393). The remedy on upgrade is to regenerate the snapshot or drop tl_snapshot from the config and start from cache_dir — a configuration change, not a code change, and the kind of step a DSS-version bump of a deployment already implies. - Behaviour is tested: TlSnapshotTest.java:161-162 ("written with DSS 5.0"), 163-165 (countries, tl_sync, pivot_support), 166-180 (OJ keystore); rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:460 tl_snapshot_errors_are_typed; DssJsonApiTest.java:188. The residual, if any, is a documentation nicety (an explicit "upgrade runbook" sentence saying "regenerate snapshots after upgrading the library or rotating the OJ keystore"), which is info/low, not an operations defect. Fail-closed at start-up for a trust-anchor file that cannot be verified compatible is a reasonable and chosen behaviour; a silent fallback to the cache would hide that the deployment's intended trust source was not used.
  • Impact: The code reads as the finding says: TrustedListManager.checkCompatible (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:341-365) throws TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED on a DSS-version or settings mismatch, DssEngine's constructor (DssEngine.java:101-106) calls importSnapshot when tl_snapshot is set and rethrows, and dss-server exits with status 2 on any engine start failure (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:201-204). But the claimed impact ("outages on routine maintenance", "crash-loop", "no cache fallback" as a defect) does not hold up in this system. 1. Documented, intentional decision with the trade-off stated. docs/DECISIONS.md:935-936: "What the library still checks (TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED, failing dss_init, as the user asked for rejected snapshots; no fallback to the cache)". DECISIONS.md:947: "The price: a snapshot only loads under the DSS version that wrote it." README.md:500-505 lists every rejection condition, and docs/server.md:23-24 states the sidecar behaviour outright: "A snapshot that cannot be used stops the server with status 2, like any other engine start failure." The finding's "runbook" already exists in these three places. 2. Fail-closed is the reasonable choice for a trust-anchor store. A snapshot is the engine's trust pool, which the application vouches for (README.md:506-511). A silent fallback to <cache_dir>/tl would start the engine on a trust pool other than the one the operator configured, or on an empty cache with TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED until an online refresh; for a component whose output is "is this signature trusted", refusing to start on a configuration mismatch is the safer behaviour, not an oversight. 3. Mitigation exists for the primary deployment form (a library in a host). dss_init returns a typed error (TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED, DssError.java:45-49; rust/dss/src/error.rs:38-41) with an actionable message ("written with DSS X; this library uses DSS Y", "...write a new snapshot", TrustedListManager.java:344, 410). The host can simply call init again without tl_snapshot; DssJsonApiTest.java:186-189 shows a rejected init is non-destructive (the previous engine keeps running). The "fallback option" the finding asks for is a two-line matter in the host, by design. 4. The triggering events are not routine runtime maintenance. A DSS-version mismatch only arises when the library itself is upgraded, and the OJ keystore is shipped with the library (README.md "The OJ keystore": trust/oj-keystore.p12 from the DSS 6.5.1 demonstrations), so an "OJ rotation" that changes oj_keystore_sha256 is also a library release. An oj_url_changed alert at runtime does not reject a snapshot (only the configured settings are compared, checkCompatible lines 346-363). Regenerating the snapshot is part of rolling out a new library build (README.md:486-487: "Make one from an engine that has lists loaded ... and store it wherever the next engine will find it"), and a deployment that ships the snapshot in its read-only image (README.md:510) rebuilds it with the image. A crash-loop would require deploying a new library against a stale snapshot while ignoring a stderr message that names the exact cause, which is an ordinary deployment error, not an outage inherent in the design. Residual kernel: dss-server has no "snapshot, else cache" flag. That is a feature request of low value given the documented behaviour, the typed error for library hosts, and the security rationale for not silently switching trust pools. Severity: low.
  • Severity and precision: The mechanism is real. TrustedListManager.java:339-344 (checkCompatible) throws TlSnapshotFile.rejected("written with DSS " + dss + ...) on a DSS version mismatch and on any difference in the trusted-list settings, and importSnapshot (around line 302) lets that exception propagate, so dss_init fails. However, this is a documented decision the user asked for. docs/DECISIONS.md, "After Phase 6: trusted-list snapshots", says: "What the library still checks (TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED, failing dss_init, as the user asked for rejected snapshots; no fallback to the cache)". It also states the version coupling outright: "The price: a snapshot only loads under the DSS version that wrote it." README.md:500-506 lists every rejection condition for operators, and README.md:517-519 names cache_dir as the fallback after start. The "routine maintenance" scenario does not hold up either. A DSS upgrade means rebuilding and redeploying the native library, and the snapshot is meant to ship in that same read-only deployment, so it would be regenerated with it. The OJ keystore is part of the engine's own config, so "OJ rotation" only rejects a snapshot when the operator changes that config without writing a new snapshot. The one time-driven path, checkUsable/requireUsable rejecting a list past its next update, only applies when accept_expired=false; the default is true, and DECISIONS.md notes that with it "this cannot fire". So this is a deliberate fail-closed design, not a defect. At most it is an informational ops note: regenerate the snapshot whenever DSS or the TL settings change.
F-184 Docker image sets no engine heap limit although the docs say to set one in containers docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:32
  • Reproduce: The literal observation holds: docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:32-33 sets only ENV DSS_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8484 \ DSS_CACHE_DIR=/var/lib/dss/cache, and docs/server.md:43 says of --max-heap / DSS_MAX_HEAP: "grows with RAM | Engine heap, e.g. 1g. Set it in containers". rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:248-249 only passes -Xmx when the option is given (if let Some(heap) = &a.max_heap { builder = builder.max_heap(heap); }), and rust/dss/src/engine.rs:56-57 documents the default as "Native Image's, which grows with physical memory". But the finding's impact and recommendation do not survive: (1) The runtime already does what the recommendation asks. GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1 (the build toolchain, java/pom.xml:47) ships container awareness in Native Image: svm.jar contains com/oracle/svm/core/container/Container.class with the strings UseContainerSupport, isContainerized, getMemoryLimitInBytes, cachedMemoryLimitInBytes, and com/oracle/svm/core/heap/PhysicalMemory.class consults Container.isContainerized before getPhysicalMemorySize; the heap cap is MaximumHeapSizePercent of that figure (genscavenge/HeapParameters.class). Nothing in the project disables it: grep -rn UseContainerSupport|MaximumHeapSizePercent|MaxRAMPercentage over java/pom.xml, rust/dss/src, scripts and docs returns nothing, and isolate_args starts empty (engine.rs:46). So in a Docker container with a memory limit (the only case where a cgroup OOM kill is possible) the default heap is already derived from the cgroup limit, not host RAM. "Grows with RAM" is true only for a container run without a memory limit, where there is no cgroup limit to be killed against. (2) The documented deployment path sets it: the Compose example at docs/server.md:188-193 has DSS_MAX_HEAP: 1g, and Dockerfile:31 states the design, "Every option is an environment variable: dss-server --help." A heap size baked into the image would be an arbitrary number for an unknown host, which is a reasonable thing to leave to the deployer. The residual concern, that 80 % heap plus the server's native memory (the request is held whole, up to --max-request-mb 100, docs/server.md:221-222) can exceed a tight cgroup limit, is generic container tuning rather than a defect in the Dockerfile, and docs/DECISIONS.md:893 already records that the image is "Not verified yet" beyond its layout. Net: the observation is accurate but the OOM-kill impact is largely covered by the runtime's cgroup awareness and the docs' explicit instruction and example; at most an informational note to mention cgroup awareness in server.md.
F-185 TLS trust is the CA bundle captured at build time; host CA store ignored and override replaces rather than adds java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:151
  • Reproduce: The behaviour the finding describes is real and reproducible from the code, but it is an explicitly documented, deliberate and reasonable design decision with documented escape hatches, so it is not a defect. What the code does (confirmed): - java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:151-159: if (config.httpsTrustStorePath != null) { // Replaces the default CA set (in the native library: the build JDK's cacerts, embedded at build time). ... loader.setSslTruststore(new FileDocument(...)); ... }. Nothing else touches TLS trust for the CRL/OCSP/AIA/TSA loaders; the TL loader additionally gets TrustAllStrategy when tl_verify_tls is false (DssEngine.java:123-128). - java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/EngineConfig.java:57-58 Javadoc: "Null: the CA set built into the library (the build JDK's cacerts). When set it <em>replaces</em> that set." - There is no extra_ca_certificates-style option; extra_trusted_certificates (EngineConfig.java:132, DssEngine.java:164-176, 463-464) feeds the signature-validation trust sources, not TLS. grep of the whole repo finds no other TLS trust knob. Why it is refuted as a finding: - It is documented in three places as intended behaviour: docs/native-library.md:143-154 ("native-image stores the default trust store of the JDK running the build ... inside the library. No certificate file is needed at run time, and the host's system CA store is *not* consulted. To embed a different bundle, build with -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=<file> ... Updating the embedded bundle means rebuilding." and "http.trust_store ... replaces the embedded set; it does not add to it."), docs/DECISIONS.md:298-303 (Build-time capture of GraalVM CE's cacerts; per-engine runtime override that "replaces the embedded set"), and README.md:278 ("trust_store ... replaces the CA bundle built into the library"). - The behaviour is tested: HttpsLoopbackTest.java:172-193 (verifiedTlsWithTrustStoreOverrideLoadsTheLists, builtInCaBundleRejectsAnUnknownServerCa expecting PKIX), plus scripts/smoke-test-c.sh:29-40. - The design is reasonable for a native shared library: there is no portable host CA store for a GraalVM native image to consult, the embedded bundle is replaceable at build time (NATIVE_IMAGE_OPTIONS="-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=..."), and an operator who needs one internal CA can build a PKCS#12 containing the public bundle plus that CA and pass it as http.trust_store. The default TL path does not even depend on TLS trust (XML-signature verification, DECISIONS.md:194-197). Net: the finding restates a documented decision and proposes a feature ("add extra_ca_certificates and report the bundle date"); it identifies no incorrect behaviour, unreachable or mis-handled case. Severity at most info; as a defect report it is refuted.
F-189 Engine API copies every document buffer in and out (to_vec), and is blocking-only rust/dss/src/engine.rs:159
  • Reproduce: The behaviour exists as described but is a documented, reasonable design decision, and the stated impact is overstated. (1) Input copy: rust/dss/src/engine.rs:159 document: document.to_vec() (also :190, :218, :257). docs/DECISIONS.md:357-358 states the choice explicitly: "Calls are blocking, with a reply channel per call. Documents are copied into the job; that copy is negligible next to validation." The Job is moved over an mpsc channel to a worker (engine.rs:601-653) and the Vec is dropped when the match arm finishes, so the extra allocation lives only for the call. (2) Output copy: engine.rs:520 from_raw_parts(out, out_len).to_vec() followed by sys::dss_free(self.0, out) at :521. The buffer is malloc'd by the isolate and must go back through dss_free; a Rust Vec cannot adopt it, so a copy is the only way to return Vec<u8> short of a custom owned wrapper. (3) Java copy: java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssJsonApi.java:95 engine.validate(copy(document), ...) is deliberate per docs/DECISIONS.md:277-284: the entry point passes a read-only ByteBuffer view and copies inside its own error handling so OutOfMemoryError cannot unwind past the C entry stub (that fix is what makes a 128 MB doc on a 64 MB heap return INTERNAL_ERROR instead of aborting the process). (4) Blocking-only: docs/DECISIONS.md:375 "The core API stays runtime-agnostic"; the async consumer dss-server already wraps every call in tokio::task::spawn_blocking (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:303-310, "The engine's own workers do the work; this thread waits"). The FFI call is synchronous on an attached worker thread regardless, so an async method would only unpark the caller, not change memory. (5) "Doubled peak memory" is unsupported: the Rust copy adds one document-sized buffer (37 MB in the finding's own example) to a 390 MB RSS; the 176-192 MB heap need comes from DSS parsing the CMS into in-memory BouncyCastle structures (dss-cms-object, docs/DECISIONS.md:52), not from to_vec. That is ~10% overhead, not 2x. Owned-buffer/Bytes/async variants would be an API enhancement, not a defect.
F-193 Trusted-list snapshot export runs on the control thread and blocks status/health rust/dss/src/engine.rs:587
  • Reproduce: The export does run on the control thread: control_main (rust/dss/src/engine.rs:579-596) serves Control::Status, Control::Version and Control::ExportTlSnapshot sequentially. But this is a documented design decision, not a defect: export_tl_snapshot's doc (engine.rs:323) states "Runs on the thread that answers trusted_list_status", and docs/DECISIONS.md:355 defines the control thread as the one that "serves status/version". More importantly, the claimed impact ("health stalls during exports") is unreachable in this repository: dss-server's router (rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:105-117) exposes no snapshot endpoint, and /health (lib.rs:251-256) only calls trusted_list_status; the sole caller of export_tl_snapshot is dss-cli tl snapshot (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:448-449), a one-shot process with no health endpoint. Only an external embedder of the dss crate calling export and status concurrently could see a delay, bounded by serialising a 14 MB file (README.md:482-485) for a rare administrative operation. The buffer claim is already handled: TlSnapshotFile.java:154 is new ByteArrayOutputStream(1 << 20), pre-sized to 1 MiB; growth beyond that is standard amortised doubling (about four reallocations for the full-EU snapshot), negligible next to Java-serialising ~4,910 CertificateTokens in TrustedListManager.exportSnapshot (TrustedListManager.java:410-434), and the exact size cannot be known before serialisation. The recommendation "pre-size the buffer" is therefore already implemented, and "use another thread" would change a documented, reasonable thread model for a path no shipped binary contends on.
F-194 Per-validation WARN logging to stderr by default in the server rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:85
  • Reproduce: The cited line exists as stated: rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:85 #[arg(long, env = "DSS_LOG_LEVEL", default_value = "warn")], forwarded at main.rs:240 config.log_level = Some(a.log_level.clone()) and applied in java/.../DssJsonApi.java:243-247 as org.slf4j.simpleLogger.defaultLogLevel with output to System.err. But the quantitative claim "DSS logs 2-3 WARN lines per validation" does not reproduce. Experiment (read-only, offline, built release dss-cli + libdssnative.dylib, cache in the scratchpad): validating individual fixtures at --log-level warn gave pades/b-lta.pdf: 2 WARN lines, pades/b-b.pdf: 3, cades/attached-der.p7m: 3, cades/multi-signer.p7m: 4. The two lines common to every run are [dss-tl-1] WARN ...FileCacheDataLoader - Empty array obtained for url [https://ec.europa.eu/tools/lotl/eu-lotl.xml] and [dss-tl-1] WARN ...AbstractAnalysis - Cannot retrieve data from url [...]: they come from the trusted-list load thread at engine start (empty cache, no network), not from validation. A validate-batch of 5 documents (3x b-lta, b-lt, b-b) in one engine produced 3 WARN lines total: the same 2 TL-load lines once, plus one [System-0] WARN ...SignatureValidationContext - No revocation found for the certificate C-7B32... for the single B-level document. The four LT/LTA validations emitted zero WARN lines. So per validation the count is 0 for complete signatures and 1 per certificate that lacks revocation data (a genuinely useful diagnostic for the verdict), scaling with the document, not a fixed 2-3. In the server, with real trusted lists and online revocation, "No revocation found" is the exception, not the rule; the TL lines appear once per start/refresh, not per request. The default is also a documented, deliberate and conventional choice: docs/server.md:52 (--log-level | DSS_LOG_LEVEL | warn), docs/native-library.md:124 ("at config_json.log_level (default warn)"), README.md:289, java/pom.xml:259 and EngineConfig.java:145 logLevel = f.string("log_level", "warn"). warn is slf4j-simple's conventional default, and operators who want silence set DSS_LOG_LEVEL=error (which the test suites do: rust/dss/tests/common/mod.rs:48, rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:41). The "lock contention" impact is speculative with 0-1 lines per validation. At most this is a style/consistency note (dss-cli defaults to error at rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:104 while dss-server defaults to warn), which is arguably correct for a long-running service versus a one-shot CLI. Not a defect.
F-200 OpenAPI error-code list omits TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED docs/openapi.yaml:464
  • Reproduce: Textually, docs/openapi.yaml:461-467 omits TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED while README.md:534-536, DssError.java:49 and rust/dss/src/error.rs:41 define it. But the OpenAPI Error schema describes HTTP error bodies, and this code is unreachable over HTTP: its only raiser is TlSnapshotFile.rejected (TlSnapshotFile.java:243) via TrustedListManager.importSnapshot (TrustedListManager.java:303, "Fails with TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED, before anything is published"), called only from the DssEngine constructor (DssEngine.java:101), i.e. dss_init. dss-server builds the engine once at startup (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:137-141) and on failure calls fail() -> std::process::exit(2) (main.rs:201-204); there is no re-init route (lib.rs:107-117). docs/server.md:23-24 documents exactly this: "A snapshot that cannot be used stops the server with status 2, like any other engine start failure", and server.md's own status table (lines 102-110) also omits the code. The schema further states "New codes may be added" (openapi.yaml:467). So there is no contract mismatch for any HTTP client; the finding misreads the scope of the list. Residual nuance: INVALID_CONFIG is listed although all its raisers are also init-only (EngineConfig.java:130,192,194; DssEngine.java:154,172; TrustedListManager.java:132-144), so the list's criterion is not strictly reachability; adding TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED (or dropping INVALID_CONFIG) would be a cosmetic consistency tweak at most. The existing openapi sync test (rust/dss-server/tests/http.rs:463-466) checks operations and auth, not code lists.
F-202 Enumerated values use inconsistent casing between input and output (packaging, container, mode) java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/SigningResult.java:29
  • Reproduce: The surface observation is accurate: the request schema spells packaging as enum: [detached, enveloping] (docs/openapi.yaml:567-569) while SignResult spells it enum: [ENVELOPED, DETACHED, ENVELOPING] (docs/openapi.yaml:790-791), and the Java code emits DSS enum names (parameters.getSignaturePackaging().name() at java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ExternalSigning.java:158, packaging.name() at :204, literal "ENVELOPED" at :150). But the finding's impact and the "ENVELOPED cannot be given as input" point do not hold up: 1. Input is explicitly case-insensitive, so clients need not normalise anything. docs/openapi.yaml:527 states "Enumerated values are case-insensitive", and the parser does Packaging.valueOf(f.requiredString("packaging").toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)) (SigningOptions.java:200). A client may send DETACHED and read back DETACHED unchanged. The output spelling is a fixed, documented enum (openapi.yaml:790-791, README.md:404 "packaging": "ENVELOPED" } // or DETACHED, ENVELOPING, rust/dss/src/types.rs:131) and is pinned by tests (SigningTest.java:267/274/337/473 assert "DETACHED"/"ENVELOPING"; rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:218-267 assert the same strings; dss-server/src/lib.rs:197-201 switches on Some("DETACHED")). 2. ENVELOPED not being an input value is by design, not a gap: packaging is "CAdES only" (openapi.yaml:569), PAdES is always inside the PDF, and a packaging on PAdES is rejected with a clear message: throw f.error("'packaging' applies to CAdES only (a PAdES signature is always inside the PDF)") (SigningOptions.java:204-206, same check at ExternalSigning.java:97-99). ENVELOPED is an output-only fact about PAdES. 3. "container" and "mode" are not input/output pairs of the same field: container (openapi.yaml:676-677, 747-748) is output-only (PDF/CMS); mode in SignOptions (:531, cms/signature_value) and mode in RefreshRecord (:859, offline/online/snapshot) are unrelated fields on different objects. There is no casing round-trip issue there. The design is coherent: inputs are human-friendly and case-insensitive; outputs echo DSS's own enum names (SignaturePackaging.name(), SignatureLevel.toString() giving "PAdES-BASELINE-LT"). The Rust CLI even lowercases for display (dss-cli/src/main.rs:868), showing the author is aware of the two spellings. What remains is a purely cosmetic style preference with no functional consequence, so the claimed impact ("Clients must normalise case") is false and the finding does not stand as described.
F-206 OJ keystore provenance and lifetime are under-documented: earliest certificate expires 2027-04-26 and expiry means a fail-closed outage trust/README.md:17
  • Reproduce: Reproduced the raw facts: keytool -list -v on trust/oj-keystore.p12 (SHA-256 98a76fbc… matches trust/README.md:15) shows six certs expiring 2027-04-26, 2027-05-06, 2027-11-17, 2028-05-31, 2029-11-23 and 2029-12-17. So "validity up to 2029" (trust/README.md:17) is a correct upper bound and the earliest expiry is indeed 2027-04-26. But the finding's substantive claims do not hold up. (1) "Provenance under-documented / not cross-checked": the README states the upstream source and path (line 12), the file SHA-256 (15), the matching OJ URL (16), and an empirical verification stronger than reading the notice: "Real-LOTL integration test on 2026-10-28: LOTL signature TOTAL_PASSED" (18); it also gives the exact keytool -list -v command (22-24) that prints every fingerprint and expiry the recommendation asks to list. (2) "No expiry alert": keystore-certificate expiry is not the failure trigger. LOTL validation breaks only when the EC signs with a certificate the engine does not know, and the engine already handles rotation and signals it: TrustedListManager.java:152 lotl.setPivotSupport(config.pivotSupport) (default true at EngineConfig.java:100) lets pivot LOTLs carry new signers without a keystore change; TrustedListManager.java:199-202 emits oj_url_changed ("LOTL announces new signing certificates at …; update oj_url and the OJ keystore") when a new OJ publication appears; per-list signature validation status is exposed in tl_status. trust/README.md:28-30 documents both signals and that pivots bridge most rotations. An expiry-date alert on the keystore would be a weak proxy for signals that already exist. (3) "Fail-closed outage": the strict ExpirationAndSignatureCheckStrategy (TrustedListManager.java:183-188) is a documented, user-confirmed decision (docs/DECISIONS.md:85-97 and 189-191 "TL sync: strict, as implemented"), with documented mitigations (oj_keystore.path override without rebuilding, trust/README.md:45-46; snapshots). Residue: a one-phrase doc nicety, "validity 2027-04 to 2029-12" instead of "up to 2029", which is cosmetic and does not justify the finding as stated.
F-209 The effective validation time is not echoed in the result, although validation_time is an untrusted per-call option in the HTTP sidecar java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ValidationResult.java:103
  • Reproduce: The literal observation is accurate but the conclusion ("no trace in the JSON", "a TOTAL_PASSED computed at a caller-chosen past instant looks the same as a current one") is false: the instant actually used IS in every result, inside the always-included simple report. Code path: DssEngine.java:246-248 applies validator.setValidationTime(Date.from(options.validationTime)). DSS then propagates it: SignedDocumentValidator.java:502 executor.setCurrentTime(documentAnalyzer.getValidationTime()) and SimpleReportBuilder.java:255-256 addValidationTime(...) { report.setValidationTime(currentTime); }; the SimpleReport XSD declares <xs:attribute name="ValidationTime" type="xs:dateTime"/> on the root element. DssEngine.java:261-262 puts the simple report in the result unconditionally (xml.put(ReportKind.SIMPLE, dssReports.getXmlSimpleReport()), independent of the requested reports), and ValidationResult.toMap (ValidationResult.java:111-113) emits every entry, so simple_report_xml is always in the JSON (README "Validation result" documents it as always present; dss-server returns "the library's result JSON" verbatim, lib.rs:9,151). Reproduction against the built library (scratchpad cargo program, testdata/fixtures/pades/b-lt.pdf, offline config): validation_time=None -> TOTAL_PASSED, ValidationTime="2026-11-06T13:24:07Z"; validation_time=2020-01-01T00:00:00Z -> TOTAL_FAILED/NOT_YET_VALID, ValidationTime="2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"; validation_time=2031-06-01T00:00:00Z -> TOTAL_PASSED, ValidationTime="2031-06-01T00:00:00Z". The attribute always equals the instant the verdict refers to, so a verdict at a caller-chosen instant is distinguishable and auditable from the response. Correct parts of the finding: toMap (ValidationResult.java:103-122) has no top-level validation_time key (probe: top-level keys are container, ok, signatures, simple_report_xml, transformations), and openapi.yaml:490-494 / README.md:302 do not caveat the option. Incorrect part: "revocation (online/offline)" is not a per-call option at all; ValidationOptions.java:56 .allowOnly(Set.of("reports", "detached_contents", "validation_time", "filename", "unwrap_nested")) rejects anything else, and revocation mode is engine config (README "revocation"), so it cannot be chosen by an untrusted caller. dss-server is also token-authenticated (--token-file), so the options part comes from the authenticated application, not from end users, unless the application forwards it, which is outside this repository. What remains is a convenience/documentation nit (surface ValidationTime as a top-level JSON field so clients need not parse the XML; add a one-line caveat to the option's description), not a security defect as described. Severity info.
F-210 Trusted-list status and refresh records expose server file-system paths and raw exception text through GET /tl/status java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:329
  • Reproduce: The behaviour reproduces exactly as described, but it is a documented, intentional API contract rather than a defect, and the only residual risk is F-205's, not this finding's. Mechanics confirmed: TrustedListManager.java:328-331 info.put("path", file.toString()); info.put("size", bytes.length); and :462 m.put("tl_snapshot", snap.tlSnapshot());; :289-290 new RefreshRecord(mode, start, Instant.now(), false, e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage(), ...); :545 per-list m.put("error", r.getExceptionMessage());. rust/dss/src/engine.rs:310-314 trusted_list_status_json returns the Java JSON untouched and rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:206-209 let json = run(engine, |e| e.trusted_list_status_json()).await?; Ok(json_response(StatusCode::OK, json)) serves it verbatim. /version (lib.rs version()) includes v.runtime, which DssJsonApi.java:223 fills with java.vm.name + " " + java.vm.version. main.rs:114-130 emits no warning when no token is set; docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:32 sets DSS_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8484. Why refuted as a security finding: 1. tl_snapshot.path is an explicit, documented contract field, not a leak: docs/openapi.yaml:805-812 ("The trusted-list snapshot the lists came from (tl_snapshot in the server's --config file): its header, path and size"), docs/DECISIONS.md:971 ("Status: tl_snapshot (header, path, size)"), README.md:516,525, and two tests assert it (DssJsonApiTest.java:183 assertEquals(file.toString(), ((Map) status.get("tl_snapshot")).get("path")), TlSnapshotTest.java:95). RefreshRecord.error and per-list error are documented fields too (openapi.yaml:874, :930). The path is the operator's own configured tl_snapshot value, so an operator reading status learns nothing they did not set. 2. The trust model is documented and reasonable: docs/server.md:214-218 "No TLS. Run the sidecar on the same host or on a private network ... never expose it publicly. The token stops other containers on the same network from using it"; DECISIONS.md:855-857 same. docs/DECISIONS.md:851-852 states /tl/status deliberately "passes the library's JSON through like every other endpoint". 3. Same auth boundary as every privileged endpoint: lib.rs:104-112 puts /tl/status and /version under the identical authorize route_layer as /validate, /extend, /sign/*, /tl/refresh. A caller who can read the status can already trigger online refreshes and sign/validate documents, so the disclosed snapshot path, exception strings and JVM version are strictly less valuable than the capabilities that caller already holds. The marginal risk collapses entirely into F-205 (tokenless 0.0.0.0 default), which the finding itself cites as the precondition. Residual observation (info level): the raw e.getMessage() in refresh records and DSS's getExceptionMessage() per list are diagnostic text for the operator and are not separately called out as a decision, but exposing diagnostic exception messages on an operator status endpoint behind the same auth as /tl/refresh is standard practice and carries negligible value for an attacker who already has that reach. No startup warning for a tokenless non-loopback listen would be a nicer-to-have but belongs with F-205.
F-217 DECISIONS.md still says the trusted-list job runs on a 4-thread pool; the code sizes it by tl_threads (default min(16, CPUs), range 1-64) docs/DECISIONS.md:103
  • Reproduce: The literal facts in the finding check out: docs/DECISIONS.md:103 reads "The TL job runs on its own 4-thread daemon pool (DSS's default is a non-daemon cached pool), shut down on close", while java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:177 has executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(config.tlThreads, r -> { and EngineConfig.java:106-110 has long threads = f.integer("tl_threads", Math.min(16, Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors())); if (threads < 1 || threads > 64) throw .... However, the finding misreads what DECISIONS.md is. Its preamble (line 3-4) says it is a log of "Decisions taken while building dss-native ... Newest phase last", i.e. a chronological record, and line 103 sits under "## Phase 1: Java engine on the JVM". The change away from the fixed pool of 4 is already recorded in the same document, under Phase 4, at docs/DECISIONS.md:390-392: "Trusted-list thread pool: new tl_threads config, default = number of CPUs, at most 16. Loading from the cache re-validates every list's signature. With the earlier fixed pool of 4, a full-LOTL cold start took ~11 s; with 15 threads it takes ~7.6 s." That entry explicitly names the Phase 1 pool as "the earlier fixed pool of 4" and states the current sizing, which matches the code (min(16, CPUs)). The Phase 1 entry is therefore an accurate historical record, not a stale description of current behaviour, and the document already handles the supersession the same way it handles other revisions (e.g. "## Resolved after the Phase 1 report", line 186). The daemon-pool half of line 103 is still true (TrustedListManager.java:179 t.setDaemon(true)), and README.md:273 documents the current default for users ("tl_threads": ... "default: CPUs, max 16", covered by F-146). The claimed impact, that readers tuning from DECISIONS get the wrong number, does not hold for anyone reading the log as written, since the later entry corrects it in the same file. At most, a cross-reference "(replaced by tl_threads in Phase 4)" at line 103 would be a nicety, which is below the bar for a defect. Rewriting the Phase 1 entry as the finding recommends would actually falsify the historical record that line 391 refers back to.
F-231 Config and option structs are Serialize-only: a config_json file cannot be loaded into the typed Config, so with_config_json discards every typed setting (root cause of the --config behaviour in both binaries); Config::default() also builds an invalid configuration rust/dss/src/config.rs:11
  • Reproduce: The mechanical facts are accurate but the finding describes a documented, reasonable design plus an enhancement wish, not a defect, and its stated impact is contradicted by the code. Verified true: rust/dss/src/config.rs:8 use serde::Serialize; and every type at lines 11, 71, 80, 88, 100, 110, 129, 139, 149, 168, ... derives Serialize only (grep finds no Deserialize in config.rs; Deserialize exists only in types.rs/error.rs for results). rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:561-563 and rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:217-219 do Some(path) => EngineBuilder::with_config_json(&a.cache_dir, read_to_string(path)?) and never apply --country, --trusted-certificate, --offline-revocation, --tsa-url, --log-level, --tl-snapshot in that branch. Config derives Default, so Config::default() has oj_keystore.path == "" and is rejected at build() by java/.../engine/JsonFields.java:52-58 requiredString ("'path' is required", INVALID_CONFIG). Why refuted: (1) The "replaces everything" behaviour is the documented contract, not an accident: rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:68 /// Full config_json file; replaces every option below except --cache-dir and --max-heap., rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:56 /// Full config_json file; replaces every option below except --max-heap., docs/DECISIONS.md:377 "Global flags build config_json, or --config takes a full one." Users see this in --help. (2) The impact claim "no unknown-key check before the isolate starts" is misleading: EngineConfig.java:81 and :87 call allowOnly(Set.of(...)) and JsonFields.java:28-35 throws unknown key '...' (allowed: ...) as INVALID_CONFIG; README.md:294 "Unknown keys are rejected (INVALID_CONFIG)" and DECISIONS.md:153 "Unknown keys ... are errors, so typos fail loudly." The check runs at build(), which is also when every other config error (missing keystore file, bad tsa) surfaces, so moving it earlier gains nothing. (3) Config::default() being invalid until build() is a common Rust pattern; config.rs:10 documents "Only the OJ keystore is required" and Config::new(oj_keystore) at config.rs:59 is the constructor; Default is used for ..Default::default() and the failure is a clear INVALID_CONFIG. (4) Deriving Deserialize and merging flags over a file would be a nice enhancement (no test covers --config combined with other flags; cli.rs:272/291 only pass --config with --cache-dir), but the missing derive is not the "root cause" of anything broken: the binaries would still need explicit merge logic. Residual nit worth at most info: clap defines no conflicts_with between --config and the flags it supersedes (grep shows conflicts_with only at cli main.rs:246), and dss-server reads --config from env DSS_CONFIG, so a flag passed alongside is ignored without a warning. That is a documented behaviour, not a defect as the finding frames it.
F-235 /health keeps answering 200 'ready' however many scheduled refreshes have failed and however stale or expired the trusted lists are rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:256
  • Reproduce: The cited code behaves as the finding describes: rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:251-268 health() answers 200 with only trusted_lists_loaded and refresh_in_progress; main.rs:153-161 logs scheduled refresh outcomes via eprintln!(describe_refresh(..)) (lib.rs:125-138, which does report "online trusted-list refresh failed after ... ms: ..."); EngineConfig.java:104 defaults accept_expired to true. But this is a documented, reasonable design rather than a defect. /health is specified as a readiness probe for container health checks only: docs/openapi.yaml:330-331 "summary: Readiness ... 200 once the engine is up, 503 while it starts. For container health checks", and docs/DECISIONS.md:845-848 explains it exists so the orchestrator sees "starting" rather than "refused". Making it 503 on stale or expired lists would break depends_on: condition: service_healthy (docs/server.md:198-200) and the Docker HEALTHCHECK (docker/dss-server/Dockerfile:39) for a condition a restart cannot fix, which is the standard reason readiness probes do not depend on upstream freshness. The claim of "no alert path" is false: /tl/status (lib.rs:206-210) exposes last_online_refresh.completed/error (rust/dss/src/types.rs:173-182), alerts[] including tl_expired (types.rs:259-266) and per-list expired (types.rs:226), documented in README.md:522-530 and pointed to by server.md:79-80 and DECISIONS.md:849-852; the Java engine logs alerts at warn (TrustedListManager.java:240) and refresh failures at error (:288), and the server's default --log-level is warn (server.md:52), so both reach stderr by default. Keeping expired lists in use is an explicit recorded user decision (DECISIONS.md:94-95, 190-191) with the mitigation that qualification flags the expired list in the validation result (README.md:271). The only residual is a documentation nicety (server.md could list the /tl/status fields to alert on), which is info-level, not a correctness or security issue.
F-237 DECISIONS.md says the bearer token is 'compared in constant time', but same() short-circuits on length (and runs after prefix parsing), so timing leaks the token's length rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:299
  • Reproduce: The code reads exactly as the finding quotes it. /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/rust/dss-server/src/lib.rs:297-300: /// Constant-time comparison: the response time does not tell how much of the token matched. followed by fn same(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> bool { a.len() == b.len() && a.iter().zip(b).fold(0u8, |acc, (x, y)| acc | (x ^ y)) == 0 }. It is called from authorize at lib.rs:285 only after strip_prefix("Bearer ") succeeds. docs/DECISIONS.md:855-857 says: "Optional bearer token, read from a file. ... It is compared in constant time." So the length short-circuit is real, but it is not a defect and the documentation does not overstate anything by the accepted meaning of the term. Every standard "constant-time comparison" primitive behaves identically: subtle's ConstantTimeEq for [T] returns Choice::from(0) early on a length mismatch, Go's crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare returns 0 immediately when lengths differ, and the constant_time_eq crate does the same. The finding itself concedes this ("subtle's ct_eq also returns early on a length mismatch") and that "knowing the length does not help an attacker". The lib.rs doc comment states the actual guarantee precisely ("does not tell how much of the token matched"), and DECISIONS.md uses the conventional term for exactly that guarantee. Hiding the length would require hashing both sides first, which no mainstream library does for bearer-token checks; demanding it is a stricter definition than the industry uses, not a documentation inaccuracy. Practically, the leak is also unobservable: the difference between skipping and running a ~32-byte XOR fold is nanoseconds against an HTTP round-trip through axum/tokio, and the token is an operator-chosen file (rust/dss-server/src/main.rs:39-41, 114-125) with no useful structure to recover from its length. This is at most an optional wording tweak, not a security or correctness finding; it is a documented and reasonable decision consistent with standard practice, so the claim as framed ("documentation overstates what the code does") is refuted.
F-246 diff-vs-jvm.sh swallows a failed real-LOTL refresh, so the private-document comparison can pass with an empty trust pool scripts/diff-vs-jvm.sh:93
  • Reproduce: The premise is accurate but the consequence is not. tl refresh really exits 1 on failure (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:482-486: Ok(if record.completed && status.loaded { SUCCESS } else { ExitCode::from(1) })) and scripts/diff-vs-jvm.sh:93 swallows it with || true. However the claim that "both sides validate against an empty pool, agree on INDETERMINATE, and the script exits 0" misreads the pipeline: 1. The config the script writes at line 87 ({"oj_keystore":...,"revocation":"online","log_level":"error"}) does not set require_trusted_lists, whose default is true: java/.../EngineConfig.java:131 requireTrustedLists = f.bool("require_trusted_lists", true); README.md:283 and docs/DECISIONS.md:99 document this ("Empty cache: validate returns TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED"). 2. DssEngine.validate() calls trustSnapshot() (DssEngine.java:217), which throws DssError(TRUSTED_LISTS_NOT_LOADED, "trusted lists not loaded: the cache is empty or unreadable; run an online refresh first") (lines 417-422). Startup only runs offlineRefresh() (DssEngine.java:102), so nothing silently fills the pool. batch_line (main.rs:547-551) therefore emits {"file":..., "ok": false, "error": {"code": "TrustedListsNotLoaded", ...}} for every private case. Reproduced offline: cargo test -p dss --test engine empty_cache_refuses_to_validate passed (rust/dss/tests/engine.rs:481-492, which asserts status.trusted_certificates == 0 and err.code() == Some(ErrorCode::TrustedListsNotLoaded)). 3. DiffVsNative.java:54-56 turns an ok:false line into Outcome.rejected(code). PlainDssReference (java/src/test/.../PlainDssReference.java:121-171) has no such guard and returns new Outcome(null, sigs, nested) after validating with zero anchors. Outcome.java:74-77: if ((e.error == null) != (a.error == null)) { out.add(path + "rejected: plain DSS=no, other=TrustedListsNotLoaded"); return; } — a difference for every document. DiffVsNative.java:118 System.exit(differing == 0 ? 0 : 1), the script's || status=1 (line 52) and exit "$status" (line 101) make the run exit 1, with the cause printed per document (line 117). 4. "No report marks the trust pool as empty" is also wrong: DiffVsNative.java:100 writes "trusted certificates from the cached lists: <n>" into build/diff/private.md, which reads 0 here. The only way both sides agree on an empty pool is a user-supplied testdata/private/config.json with require_trusted_lists: false, which is an explicit opt-in for private PKIs (DECISIONS.md:99) and not present in this checkout (ls testdata/private shows no config.json). Dropping || true would merely surface the same failure one step earlier; the engine's own guard already prevents a green result with nothing loaded. Residual nit (not the finding): a refresh whose completed is true but with some national lists failed is published on both sides identically, and the certificate count in the report is the signal for that.
F-251 No maximum age or staleness warning for trusted-list snapshots: with accept_expired=true a snapshot's trust anchors stay authoritative indefinitely, and verdicts carry no trust-pool age java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:372
  • Reproduce: The premise that checkUsable only re-applies tl_sync is accurate (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TrustedListManager.java:372-401; docs/DECISIONS.md:941-943 "With accept_expired true (the default) this cannot fire"). But the finding's substantive claims — no staleness warning, no way to refuse, no exposed age/provenance, verdicts silent — misread what exists. 1. Refuse knob exists and is tested: with tl_sync.accept_expired=false, requireUsable throws TL_SNAPSHOT_REJECTED "the snapshot trusts <url>, which tl_sync no longer allows (next update was …); write a new snapshot" (TrustedListManager.java:396-401). TlSnapshotTest.listsThatExpiredSinceTheExportAreRejectedWhenExpiredListsAreRefused (java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/TlSnapshotTest.java:208-232) exercises both branches. 2. Age and provenance are exposed: status() returns snapshot_published_at, tl_snapshot (the header with created_at and lists_loaded.finished_at; TrustedListManager.java:428-429, :461-462) and per-list next_update and expired (:516-517); dss-cli tl status prints "snapshot {} written {}, lists loaded {} at {}" (rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:984-990). README.md:516-528 documents this. 3. Verdicts do carry a staleness signal. The engine uses DSS's default validation policy (no custom policy anywhere under java/src/main; DssFeature.java:77 only bundles policy/*.xml). That policy's <eIDAS> block has TLFreshness Level="WARN" Unit="HOURS" Value="6" and TLNotExpired Level="WARN" (dss-policy-jaxb-6.5.1 policy/constraint.xml:642-643). SignatureQualificationBlock.collectAdditionalMessages merges every related XmlTLAnalysis conclusion into the signature's qualification conclusion (dss-validation-6.5.1 sources, SignatureQualificationBlock.java:258-266); DetailedReportMessageCollector.collectSignatureQualification reads that conclusion's warnings (:440-444); and ValidationResult.summarize puts report.getQualificationWarnings(id) into each signature's warnings (java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/ValidationResult.java:78). So a QESIG/TOTAL_PASSED verdict over an expired list carries "The next-update time of the trusted list is in the past!" and any list loaded >6h ago carries "The trusted list is not considered as fresh!". README.md:271 "(qualification flags it)" and DECISIONS.md:95 are accurate. 4. The remaining behaviour is a recorded decision: accepting expired lists by default was asked and answered (DECISIONS.md:94-96, :190-191), and the snapshot trust model is explicitly "the application that stores and hands over a snapshot vouches for it" (DECISIONS.md:928-934; README.md:508-511). Snapshot deployments can still call the online refresh (README.md:517). Withdrawn services going unnoticed until re-export applies equally to any offline cache deployment and is inherent to accept_expired=true, not to snapshots. What is genuinely absent is only a wall-clock max-age separate from NextUpdate and an explicit rotation-cadence sentence in the README. Neither is a defect given the existing accept_expired=false refusal, the status fields, and the per-verdict DSS warnings; at most an info-level documentation nit.
F-252 The validation policy is fixed to DSS's bundled constraint.xml (revocation freshness IGNORE, TL freshness WARN 6 h), with no way to tighten it and no documentation java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:255
  • Reproduce: Mechanics reproduce as stated: /Users/gsguglielmo/Programming/dss-rust/java/src/main/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/DssEngine.java:255 is dssReports = validator.validateDocument(); with no policy argument, and nothing else in java/src/main or rust/*/src references ValidationPolicy/setValidationPolicy (only the reachability metadata lists eu.europa.esig.dss.policy.EtsiValidationPolicyFactory, i.e. DSS's default loader). ValidationOptions.java exposes only reports/detachedContents/validationTime/filename/unwrapNested (lines 27-35), and the EngineConfig key set (accept_expired, accept_invalid_signature, aia, connect_timeout_ms, log_level, lotl_url, oj_url, online, online_cache_expiration_ms, password, path, pivot_support, require_trusted_lists, response_timeout_ms, revocation, tl_snapshot, tl_threads, tl_verify_tls, type, url, use_sunset_date, username, warn) has no policy knob; README states unknown keys are rejected. The cited constraint.xml evidence checks out against the shipped dss-policy-jaxb-6.5.1 jar: line 94 <RevocationFreshness Level="IGNORE" Unit="DAYS" Value="0" /> (repeated at 139, 243, 286, 382, 418, 491, 521) and line 642 <TLFreshness Level="WARN" Unit="HOURS" Value="6" />. However, the finding's "no documentation" claim misreads the repo: docs/DECISIONS.md:201 records it explicitly under "Resolved after the Phase 1 report": 4. Validation policy: DSS's default constraint.xml only. No custom policy support for now. That makes this a documented, reasonable project decision (the finding itself says "standard DSS behaviour and not a defect"), which per the audit method refutes it. What remains is a minor doc gap: README.md (the user-facing API doc, config section lines 255-290) never mentions the policy or that revocation freshness is IGNORE and TL freshness a 6 h WARN, so a reader of the README alone cannot see which policy produced a verdict. That is an info-level suggestion for the README, not a defect.
F-279 Release seed trusted-list cache is downloaded with TLS verification off, although the pipeline already uses verified TLS for its online smoke test .github/workflows/ci.yml:171
  • Reproduce: Mechanism confirmed literally, but the finding misreads the pipeline and duplicates covered risk, and its recommendation is unsound on the project's own evidence. What is true: .github/workflows/ci.yml:171 runs "$cli" --oj-keystore trust/oj-keystore.p12 --cache-dir build/tl-seed tl refresh with no --config. rust/dss-cli/src/main.rs:562-586 then takes the None branch, Config::new(oj_keystore(a)?), which leaves http.tl_verify_tls: None (rust/dss/src/config.rs:95, skip_serializing_if none), so the Java side applies tlVerifyTls = http.bool("tl_verify_tls", false) (EngineConfig.java:116) and tlLoader.setTrustStrategy(TrustAllStrategy.INSTANCE) (DssEngine.java:123-128). The status JSON indeed has no TLS-mode field (rust/dss/src/types.rs:199-215). Why it is refuted as a finding: 1. Documented, user-signed-off decision, not an oversight. docs/DECISIONS.md:193-199 ("TLS for trusted-list downloads: not verified... a man-in-the-middle can block a list but cannot inject one... http.tl_verify_tls: true turns checking back on") and README.md:281, docs/native-library.md:142. The seed step simply uses the engine default that every online refresh uses, including the JVM online suite in the same job: OnlineTrustedListTest.java:104-108 asserts "TL downloads skip TLS server checks (tl_verify_tls=false), so certificate-path errors must not occur". 2. The central premise ("the pipeline already uses verified TLS ... against the real LOTL in CI") misreads scripts/smoke-test-c.sh:31: that config is "countries":["IT"],"http":{"tl_verify_tls":true} — it downloads the LOTL and only the Italian TL. The full-EU seed is a different case: DECISIONS.md:193-194 records that the ES (tsl.digital.gob.es) and HU (www.nmhh.hu) TL hosts fail with PKIX against the JDK trust store, and the bundle used by tl_verify_tls:true is exactly the build JDK's cacerts (docs/native-library.md:146-147). Following the recommendation would, on the project's own evidence, publish a seed missing ES and HU (download errors), i.e. a worse artifact. 3. Half of the recommendation is already implemented: ListStatus carries sequence_number, issue_date, next_update, used_for_trust per list (rust/dss/src/types.rs:219-233), and ci.yml:172-173 publishes that JSON alongside the tarball. 4. The residual risk the finding itself names (replay of an older, validly signed list; withheld list) is explicitly attributed to F-003 and F-243 and is not specific to the seed step; XML signatures are still verified against the OJ keystore (DssEngine.java:124-127), and a server started from the seed is superseded by its first scheduled online refresh (docs/server.md:28-29). The only unaddressed remainder, that the status JSON does not say which TLS mode produced it, is cosmetic (info), not a supply-chain defect.
F-281 Re-running a release replaces published assets with new, non-reproducible bytes (--clobber) and leaves the old dated seed cache beside the new one .github/workflows/ci.yml:212
  • Reproduce: The quoted lines exist as cited: .github/workflows/ci.yml:205 "# --clobber: a re-run replaces the assets it uploaded before.", :212 gh release upload "$TAG" release/* --clobber, :169 stamp="$(date -u +%Y%m%d)", :173-175 the dated dss-native-tl-cache-$stamp.{status.json,tar.gz,tar.gz.sha256} names, and README.md:209 describes a single dss-native-tl-cache-<date>.tar.gz. scripts/package.sh:66 uses plain tar -czf with no mtime/sort/owner normalisation, so a rebuild would indeed produce different bytes. But the finding fails as a defect for three reasons. 1. The causal chain is wrong. ci.yml:183-186: release-assets has needs: [build, online] and if: github.event_name == 'release'. When "a failed leg leaves a visible release without assets" (the F-110 premise), release-assets never ran, so nothing was uploaded and a re-run uploads for the first time: --clobber replaces nothing. If the only failure was inside the upload step itself, "re-run failed jobs" re-executes just release-assets, which re-downloads the same artifacts of the same run (ci.yml:194-203, download-artifact by pattern: dss-native-* / name: tl-cache-snapshot; artifacts belong to the run, not the attempt), so the bytes are identical and --clobber is exactly what completes the partial upload. The "different bytes under the same version" outcome only arises if a maintainer deliberately chooses "re-run all jobs" on a release workflow that already succeeded, which is an explicit operator action whose effect is stated in the workflow comment. 2. It is a documented, deliberate decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:486 "| Published release | release-assets: gh release upload --clobber of every platform package, the seed cache and the OJ keystore to that release (only GITHUB_TOKEN, no third-party action). |". Using --clobber is the standard pattern for idempotent release uploads; without it a partial-upload retry would fail. 3. The duplicate-seed-cache case needs the online job to run twice on different UTC dates with release-assets succeeding both times, i.e. again a deliberate full re-run of an already-successful release on a later day. Even then each dss-native-tl-cache-<date> set is a complete, self-describing snapshot with its own status JSON and .sha256; a second, fresher one beside it is cosmetic, not a supply-chain fault, and README.md:209 ("extract dss-native-tl-cache-<date>.tar.gz") works for either. No positive evidence that the described outcome occurs on any realistic re-run path; the residual (hardening with a draft release or an assets-present guard) is a nice-to-have, so severity info and refuted.
F-283 The tracing-agent caller filter excludes the engine's own production code as a caller, contrary to run-agent.sh's description of main/ scripts/agent/caller-filter.json:7
  • Reproduce: The code facts reproduce, but the headline defect is already fixed and the exclusion is a documented decision, leaving only a latent, hypothetical gap that other test layers partly cover. Reproduced: scripts/agent/caller-filter.json:7 is {"excludeClasses": "it.codingduck.dssnative."}, so engine/ffi/visible production classes are excluded as callers in the main/ run (run-agent.sh:32-33 filter=",caller-filter-file=..."; run main "$filter"). scripts/merge-metadata.py:161-184 builds the library metadata from main/ and puts anything in full/ not already in main into the test metadata (return key(entry) not in in_main). So an engine-originated dynamic call with a non-constant argument would land only in the test-only JSON. Today's engine dynamic sites are all constant or hand-registered: BuildInfo.java:31 getResourceAsStream("/it/codingduck/dssnative/version.properties") and AwtFreeSignatureDrawer.java:354 getResourceAsStream(DEFAULT_FONT) are covered by DssFeature RESOURCE_GLOBS (DssFeature.java:76-84: "it/codingduck/dssnative/version.properties", "fonts/PTSerifRegular.ttf"), and TlSnapshotFile's ObjectInputStream reads are covered by registerTlSnapshotClasses (DssFeature.java:99). No current instance of the gap exists, as the finding itself concedes ("latent"). Why refuted: (1) The title's "contrary to run-agent.sh's description" holds only for the committed text (git show HEAD:scripts/run-agent.sh lines 8-9: "DSS, its dependencies, our engine. JUnit, Surefire and our test support code are excluded"). The working tree already corrects it (git diff scripts/run-agent.sh): "DSS and its dependencies. JUnit, Maven/Surefire and all of our own code (engine and test support) are excluded as callers". The comment, not the filter, was the inconsistent half. (2) The exclusion is a recorded decision: docs/DECISIONS.md:239 "with a caller filter excluding JUnit, Surefire and our own code, giving library metadata". It is also reasonable: test classes live in the same packages as production code (java/src/test/java/it/codingduck/dssnative/engine/{ConcurrentRefreshTest,DssJsonApiTest,ExtensionTest,...}.java), so the finding's recommended package-level narrowing (testsupport., diff.**) would reintroduce *Test classes in engine/ and visible/ as callers; only a class-name pattern could work. (3) The impact claim that the shipped library's gap would go uncaught ignores the layers that run against the shipped library with main-only metadata and MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Throw (java/pom.xml:50, :314-316 --exact-reachability-metadata): DECISIONS.md:484 describes the release chain "shared library → native tests again in Exit mode → C smoke → Rust fmt/clippy/tests → differential test", and rust/dss/tests/*, rust/dss-cli/tests/cli.rs, rust/dss-server/tests/* link libdssnative (rust/dss-sys/build.rs:15-19). An engine-originated registration gap on any path those exercise would fail there. Residual, at most info-level: neither DECISIONS.md:239 nor the corrected run-agent.sh comment states the consequence that engine-originated dynamic access must be registered in DssFeature by hand rather than harvested from the agent, which is what the project already does in practice. Not a defect in the filter, and no code change is warranted.
